text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **The two-narrative trap, and WFIOs.** Post dot-com, the official Loudcloud story was plenty of cash and customers signing at an impressive rate; the dark story was a crippled business and devastated balance sheet. He asked himself which was true "about 3,000 times" and concluded both led to "I should be removed from my position immediately" (the essay's own paraphrase of the two framings). Rule: "The key to getting to the right outcome was to keep from getting married to either the positive or the dark narrative." He also names the WFIO ("We're F#%ked, It's Over," coined or relayed by partner Scott Weiss; he says he had "at least a dozen" at Opsware): "In all cases, WFIOs feel much worse than they are—especially for the CEO." (2011 essay)

I should be removed from my position immediately
The key to getting to the right outcome was to keep from getting married to either the positive or the dark narrative.
We're F#%ked, It's Over,
at least a dozen

title: The two-narrative trap, and WFIOs

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **Calm the head: survivors, paper, road, persistence.** Four techniques from the same essay. (1) Make friends who have been through the same decision; Bill Campbell was most useful for his failure at GO and his worst days at Intuit (laying off a third of the company), not his successes. (2) Write the reasoning down: to propose, as a public company, selling all customers and revenue and changing the business, he wrote a detailed logic document; "The process of writing that document separated me from my own psychology and enabled me to make the decision swiftly." (3) "If you focus on the wall, you will drive right into it. If you focus on the road, you will follow the road." (4) Do not quit. (2011 essay)
quotes: The process of writing that document separated me from my own psychology and enabled me to make the decision swiftly.
If you focus on the wall, you will drive right into it. If you focus on the road, you will follow the road.
title: Calm the head: survivors, paper, road, persistence

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **Even with elite advice, the final decision is lonely.** His worked example is someone else's: Jason Rosenthal becoming CEO of Ning with three options (radically reduce staff, sell, or raise money dilutively), each sacrificing a different promise to employees. He chose layoffs concentrated on the most recent hires; Horowitz reports revenue "soaring" and morale high afterward. The stated lesson: even with elite advice, "ultimately he was completely alone in the final decision." Also: never discuss viability questions in raw form with employees in your darkest moments. (2011 essay)
quotes: ultimately he was completely alone in the final decision.
title: Even with elite advice, the final decision is lonely

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **One bullet, no odds (Ferriss framing).** Distinct from the book's "don't play the odds" line: do not think like an investor in probabilities (90 percent chance to miss the deal, so miss the quarter, so can't raise, so layoffs). His self-talk: "I’ve got one bullet in the gun. I have got to hit the target." with "no contingency plan, and no way out" (Ferriss transcript, spelling as in the transcript). He is candid about the cost: "I was up at 2:00 in the morning in a cold sweat with my guts boiling," and says talking it out with Bill Campbell helped even though "It wasn’t like he had any answers either."

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **Nobody cares (Al Davis's line, his use).** Feeling sorry for himself at Loudcloud (half the customers going out of business, "221 IPOs in 2000 and 19 in 2001"), he saw Bill Parcells recount asking Raiders owner Al Davis how to win with an injured roster; Davis: “Bill, nobody cares, just coach your team.” Horowitz: "That might be the best CEO advice ever." His gloss: "A great reason for failing won’t preserve one dollar for your investors, won’t save one employee’s job, or get you one new customer." Rule: "It’s best to spend zero time on what you could have done and all of your time on what you might do. Because in the end, nobody cares, just run your company." ("Nobody Cares," 2011; the book variant via Goodreads is in Signature quotes)

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **Lies that losers tell: the truth is the first casualty.** "When a company starts to lose its major battles, the truth often becomes the first casualty." His catalogue: attrition quietly reclassified as people "who quit, but it’s OK because the company didn’t want them anyway"; "We would have won, but the other guys gave the deal away" ("try to validate this claim with the actual customer. I’ll bet you can’t."); missed milestones that supposedly do not threaten the ship date; churn that email marketing will fix ("we have not been sending them enough spam"). Root cause via Andy Grove, whom he asked in 2001 why Cisco, Siebel and HP CEOs reiterated guidance until they whiffed: Grove "said they were not lying to investors, but rather, they were lying to themselves," because builders "only listen to leading indicators of good news." Horowitz's close: "And if you believe them, you are lying to yourself." ("Lies that Losers Tell," 2012)

text: [Fear, psychology and the CEO's own head] **Bill Campbell and the EDS announcement: be the one who talks to the employees.** When Loudcloud sold its old business to EDS to escape bankruptcy, Horowitz planned to fly to New York for the announcement. Campbell told him "No, no. You can’t go," because the deal sold employees and caused layoffs and he had to be the person in the company talking to them. Horowitz sent a colleague and stayed; his judgment: "had I not stayed back and had that conversation, I don’t think we would have made it as a company." (Ferriss #392; wording of the Campbell and Horowitz lines is as transcribed in the notes)

text:
[Decisions, people and process] **All Points of View (the one management concept).** The Stanford CS183B lecture compresses the 300-page book to one rule: "when you're making a critical decision you have to understand how it's going to be interpreted from All Points of View not just your point of view and not just the person you're talking to but the people who aren't in the room" (auto-caption). His gloss: "it's the easiest thing to say and the most difficult to master", because "at the point when you're making a decision you're often under a great deal of pressure." Four worked cases follow as separate bullets. He opens the lecture with a Sly and the Family Stone lyric ("sometimes I'm right and I can be wrong"), which is Sly's, not his. (How to Manage, YouTube auto-captions)
- *Worked example A, the raise.* An excellent employee asks for a raise; your view is retain and be fair, theirs is that they may have another offer, the missing view is the equally good employee who did not ask and concludes "whoever asks gets." Result if you pay on request: everybody in your company "is going to feel that they now have a fiduciary responsibility to their family to ask for a raise all the time" (caption wording). His fix: a formal cycle every six months or quarter, never off cycle, and no lobbying after it closes ("I'm not going to do things off cycle"; "you have to be formal to save your own culture"; "the process actually protects um it protects the culture"). Giving raises whenever people ask "is called encouraging behavior." (auto-caption)
- *Worked example B, demote or fire the outmatched executive.* A hardworking head of sales is out of his depth: demoting keeps a hard worker with many friends, and is easier for him to explain than a firing. Horowitz's test questions: what equity does he hold (his illustration is 1.5 percent versus an engineer's 0.1 to 0.2 percent), will you take it back, and will people give a demoted person the same respect? The real decision is what it takes to keep top-tier equity, effort or result, and you are deciding for the whole company, not one person. The figures are spoken estimates. (auto-caption)
- *Worked example C, Sam Altman's 10-year option exercise window.* Before changing the 90-day rule he asks why it existed for about 30 years: until 2004 accounting treatment (APB Opinion No. 25) made a long exercise period an unforecastable compensation expense, so the rule answered a law that no longer exists. He then walks four parties (the fired employee, the stayer, the option pool, retention "handcuffs") and concludes "I wouldn't go as far as to Sam that it should be adopted by every company"; the adopter should state a coherent culture either way, straightforward 10 years regardless of wealth, or an explicit stay culture where "10% of nothing is nothing." Altman answered in the room that he would add a stay incentive. (auto-caption)
- *Worked example D, Louverture's conquest decisions.* Three perspectives each time (soldiers, the enemy, and the culture, since "the Army was going to be the seed corn for the culture of the whole country"). Conquered European officers were made generals (a Julius Caesar technique); slave owners kept land, paid workers, and got lower taxes to fund it. The export and Napoleon claims are spoken, unsourced, and contested by a historian (see Blind spots). (auto-caption)

text: [Decisions, people and process] **The kimchi problem.** Burying a decision or an emotional issue makes it worse: "the kimchi problem the deeper you bury it the hotter it gets" (lecture auto-caption), and "the deeper you bury it the hotter it gets" again at the Computer History Museum (auto-caption). Worked example: the "confidential" raise that surfaces later. A "little emotional problem" becomes "a forest fire" in three weeks, three months or a year.

the deeper you bury it the hotter it gets
little emotional problem
a forest fire
title: The kimchi problem

text: [Decisions, people and process] **The pause protocol.** When something important arrives and you have not thought it through, say you take it seriously and must think it through from all perspectives, then come back; "the most important thing is to pause." He admits the pressure to answer is the failure: "if I don't know the answer I'll make something up uh because I want you to think I'm real smart." Worked example: the great employee asking for a raise on the spot. (auto-caption)
quotes: the most important thing is to pause.
if I don't know the answer I'll make something up uh because I want you to think I'm real smart.
title: The pause protocol

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Firing an executive: own your hiring error, protect the reputation.** In the lecture he says the number-one reason is that you "didn't match them to the needs of your company accurately enough," so lead with what you did not recognize about the company and the person, avoiding both "you just suck" and "it's not you, it's me". At the all-hands, thank them and skip personal detail, because "what you say at that meeting that's their reputation because everybody in your company is going to get a call on that person when they try and get their next job." Bill Campbell's version, as he relays it: "you can take somebody's job you have to take their job and this is something Bill Campbell taught me but you don't have to take their dignity." (lecture auto-caption; complements "Preparing to Fire an Executive")

you just suck
it's not you, it's me

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Culture act versus individual cost: Grove's late-meeting rebuke.** Grove's line to a latecomer, as Ferriss quotes and Horowitz confirms: "All I have in this world is time and you are wasting my time." Horowitz's reading: "It's kind of a Confucian approach that the individual must be sacrificed for the good of the whole." Conditions he states: not gratuitously, and mostly when the culture is in place and the person is willfully ignoring it. It breaks the basic rule never to embarrass an employee publicly, and works only because Grove was "like God" in Horowitz's phrase, an authority-dependent exception. (Ferriss #392)
quotes: All I have in this world is time and you are wasting my time.
It's kind of a Confucian approach that the individual must be sacrificed for the good of the whole.
title: Culture act versus individual cost: Grove's late-meeting rebuke

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Sharpen the contradictions.** A phrase Horowitz says originated with Marx and was used by Lenin (whom he calls wrong about everything but a rhetorical genius). Management use: when two people or two strategy statements disagree, do not smooth it over, because "there’s information in that contradiction." and "that’s where the truth is." His own caution: "it’s also a good way to start a revolution, so you’ve got to be careful." Told that a dispute is just a miscommunication, he answers it is "probably a systemic miscommunication." (Ferriss #392)
quotes: there’s information in that contradiction.
that’s where the truth is.
it’s also a good way to start a revolution, so you’ve got to be careful.
probably a systemic miscommunication.
title: Sharpen the contradictions

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Performance review: put it in the review.** Paraphrasing Grove's *High Output Management*: if something needs improvement that you never told the employee, you must put it in the review, because "it’s bad that you didn’t tell him, but it’s worse to not tell him now" (Horowitz's rendering of Grove, not Grove's verbatim text). (Ferriss #392)
quotes: it’s bad that you didn’t tell him, but it’s worse to not tell him now
title: Performance review: put it in the review

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Hire the role you have now, not the platonic CFO.** First-time CEOs hiring executives should define criteria for this company today: talk to CFOs to define the role, test in the interview, then onboard "hand-over-hand." On the interview itself: "It’s sort of like interviewing a Japanese interpreter if you don’t know Japanese. They are going to sound wonderful, right?" And on his own record: "We’ve never had a first-time CEO who is good at this, and I know I wasn’t good at it when I started." The biggest resume often brings a person who wants to be CEO and grabs territory (Ferriss #392; last point is a paraphrase).
quotes: It’s sort of like interviewing a Japanese interpreter if you don’t know Japanese. They are going to sound wonderful, right?
We’ve never had a first-time CEO who is good at this, and I know I wasn’t good at it when I started.
title: Hire the role you have now, not the platonic CFO

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Hire for strength, via Colin Powell.** The book names the source of the strength-not-absence-of-weakness rule: "I’d learned the hard way that when hiring executives, one should follow Colin Powell’s instructions and hire for strength rather than lack of weakness." At the Computer History Museum he restates it: "you value people on the magnitude of their strength not their lack of weakness" (auto-caption). (*The Hard Thing About Hard Things*, via Goodreads)
quotes: I’d learned the hard way that when hiring executives, one should follow Colin Powell’s instructions and hire for strength rather than lack of weakness.

title: Hire for strength, via Colin Powell

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Motivation and training are the only two levers on output.** "there are only two ways for a manager to improve the output of an employee: motivation and training." The argument for training: "People at McDonald’s get trained for their positions, but people with far more complicated jobs don’t. It makes no sense. Would you want to stand on the line of the untrained person at McDonald’s? Would you want to use the software written by the engineer who was never told how the rest of the code worked? A lot of companies think their employees are so smart that they require no training. That’s silly." (*The Hard Thing About Hard Things*, via Goodreads and Shortform). Origin of Good Product Manager/Bad Product Manager, per Ferriss #392: written out of frustration at repeating the same conversation ("This is going to be like dog training"), it became a Netscape-wide document; the lesson was that anyone, "no matter if they went to Stanford or Harvard", can use training in the job you want them to do.

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Three small engineering-flavored rules from the book.** (1) "Early in my career as an engineer, I’d learned that all decisions were objective until the first line of code was written. After that, all decisions were emotional." So settle scope before commitment. (2) "whenever a large organization attempts to do anything, it always comes down to a single person who can delay the entire project": find that person first. (3) "Sometimes an organization doesn’t need a solution; it just needs clarity." The page that carries them (Goodreads) gives no stories for these, so no worked example is attached. (*The Hard Thing About Hard Things*, via Goodreads)

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Eat the whole bad decision at once (a chapter title).** The book has a chapter titled in capitals "IF YOU ARE GOING TO EAT SHIT, DON’T NIBBLE" (Goodreads snippet). text: [Decisions, people and process] **The map and the terrain: CEO owns the terrain, CFO owns the map.** "Just like the map is not the terrain, the spreadsheet is not the business." "In a well run company, the CEO typically owns the terrain and the CFO owns the map." Worked example against himself: he once shouted "Goddammit, Dave, the spreadsheet is not the business!" at CFO Dave Conte after a model raised revenue by "adding more sales people earlier, but with no other changes" (revenue also depends on rep quality, onboarding, competitors, enablement, lead count). But "Dave should have yelled at me right back": "Ben, you cannot run around the terrain without a fucking map and expect to go anywhere good." (The Map and the Terrain)

title: The map and the terrain: CEO owns the terrain, CFO owns the map

text: [Decisions, people and process] **When to build the map.** Before product/market fit the business is "simple enough that a) you really don’t need a map and b) the map that you have is always so out of date that it’s almost a waste of time." Later it becomes the alignment device: "A good map will provide you with the straightest path to a much more valuable company long term." Each side needs the other's half: a CFO who knows ideal metrics but not this company's terrain "might give very bad advice"; a CEO who cannot translate terrain into value "might make costly tradeoff mistakes and drive the company into a wall." (The Map and the Terrain)
quotes: simple enough that a) you really don’t need a map and b) the map that you have is always so out of date that it’s almost a waste of time.
A good map will provide you with the straightest path to a much more valuable company long term.
might give very bad advice
might make costly tradeoff mistakes and drive the company into a wall.
title: When to build the map

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Hire a CFO by three tests.** "Which one of these candidates can I trust to map my business with great accuracy?" / "More importantly, who do I want to review every single number in a giant financial model with and explain to her where her assumptions are right and where they are house of cards?" / "Most importantly, who will I trust when they say I am headed in the wrong direction?" In short, hire the one who will contradict you; keep a standing "constant dialogue." (The Map and the Terrain)
quotes: Which one of these candidates can I trust to map my business with great accuracy?
More importantly, who do I want to review every single number in a giant financial model with and explain to her where her assumptions are right and where they are house of cards?
Most importantly, who will I trust when they say I am headed in the wrong direction?
title: Hire a CFO by three tests

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Cash flow and destiny.** Positive cash flow buys the freedom to ignore bad outside advice: "Until you generate cash, you must heed investors even when they are wrong. If investors wake up one day and think you are toast, you are indeed toast." Worked example: Loudcloud/Opsware after the crash; he committed to Wall Street to be cash-flow positive no later than Q2 2003. A strong team member asked, "Why draw a line in the sand if we don’t have to?" His answer: "We should first decide how much we like laying people off, because if we love it then lets stay cash flow negative, because when we don’t generate cash, the capital markets decide when we have to lay people off." Outcome: "Over those five years the company’s value grew 40-fold as a result of controlling our own destiny and being able to make our own decisions." (Cash Flow and Destiny, 2013)

Why draw a line in the sand if we don’t have to?

We should first decide how much we like laying people off, because if we love it then lets stay cash flow negative, because when we don’t generate cash, the capital markets decide when we have to lay people off.

title: Cash flow and destiny

text: [Decisions, people and process] **When profitless growth is acceptable.** From the same essay, two conditions: you are building something massively important with a credible expectation of huge future cash, and the capital markets are currently willing to fund it. Otherwise, or if times change, "be careful." He treats Twitter as qualifying for the exception, a nuance not an attack. This reads together with "The Case for the Fat Startup" (fat to win and not run out of cash) and differs on the funding source; both are Loudcloud/Opsware survival logic. (Cash Flow and Destiny)
quotes: The Case for the Fat Startup
title: When profitless growth is acceptable

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Be yourself, case 1: "Manager Stan."** Stan, an excellent co-worker, is promoted and "stops being Stan and becomes “Manager Stan”" and "magically transforms into a dick" because he feels he must establish authority. "Nobody likes or follows “Manager Stan.”" Mechanism: performing authority replaces the authentic relationship. (The First Rule of Leadership)
quotes: because he feels he must establish authority.
title: Be yourself, case 1: "Manager Stan."

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Be yourself, case 2: the rank-and-yank trap.** A CEO reads about Jack Welch ranking GE employees and adopts it with no thought deeper than "Jack Welch did it." A manager points out that the company's hiring bar means the bottom 10 percent is already strong; the CEO privately agrees, then must defend a view he does not hold or reverse on the spot. Horowitz's diagnosis: he "painted himself into a corner by trying to be Jack Welch rather than be himself." Heuristic: test any borrowed practice against your own facts before announcing it. (The First Rule of Leadership)
quotes: Jack Welch did it.
painted himself into a corner by trying to be Jack Welch rather than be himself.
title: Be yourself, case 2: the rank-and-yank trap

text: [Decisions, people and process] **Be yourself, case 3: the board member who says your CFO is weak.** Wrong move: relay the judgment to the CFO, which means the CEO "has refused to have a point of view and make a stand" and may make the CFO "lose his leadership mojo." Right move: ask the board member what is better about those CFOs and for introductions ("Great. Please let me know what about those CFOs you think is better and introduce me to them."), meet them, form your own assessment, decide how much the skills matter, and only then talk to your CFO, being yourself. Anchor image: Charles Barkley's "I am not a role model" versus Hakeem Olajuwon's "I am a role model" (their words, not his); Horowitz's gloss on Barkley is his own: "Don’t follow me. I don’t even like me." (The First Rule of Leadership)
quotes: has refused to have a point of view and make a stand
lose his leadership mojo.
Great. Please let me know what about those CFOs you think is better and introduce me to them.
I am not a role model
I am a role model

title: Be yourself, case 3: the board member who says your CFO is weak

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Values versus virtues, and the "weaponized value."** "a value is what you believe what you want to be what you aspire to a virtue is what you do" (CHM Live, auto-caption). A vague value can be turned against its author. Worked example: Slack's Stewart Butterfield wrote "empathy" as an early value (understand the other person's view before arguing); with no boundaries, managers wrote reviews saying an employee was "not being empathetic," and Butterfield dropped it. Counter-example: the samurai paired a hair-trigger honor virtue with an elaborate politeness virtue and required the politeness to be sincere; "politeness without veracity is empty." A virtue needs a balancing virtue and an honesty test. (CHM Live)
quotes: a value is what you believe what you want to be what you aspire to a virtue is what you do
not being empathetic,
politeness without veracity is empty.
title: Values versus virtues, and the "weaponized value."

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **A story carries what a value statement cannot.** Horowitz's samurai loyalty story: a lord's house burns with his genealogy scroll inside; a mediocre but sincere samurai runs in against orders, dies, and is found with the scroll sealed inside a cut in his own stomach; it becomes "the blood genealogy." A story people cannot get out of their head does what a value statement cannot. (CHM Live; the caption garbles the names, so none are given here)
quotes: the blood genealogy.
title: A story carries what a value statement cannot

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Orientation is whatever the new hire sees (Senghor's first day).** Shaka Senghor's first day in prison: a prisoner stabs another in the neck, throws the shank in the trash and eats a sandwich. Horowitz: that is orientation. In companies the new hire looks at whom everyone admires, sees the golden boy take credit for someone's work, and concludes "that's what I have to do to succeed here" (caption wording). Prescription: take onboarding seriously and train managers on expected behavior from day one, which has "way higher impact" than a value statement. (CHM Live, auto-caption)
quotes: that's what I have to do to succeed here
way higher impact
title: Orientation is whatever the new hire sees (Senghor's first day)

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **A cultural problem, not an actual problem (NationBuilder).** The portfolio company's cash collections were late and incomplete. Horowitz applied Senghor's technique of forced proximity and daily repetition: an 8:00 a.m. collections meeting every day, the CEO's first sentence "where's my money." The excuses were trivial (a badly written auto-email nobody knew how to fix); cash collected roughly doubled. His diagnosis: "it's a cultural problem not an actual problem," and many CEOs assume cultural baselines that do not exist. (CHM Live, auto-caption)
quotes: where's my money.
it's a cultural problem not an actual problem,
title: A cultural problem, not an actual problem (NationBuilder)

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Culture must fit strategy: Amazon and Apple.** Amazon's frugality (door desks) fits a low-cost-leader strategy; Apple's no-expense design culture (costly campus, expensive doorknobs) fits a best-product strategy. Apple adopting Amazon's culture would have been counterproductive. This is the strategy-fit test layered on the book's three questions about virtues. (CHM Live)
title: Culture must fit strategy: Amazon and Apple

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Make ethics explicit (the Uber case).** His read: Kalanick had 99 percent of a great culture (Uber University trained it; competitiveness was the defining virtue) but never stated the ethical line, so "winning" got read as "at all costs." Worked example: Susan Fowler reported harassment in writing on day one and HR said the manager was a high performer. His principle: "you have to make ethics explicit" and "you can't just say do the right thing you have to say here's what we're doing and here's why we're doing it." The Uber and Boeing judgments are made from outside, from press reports, so weight them as opinion. (CHM Live, auto-caption)
quotes: at all costs.
you have to make ethics explicit
you can't just say do the right thing you have to say here's what we're doing and here's why we're doing it.
title: Make ethics explicit (the Uber case)

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **A shocking rule has a shelf life.** Facebook's "move fast and break things" was a great shocking rule for outrunning Myspace; Zuckerberg consciously retired it when Platform and Connect partners kept getting broken. A rule that wins one phase must be rewritten for the next. The same event has him correct the word "pivot" for Hastings: streaming was planned from the start, DVDs were the pacing business, and Hastings removed the DVD leaders from the executive staff meeting although DVD was 100 percent of revenue. (CHM Live)
quotes: move fast and break things
title: A shocking rule has a shelf life

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **The lateness fine, in full.** The book-era summary says $10 a minute. At CHM he gives the schedule: $10 per minute late to an entrepreneur meeting, $50 for a bathroom break, $100 for an important phone call, so staff plan their day around the rule and recall why. In Ferriss: "I collected $50 a day. It's $10 a minute," with no excuses ("What if I had to go to the bathroom?" "I don't care."), and the answer to "why" is "because building a company is really, really hard." Culture is "how people are behaving when you're not looking." (CHM Live; Ferriss #392)
quotes: I collected $50 a day. It's $10 a minute,
What if I had to go to the bathroom?
I don't care.
because building a company is really, really hard.
how people are behaving when you're not looking.
title: The lateness fine, in full

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Culture-fit screening must be specific.** a16z will not let anyone sign an offer letter without agreeing to the written culture document. "Not a fit" has to say what exactly, and whether we want that element in our culture; fuzzy fit means homogeneity. People can also change. (CHM Live) At the a16z LP Summit he adds: "We will not let you sign your offer letter if you haven't signed your culture document that you agree to behave according to the culture." and "Nobody joins a firm without hearing from me about what the culture is for an hour." (The Evolution of the Firm, machine transcript, speaker inferred as Horowitz)
quotes: Not a fit
We will not let you sign your offer letter if you haven't signed your culture document that you agree to behave according to the culture.
Nobody joins a firm without hearing from me about what the culture is for an hour.
title: Culture-fit screening must be specific

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Peer enforcement: "That's off culture."** Worked example at a16z: a partner who is a security expert tweeted that a portfolio project's security decision made no sense; teammates intervened with the firm's norms, "we never criticize entrepreneurs in public" and "we're not dream killers, we're dream builders" (the team's words, relayed by Horowitz). Criticism goes by phone, not Twitter. His line: "The culture gets enforced by the whole team, and that's what makes it work." and, from the military, "the standard is the standard." (The Evolution of the Firm)
quotes: That's off culture.
we never criticize entrepreneurs in public
we're not dream killers, we're dream builders
The culture gets enforced by the whole team, and that's what makes it work.
the standard is the standard.
title: Peer enforcement: "That's off culture."

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **A profitable line that contradicts the mission: private equity.** Asked whether a16z should be in private equity, the position is that "cutting a company in half" is off culture and off mission, so the firm might decline it even if it can "make a lot of money" (paraphrase of the passage). The firm's stated mission, as relayed: help people build better companies and more of them. (The Evolution of the Firm, paraphrase; machine transcript)
quotes: cutting a company in half
make a lot of money
title: A profitable line that contradicts the mission: private equity

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Diversity by outcomes, not inflow.** An NFL analogy: a team of all 350-pound linemen or all 180-pound sprinters loses; you need to see talents you do not have. The metrics he asks CEOs for at board level: onboarding time to productivity, satisfaction, attrition, and promotion and attrition across race and gender, not how many underrepresented people come through the door. Using race or gender as a proxy for unseen talent, to "get the gold sticker," makes employees miserable (paraphrase of his argument). (CHM Live, paraphrase)
quotes: get the gold sticker,
title: Diversity by outcomes, not inflow

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Reality distortion versus lying.** Founder conviction is believing something others deny: "that's believing something but not knowing it." Lying is stating what you know is false. He dislikes "fake it till you make it" for its cultural implications. (CHM Live, auto-caption)
quotes: that's believing something but not knowing it.
fake it till you make it
title: Reality distortion versus lying

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Boeing 737 MAX (Nov 2019).** When schedule or earnings outranked safety where lives are at stake, he leans toward removing the leaders: "you have to shock the system hard enough to reset the culture." A culture judgment made from press reports, not inside data. (CHM Live, auto-caption)
quotes: you have to shock the system hard enough to reset the culture.
title: Boeing 737 MAX (Nov 2019)

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Join test and the outside view.** If you disagree with a company's behaviors as an individual contributor, leave early, because "culture will change you" (paraphrase of the video). An individual cannot change culture from below if the top violates it (a CEO always half an hour late). To judge a culture from outside, ask about specific behaviors: how fast a message gets answered, whether people are on laptops in the meeting. His own bound: "I'm not anti word," and nobody can see their own culture. (CHM Live)
quotes: culture will change you
I'm not anti word,
title: Join test and the outside view

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Culture is not the whole company.** The book states its own qualifier: "Culture does not make a company." A great culture with a product nobody wants goes out of business, but the lasting value is "what that time was like": how people treated each other. His one-word advice for the museum's initiative: "persistence." (CHM Live; *The Hard Thing About Hard Things*, p.179 per Thrive Street Advisors)
quotes: Culture does not make a company.
what that time was like
title: Culture is not the whole company

text: [Culture, applied (What You Do Is Who You Are, and a16z's own practice)] **Hypocrisy as the default failure.** "it's not what you believe, it's not your values, it's not what you tweet, it's not your social signal, it's what you actually do, that's who you are." and "if you talk it and don't do it, then your culture becomes your hypocrisy." On scale: "It's really hard to get 10,000 people to behave the way you want them to," and the default is that "everybody's culture is screwed up." (Ferriss #392)
quotes: it's not what you believe, it's not your values, it's not what you tweet, it's not your social signal, it's what you actually do, that's who you are.

everybody's culture is screwed up.

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **How a16z evaluates a CEO (three questions).** "1. Does the CEO know what to do? 2. Can the CEO get the company to do what she knows? 3. Did the CEO achieve the desired results against an appropriate set of objectives?" On the first: "in good companies, the story and the strategy are the same thing," and decisions are made with "less than 10% of the information typically present in the ensuing Harvard Business School case study." Worked example: his best decision, selling the Loudcloud business to EDS, "would have lost by landslide had I put it to vote with my employees, my investors, or my customers." On the second, his test question: “how easy is it for any given individual contributor to get their job done?” On the third, set objectives against this company's opportunity, illustrated by Baidu's Robin Li dreading an IPO that priced at $27 and closed at $122. Close: "All people, including CEOs, will perform better on a test if they know the questions ahead of time." ("How Andreessen Horowitz Evaluates CEOs," 2010)

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Configure the organization to the size of the market.** "When Marc and I started the firm in 2009, the conventional wisdom in Venture Capital was that in any given year, only 15 companies would ever generate $100M in revenue and those 15 companies would drive almost all of VC returns." And: "At that time, the conventional wisdom was right." Software expanded every submarket, so the right design changed from "a $300M fund and 2 General Partners" to dedicated funds with dedicated expert teams (the April 2024 raise: $7.2B across American Dynamism, Apps, Games, Infrastructure and Growth). On specialization: "Each area requires deep expertise, so it’s not wise to try to cross-train someone in, for example, Games and Infrastructure." (New Funds, New Era; the lecture's formal-process logic and this are the same move, fit structure to scale)

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Shared economics without shared control.** "if you share control, you can't scale, because if you share control, you can't reorganize." and "if you're an equal partnership with equal control, then doing something new gets very hard." a16z shared economics but not control, so it could reorganize into crypto, AI infrastructure and American Dynamism with a single decision point. Worked example: the crypto RIA came out of a conversation among Horowitz, Andreessen and Chris Dixon; other firms balked at the reporting burden. His claims that rival top-tier firms mostly missed these areas are a boast at an LP summit, unverifiable in the source. (The Evolution of the Firm, machine transcript, speaker inferred)
quotes: if you share control, you can't scale, because if you share control, you can't reorganize.
if you're an equal partnership with equal control, then doing something new gets very hard.
title: Shared economics without shared control

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Succession is a tactic; training is the mechanism.** "I think succession planning is kind of like a tactic." Martin Casado succeeded Horowitz as head of infrastructure ("And he's, by the way, better head of infra than I was."). The durable thing is a way of doing things taught in classes (Dixon teaches investing, Horowitz teaches how to be effective on a board) plus hard hiring ("We interview them hard"). (The Evolution of the Firm)
quotes: I think succession planning is kind of like a tactic.
And he's, by the way, better head of infra than I was.
We interview them hard
title: Succession is a tactic; training is the mechanism

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Venture as a product with a gap.** The firm's founding thesis: top-tier VC was a really good product for LPs and a really mediocre one for entrepreneurs (his characterization, paraphrased from the transcript, not verbatim), so a16z built a platform to turn a founder into a CEO: a network (any CEO, any executive, the US government), in-house ex-CEOs, a book, marketing. The test image is Bob Iger's network. The same view appears in the 2014 lecture: "the founder inventor is special" and "if you want to advise the CEO you have to have kind of been a CEO." (The Evolution of the Firm; How to Manage, auto-caption)
quotes: the founder inventor is special
if you want to advise the CEO you have to have kind of been a CEO.
title: Venture as a product with a gap

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Firm, not a fund; power, not advice.** Under his byline but in the firm's "we" voice (June 2026): "From the outset, a16z has been organized as a firm, not a fund whose purpose is to help founders build amazing businesses, and to do it as much as possible." and "the thing you want from your VC is ability to confer power, not just advice." The announced structure adds Anne Neuberger as General Partner and Head of Global Affairs, a Global Partnerships team, and a Tokyo office. Treat as an institutional announcement, not a personal opinion. (a16z's Global Mission)
quotes: From the outset, a16z has been organized as a firm, not a fund whose purpose is to help founders build amazing businesses, and to do it as much as possible.
the thing you want from your VC is ability to confer power, not just advice.

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Little Tech: three kinds of politicians (co-authored).** Supporters of Little Tech: support them. Opponents: oppose them. The middle, "they want to be supportive, but they have concerns": "We work with them in good faith." Applied "regardless of party and regardless of their positions on other issues," on a single issue: how startups are treated. The founders' stated reason for spending political resources is absence: startups "as an industry do not show up in Washington D.C. and in the political system the way big companies do." (The Little Tech Agenda; co-authored by Andreessen and Horowitz)

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **The incumbent lifecycle to regulatory capture (co-authored).** Startup, dominant incumbent, "pull the rope ladder up," regulation too heavy for new startups, government-backed cartels, stagnation. Their claims: "Dominant companies don’t start out that way. In fact, they start as startups, fighting their way uphill until they reach a position of power where they seek to lock in their gains, to pull the rope ladder up behind them." and "the motto of every monopoly and cartel is, “We don’t care, because we don’t have to.”" The evidence offered (productivity growth "lower than before the 1970’s") is asserted without citation. (The Little Tech Agenda; co-authored)

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **AI structure: open source and decentralization above safety (Dec 2023).** After Marc laid out the "god models" versus commoditization scenarios (Marc's, not Horowitz's), Horowitz said the more important policy question is open source and decentralization: whether open source is legal and whether crypto and blockchain help decentralize the data question, as a counterweight to "giant corporations being like our literal tech overlords" (caption wording, paraphrased). Dated precursor to his 2024 to 2026 open-weights stance. (Ask Us Anything, auto-caption, speaker inferred)
quotes: giant corporations being like our literal tech overlords

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **Regulate harms at the application layer: the deepfake example (joint, speaker-blind).** In the Nov 2024 episode the hosts (Andreessen and Horowitz, speakers unlabeled) argue for defining concrete harms and criminalizing them: an AI deepfake that leads to a death, interferes in foreign affairs or fakes an alibi gets the penalties for falsifying evidence, while preserving satire (SNL has done fake politician videos for 50 years). Technical complement: politicians sign content on a blockchain so platforms and users can distrust unsigned content. (New AI Policy Update, YouTube auto-captions; credited to the hosts jointly)
title: Regulate harms at the application layer: the deepfake example (joint, speaker-blind)

text: [Firm design, venture and policy] **The "we must do something" cycle and the takeoff bottleneck chain (joint, speaker-blind).** The hosts describe a three-step Washington adage (we must do something; this is something; therefore we must do this). The bottleneck argument, which the notes assign "per content" to Horowitz's technical turn: even a self-improving AI hits chips, then power, then cooling; self-improvement research so far is "little things", not genius re-architecture. Treat both as the hosts' joint positions in this dossier. They are falsifiable 2024 claims; the 2026 recursive-self-improvement episode already cited here frames the question differently and has not been reconciled with them on the record. (New AI Policy Update, auto-captions)

title: The "we must do something" cycle and the takeoff bottleneck chain (joint, speaker-blind)

text: Before choosing a management style, ask **which game you're in: peacetime or wartime.** Don't apply growth-mode techniques to a survival situation.

If you're hunting for a **silver bullet, stop.** Diagnose whether the real problem is the product/competitive position; if so, fire lead bullets, do the unglamorous core work, and aim for 10x, not slightly-better.

**Run at the fear.** When two options are both bad, the failure mode is hesitation; decide and move. "Your job is to act under uncertainty… What can I do? And I better do that right now" (a16z Speedrun).

text: **Take care of people first**, which *includes* doing layoffs and firings cleanly and respectfully when survival requires them, rather than avoiding them. Do it fast once decided, be honest about why, don't delegate it away, and let managers deliver the news to their own people.

text: **"Don't bring me problems": a tension, resolved as a role contract (partly inference).** An earlier version of this dossier had Horowitz warning that the maxim "don't bring me a problem without a solution" silences the report you most need. No verbatim Horowitz line to that effect appears in the sources checked in this pass. What is documented points the same direction: "Bad news travels fast" culture design, the one-on-one question "What's the No. 1 problem with our organization?", and "Almost all CEOs know where the problems are." The counter-evidence: in the Hobson interview her mentor's rule ("you do not bring me any problems I give you problems to solve") is Hobson's, relayed from her mentor, and Horowitz only asks whether it was special to her and calls it "amazing," without challenging it. Reconciliation (the dossier's inference, not his statement): he treats the maxim as dangerous when applied to a whole organization's bad news, and as legitimate when it is a bespoke contract between a principal and a deputy whose job is to take problems off the principal's desk.

text:
Blunt, profane when it serves a point, and allergic to romanticizing entrepreneurship. He opens chapters and essays with hip-hop and rap lyrics (Nas, Jay-Z, Kanye, DMX, Dr. Dre, Rick Ross, Lil Wayne) as genuine epigraphs: the worldview of hustling under existential pressure maps onto running a startup (a stylistic choice one critic, Ryan Craggs, calls out as ill-judged when a slur-laden lyric is used purely for cool-factor rather than content). Heavy use of dark humor about how genuinely awful the lows are (cold sweats, not being able to taste food). He teaches by analogy to outside-tech figures (Andy Grove, Cus D'Amato, Genghis Khan, Toussaint Louverture, Colin Powell, John Madden, Phil Jackson) and tells stories on himself, including his near-failures and moments he says he "cried because I didn't know" the true cost of what he'd asked of his team, rather than posing as the infallible genius. Short declarative sentences, war and sports metaphors, named acronym-like coinages for nearly every idea (Management Debt, the Law of Crappy People, the Reflexive Principle of Employee Raiding), and a refrain that the textbook answer misses "the hard thing about the hard thing." In recent interviews he leans on a "laws of physics have changed" framing for the AI era, and repeats several rhetorical set-pieces, the "regulating math" line, the "nobody has built anything on the way to sentience" rebuttal to AI-safety fears, nearly word-for-word across different audiences and years, suggesting rehearsed talking points rather than off-the-cuff positions.
Additions from the 2026 rebuild. His epigraph habit extends to a rap or pop lyric on nearly every post (Kanye West on the Maude Building essay, Chance The Rapper on "The First Rule of Leadership," Easy E on "The Map and the Terrain," Geto Boys, Nas and Otis Redding on the 2011 psychology essay); in every case the epigraph is the artist's, not his. He argues against himself on the record ("Dave should have yelled at me right back"; "I wasn't good at it when I started"), which is the main reason the self-critical passages read as credible. He compresses a hard idea into a single reusable image (map and terrain, kimchi, one bullet, the dread signal) and then tells the story where the image cost him money. On stage he is looser, more filler-heavy and more willing to say he has no answer ("I'm not anti word"), so auto-captioned quotes should be treated as spoken register, not essay register. When he argues for a policy with Andreessen, the two voices overlap in the transcripts; a "we" in those episodes is joint, and Horowitz tends to take the operational and technical turns while Andreessen takes the history and the sweeping analogies.

[The Hard Thing About Hard Things (2014)] **Shape of the book.** Per the British Library catalogue, nine chapters. The first five: (1) From Communist to venture capitalist; (2) "I will survive"; (3) This time with feeling; (4) When things fall apart (The struggle; CEOs should tell it like it is; The right way to lay people off; Preparing to fire an executive; Demoting a loyal friend; Lies that losers tell; Lead bullets; Nobody cares); (5) Take care of the people, the products, and the profits, in that order (A good place to work; Why startups should train their people; Is it okay to hire people from your friend's company?; Why it's hard to bring big company execs into little companies; Hiring executives: if you've never done the job, how do you hire somebody good?; When employees misinterpret managers; Management debt; Management quality assurance).

text: [The Hard Thing About Hard Things (2014)] **Shape of the book, continued.** (6) Concerning the going concern (How to minimize politics; The right kind of ambition; Titles and promotions; When smart people are bad employees; Old people; One-on-one; Programming your culture; Taking the mystery out of scaling a company; The scale anticipation fallacy); (7) How to lead even when you don't know where you are going (The most difficult CEO skill; The fine line between fear and courage; Ones and twos; Follow the leader; Peacetime CEO/wartime CEO; Making yourself a CEO; How to evaluate CEOs); (8) First rule of entrepreneurship: there are no rules (Solving the accountability vs. creativity paradox; The freaky Friday management technique; Staying great; Should you sell your company?); (9) The end of the beginning, with an appendix of questions for the head of an Enterprise sales force. text: [The Hard Thing About Hard Things (2014)] **The organizing move is to reject the genre.** Most management writing teaches you how to hit the goal; the job is what happens when you miss it. "Every time I read a management or self-help book, I find myself saying, “That’s fine, but that wasn’t really the hard thing about the situation.”" (Shortform's reproduction). The four-beat passage is in Core ideas; the book's thesis line is "That’s the hard thing about hard things—there is no formula for dealing with them." and "Sadly, there is no secret, but if there is one skill that stands out, it’s the ability to focus and make the best move when there are no good moves."

text: [What You Do Is Who You Are (2019)] **Premise.** A book-length answer to how you make a culture rather than write one down. Its cold open (per Eric Nehrlich) is a confession: at Loudcloud, Horowitz discovered a marketing employee was a compulsive liar who had gone undetected for years because he delivered the numbers, evidence that an unmanaged culture had decided lying was fine as long as the metrics looked good. Architecture per the table of contents: each historical case is paired with an "...Applied" chapter (Toussaint Louverture Applied; The Way of the Warrior; Shaka Senghor Applied; Genghis Khan, Master of Inclusion; Inclusion in the Modern World; Be Yourself/Design Your Culture; Edge Cases and Object Lessons; Final Thoughts). On the stage version: "a culture is not a set of beliefs it's a set of actions" (CHM Live, citing Bushido; auto-caption).

text: [What You Do Is Who You Are (2019)] **The samurai / Bushido.** The source of the culture-as-actions-not-beliefs idea, tested by three questions: is the virtue actionable, does it distinguish your culture from the default, and will you pass the test when it costs you something. Fuller version of the thesis (Sajith Pai's excerpt): "If you don't methodically set your culture, then two-thirds of it will end up being accidental, and the rest will be a mistake." The loyalty-story and honor-versus-politeness material is in Mental models.

The rule itself: officers were forbidden concubines, with the rationale made explicit: "your word matters most, and if we can't expect you to keep your word to your wife, how can we trust you to keep your word to us?"

He cites Louverture's reading of Caesar and recommends *The Black Jacobins* (C.L.R. James, 1937). The CHM version adds "culture not color," tracing the phrase to his 1797 rebuttal, and the stage claim that Louverture used "the same guys" who had been slaves, so culture can change without replacing everyone.

No one person makes or takes all these actions." His Haiti figures (about 900,000 enslaved people brought to Haiti and 465,000 left at the revolution's start, versus 500,000 brought to the US and 700,000 left) and the claim that it was "the only slave revolt in human history that ever resulted in an independent state" are his spoken claims, unchecked here. A genuine Haiti historian (Julia Gaffield) disputes the chapter's history as reductive (see Blind spots).

text: [What You Do Is Who You Are (2019)] **Genghis Khan.** Meritocracy and inclusion as a competitive weapon (promote by ability across tribe, class and religion; absorb conquered peoples) paired with ruthless, non-transactional loyalty enforcement: he is reported to have executed enemy commanders who defected to him by betraying their own khan, specifically to make loyalty absolute rather than negotiable. Parallels: Don Thompson (McDonald's), Maggie Wilderotter (Frontier). In the Ferriss interview Horowitz's only comment on Genghis is that he is "underrated"; no further mechanism detail was recovered.

text: [What You Do Is Who You Are (2019)] **Shaka Senghor (prison yard).** The starkest proof that people believe your actions, not your words. Prison is culture's hardest test case because inmates typically arrive from broken cultures with no shared basis for trust. Senghor's own account describes an internal split (one voice from Malcolm X, one from the prison code) resolved into a three-step, nine-year personal change process (learn there is a different way; master the new skills; decide to live it), and a concrete lever: requiring his crew to eat, train and study together so the new culture stayed visible. Horowitz's own summary in Ferriss: Senghor changed a violent gang "to be remarkably empathetic," though "It's still a prison gang." The forced-proximity technique travels (NationBuilder, in Mental models), and the first-day stabbing story is the template for onboarding-as-orientation.
