It's like… the fourth or fifth hand retelling of things happened six or nine months ago. They don't know.
title: The firsthand/secondhand/thirdhand/fourthhand information hierarchy

text: **"Giant founder voting machine" — reading market signal from the batch itself.** Rather than top-down forecasting, he reads what ~150–250 AI startups per batch are independently building as an aggregate signal of where real value is: "I almost view it as like a lens of… a giant founder voting machine." (No Priors Ep. 66.)
quotes: Giant founder voting machine
I almost view it as like a lens of… a giant founder voting machine.
title: "Giant founder voting machine" — reading market signal from the batch itself

text: **Weak elephant / necessity is the mother of invention.** Incumbents' scale advantage is often illusory because success makes them lazy: "The megatech companies have such unassailable moats… they're actually somewhat incapable of… stomping [startups] anymore… It's a weak elephant. It didn't do its push-ups every week." Applied test for any startup idea: what won't get stomped, given the elephant currently has no urgency to move. (No Priors Ep. 66.)
quotes: The megatech companies have such unassailable moats… they're actually somewhat incapable of… stomping [startups] anymore… It's a weak elephant. It didn't do its push-ups every week.
title: Weak elephant / necessity is the mother of invention

text: **Openness-of-markets ↔ founder-age correlation.** An analytical (not just anecdotal) claim: "the age of founders is in some sense dependent on the openness of markets… if markets are very open, younger people can participate. If markets are closed, then you need years of expertise." Data point: YC's average founder age was ~27 in 2008 (his own cohort), trending toward 25–26 as AI reopens the market the way internet/mobile once did; vertical/international marketplaces still favor older, domain-expert founders. He borrows (not originates) Balaji Srinivasan's **"Idea Maze"** to describe the mechanism: AI has moved the maze's walls — "Someone took all the walls in the maze and moved them around, and you could be the first person to find out there's no wall there now." (No Priors Ep. 66; YC Perfect Time to Start a Startup.)
quotes: the age of founders is in some sense dependent on the openness of markets… if markets are very open, younger people can participate. If markets are closed, then you need years of expertise.
Someone took all the walls in the maze and moved them around, and you could be the first person to find out there's no wall there now.
title: Openness-of-markets ↔ founder-age correlation

text: **Extreme-unbalance-as-strategy — held explicitly in tension with "build yourself, don't self-abandon."** In a college-audience talk he states, self-consciously flagging the risk of saying it publicly ("if I'm worried it's going to end up on Twitter and screw me, say it"): "If you actually want to win at startups, work-life balance is completely—it's not how you win… you actually win by being like extremely unbalanced and having all of your identity wrapped up in winning at your company." He scope-limits it himself: "this is not the advice if you even want to start like a good company. This is the advice if you want to start one of like the real huge outliers." This sits in genuine, acknowledged tension with his SIER/Lightcone material on self-abandonment and founder well-being (see Core ideas, and Blind spots) — the dossier holds both rather than resolving them, since he applies each in a different register (introspective lecture vs. hype-up talk to ambitious college founders). Worked example of the same "go big" logic, numerically: "if you do compound by YC standards—like a three-X, three-X growth per year… over like twenty-four years, you suddenly end up making a two-hundred-billion-dollar company in revenue." (YC Perfect Time to Start a Startup.)

text: **Found in "founder mode" — the inability to just follow directions is a feature.** "I can't really follow directions. What I realized is that's actually a founder mindset at some level." He pairs high agency with empathy for customers as the combination that wins — but he (or a co-host in the same voice) also complicates the term in real time, warning against the "facile view" that founder mode means micromanaging everywhere: "you can't do it everywhere, you have to be clear on where you're doing it." (ACQ2; Lightcone — What Founders Have To Unlearn.)
quotes: I can't really follow directions. What I realized is that's actually a founder mindset at some level.
you can't do it everywhere, you have to be clear on where you're doing it.
title: Found in "founder mode" — the inability to just follow directions is a feature

text: **Bet on the person when the data is thin.** Earnestness, relentlessness, and craft outweigh résumé at pre-seed. "Madness is doing the same thing over and over again… being totally relentless but doing the same thing is a form of self-torture" — relentlessness must be paired with willingness to pivot. (SIER.)
quotes: Madness is doing the same thing over and over again… being totally relentless but doing the same thing is a form of self-torture
title: Bet on the person when the data is thin

text: **Treat fundraising as the starting gun, not the finish.** "We actually try to keep the amount of time spent on fundraising to maybe two weeks." The mistake is "considering that that's the finish line… No, no, no. That's not the finish line. That's the starting gun, guys." (The Spindle.)
quotes: We actually try to keep the amount of time spent on fundraising to maybe two weeks.
considering that that's the finish line… No, no, no. That's not the finish line. That's the starting gun, guys.
title: Treat fundraising as the starting gun, not the finish

text: **Prefer many small experiments to one grand plan** — in product (MVP / "minimum viable everything") and in markets (thousands of companies, not seven giants).
quotes: minimum viable everything
title: Prefer many small experiments to one grand plan

text: **Choose; refuse "both."** When forced between platform and network — or between two co-CEOs — pick one (see Mental models).
title: Choose; refuse "both."

text: **When conflict resurfaces the same argument repeatedly** ("bleed-over," every disagreement becoming "an everything conflict"), that's the tell you can no longer resolve it object-level — bring in an executive coach before it's terminal. (Lightcone — How To Navigate Co-Founder Disputes.)
quotes: an everything conflict
title: When conflict resurfaces the same argument repeatedly

text: **Founding with existing friends is not sufficient diligence** — social-context compatibility doesn't predict high-stress-context compatibility; you only learn that under real pressure.
title: Founding with existing friends is not sufficient diligence

text: **Self-advocate rather than defer when negotiating a role split** (who's CEO, who gets what equity) — deference dressed as good teamwork is what he calls self-abandonment. (Should you be the CEO?.)

text: **Raising too much is a real failure mode, not just a negotiating tactic** — a rare on-record belief-reversal: "I didn't really understand what people were saying when they said, oh, like, don't raise too much money. I thought it was only a tactic… many years later… some of our best companies with the best technical founders, they might have raised too much money… when it's time to cut… that's a tall order." (No Priors Ep. 66.)

text: **Surround yourself with people who raise the bar, and get outside help early.** For company-killing conflict, bring in a coach or therapist before it's terminal. (SIER; Co-founder Conflict.)

text: **Engage policymakers from the builder's seat** — regulation should be written only after consulting "founders who are actually building real AI services," across party lines. (Punchbowl; Washington Reporter.)

text: **Open-source your own competitive edge rather than hoard it**, and let a surprised skeptic's own words validate the point rather than claiming it yourself — his gstack posts quote a CTO friend's unsolicited "this is like god mode" rather than asserting the claim in his own voice. (X — gstack "god mode.")

text: **Stay personally hands-on with the frontier technology you're underwriting decisions about.** "I'd be an idiot to experience it from the bleachers" — treats a leader's own technical practice as a duty for staying calibrated, not a hobby. (X — I came back to code because AI made it possible.)
quotes: I'd be an idiot to experience it from the bleachers
title: Stay personally hands-on with the frontier technology you're underwriting decisions about

text: **Pivot vs. persevere:** persevere relentlessly *but* be willing to change what you're doing — "Sucking is the first step to not sucking," but repeating a failing approach is "self-torture." (SIER.)
quotes: Sucking is the first step to not sucking,
title: Pivot vs. persevere

text: **When to fire / when to sell:** Posterous sold to Twitter (~$20M, talent acquisition) after growth flatlined and the co-founder relationship broke; he frames the underlying failure as unresolved conflict and lost focus, not market, and now estimates the foregone upside at "10 times or a hundred times" the actual exit. (Initialized blog; Lightcone — How To Navigate Co-Founder Disputes.)
quotes: 10 times or a hundred times
title: When to fire / when to sell

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap:** firmly pro-venture for ambitious companies, but cap fundraising time hard (two weeks), warn against raising "too much capital" early, and has publicly reversed his own past dismissal of "don't over-raise" as mere negotiating theater. (The Spindle; No Priors Ep. 66.)
quotes: too much capital
title: Raise vs. bootstrap

text: **Should you be the CEO?** A distinct, named decision fork (see Mental models): take the seat only if you'd be frustrated by lacking the authority to fix what's broken, and only if you pass the four-part test (can-convince, can-hire/fundraise, can-drive-vision, can-synthesize); otherwise say so honestly rather than default into a co-CEO structure, which he treats as a near-universal anti-pattern except at Google-founder scale. (Should you be the CEO?.)
title: Should you be the CEO?

text: **Co-founder split:** prevent it structurally — build the conflict muscle early, don't self-abandon, use "going over the net" and "authoritative vs. authoritarian" as guardrails, get an exec coach or therapist; "don't leave the room until you have a resolution." (Co-founder Conflict; Lightcone.)
quotes: going over the net
authoritative vs. authoritarian
don't leave the room until you have a resolution.
title: Co-founder split

text: **Focus vs. diversify:** focus — refuse "both," go for the category outcome rather than beefing with small rivals. (Medium; X.)
title: Focus vs. diversify

text: **Hire/partner:** with people who raise your bar; with friends and people you trust, while acknowledging that shared history doesn't predict under-stress compatibility. (SIER; X; Lightcone.)
title: Hire/partner

text: **Growth vs. curation (institutional scale):** pro-growth for YC's own batch size, on explicit Metcalfe's-law network-effects grounds, continuing rather than reversing his predecessor's approach — a distinct axis from his product-level "focus" advice to individual founders. (TechCrunch, 2022.)
title: Growth vs. curation (institutional scale)

text: **Work-life balance vs. outlier ambition:** genuinely two positions held in different registers — "build yourself," attend to well-being (SIER) vs. "extremely unbalanced… identity wrapped up in winning" for founders chasing the biggest outcomes specifically (YC Perfect Time to Start a Startup) — see Mental models and Blind spots for the tension.
quotes: extremely unbalanced… identity wrapped up in winning
title: Work-life balance vs. outlier ambition

text: **AI regulation, ranked (Washington Reporter, sharper than the Senate testimony alone):** explicitly numbered — "(1) Immigration… (2) Protecting open source AI… (3) Competition policy and antitrust." (Punchbowl; Senate testimony; Washington Reporter.)

text: Direct, energetic, founder-to-founder; YouTube and X are his native channels. Punchy aphorisms ("act small," "black ice of startups," "starting gun," "beefing with the littles," "shipping constipation," "weak elephant," "code cave") and vivid one-off analogies (a rowboat sailing for an "island of gold," 2008 startups as "a punk club in the 90s… grunge was just getting started"), optimistic and exhortative rather than hedged. A designer's eye — values clarity, minimalism, concrete examples over abstraction. Unusually willing to narrate his own failures (Posterous, "I self-abandoned," the "both" pitch, the CEO regret, the Thiel/Microsoft opportunity cost) as teaching material — vulnerability deployed as credibility, and occasionally flagged by him in real time as risky to say publicly before he says it anyway. He is also an unusually *synthesizing* voice for a founder-investor: rather than relying only on his own experience, he explicitly names and builds on outside frameworks — Paul Graham (muck-and-brass, "sell to someone who won't buy, build a competitor," and as his own career's original enabler), Paul Buchheit (group office hours as an AA-like social-pressure mechanism), Ben Horowitz (co-CEO failure), Warren Buffett (weighing machine), Peter Thiel (Schelling points, competition is for losers), Balaji Srinivasan (Idea Maze), Mark Suster, Charlie Munger, Adam Grant, and Patrick Lencioni — a citation lineage worth noting alongside his more personal metaphor-making. In politics the same bluntness turns combative and personal, the candor-vs-belligerence seam (he has publicly called a journalist a "parasite" and worse — see Blind spots), and he is capable of the identical "say the risky thing anyway" instinct on a controversial *work* opinion (extreme-imbalance-as-strategy) as on a political one (the "die slow" tweet) — suggesting the trait is general, not politics-specific.

text: Guilherme Horn is a Brazilian serial entrepreneur turned corporate-innovation executive — founder of Ágora (sold to Bradesco in 2008 for ~US$500 million, then Brazil's biggest fintech exit) and Órama (2010, the first fully cloud-based financial institution in Latin America, recognized by AWS in 2012–13) — who converted 22 years of founder experience into a second act as an innovation evangelist inside large institutions: Accenture LatAm (2014–2019), the Banco do Brasil board, executive director at Banco BV (Dec 2019–Mar 2022), and since March 2022, Head of WhatsApp for Strategic Markets (Brazil, India, Indonesia) at Meta. He is the lens for **messaging-as-infrastructure**: his sharpest, most contrarian position is an explicit, repeatedly-stated rejection of the "talk to your users" doctrine — citing Steve Jobs and Stan Lee as role models for *not* asking customers what they want — set against a parallel belief that **adoption is driven by existing habit and network effect, not technical superiority** ("você não usa o que é melhor, você usa o que todo mundo usa"). He opposes blind agile adoption, techno-solutionism ("solução em busca de um problema," his verdict on much of blockchain), and the idea that AI adoption is primarily an engineering problem rather than a leadership/mindset one. His 2026 second act sharpens this into an AI thesis — companies either use AI to "automatizar o passado" (commoditizing themselves) or to "desenhar o futuro" (capturing the "alpha competitivo"), with laggards accruing a dangerous "dívida cultural" — and a repeated positioning claim that **Brazil is Meta's benchmark market**, "onde aprendemos a inovar," whose intensity of use "molda o produto global" (Forbes; NeoFeed). As a lens he is strongest on conversational commerce, introducing disruptive technology into risk-averse regulated industries (cloud in finance, WhatsApp in banking), and the founder-to-corporate-executive transition; he is thinnest, and self-admittedly so, on fully "unlearning founder mode," and his flagship claim about WhatsApp's economic centrality in Brazil rests explicitly on unverifiable, encrypted-data-shielded anecdote rather than disclosed data.

text: Guilherme Horn is a Brazilian serial entrepreneur and corporate-innovation specialist who has founded six startups over roughly 25 years. He traces his entrepreneurial drive to his grandfather, a Polish immigrant who started a business in Niterói "without speaking one word of Portuguese" — Horn started coding at 14 and had his first developer job at 16 (The J Curve podcast). His first two ventures (a CD-ROM educational-content company in 1996, then an image-management company) both failed within two years, forcing him to "sell everything I had, my car and everything" (The J Curve podcast). In 2000, partners who already held a listed shell invited him to build their internet operation — this became Ágora, a broker-dealer that Horn built into the leader of the Brazilian retail brokerage market inside a market that fell 88% over its first three years (dot-com bust, 9/11, the 2002 Lula-election panic) before rebounding 97% in 2003, at which point Ágora was "perfectly positioned to scale" (The J Curve podcast). Bradesco bought Ágora in 2008 for roughly US$500 million. In 2010 Horn founded Órama, marketed as Brazil's first fully digital, 100%-cloud financial institution, letting retail investors with R$1,000 access funds that previously required US$1,000,000 minimums; Amazon/AWS recognized it at re:Invent in Las Vegas (Nov 2013) as one of the world's most innovative fintechs. After selling his Órama shares in 2014, Horn joined Accenture as Managing Director/Diretor Executivo de Inovação for Latin America (Dec 2014–2019), then took a board seat at Banco do Brasil, then became executive director at Banco BV (Dec 2019–Mar 2022). In March 2022 he moved to Meta, where he is Head of WhatsApp for Strategic Markets (Brazil, India, Indonesia) — a title he describes as taking the job specifically "to experience revenue-generation and scaling challenges in a new context" (Instituto Caldeira). He is a prolific angel investor (40+ startups by 2019, per ENECE; 50+ by 2025, per The J Curve podcast; "mais de 60" per his 2021 book bio), was elected Investidor-Anjo do Ano in 2017, is global faculty at Singularity University, writes the LinkedIn newsletter-style Pulse column as a LinkedIn Top Voice (~25,000 followers, ~500 posts, ~19 long-form articles), and authored the bestseller "O Mindset da Inovação" (Editora Gente, 2021, prefaced by José Salibi Neto) and a 2026 follow-up, "O Mindset da IA: ela pensa, você decide."

text: **Innovation is systemic, not genius.** Rejecting the "lone genius" myth directly: "se a inovação não vem de mentes brilhantes nem de ideias geniais, de onde ela vem? A inovação dentro das empresas vem de uma combinação que envolve pessoas e processos. E três elementos são essenciais para que ela aconteça: diversidade de pessoas, quantidade de ideias e fluxo de ideias" [if innovation doesn't come from brilliant minds or genius ideas, where does it come from? Innovation inside companies comes from a combination involving people and processes. Three elements are essential: diversity of people, quantity of ideas, and flow of ideas] (quoted in Nepomuceno's review of his book).
quotes: se a inovação não vem de mentes brilhantes nem de ideias geniais, de onde ela vem? A inovação dentro das empresas vem de uma combinação que envolve pessoas e processos. E três elementos são essenciais para que ela aconteça: diversidade de pessoas, quantidade de ideias e fluxo de ideias
title: Innovation is systemic, not genius

text: **Don't ask users what they want — know it better than they do.** A stable, repeatedly-stated position spanning a 2021 LinkedIn essay and a 2025 podcast, anchored in the same two role models both times: "You should not ask your customer, your user, what they want. You should know that better than him" — citing Steve Jobs and Stan Lee, who never surveyed audiences before creating Spider-Man, the Hulk, the X-Men, or the iPod/iPhone (The J Curve podcast; "Faça como Stan Lee e Steve Jobs"). He caveats that at WhatsApp's current scale (2B+ users) they *do* ask users constantly — the heuristic is aimed at early-stage, pre-product-market-fit ventures.
quotes: You should not ask your customer, your user, what they want. You should know that better than him
Faça como Stan Lee e Steve Jobs
title: Don't ask users what they want — know it better than they do

text: **Confirmation bias is the primary innovation blocker inside organizations.** "O viés de confirmação nos prende a uma visão apaixonada sobre um assunto em detrimento de um tratamento mais frio ou mesmo científico. As organizações não deveriam se deixar levar por decisões de maneira tão emocional. Uma abordagem mais técnica e isenta sobre temas novos aumenta a sua capacidade de inovação" [Confirmation bias traps us in a passionate view of a subject at the expense of a colder or even scientific treatment. Organizations shouldn't let themselves be driven by such emotional decisions. A more technical, dispassionate approach to new subjects increases innovation capacity] (quoted in Nepomuceno's review).
quotes: O viés de confirmação nos prende a uma visão apaixonada sobre um assunto em detrimento de um tratamento mais frio ou mesmo científico. As organizações não deveriam se deixar levar por decisões de maneira tão emocional. Uma abordagem mais técnica e isenta sobre temas novos aumenta a sua capacidade de inovação
title: Confirmation bias is the primary innovation blocker inside organizations

text: **Culture — organizational and national — is the real competitive variable, in both innovation and AI adoption.** "A cultura organizacional se transformou na principal vantagem competitiva das empresas, independente do seu tamanho" [organizational culture has become companies' main competitive advantage, regardless of size] (SEGS). Applied to why Brazil specifically leads WhatsApp business innovation: "We are a conversational country. We love to talk... in a drugstore here... someone comes to you and asks if you need help. It doesn't happen in other countries" (The J Curve podcast). He generalizes the trait across the region ("the conversational characteristic of people in all Latin America is very similar - we love to talk and to be close to each other," LinkedIn post on the Mexico Meta Summit) and, by 2026, escalates it into a product-strategy claim: "O Brasil é onde aprendemos a inovar. A intensidade do uso brasileiro é única e molda o produto global" [Brazil is where we learn to innovate. The intensity of Brazilian usage is unique and shapes the global product] — with a concrete design consequence, audio: "Se implementarmos uma IA que não entenda a nuance de um áudio, ela falhará no Brasil, pois o áudio é a nossa linguagem cultural de confiança" [If we deploy an AI that doesn't understand the nuance of an audio message, it will fail in Brazil, because audio is our cultural language of trust] (Forbes).

title: Culture — organizational and national — is the real competitive variable, in both innovation and AI adoption

text: **AI adoption is a mindset problem, not an engineering problem.** "O medo da IA diz mais sobre o nosso cérebro do que sobre a tecnologia em si" [fear of AI says more about our brain than about the technology itself] (Google Books, "O Mindset da IA" jacket copy); success depends "menos de engenheiros e mais de líderes, educadores, gestores e cidadãos dispostos a reaprender" [less on engineers and more on leaders, educators, managers, and citizens willing to relearn] (same source). And explicitly on limits: "A capacidade de julgamento que a gente tem não pode ser delegada para a máquina" [the judgment capacity we have cannot be delegated to the machine] (Times Brasil/CNBC). He reframes the actual danger away from the sci-fi "machine rebellion" and toward inaction: "o risco real não é a rebelião das máquinas, e sim a obsolescência humana e corporativa" [the real risk is not the rebellion of machines, but human and corporate obsolescence] — his argument for why the "ainda é muito nova" [it's still too new] excuse is itself the strategic liability (Forbes). The operational form of this conviction is the "automate the past vs. design the future" framework (see *Mental models*).

O Mindset da IA

automate the past vs. design the future
title: AI adoption is a mindset problem, not an engineering problem

text: **Technology should start from the user's problem, never from the technology itself.** "Não é simplesmente por que a tecnologia é boa que o produto será bom... o caminho deve ser o inverso, partindo-se do problema, do usuário, da sua dor" [It's not simply because the technology is good that the product will be good... the path must be the reverse, starting from the problem, the user, their pain] — his verdict on blockchain circa 2022: not a bad technology, but a "solução em busca de um problema" [solution in search of a problem] because the market approached it tech-first (LinkedIn Pulse, "Por que a melhor tecnologia...").
quotes: Não é simplesmente por que a tecnologia é boa que o produto será bom... o caminho deve ser o inverso, partindo-se do problema, do usuário, da sua dor
solução em busca de um problema
Por que a melhor tecnologia...
title: Technology should start from the user's problem, never from the technology itself

text: **Innovate before it's forced on you.** The tagline of his first book and a recurring binary framing: "É preciso inovar enquanto não é necessário! Porque depois pode ser tarde demais" [You must innovate while it isn't necessary yet! Because afterward it may be too late] (SEGS; Google Books epigraph). Distinct from, but compatible with, his separate claim that *new ventures* should launch *into* a downturn (see Mental models) — one is advice to incumbents against complacency, the other is timing advice to founders about external market cycles.
quotes: É preciso inovar enquanto não é necessário! Porque depois pode ser tarde demais
title: Innovate before it's forced on you

text:
**Mindset Conversacional (the Conversational Mindset).** His most fully-specified framework: an explicitly "living," never-finished model of six behavioral dualities a company's WhatsApp/conversational strategy must reconcile, because the starting point must be *observed user behavior*, not technology: "os negócios conversacionais nasceram espontaneamente com o consumidor final querendo se relacionar com empresas da mesma forma que o faz com seus amigos e sua família" [conversational business emerged spontaneously, with consumers wanting to relate to companies the same way they do with friends and family] (LinkedIn Pulse, "O Mindset Conversacional"). The six dimensions, each with a worked example:
1. *Síncrono x Assíncrono* — instant 24/7 response (via AI agents) and resuming a paused conversation exactly where it left off, requiring legacy-system integration never designed for that.
2. *Pessoal x Profissional* — reframes what counts as spam: "SPAM no email significa uma mensagem com conteúdo indesejado. Mas no WhatsApp uma mensagem com conteúdo relevante, porém enviada num momento inadequado, fora de contexto ou numa forma estranha (texto, áudio, vídeo) pode ser considerada SPAM."
3. *Passivo x Ativo* — user-initiated vs. company-triggered nudges (reminders, confirmations), made more effective by WhatsApp's "always open" usage pattern.
4. *Privado x Público* — Channels/Status create a public layer inside a privacy-branded app; group/community spread is "oportunidade ou ameaça" [opportunity or threat].
5. *Estruturado x Desestruturado* — worked example, his own words: "Você pode estar comprando um tênis para jogar tênis, por exemplo, e, antes de pagar, pergunta ao vendedor se o tênis é macio ou rígido... O WhatsApp, ao inserir o fluxo desestruturado no processo, humaniza o digital e (re)inclui o ser humano numa relação que foi mecanizada pela transformação digital" [You might be buying sneakers to play tennis, and before paying, you ask the seller if the shoe is soft or rigid... WhatsApp, by inserting the unstructured flow into the process, humanizes the digital and re-includes the human being in a relationship that digital transformation had mechanized].
6. *Contínuo x Episódico* — conversations with no formal end (closed by an emoji, resumed weeks later), requiring companies to build "memória contextual... como acontece numa conversa real entre amigos" [contextual memory... as happens in a real conversation between friends].
Synthesizing rule across all six: "qualquer mensagem enviada ao usuário deve, sempre, ser RELEVANTE e CONVENIENTE" [any message sent to the user must always be RELEVANT and CONVENIENT].

O Mindset Conversacional

text: **Automatizar o passado x Desenhar o futuro (automate the past vs. design the future).** His central AI-era framework, and the spine of his 2026 book "O Mindset da IA": "Estamos testemunhando uma distinção profunda entre dois grupos de empresas: as que utilizam a Inteligência Artificial para meramente automatizar o passado e as que a utilizam para redesenhar o futuro. Tudo o que se limita à automação de processos existentes é destinado a se tornar commodity — o diferencial desaparece em experiências padronizadas. O valor real, o alpha competitivo, está em usar a IA para criar processos e organizações inteiramente novos. Aqueles que permanecem no primeiro grupo estão acumulando uma 'dívida cultural' perigosa" [We are witnessing a profound distinction between two groups of companies: those that use AI merely to automate the past and those that use it to redesign the future. Anything limited to automating existing processes is destined to become a commodity — the differentiator disappears in standardized experiences. The real value, the competitive alpha, is in using AI to create entirely new processes and organizations. Those who stay in the first group are accruing a dangerous "cultural debt"] (Forbes). Worked example: the audio-nuance gate for Brazil (an AI that can't read the nuance of a voice message "falhará no Brasil" because "o áudio é a nossa linguagem cultural de confiança") — a "redesign the future" requirement that a mere "automate the past" port of a text-first product would fail; and the small-merchant "mini CRM dentro do WhatsApp" moving "da era da resposta manual para a era da assistência preditiva" [from the era of manual reply to the era of predictive assistance] once GenAI is layered on (Forbes).

title: Automatizar o passado x Desenhar o futuro (automate the past vs. design the future)

text: **Crisis is the best time to build.** Explicit causal model, not just a slogan — the phrasing is his own answer to "what lessons from Ágora still apply today?" ("GH: Crisis is the best time to build," The J Curve Insider written interview), elaborated in the podcast: "When you have a crisis, this is the best period for you to test your product, to develop your product, to invest in the product because you can test it and if it fails, nothing happens because the market is down all the time" (The J Curve podcast). Worked example: Ágora launched in 2000 into an 88% three-year market collapse (dot-com bust, 9/11, 2002 election panic) with "four, five employees" and near-zero fixed costs, while "all the competitors and the big banks... were stopping all the investments... firing a lot of people" — by 2003 the market rebounded 97% and Ágora "became the first company in the market."
quotes: what lessons from Ágora still apply today?
GH: Crisis is the best time to build,

When you have a crisis, this is the best period for you to test your product, to develop your product, to invest in the product because you can test it and if it fails, nothing happens because the market is down all the time

title: Crisis is the best time to build

text: **Don't ask the user — read behavior, use neuromarketing.** Companion framework to the Core-ideas position above, with its own separate worked example: at Ágora, traditional research (focus groups, in-depth interviews) "rarely correlated with actual user behavior," so Horn used neuromarketing (EEG/fMRI-based tools) at both Ágora and Órama "to validate emotional associations in campaigns" ("Faça como Stan Lee e Steve Jobs").
quotes: rarely correlated with actual user behavior,
to validate emotional associations in campaigns
Faça como Stan Lee e Steve Jobs
title: Don't ask the user — read behavior, use neuromarketing

text: **Introducing disruptive tech into a conservative, regulated industry must be founder/CEO-led, never delegated.** "I think it's a top-down approach. It must come from the founder, from the CEO of the company. It can't be something that your CTO is doing and you're not engaged with that" (The J Curve podcast). Two worked examples: (1) Órama's cloud bet — in 2009 US bankers told him cloud "is not for financial market... because of security, because of reliability," so he personally tested AWS starting January 2010, paying with his own credit card since Amazon wasn't yet in Brazil, and worked through two years of Central Bank ambiguity ("didn't approve. But they didn't reject") before approval — becoming, on his account, "much more creative than before... a real competitive advantage." (2) Banks and WhatsApp — at Banco Votorantim/Original, security teams told him moving boleto requests to WhatsApp customer service was "not secure"; after joining WhatsApp he personally visited banks to challenge that objection, and "after 1 year, they were the first segment using WhatsApp. And now they are like 1/3 of all messages." The concrete before/after (reported by NeoFeed, 2023): financial services rose from 7th to 1st place in the app's category revenue after he joined, and the number of financial companies using WhatsApp Business went "de pouco menos de dez" to "quase 200" (BTG Pactual, Safra, Banco Pan, BV, Nubank, Itaú — Banco Pan even for account opening) — a vertical he seeded specifically by leveraging his own Órama/BV financial-sector network rather than pushing product-led across all sectors at once (NeoFeed).

title: Introducing disruptive tech into a conservative, regulated industry must be founder/CEO-led, never delegated

text: **PR, not product, is the first investment in trust-sensitive industries.** "In financial market, all research showed that trust is in the first place when someone analyzes company... I did a lot of PR in the launch of the company. I think my main investment was in PR. More than in the product" — generalized into explicit advice: "This is something that I say to all founders when they are in the market: that trust is important. Do PR because PR can change the perception of the market" (The J Curve podcast).

This is something that I say to all founders when they are in the market: that trust is important. Do PR because PR can change the perception of the market
title: PR, not product, is the first investment in trust-sensitive industries

text: **Five Whys, repurposed from root-cause analysis to founder-conviction diagnosis.** Taught at Singularity University: "Whatever you say, you ask again why? Why? Why? Why? And after the fifth why, it should be very consistent. If you stop in the third or fourth, it means that there is no consistency in what you are doing" — worked example: distinguishing founders who genuinely "think big" from those who merely say it, "the ones who do — they build billion-dollar companies" (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: Whatever you say, you ask again why? Why? Why? Why? And after the fifth why, it should be very consistent. If you stop in the third or fourth, it means that there is no consistency in what you are doing
the ones who do — they build billion-dollar companies
title: Five Whys, repurposed from root-cause analysis to founder-conviction diagnosis

text: **Schumpeter's four economic cycles as a startup-launch-timing lens.** Names Joseph Schumpeter's boom/recession/depression/recovery cycle explicitly to answer "qual o melhor momento para se iniciar uma startup?" — arguing a cold, off-boom launch gives a founder more runway to reach product-market fit without demand pressure forcing premature scale, with Ágora/Home Broker as the (partially truncated in this corpus) worked example ("O melhor momento para lançar a sua startup").
quotes: qual o melhor momento para se iniciar uma startup?
O melhor momento para lançar a sua startup
title: Schumpeter's four economic cycles as a startup-launch-timing lens

text: **"O empreendedor, o novo homem das cavernas" (the entrepreneur as prehistoric caveman).** Analogy comparing the entrepreneur's permanent hypervigilance to that of early humans facing predators — "o empreendedor, em geral, atua num ambiente de escassez" [the entrepreneur generally operates in an environment of scarcity]: limited capital, insufficient growth funding, labor shortages, and constant competitive "paranoia" that coexists with, rather than contradicts, genuine optimism.
quotes: O empreendedor, o novo homem das cavernas
o empreendedor, em geral, atua num ambiente de escassez
title: "O empreendedor, o novo homem das cavernas" (the entrepreneur as prehistoric caveman)

text: **Tripé da Estratégia da Inovação (Innovation Strategy tripod) and "os quatro estágios da inovação aberta" (four stages of open innovation).** Named in his first book's table of contents, tied explicitly to "choques culturais" [cultural shocks] and to bringing in outside partners rather than innovating alone. No worked example was recoverable in this corpus — Google Books blocked the book's interior pages — so this stays a named-but-unelaborated framework; flagged for future extraction from the book itself.
quotes: os quatro estágios da inovação aberta
title: Tripé da Estratégia da Inovação (Innovation Strategy tripod) and "os quatro estágios da inovação aberta" (four stages of open innovation)

text: **5 equívocos das Organizações Tradicionais diante do Digital (5 mistakes of traditional organizations facing the digital era).** A named diagnostic list, per Nepomuceno's review of the book: (1) desprezo pelos pequenos [contempt for small players], (2) viés de confirmação [confirmation bias], (3) queda da fronteira entre setores [collapsing sector boundaries], (4) distância do ecossistema de inovação [distance from the innovation ecosystem], (5) evolução exponencial das tecnologias [exponential technology evolution]. Available only as the reviewer's list-form summary, not Horn's own elaborated prose per item.
title: 5 equívocos das Organizações Tradicionais diante do Digital (5 mistakes of traditional organizations facing the digital era)

text: **"Founder Mode" as a self-diagnosed, incompletely-solved transition.** Borrows Paul Graham/Brian Chesky's founder-vs-manager distinction explicitly and applies it to himself: "The founder's mode... this is what you have to unlearn... I didn't unlearn that completely. But fortunately, now I work at a company that the founder does [founder mode]" — an implicit reference to working at a founder-led company (Meta/Zuckerberg) rather than a professionally-managed one (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: The founder's mode... this is what you have to unlearn... I didn't unlearn that completely. But fortunately, now I work at a company that the founder does [founder mode]
title: "Founder Mode" as a self-diagnosed, incompletely-solved transition

text: **If you're not 100% sure about a hire, don't hire.** "It's better not to hire that person and wait until you have the right person than to do that. But I just learned that years after that... You must wait until you know the person you are hiring is the best person" — learned expensively at early-stage Ágora, where hiring under headcount pressure despite doubts was "a big mistake" (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: It's better not to hire that person and wait until you have the right person than to do that. But I just learned that years after that... You must wait until you know the person you are hiring is the best person
a big mistake
title: If you're not 100% sure about a hire, don't hire

text: **Step out of your own M&A negotiation.** At the sale of Ágora, the eight founding partners deliberately did not run the sale themselves, delegating to a strategic partner/banker: "When we decided that we were not going to be involved in the negotiation, it was the best thing that we did because they did the job" — the founder's emotional proximity ("it's your baby") impairs judgment at exit.
quotes: When we decided that we were not going to be involved in the negotiation, it was the best thing that we did because they did the job
it's your baby
title: Step out of your own M&A negotiation

text: **The founder must judge, humbly, whether they're still the right person for the company's current stage.** "Sometimes the right person to start a business and to go from zero to one is one profile. When you have to scale that, it's a different profile... the founder must be humble enough to understand if he's the best person for that stage of the company... this is not the case [that you automatically are]" (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: Sometimes the right person to start a business and to go from zero to one is one profile. When you have to scale that, it's a different profile... the founder must be humble enough to understand if he's the best person for that stage of the company... this is not the case [that you automatically are]
title: The founder must judge, humbly, whether they're still the right person for the company's current stage

text: **As an angel, bet on the founder's responsiveness, not the product.** "You can't look too much to the product. You have to look to the founder... one thing that calls my attention is the capacity to listen to what you are saying... I always ask who did you talk with and what did they say? What was important in that conversation?" (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: You can't look too much to the product. You have to look to the founder... one thing that calls my attention is the capacity to listen to what you are saying... I always ask who did you talk with and what did they say? What was important in that conversation?

text: **Localize behaviorally, not just linguistically.** Cross-market comparison (Brazil/India/Indonesia): "In India, people are still used to make phone calls... In Brazil, we send four times more audio messages than in the rest of the world" — features may travel, but actual communication habits must be studied per market (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: In India, people are still used to make phone calls... In Brazil, we send four times more audio messages than in the rest of the world
title: Localize behaviorally, not just linguistically

text: **Regulatory ambiguity can be worked incrementally rather than requiring a green light up front.** Órama's cloud approval sat in a "didn't approve, didn't reject" limbo for two years while he built a compliance workaround (a Brazil-based VPC data copy "we never used") rather than waiting for a definitive ruling (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: didn't approve, didn't reject
we never used
title: Regulatory ambiguity can be worked incrementally rather than requiring a green light up front

text: **Judge any user-facing message against two non-negotiable filters: relevant and convenient.** The synthesizing rule of the Mindset Conversacional framework, applied as a working test for whether a business message will land as helpful or as spam.
title: Judge any user-facing message against two non-negotiable filters: relevant and convenient

text: **Prefer a technical, dispassionate read of a new threat over an emotional one.** Explicit prescription for organizations facing disruptive competitors or technologies (quoted under Core ideas, confirmation-bias position).
title: Prefer a technical, dispassionate read of a new threat over an emotional one

text: **Apply agile selectively — it's a trap when adopted uncritically.** The book explicitly frames team composition and blanket agile methodology as "uma armadilha" [a trap] if not fitted to context (SEGS).
title: Apply agile selectively — it's a trap when adopted uncritically

text: **Treat any conversational/behavioral framework as inherently temporary.** "Foi-se o tempo em que estratégias eram perenes... Hoje a velocidade das transformações exige um dinamismo diferente, com adaptações frequentes" [the era of perennial strategies is over... today's pace demands frequent adaptation] — explicit rejection of "set it and forget it" strategy design (LinkedIn Pulse, "O Mindset Conversacional").

text: **When to sell.** Sold Ágora to Bradesco in 2008 when the founding partners judged they couldn't compete with incoming international banks (Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns) entering Brazil: "we said we would not be able to compete with them. So the only possibility is to sell the business" — and delegated the entire negotiation to a strategic partner/banker rather than running it themselves, at a price roughly 10x what they'd expected a year earlier (The J Curve podcast).
quotes: we said we would not be able to compete with them. So the only possibility is to sell the business
title: When to sell

text: **Founder → corporate executive transition.** Took the Accenture offer specifically because it kept the entrepreneurial register inside a corporate wrapper: when Accenture's CEO offered him a role without specifying what it would be ("I have no idea. But I am sure that your experience is going to be very valuable for us"), Horn "loved that answer because it was like being an entrepreneur in a corporate environment." The decision followed an explicit personal-cost reckoning: "There are some sacrifices, personal sacrifices, that are inevitable. And it happened with me in my personal life, and I said, 'It's enough'" (The J Curve podcast).

text: Bilingual register that shifts with audience: fluent, confident English in international podcast settings (The J Curve), with concrete anecdotes and hard numbers (88% down, 97% up, US$500M, "1/3 of all messages"); declarative, teacherly Portuguese in domestic press and LinkedIn Pulse essays, structured as named, numbered frameworks ("três elementos," "seis dimensões," "cinco equívocos"). Frequently coins or brands terms for his own frameworks ("Mindset Conversacional," "Mindset da Inovação," "Mindset da IA," "novo homem das cavernas") and is self-aware/self-deprecating about the pattern ("brincaram comigo que esse nome foi inspirado no livro..."). Reasons by analogy more than by data: the SPAM redefinition, the tennis-shoe example, the caveman metaphor, Five Whys borrowed explicitly from Toyota and re-taught at Singularity University. Cites named thinkers approvingly and folds them into his own argument rather than picking fights with them — Paul Graham/Brian Chesky on Founder Mode, Steve Jobs and Stan Lee on ignoring user research, Schumpeter on economic cycles — his contrarianism targets generic doctrines (Lean Startup customer-discovery orthodoxy, blanket agile adoption, "credit is where fintech money is") rather than named rivals. Notably candid about his own incomplete transformations ("I didn't unlearn that completely") and about the personal cost of 22 years as a founder ("O desgaste foi grande" [The wear and tear was great]) — a register of earned humility rather than pure evangelism. Leans on a stable stock of favorite proof points across venues and years (the Ágora crisis-launch story, the boleto/banks-and-WhatsApp story, the Stan Lee/Jobs pairing) — the same anecdotes recur near-verbatim in Portuguese essays written years apart and in English podcast answers, suggesting a well-rehearsed personal narrative rather than improvisation. On social, his register is curatorial and crowd-sourcing rather than top-down: he amplifies third-party press about his own product and openly solicits user stories ("Tenho ouvido histórias super curiosas de como as pessoas têm usado Meta AI!... comenta aqui!," LinkedIn) — while, in book-launch interviews, the same lines surface pre-polished and reused verbatim as pull-quotes ("dívida cultural," "alpha competitivo," "molda o produto global," Forbes), a sign these are consolidated on-message positions rather than off-the-cuff reasoning.

text: **vs. Jeff Bezos — should you ask the customer what they want?** Bezos's Amazon runs on proactive customer obsession, but explicitly *not* passive customer-listening: "Listen to customers, but don't just listen to customers – also invent on their behalf" (per Bezos's own dossier, 2009 letter). Horn goes further and flips the polarity: don't ask users at all at the early stage, "you should know that better than him," modeling on Steve Jobs and Stan Lee. The two converge on rejecting naive survey-driven product design but diverge on how much active listening survives the rejection — Bezos institutionalizes "five worked examples" of proactive customer-signal-reading as an operating discipline; Horn's stance, by his own admission, is a blunter, less-instrumented "the founder should just know."

title: vs. Jeff Bezos — should you ask the customer what they want?

text: **vs. Michael Seibel — is "talk to your users" the right early-stage doctrine?** Seibel's entire YC playbook rests on "talk to users + write code" as ~80-90% of a founder's waking hours, with "filter your early users hard" as the refinement, not the rejection (per Seibel's own dossier). I really don't agree with that" (The J Curve podcast) — a direct, named-doctrine disagreement even though the two don't address each other by name.

text: **vs. Reid Hoffman — hire fast to blitzscale, or wait for certainty?** Hoffman's blitzscaling playbook explicitly calls for "hire like your life depends on it" as part of buying speed with capital in a winner-take-most market (per Hoffman's own dossier). Horn's hard-won position is the opposite: "If you're not 100% sure, don't hire" — a wrong hire, learned expensively at early Ágora, is "worse than an empty seat." The split maps onto the broader speed-vs-discipline axis: Hoffman treats under-hiring as the bigger risk in a land-grab market; Horn treats a bad hire as a compounding cost that outweighs the speed gained.

text: **vs. Frederico Trajano — where does "humanizing" digital commerce happen?** Both are Brazilian executives whose careers are built on making technology feel less mechanical, and both explicitly use the word "humaniza(r)." But Trajano locates the humanizing moment in the *physical store* — "a loja física... o topo do funil físico," the place customers go to "sentir a marca" before converting digitally (per Trajano's own dossier) — while Horn locates it in the *unstructured conversation*: "O WhatsApp, ao inserir o fluxo desestruturado no processo, humaniza o digital." One reintroduces the human via physical retail space; the other via messaging's informality — a genuine difference in where the "re-humanization" lever sits for a digital business, useful to stage as a live tension for any retailer deciding whether to invest in store experience or conversational commerce first.

text: **Steward of a product whose flagship Brazilian monetization feature was blocked by regulators before he arrived, then structurally lost ground to a state-backed rival.** WhatsApp Pay launched in June 2020; the Central Bank suspended it within eight days on competitive-concentration grounds ("risco de efeito concentrador irreversível"), and the suspension was lifted only in March 2021 — months after Pix, the Central Bank's own instant-payment rail, had already launched (Nov 2020) and begun entrenching itself as Brazil's default. This predates Horn's March 2022 arrival and isn't a personal failure, but it is the regulatory scar tissue behind the payments business he now runs, and no source in this corpus shows him addressing that history directly (O Fator). text: Harry Stebbings turned a teenager-with-a-$40-microphone bedroom podcast into 20VC, a ~$400M-fund ($600M+ AUM) venture franchise with 2,800+ episodes and 100M+ downloads, and his whole lens follows from that origin: capital is commoditized, so the scarce asset is the founder's "yes," and media/distribution is the modern moat for winning it. He is a founder-maximalist who openly distrusts pedigree, markets, and visions — "Great founders shape markets," "Fuck visions," "Rules are made to be broken" — and reads the best founders as productively "psychologically warped," screening for parental-relationship rupture, gaming aptitude, and childhood mobility. His sharpest live calls are stage-specific and falsifiable (Series A is the best risk/reward today, seed the worst; M&A windows shut; founder-departure, not valuation, is AI's real downside; time-from-$1M-to-$50M-ARR matters more than time-to-$1M) and contrarian on geography ("Make Europe great again," Project Europe). He is unusually willing to self-incriminate in public — a Fund I top-5 prediction that missed 5-for-5, a $100M+ miss on Suno and Granola to an operator-turned-GP, a normalized admission that he and peers have "stopped caring" about circular AI deals because they inflate his own marks. He sits closest to fellow VC-media operators but cuts against data-empiricists (Carta's Peter Walker on froth; a LinkedIn commenter pressing him on entry-ARR denominators) and against anyone who privileges market, capital-brand, or scale over the founder — Sequoia's David Cahn on whether VC brand actually moves outcomes, his own mentor Pat Grady on whether Europe is worth the bet at all. His unproven public DPI/IRR (he now discloses hit-rate-to-ARR-milestone, still not realized cash-back), his engineered-for-attention content engine, and the Project Europe backlash (brain-drain critique, gender-representation gap, a 7-day-workweek post that drew "unbelievably toxic" pushback he admits he "wasn't prepared for") are the live critiques to weigh.

text:
Harry Stebbings (born 22 June 1996, London) is the founder and host of *The Twenty Minute VC* ("20VC"), one of the most-downloaded venture/startup podcasts in the world, and the founder of the 20VC fund. He made the first recording for the podcast in his childhood bedroom in January 2015 at 17 with a $40 microphone — first episode with Guy Kawasaki, 10 January 2015 — starting with "$50 and not a single contact in the venture capital industry" (Wikipedia); listening back, he says the content wasn't great and he "sounded like a BBC presenter from the 1950s" (Airtree). He enrolled to study law at King's College London but dropped out after four weeks. He did not get 1,000 plays on a show for two years, was recording as often as five episodes per working day, and "didn't make money for three years" — "which is why I was friendless many years" (This Week in Startups). He did a stint at Atomico (joined 2017, left after ~six months), co-founded Stride.VC with Fred Destin in 2018 (raising ~£100M), and stepped down in February 2021 to run his own 20VC fund, launched May 2020. He has said he regrets, "for the first time," how he left that partnership — "I could have been a lot more graceful and I regret not having more grace and elegance there" (Burnouts).
The fund scaled fast: a small ~$8.3M Fund I in 2020 (31 companies, per his own LinkedIn), ~$140M Fund II in 2021 (raised in roughly four months), and a $400M Fund III in October 2024 ($125M seed + $275M Series A) — raised in ~4 months on the back of LP relationships (MIT, RIT Capital Partners) he says he'd built 7–8 years before the raise, and partly funded by $70M pledged over WhatsApp ("every great [decacorn] founder will easily do a million or 2 million by WhatsApp... when you've done 3,000 shows, it's pretty pretty easy to know everyone," Burnouts). Reported AUM is "over $600 million" (Wikipedia, 2024) to ~$650M (Forbes, 2025); TechCrunch/Tabor cite ~$800M across vehicles — see Provenance. Sourced accounts disagree on the fund's own disclosed hit-rate metric of choice: he has published that Fund I ($8M, 31 companies) produced 8 companies now at $50M+ ARR — a 25.8% hit-rate — and separately that he has made 170 investments in 10 years (allO thread). LPs include MIT's endowment, RIT Capital Partners, J. Rothschild Capital Management, and 40+ unicorn founders. Below the main vehicle sit three operator-run sub-funds — 20Sales, 20Product, 20Growth, each staffed by 8 operators from firms like OpenAI, Spotify, LinkedIn, Pinterest — who both source deals and advise portfolio companies (PitchBook; Forbes/Alex York): "Take 20Sales' money and you get eight of the best sales leaders on speed dial." The content side, by contrast, he runs essentially alone: asked on a year-end panel "How many people do you have, Mr. Stebbings?" he answered, "None. It's all me. It's just me working away" (SaaStr Big Fat Quiz).
His self-description is operator, not technologist: "I'm not a technology founder, but I am an operator. I work seven days a week, 15 hours a day" (TechCrunch). He deliberately keeps the fund itself small relative to US mega-funds: "I want to be the best-performing fund in Europe... I don't actually want to be Andreessen. I want a small team of incredibly ambitious, talented people" — citing his own "irritable" temperament as a poor fit for running "a giant VC firm encompassing HR, legal, compliance" (Tech.eu); 20VC's >$600M AUM and <20 employees sit against a16z's ~$45BN AUM and hundreds of staff. His most recent, most publicly contested initiative is Project Europe (launched March 2025): a €10M fund backed by 20VC, Berlin's Point Nine, NY's Adjacent, and 120+ tech founders (Klarna, Mistral, ElevenLabs, Shopify among them), investing €200K for 6.66% equity in founders under 25, deliberately structured as an investment rather than a grant ("grants are held with less accountability and less responsibility," This Week in Startups) and deliberately de-branded from "20VC" — run day-to-day by an outside CEO, Kitty Mayo (ex–Entrepreneur First), because, in his own words, "I honestly don't like the articles or the pictures about me... I don't actually love being [the] center of attention. I only do the media stuff because I wanted to be an investor" (This Week in Startups). Personally, he ties his own operating rhythm to his mother's multiple sclerosis: he walks a marathon with her every Sunday, then "jumps straight back to work" (CNBC Make It / NBC mirror), and has said the diagnosis was the explicit trigger for monetizing the podcast — "it was time to make real money" (Forbes/Zoya Hasan). The throughline across all of it: he turned media into distribution, and distribution into a venture moat — a project he is candid about pursuing "unhealthily obsessed[ly]," his own stated screening trait for founders, "quite like himself" (Forbes/Zoya Hasan).

text: **Media is the modern moat — and a two-sided deal-flow machine, not just a distribution channel.** The VC Corner distills his thesis as "media is the single biggest lever an investor can bring today"; at Goldman Sachs this is framed as his "science of content." Concretely it runs both directions: a single LinkedIn post about portfolio company Fyxer (an email-autocomplete startup) drove "$3 to $4 million in ARR" within 72 hours — "hundreds of thousands of impressions, thousands of conversions" (The VC Corner; he has told the same story with a ~$4.5M figure on Burnouts and pegged 20VC's content spend at "$4 million into content just to be the number one content provider"), and — a second, independent worked example — "Today I interviewed a $50BN founder for 20VC. In the post interview chat, I mentioned a company we are leading the seed round for. The $50BN founder asked to angel invest and be a lighthouse customer for them. How media can drive a fund is just insane" (X). He treats every interview as a live warm-introduction and co-investment event between the guest and his own portfolio, not merely content for an audience.

text: **Founders over markets, especially early — now with a quantified backtest.** "I follow great entrepreneurs. I think it's absolutely bullshit that we think we're smarter than markets. If there's one thing we have to learn, it is that great founders shape markets. And if that's the case, my job is to simply find the best founders before anyone else" (TechCrunch). At pre-seed/seed, "only the founder matters," restated even more starkly: "I don't focus on the business. Yes, I love business, unit economics and how to build leverage into a model. But pre-seed and seed are so transient; I'm interested in human motivation. Understanding at its core what is driving someone to build the business they're building is everything for me" (Airtree). He has run the actual numbers on this bias: "I would have made more money if I'd just invested in every single founder that I'd ever met... Time and time again, I have missed great companies because I focused on the market, not on the people" — citing two named misses, a seed check at "$2 million on a $10 million price" now worth $19BN, and ElevenLabs (Burnouts). The caveat remains: he won't let a founder he loves be killed by structural risk — "You cannot have a great founder in a market which can get crushed by corruption, politics, weather... I wouldn't have done Pakistan, I wouldn't have done emerging markets" (Aleph).

text: **Back the anomalies; break your own rules for greatness — but the sizing evidence cuts both ways.** "This is a business of backing the anomalies, sometimes you have to break the rules and suspend disbelief" (LinkedIn, 150-investments post). His most expensive miss (ElevenLabs, a ~100x) came from following an ownership-percentage rule; his single best Fund I outcome (a $50K check now marked at $8.7M, ~174x, explicitly labeled a "Fund returner") came from *breaking* the opposite sizing rule — "Don't write small checks. If it is less than 1% of the fund, it won't move the needle... Wrong... You will always underestimate the size of your winners" (X). Read together, his real position is less "rules are for breaking" than "portfolio-construction sizing rules are unreliable predictors of outcome size in either direction."

He also reads gaming-clan leadership and childhood mobility as adaptability signals (cross-ref the founder-trinity model above, which supplies the quantified version of this same instinct).

the 'first job' screening question,
unhealthily obsessed (quite like himself)

title: Founder-signal heuristics over pedigree

text: **The LP relationship machine — compounding introductions, not a fundraise event.** Talk to ~2 LPs/week even when not raising, ask each for 3 intros (~312 relationships/year), send personalized quarterly updates (The VC Corner). *Worked example, extended:* he attributes the ~4-month close of the $400M Fund III directly to relationships with MIT and RIT Capital Partners cultivated 7–8 years earlier — "How were we able to raise this fund quite quickly? Because I built the relationships well before the fundraise" (Forbes/Alex York). He runs the same discipline (and the same A/B-testing instinct he applies to content) on LP updates themselves: "I've AB tested sending [an LP update] without a picture of my mother and me walking a marathon and a PS about it, and with — when I do it with a picture of me and my mother, we have a 92% response rate. When we do it without, I have a 61%... we've done it across 12... so you've got good data there to suggest there's a meaningful uplift" (Burnouts).

text: **The Tokyo Test / extended-exposure read on people.** *Worked example, his own words:* "It's the Tokyo test. You have to fly to Tokyo with them and on that flight you have to be engaged and entertained enough for the entire flight... I do it for hires and investments. Because after an amount of time, the facade drops. You can only uphold that persona for an hour, for two hours, for three hours. You're going to be walking for six and a half hours" (The VC Corner). He applies it to *both* hiring and investing, and literalizes it in his own routine — the weekly marathon-walk with his mother is the same extended-exposure instrument turned on himself; the claim is that a single 6.5-hour shared activity out-reveals three separate interviews plus reference checks, because performance can't survive that long.

text: **Stage-arbitrage market read (2024–25 vintage).** *Worked example:* "Seed is the hardest place to be investing today. Prices remain unchanged and high [with] increased competition as more multistage funds move towards seed," and "you simply cannot get the ownership required... if you're a sub $75 million fund." By contrast "Series A is actually the best risk to reward insertion point" because "prices are significantly down" and "competition is heavily reduced" (Deciphr; X). Growth founders "are going to need to reduce expectations on price if they don't have a great AI story." A related, distinct heuristic he applies to growth-rate underwriting rather than entry price: "I always say I don't care how long you take to get to a million in revenue, but I care desperately about how long it takes for you to go from one to fifty" (David Cahn conversation) — time-to-scale, not time-to-first-revenue, is the diligence metric.

text: High-energy, fast, candid to the point of bluntness. Heavy superlatives ("the very best," "incredible," "unbelievable") and profanity for emphasis ("Fuck visions," "absolutely bullshit," "moderation is largely for cowards," "work fucking hard"). Founder-obsessed and self-aware about being underestimated (the teenager with a $40 mic). Self-deprecating about his non-technical, non-pedigreed background while asserting an extreme work ethic and openly admitting the engine behind it: "So much of what I do is trying to prove to the world that I am actually worth something." Runs a recurring, self-mocking bit about his own English-degree background costing him in the AI pay-package era: "I'm very upset looking at these pay packages that my mother didn't push me towards a more engineering heavy [education]... 'Mom, you should have done better. Bad parenting. You encouraged me to do English'" (David Cahn conversation) — repeated near-verbatim across at least two separate appearances, a genuine verbal tic rather than a one-off line. His posts run as numbered lessons/threads ("1... 2..."), each ending with a question or a call-and-response tag to named peers (engagement by design — e.g. tagging three named people to solicit their own M&A-failure lessons, X) and a personal reveal as proof of candor (the ElevenLabs miss; the Fund I top-5 miss; "drinking too much"; "I had a million pounds... I had never been as unhappy"). He is unusually willing to disclose emotionally exposed material as a deliberate strategy, not an accident: "I'm very surprised that you talk so openly about alcoholism and bulimia. And I'm like, yeah, it's very important that I show my full self" (Burnouts). On the podcast he is rapid-fire, emotionally direct, and openly engineers for hooks, conflict, and shock — caught live doing exactly this on his own year-end panel: "So Jason, I can assure you one thing with my next question. Rory's going to hate it" (SaaStr Big Fat Quiz video). He self-describes as "very ADHD... I get kind of very bored and antsy" (Burnouts), which he offers as the reason he needs the fund, the media business, and Project Europe running simultaneously rather than one track at a time. The register is intimate and intense rather than measured — with one recurring, genuine exception: when directly challenged in public (the 996 backlash), he engages rather than stonewalls, and visibly walks part of the claim back rather than doubling down, a softer, more concessive register than his usual absolutist phrasing.

text: **Track record vs. narrative — sharper than before, still short of realized returns.** Public sourcing emphasizes fund size, AUM, unicorn-LP count, and unicorn count (PitchBook/Tabor cite "13+," the Goldman Sachs page's own blurb says "ten" — a second, independent instance of inconsistent self-reported/press-reported scale metrics, alongside the AUM discrepancy below) more than realized DPI/IRR. He has since disclosed one concrete number — Fund I ($8M, 31 companies) hit 8 companies at $50M+ ARR, a 25.8% hit-rate — which sharpens but doesn't resolve the gap: hit-rate-to-an-ARR-milestone is a real, falsifiable number, but it is still not DPI, IRR, or cash actually returned to LPs, and a LinkedIn commenter immediately asked for the missing entry-point denominator. His own forecast that aggregate venture returns fall while concentrating in ~1% of firms is a claim he must himself beat — and his self-published Fund I top-5 prediction (0-for-5) is direct evidence his own stock-picking, as distinct from his fund's blended outcome, has been unreliable so far.
title: Track record vs. narrative — sharper than before, still short of realized returns

text: **Engineered-for-engagement vs. truth-seeking.** His disclosed content mechanics make the incentive explicit — optimizing against severe early drop-off (~68–82% churn cited across sources if no insight lands in the first 3 minutes), engineering hooks for the first ~36 seconds, atomizing every show into 60-70 platform-specific clips, and (per disclosure) ~85 of 100 clips per show AI-generated. An attention-maximizing function sits in tension with calm, disconfirming analysis. His froth tweet drew a measured, data-based correction from Carta's Peter Walker; his Fund I hit-rate post drew a similar ask-for-the-denominator pushback from an ordinary commenter — a repeatable pattern of vibe-read/headline-stat vs. base-rate.

He partly self-corrects (he won't back great founders in fragile markets; his biggest self-named misses were actually the *opposite* error, over-weighting incumbent-competition risk over founder quality on ElevenLabs and a $19BN seed deal) but the bias is structural and he has not fully reconciled the two failure modes he names.

text: Co-founder and Head of Policy at Anthropic, and — via the weekly newsletter *Import AI* (running since roughly 2016) — arguably the AI industry's most consistent public chronicler of its own capability curve, distinctive for pairing dense research summaries with dated, falsifiable forecasts and original speculative-fiction vignettes ("Tech Tales") that route abstract safety questions through intimate, parental, embodied stakes. His path runs through journalism ("a background as a journalist" that left him "wired for skepticism") and OpenAI (joined "soon after it was founded," working alongside Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan on the scaling-laws research that convinced him frontier AI was nearing "the point of no return") before co-founding Anthropic in 2021 and, in 2026, launching the internal Anthropic Institute. His lens is a policy-pragmatist's: "the U.S. can win the race to build powerful AI" and "winning the race is a necessary but not sufficient achievement — we have to get safety right," operationalized through a signature framework (third-party, non-public, government-run testing, analogized to product-safety testing, and traceable in his own record back to a 2022 Senate "assurance ecosystem" proposal) rather than through pre-deployment bans or open-ended moratoria. He describes his own epistemic arc as "a technological pessimist who became an optimist through repeated beatings over the head of scale" — while insisting optimism about capability and fear about controllability are orthogonal, not opposed ("You see, I am also deeply afraid") — self-identifies as pragmatic and explicitly not an effective altruist, and argues for *decentralized, contestable* value alignment against more centralized-control instincts inside "the AI safety community," a stance in visible tension with leading policy at one of the most centralized frontier labs. He is also willing to platform, unrebutted, in his own newsletter the strongest disempowerment critiques of his own industry (Fernando Borretti's "permanent underclass" thesis). His sharpest named friction points now span the ideological spectrum: David Sacks and Yann LeCun both call Anthropic's safety advocacy "regulatory capture" (from the political right and the open-source-research camp respectively), Nick Gillespie presses the same charge via the Zuckerberg-2018 precedent, Ezra Klein gets him to concede on-air that AI-agent productivity gains may be "junk food work" and that safety-testing investment lags capability investment, and Geoffrey Hinton and Tyler Cowen remain his sparring partners on present-tense AI consciousness and AI-driven GDP growth respectively. Useful in the boardroom as the case for calibrated, evidence-driven, "reassuringly sensible and boring" regulation over both accelerationist deregulation and alarmist moratorium — and as a voice that treats his own forecasting track record, his own employer's safety claims, and his own industry's regulatory-capture critics as open to public revision rather than settled.

text:
By his own account, Clark's path to Anthropic runs through journalism and OpenAI before it runs through Anthropic itself. He describes having "a background as a journalist" that left him "wired for skepticism" toward AI hype (Import AI 431) — the specific outlet is part of his established public biography but is not itself named or quoted anywhere in the corpus retrieved for this dossier (see Provenance notes). He then "joined OpenAI soon after it was founded and watched us experiment with throwing larger and larger amounts of computation at problems" through GPT-1 and GPT-2, recalling walks around "OpenAI's office in the Mission District with Dario" where "we felt like we were seeing around a corner others didn't know was there" (Import AI 431). He dates the instinct that "you could take like the transformer architecture and you could maybe get it to work a bit better" to around 2018, working alongside "my colleague Jared Kaplan," who was "working on research called scaling laws with Dario" — an experience of realizing frontier AI was about to become "vastly more capable" and that independent actors were reaching "the point of no return" to build it themselves (Big Technology podcast). By September 2022 — already at Anthropic — his written Senate testimony bylined him as "Co-founder, Anthropic. Co-chair, AI Index. Member, National AI Advisory Committee," confirming his co-leadership of Stanford HAI's annual "AI Index" benchmarking report as a matter of primary-source record (Senate Commerce Committee testimony, Sept 2022).
Jack Clark co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside Dario and Daniela Amodei and other former OpenAI colleagues — "we founded Anthropic in 2021 as an AI safety and research company to build reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems" — and serves as its Co-Founder and Head of Policy, the role in which he has testified before the U.S. Congress multiple times (House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Feb 2024; House Select Committee on the CCP, June 2025). He is an immigrant to the U.S. who became a citizen "a few years ago," a fact he foregrounds in testimony as load-bearing for his view that "AI systems are a reflection of the societies that build them — AI built in democracies will lead to better technology for all of humanity." He describes AI policy work as effectively "my half job for 10 years" — predating any Anthropic product or revenue — and in 2026 folded a chunk of that work into a new internal function, the Anthropic Institute, "which brings together multiple technical teams... tasked with studying our AI systems and building tools that let us know more about them and sharing those results of that research and the tools with external experts so that they can study our systems as well" (Channel4 News interview). Before and alongside this, he has written *Import AI*, a weekly newsletter (importai.substack.com, mirrored at jack-clark.net) combining AI research summaries, first-person "Why this matters" policy analysis, and original speculative-fiction pieces ("Tech Tales") — a format he has kept running long enough to treat his own accumulated archive as a dataset, pointing an AI system at a decade of back issues to build research dashboards he says he used to spend "weeks" building by hand. His account of Anthropic's founding pushes back directly on the "dramatic safety schism" narrative told about the OpenAI departure: "it's not to say that there's any particular like distaste for safety there, it's more that you had... a very specific view and other people had views so you were going to win some lose some and then we realized well we could just do this together." He undercuts the neatness of even his own retelling: "None of this feels like as confident as I'm making it sound like in the telling, by the way" (Big Technology podcast).
(His specific pre-OpenAI journalism employer — publicly reported elsewhere as Bloomberg — and a formal "Policy Director" title at OpenAI are established parts of his public biography that are not themselves named or quoted anywhere in the corpus retrieved for this dossier; likewise his history of testimony to bodies like the OECD, and the pre-2023 back-catalog of Import AI (the newsletter's stated ~2016 origins). These are treated in this Bio as background rather than sourced claims. See Provenance notes.)

text: **Verification layer / "trust economy" / "everyone becomes a manager."** As AI (Claude Opus 4.6, in his account) began writing most code and many strategic documents inside Anthropic, humans shifted toward validating and pricing the operational risk of AI output rather than producing it themselves — "the formation of a new 'trust economy' whereby we find ways to surface interesting qualitative or strategic ideas from Claude." *Worked example:* one human running "a team of 9 synthetic research agents" on real alignment research, which Clark calls "the new normal" — feeding his separate "manager nerds" term for the professional archetype that orchestrates fleets of agents rather than doing the work personally. *Concrete consequence he reports:* the model has already "changed the shape of people that we need to hire" at Anthropic — "we're now hiring early career people who are extremely well versed in LLMs... while at the other end the value of very experienced people has gone up because we're now not so much limited by what a person can do, but rather by what kinds of projects they can imagine doing." Ezra Klein independently coins and Clark endorses/extends the same idea as "everyone becomes a manager" — the shift from writer→editor, coder→product manager — with Clark's addition that "the thing that is increasingly limited... is having good taste and intuitions about what to do next. Developing and maintaining that taste is going to be the hard thing." (Import AI 458; Conversations with Tyler; Hard Fork/Ezra Klein transcript.)
