text: **Two-Minute Rule lineage and its self-disclosed weakness.** He credits David Allen: "Hat tip to David Allen" for the rule "If it takes less than two minutes, then do it now." Clear's version is a different rule (shrink a new habit to a two-minute start, not do tiny tasks at once). He concedes it can seem like a trick, "it may feel like you’re trying to fool yourself," and offers the fallback "do it for two minutes and then stop." He also advises ritualizing only the first two minutes of a process (same warm-up before every workout), crediting Cal Newport's shutdown ritual. (2-minute-rule essay)
quotes: Hat tip to David Allen
If it takes less than two minutes, then do it now.
it may feel like you’re trying to fool yourself,
do it for two minutes and then stop.
title: Two-Minute Rule lineage and its self-disclosed weakness

text: **Upper limit, not lower limit (Southwest and the reader Mitch).** *Example (auto-transcript, wording unverified against audio):* via Jim Collins, Southwest had offers to expand to 100+ cities in 1996 and added only four, setting an upper bound on growth. Clear's application: instead of "at least 45 minutes," set an upper limit early, because consistency is the only thing that matters at the start. Reader Mitch lost over 100 pounds over two years after telling himself he could not stay at the gym more than five minutes; "when it got to six minutes, he left." The 2-minute essay tells the same case without the Southwest frame. (One You Feed, Dec 2014)
quotes: at least 45 minutes,
when it got to six minutes, he left.
title: Upper limit, not lower limit (Southwest and the reader Mitch)

text: **Reduce the scope, stick to the schedule.** *Example (auto-transcript, wording unverified):* planning a 3-mile run with 25 minutes left, his old reflex was to do email instead; the new rule is run one mile or put on shoes and do ten sprints. For writing, "I publish new articles every Monday and Thursday," however good or bad, an idea he credits to a software company that ships on deadline even if the feature is smaller. The Mel Robbins episode (auto-transcript, paraphrase only) gives a second telling: a planned one-hour workout shrunk to one set of squats in the basement gym. Ancestor of the worst-day heuristic. (One You Feed 2014; Mel Robbins)
quotes: I publish new articles every Monday and Thursday,
title: Reduce the scope, stick to the schedule

text: **Pre-game routine: remove the decision, not the effort.** *Example:* his pitching routine ran 20 to 25 minutes and was identical every time (jog to the outfield foul pole, stretch, toss to 75 feet, bullpen, ten pitches from the windup and ten from the stretch). Three steps: so easy you cannot say no, move toward the goal, same pattern every time. "My writing routine starts by getting a glass of water." "My weightlifting routine starts by putting on my lifting shoes." "When faced with another decision, you will often decide to just quit. However, the pre-game routine solves that problem because you know exactly what to do next." "If you only work when you feel motivated, then you’ll never be consistent enough to become a pro." (how-to-get-motivated; the claim that top performers all use rituals is asserted without named examples)

My weightlifting routine starts by putting on my lifting shoes.

If you only work when you feel motivated, then you’ll never be consistent enough to become a pro.
title: Pre-game routine: remove the decision, not the effort

text: **Habit tracker: immediate evidence for delayed feedback.** *Example:* chef Gabrielle Hamilton ("we taste everything, all the time, before we commit it to the dish") gets instant feedback; habits do not (run for a month with no visible change), so the tracker supplies it. "The most effective form of motivation is progress." Rules: track few ("It is better to consistently track one habit than to sporadically track ten"), record immediately after the habit, and track avoidance habits (no soda, no Netflix). He credits Fogg for stacking: "I use the term habit stacking to refer to linking a new habit to an old one. For this idea, I give credit to BJ Fogg." (habit-tracker, Atomic Habits ch. 16; he also pitches his Habit Journal on the page)

The most effective form of motivation is progress.

text: **How long does a habit take? Forever.** He rejects "21 days, 30 days, 100 days" and the 66-day study ("even within that study the range was quite wide depending on the difficulty of the habit") and reframes to how long until it is easy. "How long does it take? The honest answer is: forever. Because once you stop doing it, it is no longer a habit." "A habit is a lifestyle to be lived, not a finish line to be crossed." Self-disclosed limit: a tracker "is not something that makes sense in every situation or for every person." (habit-tracker)
quotes: 21 days, 30 days, 100 days
even within that study the range was quite wide depending on the difficulty of the habit
How long does it take? The honest answer is: forever. Because once you stop doing it, it is no longer a habit.
A habit is a lifestyle to be lived, not a finish line to be crossed.
is not something that makes sense in every situation or for every person.
title: How long does a habit take? Forever

text: **Habits Scorecard and Pointing-and-Calling.** *Example:* Japanese rail operators point at and name signals; he cites "Pointing-and-Calling reduces errors by up to 85 percent and cuts accidents by 30 percent" (footnoted to journalism), and an NYC MTA point-only version that cut incorrectly berthed subways 57 percent in two years. The Scorecard: list daily habits, mark each plus, minus or equals, and observe "almost as if you were watching someone else" without praise or blame, then use the identity-vote question to break ties. His wife's version of calling: "I’ve got my keys. I’ve got my wallet. I’ve got my glasses. I’ve got my husband." (habits-scorecard)
quotes: Pointing-and-Calling reduces errors by up to 85 percent and cuts accidents by 30 percent
almost as if you were watching someone else
I’ve got my keys. I’ve got my wallet. I’ve got my glasses. I’ve got my husband.
title: Habits Scorecard and Pointing-and-Calling

text: **Akrasia, Victor Hugo, and the three-part anti-akrasia stack.** *Example:* in 1830 Hugo owed a publisher a book, wasted a year, got a deadline under six months out, had an assistant lock his clothes in a chest, wrote in a shawl, and *The Hunchback of Notre Dame* came out two weeks early on 14 Jan 1831. Stack: (1) design future actions with commitment devices ("A commitment device is a choice you make in the present that controls your actions in the future."), such as single-serve food packages, casino ban lists, athletes leaving wallets home before weigh-in; (2) shrink the start; (3) implementation intentions, with a 3,272-employee flu-shot study (Milkman et al.) and his gloss "2x to 3x more likely." (akrasia)
quotes: A commitment device is a choice you make in the present that controls your actions in the future.
2x to 3x more likely.
title: Akrasia, Victor Hugo, and the three-part anti-akrasia stack

text: **Four levers against procrastination, and the Ivy Lee Method.** Levers: make rewards of action immediate, make consequences of delay immediate, design future actions, make the task achievable. *Example:* temptation bundling, which he credits by name ("a concept that came out of behavioral economics research performed by Katy Milkman at The University of Pennsylvania"): "Only get a pedicure while processing overdue work emails." Immediate consequences: commit to a 7 a.m. workout with a friend, because "Miss this one workout and you look like a jerk." Ivy Lee: six tasks a night, work only on the first; "I don't believe there is anything magical about Lee's number of six important tasks per day... However, I do think there is something magical about imposing limits upon yourself." (procrastination hub)
quotes: a concept that came out of behavioral economics research performed by Katy Milkman at The University of Pennsylvania
Only get a pedicure while processing overdue work emails.
Miss this one workout and you look like a jerk.
I don't believe there is anything magical about Lee's number of six important tasks per day... However, I do think there is something magical about imposing limits upon yourself.
title: Four levers against procrastination, and the Ivy Lee Method

text: **Ivy Lee: decide the first task the night before.** *Example:* "as a writer, I can waste three or four hours debating what I should write about on a given day. If I decide the night before, however, I can wake up and start writing immediately." Rules from the same hub: "Use simple rules to guide complex behavior"; on emergencies, "Ignore them as much as possible, deal with them when you must, and get back to your prioritized to-do list as soon as possible." "Do the most important thing first each day and let the momentum of the first task carry you into the next one." He ties the six-task cap to Buffett's "25-5 Rule," which is his attribution and was not checked here. (procrastination hub)

text: **Chunking by time, not output: Trollope.** *Example (figures are Clear's, unverified here):* Anthony Trollope published 47 novels; "Instead of measuring his progress based on the completion of chapters or books, Trollope measured his progress in 15-minute increments. He set a goal of 250 words every 15 minutes and he continued this pattern for three hours each day." Clear's reason it works: satisfaction and accomplishment every 15 minutes. Visual cues do three jobs (remind, display progress, an "additive effect on motivation" he labels the Endowed Progress Effect); named tools are the Paper Clip and Seinfeld strategies. (procrastination hub)

additive effect on motivation

text: **Decision fatigue and the five-part response.** *Example:* the parole-board study (1,112 rulings over 10 months, PNAS), which he reads as favorable rulings of about 65 percent at the start of the day falling toward zero before a break; tired judges default to "Deny, deny, deny." Response: plan repeated decisions the night before, do the most important thing first, schedule rather than decide (then: writing Monday and Thursday, lifting Monday, Wednesday, Friday), eat before important late decisions, simplify. "Stop making decisions. Start making commitments." Credits John Tierney. *(Stated as settled; replication challenges are outside the source, see Blind spots.)* (willpower-decision-fatigue)
quotes: Deny, deny, deny.
Stop making decisions. Start making commitments.
title: Decision fatigue and the five-part response

text: **Plan for failure: average speed, not maximum speed.** *Example:* "it is all about average speed, not maximum speed. Daily failures are like red lights during a road trip... if you maintain a good average speed, you’ll always make it to your destination despite the stops and delays along the way." Fat-loss coach Josh Hillis looks only at weekly calorie totals. Definition: "Planning to fail doesn't mean that you expect to fail, but rather than you know what you will do and how you will get back on track when things don't work out." He attributes the claim that lacking a failure plan is the number one reason willpower fades to Kelly McGonigal without a citation. (plan-failure)
quotes: it is all about average speed, not maximum speed. Daily failures are like red lights during a road trip... if you maintain a good average speed, you’ll always make it to your destination despite the stops and delays along the way.
Planning to fail doesn't mean that you expect to fail, but rather than you know what you will do and how you will get back on track when things don't work out.
title: Plan for failure: average speed, not maximum speed

text: **If-then plan for getting back on track.** *Example (auto-transcript, paraphrase):* credited to McGonigal's *The Willpower Instinct*; list everything that could derail the habit, prevent what you can, and for the rest write an if-then plan for returning quickly (a sick child, a forgotten reminder, friends proposing dinner during a diet). The payoff he names is moving from a victim story to a recovery plan. In the Habit Guide the same move is a pre-mortem: "What are some daily emergencies that are likely to pull you off course? How can you plan to work around these issues?" (One You Feed 2014; habit-guide)
quotes: What are some daily emergencies that are likely to pull you off course? How can you plan to work around these issues?
title: If-then plan for getting back on track

text: **Premortem and motion versus action (Mel Robbins episode, paraphrase of an auto-transcript, not verbatim).** Per the extraction: imagine the plan failed six months out, find where, fix it, then return to optimism; his gym case is picking a gym on the commute, laying out clothes the night before, bringing a water bottle if there is no fountain. Motion (planning, researching) feels like progress; action produces the result. This is a labeled paraphrase because the page was reached only through a summarizing fetch tool. (mel-robbins episode)
title: Premortem and motion versus action (Mel Robbins episode, paraphrase of an auto-transcript, not verbatim)

text: **Equilibrium and the muscle analogy for rate of change.** *Example:* "You commit to going for a run each night and within a week you’re asked to stay late at work." The right dose is a muscle that adapts: "If the weight is too light, your muscles will atrophy. If the weight is too heavy, you'll end up injured. But if the weight is just a touch beyond your normal, then your muscles will adapt to the new stimulus and equilibrium will take a small step forward." A Leonard footnote: discomfort when changing "can be seen as a signal not that something is wrong, but that something is right." He rejects advice that you need "massive action." (behavior-change-paradox; argued by analogy, no study cited)
quotes: You commit to going for a run each night and within a week you’re asked to stay late at work.

If the weight is too light, your muscles will atrophy. If the weight is too heavy, you'll end up injured. But if the weight is just a touch beyond your normal, then your muscles will adapt to the new stimulus and equilibrium will take a small step forward.

text: **Keystone habits (Duhigg).** *Example (his own, introspective):* working out made him want to eat better, sleep better, and write with more clarity in the hour or two afterward; on non-exercise days: junk food, late nights on unimportant tasks, back tension. "you might need just one keystone habit before the dominoes start falling everywhere." "What are you doing when everything falls into place? What is your keystone habit? Find it and do more of it." Evidence is self-report: "I didn't check it, but my guess is that my blood pressure raised." (keystone-habits; early-era essay that still leans on willpower language)

text: **Buffett's 2 List: your enemy is the second-tier thing you love.** *Example (secondhand: Mike Flint, Buffett's pilot, via Scott Dinsmore):* Flint circled his top 5 of 25 goals and planned to work the other 20 "intermittently"; Buffett replied "No. You've got it wrong, Mike. Everything you didn't circle just became your Avoid-At-All-Cost list." Clear: "The most dangerous distractions are the ones you love, but that don't love you back." and "Spending time on secondary priorities is the reason you have 20 half-finished projects instead of 5 completed ones." He offers a weekly variant of the exercise. (buffett-focus)

text: **The life punchcard: Buffett's 20 slots.** *Example:* Buffett (via Munger's 1994 USC talk) imagines a ticket with 20 punches for all your investments; "you’d be forced to load up on what you’d really thought about." Clear transposes it to time: each slot is "a period of focused work for a year or two," and "Unlike financial investments, your 20 “life slots” are going to get punched whether you like it or not. The time will pass either way." "Don’t waste your next slot. Think carefully, make a decision, and go all in." His claim that one year of focused work can make you very good in many areas is from his own experience, not data. (buffett-slots)

title: The life punchcard: Buffett's 20 slots

text: **Inversion: find anti-advice.** "Inversion is not about finding good advice, but rather about finding anti-advice. It teaches you what to avoid." *Examples:* Nirvana recorded *Nevermind* for $65,000 while hair-metal bands spent millions; he credits inversion for his own contrarian essays ("Forget About Setting Goals," "Motivation is Overvalued"); managers ("What would someone do each day if they were a terrible manager?"); the productivity inversion of asking how you would end up distracted (phone in another room). Lineage: Jacobi, Munger, Stoic negative visualization; Jacobi's phrase is folkloric by his own footnote. (inversion)

Motivation is Overvalued

text: **Inversion, premortem, and why avoiding failure is safe.** *Example:* Gary Klein's failure premortem, imagine the project "has failed" six months out and "Tell the story of how it happened." Munger as quoted by Clear (not Clear's words): "What do you want to avoid?" Answer: "sloth and unreliability." Clear's asymmetry: "Blindly chasing success can have severe consequences, but preventing failure usually carries very little risk." His footnote separates inversion from beginning with the end in mind, which keeps the same goal from another direction. Finance case: "accumulating debt is a hair-on-fire emergency." (inversion)

text: **First principles: deconstruct, then reconstruct.** *Example:* Musk (via Wired): "Physics teaches you to reason from first principles rather than by analogy... the materials cost of a rocket was around two percent of the typical price"; Clear says SpaceX "cut the price of launching a rocket by nearly 10x while still making a profit." Other cases: John Boyd's snowmobile (bicycle handlebars, tank treads, boat motor and skis), Gutenberg's wine press plus movable type, the rolling suitcase ("While everyone else was focused on how to build a better bag (form), Sadow considered how to store and move things more efficiently (function).") text: **First principles marks the limit of continuous improvement.** His own flagship philosophy has a stated boundary: "Continuous improvement tends to occur within the boundary set by the original vision. By comparison, first principles thinking requires you to abandon your allegiance to previous forms and put the function front and center." And: "Without reasoning by first principles, you spend your time making small improvements to a bicycle rather than a snowmobile." Also "Be wary of the ideas you inherit" and "Optimize the function. Ignore the form." He calls Musk the exemplar ("no one embodies the philosophy of first principles thinking more effectively"). (first-principles)
quotes: Continuous improvement tends to occur within the boundary set by the original vision. By comparison, first principles thinking requires you to abandon your allegiance to previous forms and put the function front and center.
Without reasoning by first principles, you spend your time making small improvements to a bicycle rather than a snowmobile.
Be wary of the ideas you inherit
Optimize the function. Ignore the form.

title: First principles marks the limit of continuous improvement

text: **Deliberate practice in 1 to 3 sessions (Kathy Sierra's rule).** Sierra's definition as relayed: "Deliberate practice is when you work on a skill that requires 1 to 3 practice sessions to master. If it takes longer than that, then you are working on something that is too complex." *Example:* the clean and jerk taught as hook grip, then broomstick movement, then foot position, then set position, then first pull, each its own session. Personal case: at about age nine his father spent a whole session on a 12-inch pitching backswing with the cue "Elbow up"; weeks later the position was automatic. He calls it "the first practical definition of deliberate practice that I have come across." (deliberate-practice-strategy)
quotes: Deliberate practice is when you work on a skill that requires 1 to 3 practice sessions to master. If it takes longer than that, then you are working on something that is too complex.
the first practical definition of deliberate practice that I have come across.
title: Deliberate practice in 1 to 3 sessions (Kathy Sierra's rule)

text: **The three questions experts keep asking.** (1) "Do I understand the fundamentals?" (2) "Am I working on the next step?" (failure both ways: "There are a lot of smart people who know what the next step is, but never do it. Similarly, there are many people who take action, but waste time working on skills that don’t build upon each other.") (3) "What am I missing?" On the 10,000-hour rule he blames the audience, not Gladwell: "people quickly latched onto the number 10,000 and forgot the details of the argument." "Expertise is a process, not an outcome." (deliberate-practice-strategy)

Am I working on the next step?
There are a lot of smart people who know what the next step is, but never do it. Similarly, there are many people who take action, but waste time working on skills that don’t build upon each other.
What am I missing?

text: **Necessary but not sufficient: the limits of deliberate practice.** *Example:* Louis Rosenbaum's finding that "the average eyesight of a Major League position player is 20/11," with half of one Dodgers roster 20/10 uncorrected and the anatomical limit 20/8 (via David Epstein's *The Sports Gene*). Steffi Graf scored highest on physical attributes and on competitive desire. He quotes Robert Plomin: "we literally can't find a single one that isn't influenced by our genes," and estimates "between 25 percent to 35 percent" of performance differences from genes (uncited on the page). (deliberate-practice-myth)
quotes: the average eyesight of a Major League position player is 20/11,
we literally can't find a single one that isn't influenced by our genes,
between 25 percent to 35 percent
title: Necessary but not sufficient: the limits of deliberate practice

text: **Layer your skills; fight where the genetic odds favor you.** "If you can't win by being better, then win by being different. By combining your skills, you reduce the level of competition." The model is Scott Adams: "few people can draw well and write jokes. It’s the combination of the two that makes what I do so rare." With Sun Tzu ("the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won"), his advice is to "train hard and practice deliberately in areas where the genetic odds are in your favor (or where you can overlap your skills in a compelling way)." (deliberate-practice-myth)
quotes: If you can't win by being better, then win by being different. By combining your skills, you reduce the level of competition.
few people can draw well and write jokes. It’s the combination of the two that makes what I do so rare.
the victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won
train hard and practice deliberately in areas where the genetic odds are in your favor (or where you can overlap your skills in a compelling way).
title: Layer your skills; fight where the genetic odds favor you

text: **Time assets versus time debts.** "Time assets are choices that save you time in the future. Think: saying no to a meeting, automating a task, working on something that persists and compounds." "Time debts are choices that must be repaid and cost you time in the future. Think: saying yes to a meeting, doing sloppy work that will need to be revised." "Time assets are an investment. Time debts are an expense." Extends the saying-no essay from commitments to work quality and automation. The page names no outside source for the framing. (3-2-1, April 27, 2023)
quotes: Time assets are choices that save you time in the future. Think: saying no to a meeting, automating a task, working on something that persists and compounds.
Time debts are choices that must be repaid and cost you time in the future. Think: saying yes to a meeting, doing sloppy work that will need to be revised.
Time assets are an investment. Time debts are an expense.
title: Time assets versus time debts

text: **Muddy puddles versus leaky ceilings.** *Example:* "I split problems into two groups: muddy puddles and leaky ceilings." A puddle clears if left alone ("Is life really falling apart or am I just in a sour mood?... Drink some water. Go for a walk. Get some sleep."); a leak widens ("Relationship tension that goes unaddressed. Overspending that becomes a habit. One missed workout drifting into months of inactivity."), so "You need to intervene now." Closing question: "Are you dealing with a leak or a puddle?" Only this third item of that issue is clearly first person. (3-2-1, March 28, 2024)

text: **Body or bridge: optimize for starting or finishing?** *Example:* "In some areas of life, value is unlocked by starting. Even a five-minute workout or a short walk can reset your mood and benefit your body. In other areas, value is unlocked by finishing. It does you no good to build a bridge halfway across the river." Companion idea: "Your net productivity is the balance of the productive and unproductive forces in your life... A car will travel faster not only if you press the accelerator, but also if you remove the speed bumps." He does not say when to abandon a bridge midway. (3-2-1, Nov 3, 2022)
quotes: In some areas of life, value is unlocked by starting. Even a five-minute workout or a short walk can reset your mood and benefit your body. In other areas, value is unlocked by finishing. It does you no good to build a bridge halfway across the river.
Your net productivity is the balance of the productive and unproductive forces in your life... A car will travel faster not only if you press the accelerator, but also if you remove the speed bumps.
title: Body or bridge: optimize for starting or finishing?

text: **The five-step creative process.** Discover (read a lot, observe, notice), Collect ("Immediately record anything that strikes you."), Generate (brainstorm lots of ideas), Combine (connect previously unconnected ideas), Refine ("Edit, edit, edit. Select the best."). No worked example in that issue. Mapping to Rubin's make-30-pick-the-best (Generate then Refine) is my inference, not his. (3-2-1, Nov 14, 2024)
quotes: Immediately record anything that strikes you.
Edit, edit, edit. Select the best.
title: The five-step creative process

text: **Deconstruct the cool things you see.** *Example:* after an amazing musical performance, ask "How did they promote the event? What happens in the first ten seconds of each song? How frequently are they engaging directly with the audience? Is there a progression of energy throughout the show?" "The person who thinks, “That was cool” is a consumer. The person who thinks, “How did they make something that cool?” is on the path to being a creator." "Don't just taste the recipe, look for the ingredients." (3-2-1, Dec 15, 2022)
quotes: How did they promote the event? What happens in the first ten seconds of each song? How frequently are they engaging directly with the audience? Is there a progression of energy throughout the show?
That was cool
How did they make something that cool?
title: Deconstruct the cool things you see

text: **Comparison versus competitiveness (2014 voice).** *Example (auto-transcript, paraphrase plus short wording):* Agnes de Mille doubted her work on *Oklahoma* and asked Martha Graham whether she was cut out for it; Graham's answer as relayed was that her job is not to judge the work but to create it. His extraction: "competitiveness does not necessarily require you to compare." Diagnostic: relieve yourself of comparison and do more work, and you probably get better results. Confession: for most of his athletic career he was comparison-focused. The 2026 line "compete internally" is the matured form of a decade-old position. (One You Feed 2014)
quotes: competitiveness does not necessarily require you to compare.
title: Comparison versus competitiveness (2014 voice)

text: **Ambition and contentment are not opposites (rose seed).** *Example (auto-transcript, paraphrase):* via Gallwey's *The Inner Game of Tennis*, a rose seed is never criticized for not yet being a tree; it is perfect as it is and also never stops growing. His application: he is happy with who he is now and does not feel he must prove himself, yet will not stop growing, "not because it requires me to be unhappy." He hedges that he has not mastered the balance. This is the on-record reconciliation of his later "No sense in thinking small" (3-2-1, May 21, 2026) with satisfaction. (One You Feed 2014)
quotes: not because it requires me to be unhappy.
No sense in thinking small
title: Ambition and contentment are not opposites (rose seed)

text: **Professionals schedule, amateurs wait for motivation.** *Example:* he asked Todd Henry about writing only when inspired; Henry: "I only write when I'm motivated too. I just happened to be motivated every day at 8am." Clear's rule: "Professionals stick to the schedule, amateurs let life get in the way," and "Setting a schedule doesn't make you a professional, following it does." His caution from his own mistake: schedule actions, not results ("'Lose 5 pounds' is not an action you can perform. 'Do three sets of squats' is an action you can perform."), and commit for one week at a time (professionals-and-amateurs essay). The 2014 interview (auto-transcript) says this conversation triggered his Monday and Thursday publishing. In the same interview he says we each hold both fixed and growth mindsets in different areas, citing Dweck's *Mindset*: growth for writing, a fixed "I'm not a natural salesman" story in sales. (One You Feed 2014)

title: Professionals schedule, amateurs wait for motivation

text: **Graded exposure to failure (mental toughness).** *Example (auto-transcript, paraphrase):* train with small failures, then step to a slightly greater risk once you can overcome the small one. He admits his own failure mode was overreach, "when I've tried to do too much too fast," and warns that growing very fast is dangerous. A scientist-friend's lesson: an unexpected result is "just another data point," and a bad restaurant entree does not make you a terrible food orderer. The 2022 8-or-9-in-10 ratio is the later, numeric form. (One You Feed 2014; see also the failure-scientist essay)
quotes: when I've tried to do too much too fast,
just another data point,
title: Graded exposure to failure (mental toughness)

text: **Bright-line rules: decide once, not daily.** *Example:* the Miranda ruling as a rule "with clear interpretation and very little wiggle room"; fuzzy goals become lines: "I only process email between 11AM and 6PM," "I enjoy a maximum of 2 drinks per night," "I save $500 per month for retirement." Two payoffs: a shift from sacrifice ("Oh, I can't do it this time") to identity ("No thanks, I don't do that"), and less decision fatigue because "the decision is made ahead of time." He credits Nir Eyal's "Progressive Extremism" (no red meat first, then fish) and Brian Johnson for the drinking example. "Vague promises will never lead to clear results." (bright-lines)

No thanks, I don't do that

text: **The ice cube and stored work.** "Complaining about not achieving success despite working hard is like complaining about an ice cube not melting when you heated it from twenty-five to thirty-one degrees. Your work was not wasted; it is just being stored. All the action happens at thirty-two degrees." (quote archive, Atomic Habits ch. 1). It is the visual for the delayed payoff of compounding and the reason he tells readers to judge trajectory over early results.
quotes: Complaining about not achieving success despite working hard is like complaining about an ice cube not melting when you heated it from twenty-five to thirty-one degrees. Your work was not wasted; it is just being stored. All the action happens at thirty-two degrees.
title: The ice cube and stored work

text: **Accountability that bites: the neighbor, not the stranger.** Asked by Attia for research on partner types, he says "I don't know of any studies that distinguish clearly between those two," then reasons: a matched stranger fails because "you don't really bear much cost for them thinking you did a bad job"; a spouse or sibling is too entangled to be strict; the neighbor who sees your unmowed lawn, or a paid coach you see repeatedly, carries real social or financial cost. An honest no-evidence answer, offered as reasoning. (Attia #183 rebroadcast, auto-transcript)
quotes: I don't know of any studies that distinguish clearly between those two,
you don't really bear much cost for them thinking you did a bad job
title: Accountability that bites: the neighbor, not the stranger

text: **Seasons of life, with a writing-cadence example (Mel Robbins episode, paraphrase of an auto-transcript).** Per the extraction: he wrote two roughly 2,000-word articles a week for about three years, could not keep that pace after the book deal, spent three years on the book, and now writes a shorter weekly newsletter; he says it took about 18 months to notice the season had changed. This corroborates the essay-cadence history and is a self-admitted slowness to notice change. Paraphrase only. (mel-robbins episode)

text: **Make the good choice the path of least resistance.** Reduce friction for what you want; add friction to what you don't; concretely: put the pill bottle next to the faucet, the guitar on a stand in the living room, water bottles pre-filled around the house (choice-architecture essay).
title: Make the good choice the path of least resistance

text: **Say no as time credit, not time debt.** "No is a form of time credit. You retain the ability to spend your future time however you want. Yes is a form of time debt. You have to pay back your commitment at some point. No is a decision. Yes is a responsibility" (saying-no essay). Layered tactics he amplifies: Tim Harford's "if I had to do this today, would I agree to it?"; Derek Sivers' "Hell Yeah or No"; Greg McKeown/Shane Parrish's trade-off-forcing when declining a superior ("which of these other projects should I deprioritize?"). "Elimination is a more useful skill than optimization."

text: **Diagnose which stage failed before reacting.** When something feels broken, check tactics (HOW) first, then strategy (WHAT), then vision (WHY), because demoralization from a lower-stage failure gets mistakenly read as a vision-level failure (3-stages-of-failure essay). "Be firm on the vision, not on this particular version of your idea", nearly everything else (tactics, strategy, even business model) should flex.

Push yourself and reach beyond your current grasp... Win enough to keep progressing. Lose enough to keep learning" (3-2-1, Oct 6, 2022); a numeric calibration heuristic, distinct from "treat failure like a scientist" (which is about interpreting failure, not dosing it in advance).

text:
Clear, concrete, analogy-driven. Short declarative sentences; a single sticky metaphor per idea (the ice cube melting at 31° then 32°; the plane that shifts course a few degrees; the bow-and-arrow vs. aim-while-moving; "joy in the snow"; a jar of marbles; an election needing only a majority; red lights on a road trip; a muddy puddle versus a leaky ceiling; a car with speed bumps; a bicycle versus a snowmobile). He favors aphorisms engineered for recall and re-sharing, and leans hard on **rule-of-three** and named "laws/rules" (Four Laws, Goldilocks Rule, Two-Minute Rule, Three Meanings of Atomic, Three Stages of Failure). Heavily fond of **symmetry and antithesis**: compete externally versus internally, create versus consume, the forgiving past self, strict present self and flexible future self, "No is a decision. Yes is a responsibility," and time assets versus time debts.
Reaches for named historical or creative case studies to anchor abstract claims (Steve Martin's stand-up climb, Ben Hogan's golf practice, Benjamin Franklin's essay rewriting, Victor Hugo's locked-up clothes, Anthony Trollope's 15-minute word quotas, Nirvana's $65,000 album, Amazon's three marketplace attempts), and the newsletter and essays are dense with attributed quotations from named thinkers (Feynman, Munger, Pressfield, Tharp, Angelou, Nietzsche, Thoreau, Naval, Camus, Fuller) he curates rather than originates. The essays often carry numbered steps ("Step 1"), footnotes that credit sources, and a closing product or book tie-in; the 3-2-1 form itself is tight, modular and quotable, three ideas, two quotes, one question every issue.
Calm, practical, non-judgmental: he rarely scolds and almost never hypes; the recurring promise is something small, achievable, and doable today. He hedges on his own mastery in public ("As usual, I don't have this all figured out"; in 2014 (auto-transcript) that the ambition-versus-contentment balance is "something I certainly haven't mastered to any degree") and admits his own failures (the early product with no defined customer; being cut from varsity; overreach) as proof the method is practical, not theoretical. He does source-hygiene in public on occasion: he flags that the "insanity is doing the same thing" line is misattributed to Einstein, and he corrected the DiMaggio basement-swings story in a footnote after readers said it belonged to Brooklyn Dodgers outfielder George "Shotgun" Shuba, while leaving the body text unchanged. The 2014 spoken voice (auto-transcript) is more tentative and more confessional than the polished 2020s one, with the same habit of crediting a book or friend for each idea.

As usual, I don't have this all figured out
something I certainly haven't mastered to any degree

text: Mindset & identity | Behavior change *is* identity change; act your way into believing | **Carol Dweck** largely *agrees* (growth vs. fixed mindset); natural pairing; the seam is that Dweck centers beliefs about ability, Clear centers beliefs as a byproduct of repeated action. Documented, not just inferred: in a 2014 interview (auto-transcript) Clear cites Dweck's *Mindset* and refines it, saying we each hold both mindsets in different areas (growth for writing, fixed for sales)

Compounding & long games | Compounding via tiny daily reps and long-half-life work | **Naval Ravikant** *agrees* on compounding and leverage; natural pairing; Naval pushes harder toward equity/code/media leverage and long-term games with long-term people, where Clear stays in personal-behavior territory

Curiosity, contrarianism, and great work | Motivation is overrated in general, but *cites Paul Graham approvingly* on "work on something you're deeply interested in... curiosity, delight, and the desire to do something impressive" | **Paul Graham** himself is a natural ally here, not an opponent; Clear directly amplifies Graham's essays (on great work, and on the contrarian test "Do you have any opinions that you would be reluctant to express in front of a group of your peers?", featured in the Oct 6, 2022 issue) rather than disputing them, a rare case of near-total alignment across the roster

text: *(Rows against Bezos, Musk, Horowitz and Hoffman are my extrapolation from documented positions, not on-record exchanges. Graham, Munger, Buffett and Gladwell rows rest on how Clear quotes or describes them in his own essays and newsletter; Dweck is partly documented (2014 interview, auto-transcript); the Naval and Fuller rows rest on issues where Clear only featured their quotes, so the tension is my inference.)*

**Oversimplifies real behavior change.** The cue-craving-response-reward loop assumes executive function and environmental control many readers lack; trauma, ADHD, chronic stress, mental illness; "some habits need healing, not hacking" (Dr. Gina Cleo).
quotes: some habits need healing, not hacking

text: **The 1% / 37x math is a motivational metaphor, not science.** Real change is non-linear (jumps, plateaus, relapses): "It's a motivational metaphor. But it's not how habit change works in real life. Behavior doesn't follow clean math" (Dr. Gina Cleo). *Sharper, fact-checked version*: "There's no skill that you can improve 1% every single day... for 365 days. It's a ridiculous concept. This is just taking the idea of compound interest and pretending that it applies to skills" (*If Books Could Kill*, Peter Shamshiri).
quotes: It's a motivational metaphor. But it's not how habit change works in real life. Behavior doesn't follow clean math
There's no skill that you can improve 1% every single day... for 365 days. It's a ridiculous concept. This is just taking the idea of compound interest and pretending that it applies to skills
title: The 1% / 37x math is a motivational metaphor, not science

text: **The flagship British Cycling "marginal gains" anecdote omits a major confound.** *If Books Could Kill*'s research: after the UK National Lottery began in 1994, "In the mid-1990s, the cycling team has barely any funding. By 1999, they're receiving £2.5 million annually," and of the one gold medal Clear mentions, "What he doesn't mention is that gold medal was in the year 2000, right after the funding started pouring in"; "those aren't philosophical changes as much as they're just costly resources that they could now afford," not proof that incremental tweaks alone drove the outcome. The same host grants Brailsford's "methods are widely respected within the sport."

text: **The Karachi soap study (his own "make it satisfying" closing anecdote) also omits confounds.** The actual Stephen Luby / Procter & Gamble study involved free soap distribution *and* weekly household educational visits, not just fragrant/foaming soap; Clear "expressly dismisses the role that education played," and the podcast hosts argue he overweights the satisfaction angle as "the decisive factor" it likely wasn't alone (*If Books Could Kill*).

text: **The Thorndike cafeteria study is observational, not experimental.** "There's no control group. There's no effort to do research. They're just observing what happened in one cafeteria location" (Peter Shamshiri); a caution against Clear's confident causal framing ("nobody had said a word to anyone eating there," implying environment alone explains the shift).

text: **One environment essay still cites Brian Wansink.** The power-of-environment excerpt says "A study from Brian Wansink at Cornell University found that people eat 22 percent less food by switching from 12-inch dinner plates to 10-inch plates." *If Books Could Kill* calls Wansink, in the food choice-architecture context, "a giant fraud." *Context outside the sources:* Wansink resigned from Cornell in 2018 after a string of retractions; the page does not flag this. text: **"Habit" is used loosely across incompatible categories.** The same word covers compulsive behavior (nail-biting), rare deliberate acts (voting), and identity-level traits; critics argue this undermines applying one Four-Laws framework uniformly across all three (*If Books Could Kill*).
title: "Habit" is used loosely across incompatible categories

text: **Identity-based habits may reverse cause and effect.** The correlation between self-identifying (e.g., as a "voter") and the corresponding behavior doesn't establish that adopting the identity-language *causes* the behavior; the causal arrow may run the other way (*If Books Could Kill*): "that's not necessarily because they're identifying as voters. It's the other way around." This is also, independently, a **circularity critique**: "the key to developing habits you want is to change your identity around those habits. You change your identity by developing the habits you want... It's circular" (*If Books Could Kill*).
quotes: that's not necessarily because they're identifying as voters. It's the other way around.
the key to developing habits you want is to change your identity around those habits. You change your identity by developing the habits you want... It's circular
title: Identity-based habits may reverse cause and effect

text: **Survivorship bias / class-and-personality confound, sharper than "healing not hacking."** "In his own telling, there's no phase of his life where he's disorganized or has bad habits or anything. The adversity he overcame was getting smacked in the face with a baseball bat, that's not related to habits"; the critique that his prescriptions may reflect trait-level organization rather than a transferable learned system (*If Books Could Kill*).

text: **Not every habit is reward-driven.** Habits rooted in fear, anxiety, trauma, or compulsion need different tools than a feel-good reward loop; the Four Laws don't address them (Dr. Gina Cleo).
title: Not every habit is reward-driven

text: **Systems-over-goals is overdrawn, and may itself be a case of overclaiming precision, not just philosophy.** Goal-setting research shows clear, challenging goals are among the most proven motivators; the science supports *both*, "set a meaningful goal, then build small systems" (Dr. Gina Cleo). Clear's own "No sense in thinking small. Don't water down your vision." (3-2-1, May 21, 2026) and "goals are necessary, but not sufficient" (Rich Roll #401 notes) partly concede goals back in.
quotes: set a meaningful goal, then build small systems
No sense in thinking small. Don't water down your vision.
goals are necessary, but not sufficient
title: Systems-over-goals is overdrawn, and may itself be a case of overclaiming precision, not just philosophy

text: **The 66-day figure misleads, by his own partial disclosure.** It's an average from a study where formation ranged "18 to 254 days"; the mean obscures huge variance (Dr. Gina Cleo). Clear's own essay discloses the extrapolation's shakiness: the underlying Lally study ran only 12 weeks (84 days), so "the researchers were able to use the data to estimate the longer timelines (like 254 days)"; i.e., the long tail is modeled, not directly observed, a caveat Clear states himself but that doesn't fully appear in his popularized "66 days" framing elsewhere.
quotes: 18 to 254 days
the researchers were able to use the data to estimate the longer timelines (like 254 days)
title: The 66-day figure misleads, by his own partial disclosure

text: **Overemphasizes individual responsibility, underweights systemic barriers.** "James Clear overemphasizes on the idea of individual responsibility ignoring systematic barriers, mental health issues and other socioeconomic limitations of an individual" (Fatima & Chakraborty, IJSI 2025), Clear himself partially concedes an adjacent point in his own "3 Stages of Failure" essay, explicitly bracketing out "Failures of Opportunity" (systemic/societal barriers) as out of scope because "Failures of Opportunity are difficult to influence," choosing to focus only on individually-controllable failure modes, a self-aware limitation, but one that leaves the structural critique standing.

Failures of Opportunity
Failures of Opportunity are difficult to influence,

text: **Assumes a Western, individualistic cultural context.** "The book largely assumes a Western, individualistic context, which may limit its relevance in collectivist cultures and societies where behavior is influenced more strongly by social/family expectations" (Fatima & Chakraborty, IJSI 2025); a cross-cultural-validity critique absent from the earlier, US-centric critique sources.

text: **Little is novel.** The book synthesizes psychology rather than contributing original research, and he concedes it ("I would love to be brilliant and original and a genius, but I'm not smart enough for that," The Profile 2021). The 2025 review says the same without hostility ("The originality of the book lies not in introducing new concepts but how it synthesizes existing behavioural science") and traces his tools to Gollwitzer, Premack and Milkman; its listed weaknesses are repetition, individual responsibility and a Western frame, not plagiarism. The sharper "renaming" charge is The Guardian's (below).

text: **Harsher reads question rigor and packaging, not just content.** *The Guardian* (Steven Phillips-Horst, "Tedcore," May 18, 2022, read directly, not via Wikipedia) groups Clear with Brené Brown, Bessel van der Kolk, and Mark Manson in a genre he dubs "Tedcore": "a coalescing sub-genre of self-help books that combine the comforting yet impenetrable vocabulary of modern therapy with pseudoscientific grand theories on human behavior... backing up their circular logic with dubious 'research' and 'experts.'" Clear-specific lines from the piece: he explains habits "mostly by renaming things that already exist" (stacking, temptation bundling); the cue-craving-response-reward loop is mocked directly, "when I walk into a dark room and instinctively reach for a light switch, I am 'satisfying my craving to see.' Ah yes, my insatiable lust for vision"; a claim that "people who are high in agreeableness tend to have higher natural oxytocin levels" is flagged as a "pseudo-fact," since "soft qualifiers like 'tend to' and 'easily imagine' keep us firmly in the realm of feel-good conjecture"; and the piece notes the $299 "Habits Academy" as a monetization angle.

text: **Willpower-as-muscle and decision fatigue are stated as settled (analyst observation).** "Research shows that willpower is like a muscle. It gets fatigued as you use it throughout the day." (habit-guide); "Every time you make a decision, it’s like doing another rep in the gym." (willpower-decision-fatigue, with the parole-board curve as proof). The pages do not flag any replication dispute. *Context outside the sources, not from any critic cited here:* ego depletion and the parole-board study have faced replication failures and re-analysis (the judges' case order was not random), so treat the strong form as contested. It also sits uneasily beside his environment-over-willpower stance, and the keystone essay says "we don't have the willpower to make different decisions."

text: **The genetic ceiling cuts against the open-ended identity framing.** In the deliberate-practice essay genes "set a boundary," roughly 25 to 35 percent of performance differences (uncited), and readers should choose domains by genetic odds. The book's message is that every action is a vote for "the type of person you wish to become." He never reconciles the open-ended version with the pick-where-the-odds-favor-you version. The evidence is from extreme outlier fields (elite baseball vision) and the essay does not say where the limit does not bind. (deliberate-practice-myth)
quotes: set a boundary,
the type of person you wish to become.

text: **The deliberate-practice essay opens with a story he concedes may be misattributed.** The DiMaggio basement-tally tale is told in the body; his footnote says he "can't vouch for the authenticity" and that readers say it was originally told about George "Shotgun" Shuba. The second ("you can actually become very good in many areas—maybe even world-class—with just one year of focused work") is "my experience," with no data, and sits uneasily with "commit to working through 10 years of silence" in the same essay. text: **Several framings rest on one anecdote or analogy.** The keystone claim is introspective ("my guess is that my blood pressure raised"); the equilibrium thesis is argued by analogy (blood pressure, athletes, nations) with no study; the pre-game-routine claim that top performers all use rituals has no named examples; Pointing-and-Calling figures are footnoted to journalism; the Buffett 2 List is a three-link secondhand story (Flint to Dinsmore to Clear); the Hillis fat-loss example has no outcome data. Inversion's Nirvana example is hindsight with no way to predict which inversions will win, and "preventing failure usually carries very little risk" overlooks opportunity cost (my reading). text: **Counter-evidence to the renaming charge: he often credits.** In essays he names Fogg for habit stacking and the motivation wave, Milkman by name for temptation bundling, David Allen for the Two-Minute Rule (and Babauta for the "so easy you can't say no" phrase in 2014), Duhigg for keystone habits, McGonigal, Ivy Lee, Kathy Sierra, Leonard and Senge. That weakens The Guardian's "renaming" charge for the essay archive (he also credits Nir Eyal and Brian Johnson on bright lines, Gretchen Rubin on the four-quarter day); the charge is stronger for the book's tool names and for Gollwitzer and Premack, who are not credited on the pages read. text: Co-founder and (former) co-CEO of PostHog (open-source product analytics turned 16+ product developer suite, YC W20, ~$1.4B valuation, ~300k customers), an ex-enterprise-sales VP who built the anti-enterprise-sales company and documents every belief in public, including his own mistakes. His lens: **radical transparency is a competitive moat and a hiring filter, not a virtue**; **the enemy is obscurity, not competitors**, so brand must be weird and polarizing rather than conversion-optimized; **velocity beats validation** ("unless you already know that you're good at product you're probably bad at product"); and **org design is the product**: teams of six or fewer, engineers decide what to build, PMs as "compass," no deadlines, no formal 1:1s. Sharpest contrarian calls: 100% inbound because developers cannot be cold-sold; price on cost plus a modest margin and never "to value"; give away more to earn more; VC "is a tool, not a religion"; a "team, not a family" with four-month severance. He opposes sales-led SaaS GTM (Lemkin), PM-owns-the-roadmap orthodoxy (Horowitz), and crunch culture, and he qualifies his own advice constantly ("isn't universally good advice"). Watch the seam: an insider Glassdoor review calls the marketed autonomy day-to-day, not directional, and in 2025 he himself conceded "too much top down communication." His own texts also hold unresolved tensions (deadlines vs no deadlines, anti-measurement brand vs measured growth experiments, transparency vs the pay exception).

text: James Hawkins co-founded PostHog in 2020 with technical co-founder Tim Glaser, going through Y Combinator's W20 batch. They quit their jobs in August 2019, pivoted five times (six products and 100+ user meetings in nine months), and PostHog was the sixth idea, a tool forged from their own pain: "the first thing that worked for us... was self-hosted product analytics because we pivoted so many times and every time we had to set up product analytics over and over again and we're just getting frustrated having to implement it." (YC Podcast, auto-caption.) Before PostHog, Hawkins was VP of Sales at Arachnys, an enterprise outbound-sales background he deliberately inverted. After a Hacker News launch in February 2020 and a $3M seed (closed April 2020 on SAFEs), PostHog raised a $9M Series A and $15M Series B, over $27M in total by 2023, then a **$70M Series D led by Stripe at a ~$920M valuation** (reportedly after Patrick Collison tweeted "out of the blue" that the website was cool) and, by late 2025, a further raise at $1.4B. The company grew from 37 people (Nov 2023) to roughly 150 (Oct 2025), ~300,000 customers (mostly free) and 16-17 products. In May 2026 he and Tim split the co-CEO role by emphasis: Hawkins goes deep on AI product and engineering, Tim goes wide on execution. His judgment is worth borrowing because he has put the whole operating manual on record (handbook, pricing, raise mechanics, pivots, annual self-reviews) and built a cashflow-positive business on bets that contradict SaaS orthodoxy.

text: **The PMF Game (5-level "snakes and ladders").** Five sequential levels: find a significant problem, validate it by talking to users, get users to use the product, keep them coming back, onboard your first five reference customers. *Gist:* "Finding product-market fit is a bit like playing snakes and ladders. (PMF game; YC Podcast: "14 of them didn't even click the link... we hadn't done any of the user interviews correctly.")

text: **Writing for developers (five-part framework).** Be human, be concise, pick a side, be engaging, be precise. *Worked example:* hitting the Hacker News front page is "one of the most surprisingly important skills I've realized I have": "Out of five posts that I hoped would get there, four did." text: **How the PM reversal actually happened: a full-team feedback session.** At the first offsite in 2020, each person received feedback from everyone else, moderated "to be 70% constructive and as specific as possible." The founders heard that "we've seen product done badly in our previous careers, and as a result, we aren't building this discipline at all into the company." An engineer, Paolo, had "proactively acted like a product manager," gathering "deep feedback from dozens of users"; they moved him into product and hired Marcus as VP Product in 2021. His pre-reversal doubts, in his own words: "Don't they just dictate what to build to our team, thus annoying our team, and probably understanding our (technical) users less well than our engineers?" The condition that made it acceptable: "We've not had to sacrifice engineering autonomy. Both Marcus and Paolo can write code, and they both ship from time to time." text: **LLM-limits model and the AI chapter.** Three gaps: "LLMs have no innate goal setting," "AI is spiky," "LLMs don't self-improve." *Worked example:* a Clippy-esque one-shot chat assistant made mistakes: "FOMO got the better of me and I pushed this in our marketing too early." The fix was "a single query loop architecture, so the agent could iterate", plus regular reviews of real LLM traces; then "Last week, the majority of dashboards were created by agents." Bets: "We think PostHog's future is headless"; reactive to proactive; long-running agents. (PostHog's next chapter.)

AI is spiky,
LLMs don't self-improve.
FOMO got the better of me and I pushed this in our marketing too early.
a single query loop architecture, so the agent could iterate
Last week, the majority of dashboards were created by agents.
We think PostHog's future is headless
title: LLM-limits model and the AI chapter

text: **Co-CEO split by depth vs breadth.** "I wanted to go full founder mode and push the ambition of the AI work we were already doing." Tim "wanted to go wide and improve how we execute across everything: hiring, ops, finance, go-to-market, and engineering." Earlier, on the podcast: Tim is "clearer, more direct... a stronger communicator", James "better at just pushing up the level of ambition." (PostHog's next chapter; TL&W #189 transcript.)

text: **When in doubt, ship it.** Handbook value "Why not now?": "You do not need consensus to do things – focus your energy on shipping what's most valuable." / "If we're debating doing something, just trying it is the best way to learn." The midwit meme: "idiot and genius do the same behavior and the middle one overthinks things... It's like just try it." (Handbook: values; Executive Brand, auto-caption.)
quotes: Why not now?
You do not need consensus to do things – focus your energy on shipping what's most valuable.
If we're debating doing something, just trying it is the best way to learn.
idiot and genius do the same behavior and the middle one overthinks things... It's like just try it.
title: When in doubt, ship it

text: **Judge by what people do, not what they say.** The say/do gap is the reason to build before validating (the 15-prospect, one-click story). "If you can't stop thinking of other ideas, you probably are building something you don't like." (A story about pivots.)
quotes: If you can't stop thinking of other ideas, you probably are building something you don't like.
title: Judge by what people do, not what they say

text: **Pivot-cooling rule.** "If you decide to pivot, you have to wait at least until the next day to do it." They could build "an MVP and a new website in a single, glorious, all nighter", which "felt like progress, but in reality was just a bit dangerous." Also "Know where you sit on this line": they leaned toward pivoting too often. (A story about pivots.)
quotes: If you decide to pivot, you have to wait at least until the next day to do it.
an MVP and a new website in a single, glorious, all nighter
felt like progress, but in reality was just a bit dangerous.
Know where you sit on this line
title: Pivot-cooling rule

text: **If retention needs nudges, the product isn't valuable.** "Avoid relying on things like reminder emails or push notifications purely designed to get users to log back into your product. If it takes this sort of effort to retain users, your product probably isn't valuable to them." (PMF game.)
quotes: Avoid relying on things like reminder emails or push notifications purely designed to get users to log back into your product. If it takes this sort of effort to retain users, your product probably isn't valuable to them.
title: If retention needs nudges, the product isn't valuable

text: **Define the ICP precisely, then listen only to it.** "Do not just assume one or two things like 'engineers in startups with over 100 staff'." (PMF game.) "You should focus completely on your ICP. That's the point. Everything else comes from it." (How we found our ICP.)
quotes: Do not just assume one or two things like 'engineers in startups with over 100 staff'.
You should focus completely on your ICP. That's the point. Everything else comes from it.
title: Define the ICP precisely, then listen only to it

text: **Respond in seconds; ask in two or three sentences.** "Be as concise as you can when asking for a meeting. That means 2-3 sentences – not a wall of text." / "Speed matters. You should aim to respond within 30 seconds if someone messages you back." (PMF game.) Sales version: "We had a 90% greater chance of booking time if we called back potential customers within 5 minutes." (Startup sales.)

Speed matters. You should aim to respond within 30 seconds if someone messages you back.

title: Respond in seconds; ask in two or three sentences

text: **Charge early unless you're a network-effects consumer play.** "Unless you're building Facebook, you're always better off charging something as soon as possible." (Pricing advice, house view.) Qualified by competition: if "no one is doing your thing... it's like much more likely that no one will pay for it," charge sooner. (Executive Brand, auto-caption.) His own context-sensitive version: "Had we been building into a new market with less validation from competitors, a worse fundraising environment (like right now), or bootstrapping, then monetizing sooner would have been important." (First 1,000 users.)

title: Charge early unless you're a network-effects consumer play

text: **Cut anything that isn't fun, because "the easiest way to fail is to simply lose interest."** They abandoned self-hosted monetization because the sales and infra debugging were not enjoyable. (Pragmatic lessons from Elon.) "Had we stuck with the original plan, we'd have lost interest because we weren't doing what we enjoy." (How not to be boring.)
quotes: the easiest way to fail is to simply lose interest.
Had we stuck with the original plan, we'd have lost interest because we weren't doing what we enjoy.
title: Cut anything that isn't fun, because "the easiest way to fail is to simply lose interest."

text: **Optimize for your strongest performers**, not the average. (Pragmatic lessons from Elon.)
title: Optimize for your strongest performers

text: **Don't do measurable marketing.** "it's exactly because you can measure it that it gets saturated and you don't stand out and that's bad marketing in my opinion." No retargeting "from a brand perspective." (Executive Brand, auto-caption.) See Blind spots for the tension with measured growth experiments.
quotes: it's exactly because you can measure it that it gets saturated and you don't stand out and that's bad marketing in my opinion.

text: **Self-qualify your own advice.** The no-PM and no-deadline model gets easier "the closer you are to being a dev tool"; going all-in on one open-source project is "very bad advice for something that doesn't have competition that's making lots of revenue. So be very careful." Likewise: "This worked for us, but it isn't universally good advice." (Executive Brand; First 1,000 users.)

text: **Do more of what's working.** "In go-to-market, it's always tempting to explore new channels. However, in 2022, we really benefited from understanding where our growth was actually coming from, and doing more of those things." (CEO diary: 2022; Nail Self Serve: "So we should do more of what's working.")

text: **Growth team over outbound team.** "If we had hired a sales team, I guarantee we'd be focusing on how to send more cold emails more effectively versus the more leveraged work of improving our onboarding, activation and billing flows." One activation experiment: "one experiment has led to a 25% increase in our monthly growth, forever." (CEO diary: 2022.)

text: **Set customer-success targets on inputs.** One KR is "volume of deals in our target range per week - rather than trying to hit an overall revenue figure." (Nail Self Serve.)
quotes: volume of deals in our target range per week - rather than trying to hit an overall revenue figure.

text: **Sort customers by speed-to-close.** "Some customers are very fast (a couple of weeks, or less) to sell to, with minimal interaction, whereas others take months and are very intense." (Nail Self Serve.) Also track the anti-ICP: "Don't just monitor deals that close, but track those that are dragging on." (VC is a tool, not a religion.)

text: **Duplication is cheap, coordination is expensive.** "it's kind of like saying, oh, if I buy a Porsche, there's no point because a bird might poo on it"; just wipe it off. Mitigations: a demo section every all-hands and exec matchmaking; "There's only been like a couple of times where we've sort of built the same thing twice." (TL&W #189 transcript.)

text: **Guidance, not mandates.** The handbook gives engineers a method and a quarterly list, "this is just guidance. Like, you can ignore it if you think it's stupid." Failure rule: if an engineer keeps building off-guidance things and "their ideas are all failing, they are too rogue to work here effectively." (TL&W #189 transcript.)

(TL&W #189 transcript.)

text: **Outreach only before PMF.** "This was the only time we had to do outreach at PostHog. Once we had product market fit, this need disappeared." Channel choice: "WhatsApp / SMS > Email > LinkedIn, depending on if I had each person's contact details." (How we made something people want.)

text: **Pivot vs. persevere.** Strongly pro-pivot early: "Since most startups fail, you're probably doing something wrong if you don't pivot!" But "Fractional pivots are dangerous." (PMF game; What we've learned about PMF, house view.) Counterweight from his own pivots: "We stopped working on several ideas that probably could have worked out, if we'd been willing to persist." (A story about pivots.) On the PostHog idea: "What we didn't do was like sit cross-legged on the top of a mountain waiting for inspiration... we had to just build a bunch of things to find the thing we're excited about." (YC Podcast, auto-caption.) Hard test: "If you're pushing this hard and getting nowhere, you don't have the magic of product market fit." (A story about pivots.)

text: **How long to give a pivot test.** A one-month plan with a pre-committed kill: "If we failed to complete all four in a month, we would pivot again." They worked "from 9am to anywhere between midnight and 3am, 7 days a week," reached "300 deployments within a couple of days – five weeks after we started building," and he drew the lesson "Deadlines are motivating." (First 1,000 users.) He later adds: "I'd stress we had a hard 4-week deadline we'd set ourselves." (How we made something people want.) See Blind spots for the tension with no-deadline culture.

text: **How to price.** Usage-based, transparent, generous free tier, no "talk to sales." "Hobbyists or pre-PMF startups should be able to use PostHog for free" and "Be more generous than competitors, making it a no-brainer." (Pricing advice, house view.) "Match the cheapest for each individual product" (Handbook: how we make money). Over-simplified pricing "limits your ability to charge users for the value they receive." "Usage is a leap of faith... me kind of showing that I believe that you will find this product useful." (Churn.FM.) Self-critique: "that's probably something I would change. Like I might I would have charged a little bit sooner." (Executive Brand, auto-caption.)

text: **Who not to monetize.** "Trying to get money out of tiny startups would have been a mistake," because "We started by focussing on startups but realized our lowest churn teams were working on products that already had product market fit." (Pricing lessons, founders.)

We started by focussing on startups but realized our lowest churn teams were working on products that already had product market fit.

text: **When to charge for an open-source product.** In 2020 his stance was ubiquity first: "We'd advocate that the best way to build a really ambitious, fundable open source project is to get something to ubiquity before anything else." Rationale five years on: "none of the multi-billion dollar open-source companies I researched monetized in the first five years." Then the caveat that it "isn't universally good advice." (How we raised $3M; First 1,000 users.) In 2023 he says pre-announcing the paid tier on the pricing page from launch makes later charging not a betrayal (his paraphrased lesson), and "Charging customers for a product led to more usage." (VC is a tool, not a religion.)

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap (2020 to 2023, evolving).** 2020: choose VC for ambition: "when we're 80, we think we want to have taken a couple of big swings with our careers even if we don't own the whole pie." "Going for VC means you are committing to an exit or a failure." (How we raised $3M.) 2022, pro-VC: "Since PostHog raised Venture Capital (VC), we've had far less stress, and far more fun." "We decided it was more stressful to bootstrap than to raise VC." (Raising money is less stressful; VC is a tool.) Early on he judged bootstrapping "slow and dull for us" and capital "would always be a frustrating constraint." (Inflated risk.) He wants VC money with bootstrap values: "we're a VC backed company we have a lot of like the values of a bootstrap company" (Executive Brand.) 2023, restraint: "We raised over $27,000,000 then realized we should be growing out of our own revenue instead."

text: **Why VC is a tool, not a religion.** Hype loop: founder raises, VC sees social proof, users pick tech featured in TechCrunch, founder feels not raising "stupid." PostHog's seed was March 2020, Series A a month later, B about six months after, ending in "dark ages" of messy hiring. Developer math: "Normal companies probably should raise venture capital, since most grow by hiring a big sales team whilst the product tries to keep up. PostHog's main growth lever is shipping." Valid purposes: working capital, employee secondaries, an ideal board member. Bad reasons: "You want to hire people to find product market fit for you" / "You want to hire people to do the early sales for you" / "You want to raise money because of your ego". (VC is a tool; Raising money is less stressful.)
quotes: Normal companies probably should raise venture capital, since most grow by hiring a big sales team whilst the product tries to keep up. PostHog's main growth lever is shipping.
You want to hire people to find product market fit for you
You want to hire people to do the early sales for you
You want to raise money because of your ego
title: Why VC is a tool, not a religion

text: **Fundraising mechanics (2020 seed).** A 157-row investor sheet, ~200 calls of ~45 minutes in ~6 weeks, ~30 rejections (mostly "too early"), $3.025M closed with offers up to $5.5M, which they declined. SAFEs at a $12M post-money cap rising to $15M; planned $20M but did not because of covid recession risk. A $10k flip to a US parent: UK investors guessed ~$5M post-money against $15M in the US. Pipeline learning after four weeks: investors with open-source portfolios closed at an "astronomically higher" rate. Cold outreach failed; "investors who made the effort to reach out to us through another investor did end up making an offer." (How we raised $3M.)
quotes: investors who made the effort to reach out to us through another investor did end up making an offer.
title: Fundraising mechanics (2020 seed)

text: **How to pitch.** Be certain and opinionated: "If you act meek and ask investors to make up the price, you'll land very low. Go in high and you'll polarize people - which is what you need… a definite yes or definite no!" Seed-round confession in 2025: "we sucked at pitching. We're trying to people please I think too much" (about 160 firms met); it turned when "we started getting much more opinionated... Hey, like you're out of your mind if you think we're going to go big on like hiring a big sales team." (How we raised $3M; YC Podcast, auto-caption.) "just bear in mind the reason for rejection may not be the real reason." Do not stop for a crisis: "We promised ourselves that we would not use the virus as a reason to not raise."
quotes: If you act meek and ask investors to make up the price, you'll land very low. Go in high and you'll polarize people - which is what you need… a definite yes or definite no!

title: How to pitch

(Executive Brand, auto-caption.) Same lesson in 2020: their one cold message was ignored. (How we raised $3M.)

Usage doubling mid-raise helped, and he concludes "It would have been much harder if we were solo founders." Also admits network privilege: "I imagine this is quite socially harmful - if your network is weaker and further from the most decisive VCs, you will have a harder time raising money for your company." (How we raised $3M.)

text: **Revenue over fundraising when capacity-constrained.** In late 2021, paid-product demand and investor interest arrived together just as a serious family health matter took his time (he has written about it publicly; the details are personal and left out here). "We picked revenue." (What motivates me.) He chose the path that needed less of his own time rather than running a raise and a sales push at once.
quotes: We picked revenue.

text: **Personal crisis as a forcing function, not a pause.** During that family health matter he framed the next board meeting as a refusal to let it shrink the company's ambitions for anyone involved (CEO diary, Nov 2021; personal details omitted here). Remote work was what made it workable: "I was grateful that I was lucky enough to work from home and be present during these periods." The same diary already shows the input-metric habit: "Long term revenue is the output but we want to look upstream for a metric that is more controllable, with a faster feedback loop," via a lead-scoring algorithm on every deployment. On the revenue choice, later: "now a year and a half on, I'm very glad that's what we picked." They also declined hyped 2021 rounds: "we had demand, but ultimately chose not to move forward." Target: default alive and ~$10M ARR before raising again. (What motivates me; CEO diary: 2022; VC is a tool: "I felt that if I tried to sell and fundraise, I'd do both badly.")

A later round was easy: "perversely. It's easier... we spoke to one investor for this round." The platform bet: become "upstream of every piece of software they'll ever buy." (Crunchbase; Series D; YC Podcast.) Tension with 2023 restraint is recorded in Blind spots.

text: **When to hire a sales team.** For developers, essentially never. "I can't think of a worse group to target this way (this is coming from a place of experience as I've run outbound sales teams before)." "Nearly all our sales are self-serve and 70% of our customers find us through word-of-mouth growth." (CEO diary: 2022; Handbook: low prices.) Exception stated in 2020 in house "we" voice: "operating a B2B company without a Sales team does become impractical at a large scale." And a 2024 footnote concedes the company later built a sales and customer-success team, with the golden rule "the person who closes a deal also manages that relationship long term."

text: **Founders are the best sellers.** "A founder is, regardless of experience, the best person in the world to sell the product they made." (PMF game.) The 2024 restatement and its rules are under Mental models: founder-led sales.

text: **When a startup should do sales anyway.** Founder-led and pre-PMF: "You have one job as a founder: get to product-market fit. Outsourcing your sales will make this harder." even "if you think you'll be product-led eventually, it may be better to start with a sales-led motion, so you can learn more about your early prospects"; self-serve "would have made finding product-market fit more difficult" in the early days. Key rule: "In sales meetings, you are aiming to close down objections, and steer the customer... In product meetings, you want to let users meander." Existing customers first: "Looking after your existing customers should be your number one priority." (How to do startup sales.)

text: **How to get first meetings.** Easiest to hardest: friends and family; people you've worked with; social posts; customized LinkedIn DMs; customized cold emails; posting where users hang out. Did not work: events ("I found it awkward, but that might be a me thing") and automated outreach. (How to do startup sales.) His own first users: friends, family, the phone book, LinkedIn connections and "every developer I'd ever worked with via LinkedIn", hand-written, "All messages were totally customized to the person. Nothing automated." (How we made something people want.)

every developer I'd ever worked with via LinkedIn

text: **Who to sell to.** Engineers, not sales leaders: "building for sales people or sales leaders in particular, I feel the signal to noise ratio is pretty poor." Confirmed by deals: "if it's an engineer leading this stuff, it gets better implemented. It sells way faster." (YC Podcast; Churn.FM.) Principle: "The best products are generally built for end users." and "we want an engineer in any size organization on Earth to be able to use our software in production without getting up from their desk." (Nail Self Serve.)

text: **When to fire.** Decisively but humanely, and visibly: "our number one goal if we let someone go is that they see it coming"; "It's a team, not a family." (Executive Brand, auto-caption.) The "team, rather than a family" framing enables swift performance-based exits, balanced by "Paying generous severance (four months) to people we let go." The bargain: "we pay 4 months severance because our attitude is letting people go earlier is better for everyone and a big payout for them is kinder in return." Sharing why: "we received positive feedback from our team when we explained why we made these decisions, transparently." (Pragmatic lessons from Elon; CEO diary: 2022.) He holds this partly because of VC: "I doubt we'd have made that call if we were bootstrapped. We simply think it's cheaper to spend money here than to have an underperformer stay for longer because we feel bad." (Raising money is less stressful.)
