text: **Harsh internal culture — now documented at Blue Origin too, not just Amazon.** Brad Stone's "The Everything Store" (2013) documents a demanding, sometimes brutal Amazon management style. A parallel and separately sourced picture emerges at Blue Origin: a 2021 essay co-signed by 21 current and former employees alleged a "toxic workplace where 'professional dissent' is 'actively stifled'" and sexist behavior by certain male leaders (CNN Business, Oct 2021). CNN independently corroborates a company-distributed list of perceived "troublemakers," an internal 2018 memo proposing Blue Origin adopt SpaceX-style culture in which "burnout is part of their labor strategy," and a senior engineer's April 2020 resignation letter over "schedule-biased drive [that] is incapable of producing safe systems engineering" — directly contradicting Blue Origin's official "tortoise," safety-first brand identity. Former head of employee communications Alexandra Abrams, fired in 2019, ties the company's post-2018 use of forced-arbitration clauses directly to Bezos himself: "I was like, 'Wow, now I see how the most powerful person in the world uses their power. They use it to continually shore up their position and disempower people around them.'" [CNN Business]

text: **The conflicted owner — Washington Post, now with three dated, named 2025 incidents.** In 2026 Bezos ordered layoffs of roughly a third of the Post's staff, defending it as needing to "stand on its own two feet." More granular and more recent: NPR's October 2025 reporting (David Folkenflik) found the Post's editorial page took institutional positions favorable to Bezos's own financial interests without disclosure at least three times in two weeks — defending Trump's White House ballroom construction (Amazon a "major corporate contributor" to costs, disclosed only after outside pressure), endorsing small nuclear reactors as "a worthy gamble" (Amazon holds a stake in X-energy; Bezos personally in a nuclear-fusion venture), and opposing D.C. self-driving-car regulation (Amazon-owned Zoox had just announced D.C. as its next market). Ruth Marcus, the paper's former deputy editorial-page editor, resigned in 2025 and called the pattern "concerning – whether out of negligence or worse." Bezos's own words, quoted by NPR: "When it comes to the appearance of conflict, I am not an ideal owner of The Post," and, self-aware: "I once wrote that The Post is a 'complexifier' for me. It is, but it turns out I'm also a complexifier for The Post." A 2022-era Columbia Journalism Review analysis (Dan Froomkin) supplies the more theoretically serious version of this critique: media scholar Robert McChesney argues "Bezos didn't need to make any changes; the Post had already adopted the establishment, pro-corporate view," and proposes Bezos adopt a Le Monde-style ownership ethics charter — which he has not. [NPR ×2; CJR]

text: Co-founder/CEO of Nvidia for 30+ years (the longest-running tech CEO), Huang is the operator's case for *conviction under suffering*: re-derive every problem from first principles against the "speed of light" physical limit, broadcast strategy to 60 direct reports instead of hoarding it, and ride a decade of losses on a bet (CUDA, "the house that GeForce built") because "did physics change?" is the only question that matters. His lens is accelerated computing and "AI factories" whose output is tokens — "compute equals revenues" — not infrastructure for its own sake, built on a virtuous-cycle mechanism he now names explicitly and extends beyond CUDA to AI itself. His sharpest contrarian positions: suffering forges greatness ("I'd rather torture you into greatness") while paradoxically insisting leadership requires public vulnerability, not infallibility; export controls on China have "already largely backfired" even by his own more concessive 2026 account, and Nvidia has "evacuated"/"largely conceded" the China AI-chip market rather than merely disputing the policy; AI automates *tasks*, not *purposes*, so it creates more jobs, not fewer; and the AI capex wave is "the largest infrastructure build-out in human history," not a bubble — a claim now contested not just by vendor-financing critics (Goldman/Wedbush/Mizuho) but by short-sellers attacking a different mechanism entirely (Michael Burry and Jim Chanos, on hyperscaler depreciation schedules) and by France's competition regulator, which reads the exact CUDA "virtuous cycle" Huang celebrates as a theory of antitrust harm. He opposes information-hoarding hierarchs, China-hawk policymakers ("a badge of shame"), realist zero-sum framings of great-power competition (implicitly rejecting Mearsheimer), fellow AI-CEOs who scare the public with unhedged doom percentages, AI-doomers/bubble-callers, and anyone who plans incrementally instead of from zero.

text:
Jensen Huang was born in Taiwan; at five his father took an engineering job helping start an oil refinery in Thailand, and after a 1973 coup his parents — who "never been to United States" and had little money — sent him and his ten-year-old brother alone to the only school an uncle could find that took foreign students and that the family could afford: a boarding school in Oneida, Kentucky, in what Huang calls "the poorest county in America" then and now. He was nine. Conditions were spare ("no drawers and no closet doors... just like a prison... everybody had knives, everybody smoked") and his chores included "cleaning toilets for a dorm of a hundred boys" while his older brother worked a tobacco farm; the brothers stayed connected to their parents for two years via re-recorded cassette tapes, one of which describes a family's first McDonald's as though it were "the future" ("the food comes in a box... the hamburger is incredible"). His parents arrived in America with nothing but a suitcase and "the money they had in their pocket" — his mother worked as a maid at a Catholic school, his father as a consulting engineer found through newspaper classified ads — and the family's one vacation was a milk-crate-and-carpet ride in a seatless van from Oregon to Disneyland. Huang calls himself "the first generation of the American dream" and, more directly, "the embodiment of the American dream."
He studied electrical engineering at Oregon State, where he met his wife Lori by strategically enrolling in her lab section to narrow "the competition from 250 [boys] to 4," then delivering "the ultimate pickup line" — asking if she wanted to see his homework. He worked at AMD, which paid his tuition for a Stanford master's he took roughly eight years to finish ("the longest-running student at Stanford... nobody paid Stanford more for the education"). In 1993 he co-founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem at a Denny's in East San Jose ("It had all the coffee you could drink and no one could chase you out"), having worked as a Denny's dishwasher, busboy, and waiter as a teenager in Portland ("No one can carry more coffee cups than I can"). The founding bet was a first-principles wager on parallel, simulation-shaped computation — "computer graphics is basically a simulation of the world... the computation of simulation can be done... largely in parallel," unlike a CPU's step-by-step "recipe" — against 64 years of general-purpose CPU dominance; Huang calls the resulting business plan "impossible to fund," financed anyway by Sequoia and Sutter Hill. Nvidia nearly died at least twice: once early on, when Huang used half the company's last ~$1M in cash to buy a defunct rival's chip emulator and talked TSMC's Morris Chang into skipping the standard validate-before-produce step on an unproven chip (RIVA 128) — "Nobody has ever done that before" — a gamble that made Nvidia "the fastest growing technology company in history to go from zero to $1 billion"; and again during the decade-plus CUDA bet, when the stock cratered (accounts vary in the exact figure — "down to like one and a half billion dollars" by one telling, "down to like two or three billion... from about twelve" by another) while, in his words, "nobody believed in it... we suffered our way here... because nobody believed in it."
By 2025-2026 Nvidia repeatedly traded as one of the most valuable companies on earth, the dominant supplier of AI training and inference hardware — and the subject of a French antitrust probe examining the very CUDA "virtuous cycle" Huang treats as legitimate ecosystem value. Huang says the company runs on chronic vigilance rather than confidence: "the phrase '30 days from going out of business' I've used for 33 years... every morning... the sense of vulnerability, the sense of uncertainty, the sense of insecurity. It doesn't leave you." His public persona — leather jacket, marathon keynotes, blunt and folksy, self-correcting live on stage — now carries both the AI-buildout narrative and its sharpest critiques: bubble/circular-financing, hyperscaler depreciation-schedule risk, antitrust exposure, and a demanding, sometimes-burnout-adjacent internal culture cushioned by extraordinary equity upside.

title: Fear of failure, not desire for success, is the actual driver

text: **Leadership requires vulnerability, not infallibility.** "There's nothing inconsistent with being a leader and being vulnerable... the more vulnerable we are as a leader, the more able other people are able to tell you [things]... the more able we're actually able to pivot. If we put ourselves into this superhuman capability, then it's hard for us to pivot strategy because we were supposed to be right all along." Sits in productive tension with "torture them into greatness" — demanding of others' work, admittedly uncertain of his own judgment (see Voice & style). (Rogan #2422, Dec 2025.)
quotes: There's nothing inconsistent with being a leader and being vulnerable... the more vulnerable we are as a leader, the more able other people are able to tell you [things]... the more able we're actually able to pivot. If we put ourselves into this superhuman capability, then it's hard for us to pivot strategy because we were supposed to be right all along.
torture them into greatness
title: Leadership requires vulnerability, not infallibility

text: **Information is not power; sharing context is power.** "I don't believe in a culture, in an environment where the information that you possess is the reason why you have power." (Stanford GSB.) This underwrites the flat org and the no-succession-plan stance: continuously transfer knowledge instead of hoarding it.
quotes: I don't believe in a culture, in an environment where the information that you possess is the reason why you have power.
title: Information is not power; sharing context is power

text: **Beliefs should be stable; reactions should not.** His crisis test: "What do you believe? … Did something change? The stock price changed, but did something else change? Did physics change? Did gravity change? Did all of the things that we assumed that we believed that led to our decision, did any of those things change? Because if those things changed, you've got to change everything. But if none of those things changed, you change nothing, keep on going." (Stanford GSB.)
quotes: What do you believe? … Did something change? The stock price changed, but did something else change? Did physics change? Did gravity change? Did all of the things that we assumed that we believed that led to our decision, did any of those things change? Because if those things changed, you've got to change everything. But if none of those things changed, you change nothing, keep on going.
title: Beliefs should be stable; reactions should not

text: **A company needs a unifying theory.** Speed comes from coherence: "The reason why Nvidia can move so fast is because we always have a unifying theory for the company." (Stratechery, 2026.) The company itself is "the machinery… that produces the output," and "the architecture of the company should reflect the environment." (Lex Fridman, 2026.)
quotes: The reason why Nvidia can move so fast is because we always have a unifying theory for the company.
the machinery… that produces the output,
the architecture of the company should reflect the environment.
title: A company needs a unifying theory

text: **The mission is long; he intends to die on the job.** Continuity comes from constant teaching, not a named heir — see Decision heuristics and Positions.
title: The mission is long; he intends to die on the job

text: **First-principles re-derivation.** Strip a problem back to zero rather than patching the prior plan. *Worked example:* on the Lex Fridman podcast he describes rejecting incremental wins: "I don't like going into a problem and somebody says… 'it takes 74 days to do this today… And we can do it for you in 72 days.' I'd rather strip it all back to zero." His framing question (Stanford GSB): "Given the conditions today, given my motivation, given the instruments, the tools, given how things have changed, how would I redo this?" (Lex Fridman 2026; Stanford GSB.)
quotes: I don't like going into a problem and somebody says… 'it takes 74 days to do this today… And we can do it for you in 72 days.' I'd rather strip it all back to zero.
Given the conditions today, given my motivation, given the instruments, the tools, given how things have changed, how would I redo this?
title: First-principles re-derivation

text: **Simulation-shaped vs. recipe-shaped computation.** The physics-of-computation argument underneath every other co-design claim: parallel hardware suits problems that are inherently simultaneous, not sequential. *Worked example:* "Computer graphics is basically a simulation of the world. It's a simulation problem. In a lot of ways, artificial intelligence is a simulation of the mind... a recipe is step 1, step 2, step 3. In the case of simulation, the world is happening concurrently and in parallel all at the same time right now." This is the categorical reason GPUs, not just faster CPUs, were ever necessary. (Hoover/Rice, 2026.)
quotes: Computer graphics is basically a simulation of the world. It's a simulation problem. In a lot of ways, artificial intelligence is a simulation of the mind... a recipe is step 1, step 2, step 3. In the case of simulation, the world is happening concurrently and in parallel all at the same time right now.
title: Simulation-shaped vs. recipe-shaped computation

text: **"Speed of light" planning baseline.** Set targets against the physical limit, not competitors or last year. *Worked example:* "The speed of light is my shorthand for what's the limit of what physics can do… Memory speed, math speed, power, cost, time, effort, number of people, manufacturing cycle time." Everything below that limit is slack to attack. Later given a literal silicon instantiation: Vera's CPU fabric runs "at... 3.6 terabytes per second. No chiplet stacks, no chip boundary crossings" — his planning metaphor built directly into the chip. (Lex Fridman, 2026; GTC Taipei 2026.)
quotes: Speed of light
The speed of light is my shorthand for what's the limit of what physics can do… Memory speed, math speed, power, cost, time, effort, number of people, manufacturing cycle time.
at... 3.6 terabytes per second. No chiplet stacks, no chip boundary crossings
title: "Speed of light" planning baseline

text: **Extreme co-design.** Optimize every layer of the stack simultaneously because the problem no longer fits one chip. *Worked example:* "We're optimizing across the entire stack of software from architectures to chips, to systems, to system software, to the algorithms, to the applications" — because "the problem no longer fits inside one computer to be accelerated by one GPU… you would like it to go a million times faster." Nvidia validates a full rack/pod/data-center system in a digital twin before "a single rack lands." Quantified: NVLink72 (Grace Blackwell) delivers "ten times the performance" over the H200 "when it's only twice the number of transistors" (SemiAnalysis benchmark); Rubin reduces token costs "by a factor of ten over Blackwell... even though the number of transistors we used was only 1.7 times." (Lex Fridman 2026; Stratechery 2026; GTC Washington, D.C. 2025; CNBC/Jon Fortt 2026.)
quotes: We're optimizing across the entire stack of software from architectures to chips, to systems, to system software, to the algorithms, to the applications
the problem no longer fits inside one computer to be accelerated by one GPU… you would like it to go a million times faster.
a single rack lands.
ten times the performance
when it's only twice the number of transistors
by a factor of ten over Blackwell... even though the number of transistors we used was only 1.7 times.
title: Extreme co-design

text: **Scale up before you scale out.** Solve the hardest, most extreme version of the compute-density problem first (disaggregation, liquid cooling, NVLink) rather than defaulting to commodity horizontal scaling. *Worked example:* "there's no replacement for scaling up before you scale out. Both are important, but you want to scale up first." The multi-generation Ranger→Grace Blackwell NVLink72 hardware story is the proof; had Nvidia instead brute-forced commodity scale-out, "deep learning would've never happened" on power/cost grounds. (GTC San Jose, March 2025.)
quotes: there's no replacement for scaling up before you scale out. Both are important, but you want to scale up first.
deep learning would've never happened
title: Scale up before you scale out

text: **The Frontier Pareto (AI-factory config optimization).** Every data-center config choice trades tokens/sec-per-user (quality of service) against tokens/sec-for-the-whole-factory (throughput/revenue); millions of configurations exist, and the goal is the outer edge of that trade-off, run at the point that balances the two. *Worked example:* "Underneath the Pareto, the Frontier Pareto... are millions of points we could have configured the data center to do... which is the reason why... you want a programmable architecture that is as homogeneously fungible as possible because the workload changes so dramatically across the entire frontier." A more mechanistic sibling to the tokenomics model below — not just "tokens=revenue" but "there is a whole optimization frontier, and only a fungible architecture can reach it." (GTC San Jose, March 2025.)
quotes: Underneath the Pareto, the Frontier Pareto... are millions of points we could have configured the data center to do... which is the reason why... you want a programmable architecture that is as homogeneously fungible as possible because the workload changes so dramatically across the entire frontier.
there is a whole optimization frontier, and only a fungible architecture can reach it.
title: The Frontier Pareto (AI-factory config optimization)

text: **Flat org, ~60 direct reports, no 1:1s.** Broadcast context; don't ration it. *Worked example:* "My direct staff is 60 people. You know, I don't have one-on-ones with 'em because it's impossible." Almost everything he says, he says to everyone at once — "we present a problem and all of us attack it, because we're doing extreme co-design… all the time." (Lex Fridman, 2026; Stanford GSB.)
quotes: My direct staff is 60 people. You know, I don't have one-on-ones with 'em because it's impossible.
we present a problem and all of us attack it, because we're doing extreme co-design… all the time.
title: Flat org, ~60 direct reports, no 1:1s

text: **Manifest the future, then endure the gap to it.** Conviction precedes proof. *Worked example:* "When I believe it in my mind… You manifest a future and that future is so convincing, there's no way it won't happen. There's a lot of suffering in between, but you've gotta believe what you believe." He pairs this with persuasion: "Oftentimes, I've already made up my mind, but I'll take every possible opportunity… to shape everybody else's belief system." Given an organizational, teachable form at Hoover/Rice: "the hard part, of course, is that you're endeavoring something that has no positive feedback, no external motivation... you have to tell the story so that everybody else could see it in their mind's eye and you have to believe it yourself." (Lex Fridman, 2026; Hoover/Rice, 2026.)
quotes: When I believe it in my mind… You manifest a future and that future is so convincing, there's no way it won't happen. There's a lot of suffering in between, but you've gotta believe what you believe.
Oftentimes, I've already made up my mind, but I'll take every possible opportunity… to shape everybody else's belief system.

the hard part, of course, is that you're endeavoring something that has no positive feedback, no external motivation... you have to tell the story so that everybody else could see it in their mind's eye and you have to believe it yourself.
title: Manifest the future, then endure the gap to it

text: **"If we don't build it, they can't come."** An explicit inversion of *Field of Dreams*, and the plainest public articulation of why Nvidia invests years ahead of demonstrated demand. *Worked example:* on the mid-2000s deep-learning bet: "No one knew how far deep learning could scale, and if we didn't build it, we'd never know... Our logic is: If we don't build it, they can't come." (NVIDIA Blog, Caltech commencement, June 2024.)
quotes: If we don't build it, they can't come.
No one knew how far deep learning could scale, and if we didn't build it, we'd never know... Our logic is: If we don't build it, they can't come.
title: "If we don't build it, they can't come."

text: **Surf the waves.** Distinct from "manifest the future": manifesting sets the target; surfing describes moment-to-moment adaptive execution once you're already in motion, under a hundred unknowable variables. *Worked example:* "You have to invent a future where a hundred variables are included and there's no way you could be right on all of them... You're surfing waves of technology and innovation. You can't predict the waves. You got to deal with the ones you have." (Rogan #2422, Dec 2025.)
quotes: manifest the future

You have to invent a future where a hundred variables are included and there's no way you could be right on all of them... You're surfing waves of technology and innovation. You can't predict the waves. You got to deal with the ones you have.
title: Surf the waves

text: **Betting the company, repeatedly.** *Worked example:* CUDA was "the first strategic decision that is as close to an existential threat" — "It took a decade… but I carried CUDA on GeForce… Nvidia is the house that GeForce built," through a market cap that fell sharply (tellings vary — see Provenance notes). He says of NVLink: "if we didn't do it, nobody else would have." An earlier, more mechanical near-death moment: buying a defunct rival's last chip emulator with half of Nvidia's remaining ~$1M cash to pre-validate the unproven RIVA 128 chip, then persuading TSMC's Morris Chang to skip the standard validate-before-produce step — "Nobody has ever done that before... TSMC decided to support me... probably because they didn't have that many other customers anyway" — result: "we became the fastest growing technology company in history to go from zero to $1 billion." (Lex Fridman 2026; Dwarkesh; Rogan #2422.)

It took a decade… but I carried CUDA on GeForce… Nvidia is the house that GeForce built,
if we didn't do it, nobody else would have.
Nobody has ever done that before... TSMC decided to support me... probably because they didn't have that many other customers anyway
we became the fastest growing technology company in history to go from zero to $1 billion.
title: Betting the company, repeatedly

text: **Zero-billion-dollar markets.** Prefer creating a market that doesn't exist to fighting in a commoditizing one; retreat to do it. *Worked example:* "To retreat from a giant phone market to create a zero billion dollar robotics market." (NTU 2023.) The origin story is sharper and less voluntary than the slogan suggests: "one year we were kicked out of those markets... With no more markets to turn to, we decided to build something where we are sure there are no customers... because one of the things you can definitely guarantee is where there are no customers, there are also no competitors." (NVIDIA Blog, Caltech commencement, 2024.)
quotes: To retreat from a giant phone market to create a zero billion dollar robotics market.

one year we were kicked out of those markets... With no more markets to turn to, we decided to build something where we are sure there are no customers... because one of the things you can definitely guarantee is where there are no customers, there are also no competitors.
title: Zero-billion-dollar markets

text: **"Either you're running for food or running from becoming food… Either way, run!"** Ambient urgency regardless of position. *Worked example:* his entire NTU 2023 address built around perpetual motion; recycled at CMU 2026 as "Run, don't walk" toward AI. (NTU 2023; NVIDIA Blog CMU 2026.)

Run, don't walk
title: "Either you're running for food or running from becoming food… Either way, run!"

text: **"The more you buy, the more you save."** TCO argument for accelerated computing — higher upfront cost, lower total cost/time/energy per task. *Worked example:* on stage at Computex 2024 he winked at his own slide: "That's called CEO math. It's not accurate, but it is correct." The mechanism behind the wink, given explicitly two years later: "Software developers start with NVIDIA CUDA. And by definition, therefore, the ecosystem, the useful asset is going to be much longer... If the life of the asset is long, the TCO is low" — ecosystem breadth is the causal reason the higher sticker price pays off. (Tom Warren / The Verge; GTC Taipei 2026.)
quotes: The more you buy, the more you save.
That's called CEO math. It's not accurate, but it is correct.
Software developers start with NVIDIA CUDA. And by definition, therefore, the ecosystem, the useful asset is going to be much longer... If the life of the asset is long, the TCO is low
title: "The more you buy, the more you save."

text: **"Price it at zero" — the TCO argument as a competitive weapon.** A sharper, fully-worked extension for reading rival free/subsidized chips: "Even if they gave it to you for free, you only have two gigawatts to work with. Your opportunity cost is so insanely high, you would always choose the best performance per watt" — a ~30x performance-per-watt gap dwarfs any ~10-15 point gross-margin discount a rival ASIC vendor could offer. (BG2 Pod, Sept 2025.)
quotes: Price it at zero
Even if they gave it to you for free, you only have two gigawatts to work with. Your opportunity cost is so insanely high, you would always choose the best performance per watt
title: "Price it at zero" — the TCO argument as a competitive weapon

text: **Tokens-as-revenue (tokenomics).** A data center is a token factory; throughput-per-watt is the P&L. *Worked example:* at GTC 2026 he tied capacity directly to customer revenue — "If they could just get more capacity, they could generate more tokens, their revenues would go up." (CNBC, 2026.) He extends it internally: a "$500,000 engineer… should be consuming at least $250,000 worth of tokens annually," and an engineer running a mere "$5,000 annual AI token bill" makes him want to "go ape." (All-In at GTC 2026 / R&D World.)
quotes: If they could just get more capacity, they could generate more tokens, their revenues would go up.
$500,000 engineer… should be consuming at least $250,000 worth of tokens annually,
$5,000 annual AI token bill
title: Tokens-as-revenue (tokenomics)

text: **Tokens as a universal, modality-agnostic representation.** A prior, more basic claim than tokenomics — about ontology, not revenue. *Worked example:* "The computer doesn't know and doesn't care what kind of tokens it's generating. It could be generating a language token. It could be generating a video token... a steering wheel activation token, or... a finger articulation grasp token. The computer in the final analysis is just a bunch of numbers." This is the conceptual bridge he uses to argue humanoid robotics is imminent: if a generative model can predict a hand picking up a cup on video, the same architecture predicts a *robot's* hand picking up a cup. (GTC Taipei 2026; CNBC/Jon Fortt 2026 — repeated near-verbatim across both, indicating a rehearsed, load-bearing line.)
quotes: The computer doesn't know and doesn't care what kind of tokens it's generating. It could be generating a language token. It could be generating a video token... a steering wheel activation token, or... a finger articulation grasp token. The computer in the final analysis is just a bunch of numbers.
title: Tokens as a universal, modality-agnostic representation

text: **Retrieval-based computing vs. generative computing.** The resource-demand argument underneath "AI factories," one level more basic still. *Worked example:* "The way we used to do computing is essentially retrieval-based computing. We would pre-record information... and... go and retrieve that file for you... the way that we do computing now with artificial intelligence is... generative computing" — every request regenerates a largely new answer from a seed, which is why "we need so much more computation instead of a bunch of storage." Contrast case: recommender systems/search (retrieval) vs. a prompted brief or summary (generative). (SCSP/Memos to the President, April 2026.)
quotes: The way we used to do computing is essentially retrieval-based computing. We would pre-record information... and... go and retrieve that file for you... the way that we do computing now with artificial intelligence is... generative computing
we need so much more computation instead of a bunch of storage.
title: Retrieval-based computing vs. generative computing

text: **Agent = Model (brain) + Harness (body) + Tools/Skills (workshop) + Runtime (OS).** The architecture-level model behind Nvidia's 2026 product line. *Worked example:* "it is an agent, which consists of a large language model... sitting inside a harness, and that harness helps it, orchestrates it, to do productive work... You can think of the model as the brain, the harness as the body, the tools that it uses — working in a runtime, think of it as a workshop. So this is a person, a worker working with tools in a workshop." Instantiated as Nvidia's own stack (Nemotron models, Open Shell harness, CUDA-X tools, Vera runtime). He credits **Codex and Claude Code by name** as the best-in-class harnesses driving the model-to-agent leap: "we're big fans of Codex... and... Claude Code obviously incredibly good." (GTC Taipei 2026; SCSP, April 2026.)
quotes: it is an agent, which consists of a large language model... sitting inside a harness, and that harness helps it, orchestrates it, to do productive work... You can think of the model as the brain, the harness as the body, the tools that it uses — working in a runtime, think of it as a workshop. So this is a person, a worker working with tools in a workshop.
we're big fans of Codex... and... Claude Code obviously incredibly good.
title: Agent = Model (brain) + Harness (body) + Tools/Skills (workshop) + Runtime (OS)

text: **Three categories of chips: architectural, ASIC, and "COT" (customer-owned tooling).** A named framework for reading rival chip strategy. *Worked example:* "architectural" chips (x86/ARM CPUs, Nvidia GPUs) carry "rich IP and rich ecosystem"; "ASICs" work "when the market size is not very large" but "charge you 50, 60 points of margin"; once a market is large enough, it graduates to COT — "where will TPUs go when it becomes a large business? Customer owned tooling, there's no question about it," with Apple's own smartphone chip as the precedent. (BG2 Pod, Sept 2025.)

when the market size is not very large
charge you 50, 60 points of margin
where will TPUs go when it becomes a large business? Customer owned tooling, there's no question about it,
title: Three categories of chips: architectural, ASIC, and "COT" (customer-owned tooling)

text: **Build vertically, then open horizontally — with the tradeoff named explicitly.** Ship an integrated full stack, then let customers adopt only the layers they want. *Worked example (adoption strategy):* "We create a thing vertically and then we open it horizontally so everybody could use whatever piece they would like." (Stratechery, 2026.) *Worked example (naming the actual cost of openness, not just its benefit):* "If it were to be proprietary... closed... we'll have the benefit of monetizing the entire layer and the entire stack. But it prevents our ability to be open... I really love that our company has the ability to work with everybody" — an explicit, rare admission that Nvidia forgoes full-stack monetization for reach, applied concretely to adding Anthropic alongside OpenAI, xAI, and Google as 2026 model partners. (CNBC/Jon Fortt, Jan 2026.)

text: **Win all five layers, or lose the stack — now named ("five-layer cake") and ranked.** AI dominance is layered (energy, chips, infrastructure, models, applications) and the layers reinforce each other; cede one and you weaken all five — the structural logic behind his export-control argument. See Core ideas for the full quote and ranking. (Stratechery, 2025-2026; Hoover/Rice 2026; GTC Washington, D.C. 2025.)

text: **Task vs. purpose, fully worked (two parables).** *Radiology parable:* "10 years ago, somebody predicted that the first job that's going to go... is radiologists. That job is gone forever... The prediction was 100% right [that] AI has now permeated every aspect of radiology. The only thing that was wrong was the prediction. Radiologists are in short supply" — because "the task that we do... is programming... [but] the purpose of the job is not programming... The radiologists' purpose in life is to diagnose disease. Reading scans is a task." *Software-engineer parable, with hard numbers:* GitHub commits went "300 million" (2023) → "400 million" (2024) → "500 million" (2025) → nearly tripling in early 2026 across "30 million software developers representing about $3 trillion worth of GDP" — "effectively a $9 trillion productivity from $3 trillion of salaries," so "why wouldn't you want to hire more software engineers?" *Self-referential test, repeated verbatim across two separate 2026 speeches:* "if you apply that to me, you would come to the conclusion what Jensen does for a living is tap on phones and talk... AI has done that just fine. And therefore, my job should be gone. But I'm busier than ever." (GTC Taipei 2026; SCSP, April 2026 — cross-confirmed wording in both.)

text: **"Cautious optimist" — a named third stance.** Distinct from wild-eyed techno-optimism and from doomerism: "Cautious optimist... we have to be cautious so that we advance the technology as quickly as we can so that it works as we promised, so that it's functional as we expect, so that it doesn't produce intelligence that sounds like it's intelligence, but it's not. It's flawed. Functional things are safer." Reframes "caution" as a reliability-engineering question (does it work correctly?), not a pace-of-deployment question (should we slow down?). (Hoover/Rice, 2026.)

text: **EOIFS — early indicators of future success.** Before revenue exists, look for non-financial signals (research papers, real problem-solving, meaningful work) to decide whether to keep investing. *Worked example:* his stated test for continuing the pre-revenue CUDA/datacenter bet. (Stanford GSB.)

text: **Show your reasoning, not just your conclusion** — "I reason about things step by step by step… I'll take every possible opportunity to shape everybody else's belief system." Teaching scales judgment across the org. (Lex Fridman; Stanford GSB.)

My sales guys are going, 'Oh no, don't say that.'" (Lex Fridman; Dwarkesh; GTC San Jose 2025.)

text: **Don't plan succession; transfer knowledge daily.** "I don't believe in succession planning… if you care about the future of the company after you, then you should transfer knowledge, information, insight, skill, and experience as frequently and as continuously as you can today." (Lex Fridman, 2026.)

text: Folksy, blunt, repetitive *by design* — he hammers a small set of phrases ("pain and suffering," "speed of light," "the more you buy the more you save," "no task is beneath me," "run!," "compute equals revenues," the task-vs-purpose self-test) until they become company doctrine, and some lines recur near-verbatim across venues months apart, confirming they're rehearsed stock arguments rather than ad-libs. He teaches by narrating his own reasoning in real time ("I reason about things step by step by step") rather than handing down conclusions, and explicitly uses every conversation to "shape everybody else's belief system." He is comfortable correcting himself live and immediately on stage ("that was wrong") and joking at his own expense ("I'm the chief revenue destroyer"), which sits alongside — rather than contradicts — his demanding, "torture them into greatness" persona: he pairs relentless criticism of others' output with explicit, repeated claims that leadership requires his own vulnerability and fallibility ("we were supposed to be right all along" is the failure mode he's naming, not his own posture). His register shifts markedly by venue: internal pep talks and analytical interviews (Stanford GSB, Lex Fridman) lean into suffering and conquest; commencement addresses and anniversary events (Caltech, the Denny's return) lean into gratitude, humility, and even a gentler, non-suffering parable (a Kyoto moss gardener, "prioritize your life, and you will have plenty of time"). Reaches for engineering metaphors as moral and historical ones — "speed of light," "co-design," "the house that GeForce built," naming an operating system "Dynamo" after the device that "started the last industrial revolution," the company as "machinery that produces the output." Warm and loyalty-driven beneath the demanding exterior; frames harshness as belief in the person, "just like a Taiwanese parent." On mortality and legacy he is startlingly direct rather than evasive ("I really don't want to die"; "die on the job"); on his own motivations he is equally direct that fear, not ambition, drives him ("I just want to stay alive, Joe").

text: Critiques are sourced to Nvidia's own SEC risk factors, named short-sellers (Burry, Chanos) and sell-side analysts, and a named foreign competition regulator — not to the subject's self-description.

Jonas Marques Neto is the first CEO of Pague Menos (Brazil's second-largest drugstore chain, B3: PGMN3) from outside the founding Queirós family — a clinical psychologist and 30-year pharma-multinational executive (Roche, Bayer, Stiefel/GSK, Isdin, across Brazil, Italy, and Oceania) nicknamed the **"CEO-psicólogo"** by Brazilian business press for running a debt-laden retail turnaround through the lens of clinical diagnosis rather than a spreadsheet. His sharpest, most contrarian move is procedural, not rhetorical: on taking office he deliberately looked at *people before numbers* — touring 26,000 employees in randomized five-person listening groups before opening a single financial report — and let that listening tour, not a consultant's diagnostic, surface the two decisions that made his reputation: buying 1,500 air conditioners and 500 microwave ovens for stores where staff had been warming lunch at a neighboring gas station, and rejecting a straightforwardly profitable proposal to sell non-alcoholic beer because it could "gateway" a pharmacy customer into alcohol. He runs on named frameworks borrowed wholesale from outside pharmacy retail — Jim Collins's brutal facts, Karpman's drama triangle, Amy Edmondson's psychological safety, Bain's Founders Mentality, his own aviation-honed "complacency kills" — and insists none of it trades off financial discipline: the same CEO who calls his own numbers "smoke" ("fumaça mental") also drove net debt/EBITDA from ~4.2x to under 2x and refuses to loosen store-opening discipline even after a capital raise ("behaving in scarcity"). He tends to disagree, implicitly, with numbers-first turnaround operators (a sharp contrast with Magalu's Frederico Trajano, who states plainly "Fred só quer saber de margem") and with blunt, radical-candor management cultures, favoring instead a therapeutic, feedback-is-a-gift register — a positioning that is still, as of Q1 2026, coexisting with real financial friction (an EPS miss driven by financial expenses, leverage still above sector peers) that the warmly promotional Brazilian business press covering him has mostly declined to press him on directly.

text: Jonas Marques Neto was born and raised in Ceará in a lower-middle-class family of public servants, and describes himself as "sempre hiperativo, questionador" [always hyperactive, questioning] from childhood — he financed a home-video production business at 15, filming weddings, baptisms, and, by his own count, more than 100 births, before choosing psychology at university (Forbes Brasil). He practiced as a clinical psychologist, treating adults and children on the autism spectrum, and traces his entire later management philosophy to a single clinical observation: patients' unhappiness almost always traced back to the same root cause — "a diferença entre a vida que a pessoa tem e a vida que ela gostaria de ter... o chamado self ideal e... o self real. E essa diferença gera dor" [the difference between the life a person has and the life they'd like to have — the so-called ideal self and the real self. And that difference generates pain] (Forbes Brasil). Needing more income after the birth of twin sons, he left the clinic for pharma sales at Roche, and spent the next ~30 years climbing pharma multinationals — Roche (national sales director, oncology), Isdin (country president, Brazil), and 12 years at Bayer (consumer health), with postings in Italy and then Australia/New Zealand leading the entire Oceania consumer-health business. A family tragedy punctuates the career narrative he tells in public: one of his twin sons died in a traffic accident, an event he says triggered the move to Italy ("um verdadeiro renascimento" [a true rebirth]) and which he still discusses candidly in long-form interviews, alongside grief-work through a community organization ("Serviço Luz," "Metamorfose"). He was recruited to Pague Menos by outgoing CEO Mário Queirós (son of founder Francisco Deusmar de Queirós) after a chance reunion at an industry mission Marques was curating in Oceania; he initially refused, then accepted after founder Deusmar Queirós framed the ask around the company's 45-year survival and its 26,000-plus employees rather than short-term turnaround metrics. He took office January 4, 2024 (with a 90-day transition through April) as the **first CEO from outside the founding family** in the chain's history, inheriting a balance sheet stretched by the 2022 Extrafarma acquisition (R$700 million, ~R$600 million cash) and net debt/EBITDA above 3x. His signature first act was not cost-cutting: he pulled the names of all 26,000 employees, randomly sorted them into groups of five, and spent roughly 70 hours over several weeks listening before touching a financial report — a method he explicitly imports from clinical anamnesis. By the account he gives across multiple interviews, that listening tour is what surfaced the air-conditioner/microwave decision and dismantled a company myth that no one could be fired. Under his tenure (through Q1 2026 results) Pague Menos returned to profit after a 2023 loss, cut net debt/EBITDA from roughly 3.4x–4.2x toward under 2x, delivered nine consecutive quarters of double-digit same-store-sales growth, and built a "Continuous Care Customer" (CCC) strategy around chronic-treatment patients — while flattening the management hierarchy from six layers to three between store manager and CEO and replacing "vários executivos de operações e logística" [several operations and logistics executives]. He is a licensed small-aircraft pilot and ocean rower, and repeatedly imports both hobbies as management metaphors in interviews.

Sharpened on Pause: "se você é uma pessoa que nunca erra, se você é um cara autossuficiente, é um chefe ditador... eu não te sigo, é óbvio que eu não te sigo" [if you're someone who never makes mistakes, if you're a self-sufficient guy, a dictator boss... I won't follow you, obviously I won't follow you].
quotes: Acredito fortemente na sinergia entre autenticidade e vulnerabilidade como impulsionadores da liderança
se você é uma pessoa que nunca erra, se você é um cara autossuficiente, é um chefe ditador... eu não te sigo, é óbvio que eu não te sigo
title: Authenticity and vulnerability are the leadership drivers, not authority or infallibility

text: **Complacency, not crisis, is what kills companies — imported directly from aviation.** "A coisa que mais mata na aviação é a complacência... A complacência que mata na aviação é a mesma que mata as empresas que entram na rotina" [The thing that kills most in aviation is complacency... the complacency that kills in aviation is the same complacency that kills companies that fall into routine] (Brazil Journal).
quotes: A coisa que mais mata na aviação é a complacência... A complacência que mata na aviação é a mesma que mata as empresas que entram na rotina
title: Complacency, not crisis, is what kills companies — imported directly from aviation

text: **Every privilege carries a responsibility.** "Todo privilégio tem uma responsabilidade. Eu enxerguei como eu fui privilegiado... a volta para Fortaleza foi como devolver como responsabilidade" [Every privilege carries a responsibility. I saw how privileged I'd been... coming back to Fortaleza was like paying that responsibility back] (Diário do Nordeste) — the frame he also uses to explain leaving an eight-year international career to run a regional Brazilian pharmacy chain.
quotes: Todo privilégio tem uma responsabilidade. Eu enxerguei como eu fui privilegiado... a volta para Fortaleza foi como devolver como responsabilidade
title: Every privilege carries a responsibility

text: **Financial discipline and a "culture of love" are not in tension — deleveraging is treated as a moral commitment, not a constraint.** On the Q1 2026 call (again quoted from the official English-language transcript, not back-translated): "Our commitment, which was the first feedback that I received here nearly 2.5 years ago, is reduce your leverage. You can see here the net debt over EBITDA is decreasing from 4[.2] two years ago to under 2 in quarter one" (Q1 2026 earnings call) — delivered on the same call as "we will continue to bring health with love to all Brazilians."
quotes: culture of love

Our commitment, which was the first feedback that I received here nearly 2.5 years ago, is reduce your leverage. You can see here the net debt over EBITDA is decreasing from 4[.2] two years ago to under 2 in quarter one
we will continue to bring health with love to all Brazilians.
title: Financial discipline and a "culture of love" are not in tension — deleveraging is treated as a moral commitment, not a constraint

text: **"Complacência mata" (complacency kills) — aviation transplant into organizational diagnosis.** Learned while training as a pilot: "A companhia aérea que se torna complacente não faz a manutenção adequada das aeronaves. O piloto que se torna complacente não se desvia da turbulência a tempo. E isso vale para qualquer empresa" [The airline that becomes complacent doesn't properly maintain its aircraft. The pilot who becomes complacent doesn't steer around turbulence in time. And that applies to any company]. *Worked example*: he uses two symbolic non-repairs he personally witnessed — a broken water fountain in a five-star hotel with an elaborately handwritten "out of order" sign instead of a repair, and an airplane seat with an embroidered "broken, doesn't recline" note instead of a fix — as the diagnostic pattern he then recognized on visiting Extrafarma's worst-performing stores after the acquisition: "o que mais me impressionou foi que a energia de muitas pessoas estava apagada. As pessoas estavam complacentes" [what struck me most was that many people's energy was extinguished. People were complacent] (Forbes Brasil).
quotes: A companhia aérea que se torna complacente não faz a manutenção adequada das aeronaves. O piloto que se torna complacente não se desvia da turbulência a tempo. E isso vale para qualquer empresa
out of order
broken, doesn't recline
o que mais me impressionou foi que a energia de muitas pessoas estava apagada. As pessoas estavam complacentes
title: "Complacência mata" (complacency kills) — aviation transplant into organizational diagnosis

text: **Clinical anamnesis applied to corporate diagnosis.** The structured diagnostic interview from psychology, imported first into pharma sales technique and later into CEO onboarding. *Worked example, sales era*: "usei essa técnica desde muito cedo... aplicar essa teoria nos médicos que eu visitava" [I used this technique from very early on... applying this to the doctors I visited] got him promoted within 18 months at Roche. *Worked example, CEO onboarding*: "pegar uma lista de 26.000 pessoas, colocar no sorteador web e sortear grupos de cinco pessoas... através de uma dinâmica de anamnese mesmo: conta a história do teu nome... me fala porque que você ama trabalhar aqui" [take a list of 26,000 people, put it into a random-draw tool, and draw groups of five... through an actual anamnesis dynamic: tell me the story of your name... tell me why you love working here], 12 groups a day for the first two weeks, ~70 hours of listening total (Pause | O POVO; corroborated independently by Forbes Brasil and Portal IN).
quotes: usei essa técnica desde muito cedo... aplicar essa teoria nos médicos que eu visitava

pegar uma lista de 26.000 pessoas, colocar no sorteador web e sortear grupos de cinco pessoas... através de uma dinâmica de anamnese mesmo: conta a história do teu nome... me fala porque que você ama trabalhar aqui
title: Clinical anamnesis applied to corporate diagnosis

text: **Correlation-of-signal (a "machine-learning" logic applied to human complaints).** "Uma coisa isolada ela não vale nada, mas uma coisa dita várias vezes sem uma intercomunicação ela tem um poder muito grande, né. Esse daí é a base do machine learning" [A single isolated thing is worth nothing, but the same thing said repeatedly by people who haven't talked to each other carries a lot of weight — that's the basis of machine learning] (Pause | O POVO). *Worked example*: the air-conditioner/microwave decision and the "we can't fire anyone" myth both surfaced this way — the same complaint, from unrelated stores, repeated across the 70 listening groups.
quotes: Uma coisa isolada ela não vale nada, mas uma coisa dita várias vezes sem uma intercomunicação ela tem um poder muito grande, né. Esse daí é a base do machine learning
we can't fire anyone
title: Correlation-of-signal (a "machine-learning" logic applied to human complaints)

text: **Karpman drama triangle (victim–persecutor–rescuer).** "Toda a história às vezes tem uma vítima, um culpado e um Salvador, isso aí quebra empresas e quebra famílias" [Every story sometimes has a victim, a culprit, and a savior — that breaks companies and breaks families] (Pause | O POVO); explained more fully with editorial gloss in Forbes Brasil: "Não há segurança psicológica nas empresas. Eu encontrei muitas situações em que havia um Triângulo de Karpman" [There's no psychological safety in companies. I found many situations with a Karpman Triangle]. *Worked example*: named as a pattern he actively works to eliminate by giving employees protagonism rather than a script of blame.
quotes: Toda a história às vezes tem uma vítima, um culpado e um Salvador, isso aí quebra empresas e quebra famílias
Não há segurança psicológica nas empresas. Eu encontrei muitas situações em que havia um Triângulo de Karpman
title: Karpman drama triangle (victim–persecutor–rescuer)

text: **Jim Collins's "brutal facts of reality" (Good to Great).** "O que o Jim Collins no Good to Great ele fala dos fatos brutais de realidade. Quais são os fatos brutais de realidade que a gente encontra na nossa operação... nós vamos estabelecer missões operacionais então Nós criamos seis missões e duas delas elas são transformadoras" [What Jim Collins in Good to Great calls the brutal facts of reality. What are the brutal facts we find in our operation... we're going to set operational missions, so we created six missions and two of them are transformative] (Pause | O POVO). *Worked example*: the six named strategic pillars (atendimento, manutenção, processos, precificação, tecnologia, operação) that structured the first turnaround phase, including reforming 400 under-invested stores and clearing a 7,000-ticket service backlog (IstoÉ Dinheiro).
quotes: brutal facts of reality

O que o Jim Collins no Good to Great ele fala dos fatos brutais de realidade. Quais são os fatos brutais de realidade que a gente encontra na nossa operação... nós vamos estabelecer missões operacionais então Nós criamos seis missões e duas delas elas são transformadoras
title: Jim Collins's "brutal facts of reality" (Good to Great)

text: **Simon Sinek's "infinite game."** "A empresa é um jogo infinito, você nunca concorre com outra empresa, o grande concorrente nosso somos nós mesmos, nós colocamos as barreiras" [The company is an infinite game — you never really compete with another company, our biggest competitor is ourselves, we're the ones putting up the barriers] (Pause | O POVO). Used to reframe internal complacency, not external rivals, as the real threat.
quotes: A empresa é um jogo infinito, você nunca concorre com outra empresa, o grande concorrente nosso somos nós mesmos, nós colocamos as barreiras
title: Simon Sinek's "infinite game."

text: **Jung's typology, repurposed as a pharma sales-classification tool.** "Eu adorava Jung... ele foi para quatro tipos de comportamento, e eu decidi aplicar essa teoria nos médicos que eu visitava... trazia uma mensagem muito focada... isso acabava trazendo resultados" [I loved Jung... he moved to four behavior types, and I decided to apply that theory to the doctors I visited... it delivered a very focused message... that ended up bringing results] (Pause | O POVO) — corroborated independently, with less detail, by IstoÉ Dinheiro's reference to him drawing on "conceitos do suíço Carl Jung... a importância da psique... na busca pela totalidade."
quotes: Eu adorava Jung... ele foi para quatro tipos de comportamento, e eu decidi aplicar essa teoria nos médicos que eu visitava... trazia uma mensagem muito focada... isso acabava trazendo resultados
conceitos do suíço Carl Jung... a importância da psique... na busca pela totalidade.
title: Jung's typology, repurposed as a pharma sales-classification tool

text: **"Bela figura" vs. "bruta figura" — a named cultural-translation model for leading across countries.** Before acting in a new country he deliberately consults a local philosopher friend ("Alfredo... me conta a história dos italianos") to map "padrões culturais profundos" before intervening (Pause | O POVO). *Worked example*: at a poorly kept Italian point of sale he told the team "isso aqui não é a bela figura, isso aqui é a bruta figura" [this isn't the beautiful figure, this is the ugly/rough figure] — invoking Italian aesthetic pride as the lever, not a directive — and within a week the team returned with its own improvement plan; the chain went on to ship "110 mil displays para 10.000 farmácias na Itália, já preenchidos com os produtos dentro" [110,000 displays to 10,000 Italian pharmacies, pre-filled with product] — "foi uma grande virada" [it was a major turnaround].
quotes: Alfredo... me conta a história dos italianos
padrões culturais profundos
isso aqui não é a bela figura, isso aqui é a bruta figura
110 mil displays para 10.000 farmácias na Itália, já preenchidos com os produtos dentro
foi uma grande virada
title: "Bela figura" vs. "bruta figura" — a named cultural-translation model for leading across countries

text: **Founders Mentality (Bain) — three-legged framework, adopted wholesale.** "Um livro que eu adoro e que tô relendo agora é a questão do Founders Mentality... tem um tripé: uma missão insurgente... a obsessão pela linha de frente... a questão da cabeça de dono" [A book I love and am rereading now is Founders Mentality... there's a tripod: an insurgent mission... obsession with the front line... the owner's-mindset question] (Pause | O POVO). *Worked example, frontline obsession*: "obsessed with the front line. We went to the stores to understand what frictions were present" (3Q25 earnings call, English transcript) — used to find and fix the label-printer friction (see below).
quotes: Um livro que eu adoro e que tô relendo agora é a questão do Founders Mentality... tem um tripé: uma missão insurgente... a obsessão pela linha de frente... a questão da cabeça de dono
obsessed with the front line. We went to the stores to understand what frictions were present
title: Founders Mentality (Bain) — three-legged framework, adopted wholesale

text: **"Continuous Care Customer" (CCC) — the strategic mandala.** Reframes chronic-disease patients (hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular) as the highest-loyalty, highest-spend segment, replacing the stigmatized label "chronic patient": "the continuous care customer, who many companies call chronic patients, and we don't believe that, because chronic here is only happiness" (3Q25 earnings call). *Worked example*: CCC customers are ~26% of the client base but ~72% of revenue, visit stores 4x more often, spend 60% more, and generate 6.4x the annual revenue of a non-CCC customer; management pegs a 2-point CCC-share gain (≈350,000 new CCCs) at roughly R$500 million of incremental annual revenue (BTG Investor Day note); by Q1 2026, CCC customers had grown 10.8% since Q4 2024.
quotes: Continuous Care Customer
the continuous care customer, who many companies call chronic patients, and we don't believe that, because chronic here is only happiness
title: "Continuous Care Customer" (CCC) — the strategic mandala

text: **"Behaving in scarcity" — capital discipline as a standing policy, independent of how much cash is on hand.** "We want to keep behaving in scarcity... It's not just because we had a follow-on and we have more money... that we now can make mistakes. No, that's not the case" (Q1 2026 earnings call). *Worked example*: store-opening cohorts from 2021–2025 show gradually rising "assertiveness," not an opportunistic jump after the equity raise — only one new store opened in Q1 2026 despite available capital, with acceleration deliberately deferred.
quotes: Behaving in scarcity
We want to keep behaving in scarcity... It's not just because we had a follow-on and we have more money... that we now can make mistakes. No, that's not the case
title: "Behaving in scarcity" — capital discipline as a standing policy, independent of how much cash is on hand

text: **Telemetria — real-time store-level data as the mechanism for meritocracy and rapid turnarounds.** *Worked example*: "we took 50 stores that had negative EBITDA. And by plugging in the telemetry, by making a simple plan, talking to the people in the store, we revert these 50 stores in just three months to have a positive EBITDA" (3Q25 earnings call) — the program was later expanded from an initial 50-store pilot to a planned 200+ stores by 2026 (BTG Investor Day note).
quotes: we took 50 stores that had negative EBITDA. And by plugging in the telemetry, by making a simple plan, talking to the people in the store, we revert these 50 stores in just three months to have a positive EBITDA
title: Telemetria — real-time store-level data as the mechanism for meritocracy and rapid turnarounds

text: **"Tempo cronológico" vs. "tempo de qualidade" — a named time-management dichotomy, explicitly grounded in clinical psychology.** "Não podemos viver a vida no tempo cronológico. Precisamos direcionar nossas vidas no tempo da qualidade... Como a depressão mora no passado e a ansiedade no futuro, o ideal é sempre estarmos focados no presente" [We can't live life in chronological time. We need to direct our lives toward quality time... Since depression lives in the past and anxiety in the future, the ideal is to always stay focused on the present] (PodSempre write-up, Dois a Mais Farma). *Worked example*: strict work/home separation — full presence at work when at work, full presence with family when home, no blending — though he admits (see *Blind spots*) failing this once with his own daughter.
quotes: tempo de qualidade

Não podemos viver a vida no tempo cronológico. Precisamos direcionar nossas vidas no tempo da qualidade... Como a depressão mora no passado e a ansiedade no futuro, o ideal é sempre estarmos focados no presente
title: "Tempo cronológico" vs. "tempo de qualidade" — a named time-management dichotomy, explicitly grounded in clinical psychology

text: **Listen before you look at the numbers, every time you take a new job.** "Nunca aceito um novo trabalho sem ouvir as pessoas. No caso da Pague Menos eu conversei com meu antecessor, com os principais executivos e com a família controladora" [I never accept a new job without listening to people. In Pague Menos's case, I talked to my predecessor, the main executives, and the controlling family] (Forbes Brasil).
quotes: Nunca aceito um novo trabalho sem ouvir as pessoas. No caso da Pague Menos eu conversei com meu antecessor, com os principais executivos e com a família controladora
title: Listen before you look at the numbers, every time you take a new job

text: **Test the boundary before you plan to cross it.** He floated hypothetical, provocative ideas to the controlling family purely to map real limits, not to execute them: "eu perguntei — só para ver a reação — se poderíamos fechar as lojas do Rio Grande do Sul para cortar custos... Eu não planejava sair de nenhum estado, mas queria saber o que poderia ou não ser negociado" [I asked — just to see the reaction — whether we could close the Rio Grande do Sul stores to cut costs... I didn't plan to leave any state, I wanted to know what could or couldn't be negotiated] (Forbes Brasil).
quotes: eu perguntei — só para ver a reação — se poderíamos fechar as lojas do Rio Grande do Sul para cortar custos... Eu não planejava sair de nenhum estado, mas queria saber o que poderia ou não ser negociado
title: Test the boundary before you plan to cross it

text: **A single complaint is noise; the same complaint from unconnected people is signal — act on the pattern, not the anecdote.** The correlation-of-signal mental model, applied directly as a filter for which of the 70 listening-group findings became capital decisions.
title: A single complaint is noise; the same complaint from unconnected people is signal — act on the pattern, not the anecdote

text: **Verify a taboo before you accept it; don't rule by decree, dismantle the myth itself.** He found the company's "we can't fire anyone" belief was an unexamined artifact of quarterly-results anxiety, not policy — and treated exposing the myth as the intervention, rather than issuing a new edict: "Como a empresa tinha uma preocupação com o resultado trimestral, criou-se esse mito de que não se podia demitir... São aqueles paradigmas que se criam na incapacidade de desafiar o status quo" [Because the company was worried about quarterly results, this myth arose that no one could be fired... those are the paradigms created by an inability to challenge the status quo] (Brazil Journal).
quotes: we can't fire anyone
Como a empresa tinha uma preocupação com o resultado trimestral, criou-se esse mito de que não se podia demitir... São aqueles paradigmas que se criam na incapacidade de desafiar o status quo
title: Verify a taboo before you accept it; don't rule by decree, dismantle the myth itself

text: **When to give up on an underperforming employee — his own named test, offered with an explicit disclaimer that it's personal, not universal.** "Eu criei uma técnica para mim — não tô dizendo para ninguém usar isso — se essa pessoa quer e ela tem o mínimo das competências, eu vou investir mais. Se a gente já falou sobre isso, se tem exemplos claros que foi dado, se é baseado em resultados e também habilidades e competências e esse negócio não responde, é melhor, infelizmente, você ser sincero e fazer a troca" [I created a technique for myself — I'm not telling anyone to use it — if the person wants it and has the minimum competencies, I'll invest more. If we've already talked about it, if clear examples have been given, if it's grounded in results and skills and it still doesn't respond, it's better, unfortunately, to be honest and make the change] (Pause | O POVO).
quotes: Eu criei uma técnica para mim — não tô dizendo para ninguém usar isso — se essa pessoa quer e ela tem o mínimo das competências, eu vou investir mais. Se a gente já falou sobre isso, se tem exemplos claros que foi dado, se é baseado em resultados e também habilidades e competências e esse negócio não responde, é melhor, infelizmente, você ser sincero e fazer a troca
title: When to give up on an underperforming employee — his own named test, offered with an explicit disclaimer that it's personal, not universal

text: **Turn expenses into investment — cut what doesn't return, redeploy the margin, don't just cut.** Concrete example given unprompted on an earnings call: "We saw that we were paying BRL 450,000 for the booth, also 20 employees to be there in the conference... We're no longer participating in this conference because we cannot afford to have margins that can be expanded, and invest this margin in things that will not bring a return" (Q1 2026 earnings call).
quotes: We saw that we were paying BRL 450,000 for the booth, also 20 employees to be there in the conference... We're no longer participating in this conference because we cannot afford to have margins that can be expanded, and invest this margin in things that will not bring a return
title: Turn expenses into investment — cut what doesn't return, redeploy the margin, don't just cut

text: **After a capital raise, discipline doesn't loosen — it's a "marathon, not a sprint."** Refuses to read more cash as license for faster/lower-quality store openings; ties expansion pace strictly to operating cash generation, not to how much capital happens to be on the balance sheet (Q1 2026 earnings call).
quotes: marathon, not a sprint.
title: After a capital raise, discipline doesn't loosen — it's a "marathon, not a sprint."

text: **Fix cheap, high-friction annoyances before tackling structural problems.** The recurring, cross-audience anecdote: employees had to hand-cut price labels to fit shelves, burning "178 mil horas por ano" [178,000 hours a year] — fixed with a printer that cuts labels to size automatically, freeing staff time for customer service (confirmed near-verbatim, with the same 178,000-hour figure, across Brazil Journal, IstoÉ Dinheiro, and the 3Q25 earnings call — his most-repeated signature story).
quotes: 178 mil horas por ano
title: Fix cheap, high-friction annoyances before tackling structural problems

text: **Access, not exclusivity — even when private label crosses R$1 billion.** He caps the ambition of Pague Menos's own-brand line at "access" and explicitly refuses to let it become a margin grab that competes with the manufacturers he buys from: "We don't want to have our own brand to compete with our partner, which is the industry. We want our own brand access!... Pague Menos is an access company!" (3Q25 earnings call). *Worked example*: on the same call he reports private label passing R$1 billion in revenue for the first time and Pague Menos becoming "the largest label in sunscreen" — yet keeps the framing access-first rather than share-of-wallet maximization, structurally the same logic as the non-alcoholic-beer refusal (expand what the customer can reach, don't maximize what the company alone captures).
quotes: We don't want to have our own brand to compete with our partner, which is the industry. We want our own brand access!... Pague Menos is an access company!
the largest label in sunscreen
title: Access, not exclusivity — even when private label crosses R$1 billion

text: **Growth vs. deleveraging.** Explicitly subordinates growth ambition to a deleveraging target, repeatedly and across years: "bem mais do que 50 lojas, mas nosso compromisso vai continuar sendo com a desalavancagem" [well more than 50 stores, but our commitment will keep being deleveraging] (Brazil Journal, dez/2024). Net debt/EBITDA fell from roughly 4.2x (his first-quarter benchmark) to below 2x by Q1 2026, and separately reported at 3.4x (jun/2024) → 2.6x (jun/2025) with an internal target of 2x (Relatório Reservado, ago/2025) — even while store-opening acceleration is publicly promised "a partir do 2º tri de 2026" only once the leverage trajectory allows it.
quotes: bem mais do que 50 lojas, mas nosso compromisso vai continuar sendo com a desalavancagem
a partir do 2º tri de 2026
title: Growth vs. deleveraging

text: **People vs. straightforwardly profitable proposals (the clearest "psychologist vs. CEO" tension on record).** Rejected an early, revenue-positive proposal to sell non-alcoholic beer in stores: "Eu recebi a proposta de colocar cerveja sem álcool para vender em nossas unidades, mas fui contra, já que sei que uma pessoa que compra uma bebida dessas pode migrar para cervejas alcoólicas e isso vai 100% contra o que uma farmácia deve fazer" [I received the proposal to sell non-alcoholic beer in our stores, but I was against it, since I know a person who buys that kind of drink could migrate to alcoholic beer, and that goes 100% against what a pharmacy should do] — framed by the outlet itself as "uma disputa de ideias entre o psicólogo e o CEO que, como todos, busca lucro para sua companhia" [a dispute of ideas between the psychologist and the CEO who, like everyone, seeks profit for the company] (Brazil Economy).
quotes: psychologist vs. CEO

Eu recebi a proposta de colocar cerveja sem álcool para vender em nossas unidades, mas fui contra, já que sei que uma pessoa que compra uma bebida dessas pode migrar para cervejas alcoólicas e isso vai 100% contra o que uma farmácia deve fazer
uma disputa de ideias entre o psicólogo e o CEO que, como todos, busca lucro para sua companhia
title: People vs. straightforwardly profitable proposals (the clearest "psychologist vs. CEO" tension on record)

text: **When to fire / restructure people.** Dismantled the "no-fire" myth by verification rather than decree (see *Decision heuristics*); separately, and more structurally, cut management layers between store manager and CEO from six to three, and replaced "vários executivos de operações e logística" [several operations and logistics executives] — a harder edge of the turnaround that surfaces almost exclusively in the Forbes Brasil as-told-to profile, not in the warmer podcast/video appearances (see *Blind spots*).
quotes: vários executivos de operações e logística
title: When to fire / restructure people

text: **Build vs. buy / organic growth vs. M&A.** Explicit preference for organic growth over further acquisitions in the near term, after integrating the 2022 Extrafarma deal: "Estamos muito focados em um crescimento orgânico, sem pressa de fazer novas aquisições. Queremos acelerar nossa expansão, mas de forma equilibrada, sem comprometer a saúde financeira da empresa" [We're very focused on organic growth, with no rush to make new acquisitions. We want to accelerate our expansion, but in a balanced way, without compromising the company's financial health] (Exame INSIGHT, "Na Sua Cesta").
quotes: Estamos muito focados em um crescimento orgânico, sem pressa de fazer novas aquisições. Queremos acelerar nossa expansão, mas de forma equilibrada, sem comprometer a saúde financeira da empresa
Na Sua Cesta
title: Build vs. buy / organic growth vs. M&A

text: **Raise capital vs. wait — and how to sequence it.** Treats an equity follow-on as a lagging reward for delivered performance, not a funding event to chase on its own timeline: "Queremos crescer o negócio, arrumar os fundamentos, continuar nessa entrega acima do que o mercado espera e, com isso, ver uma valorização do papel e um possível follow-on" [We want to grow the business, fix the fundamentals, keep delivering above what the market expects, and with that, see the stock re-rate and a possible follow-on] (Brazil Journal Play). In practice this sequencing sat inside a real governance tension he did not control: Relatório Reservado documents minority shareholder General Atlantic (17% stake) pushing hard for exit-oriented follow-on timing against controlling shareholder Deusmar de Queirós's preference to delever further first — "a General Atlantic vai impor sua visão e seu senso de premência" [General Atlantic will impose its view and its sense of urgency] — with no on-record Jonas Marques statement in that specific piece.
quotes: Queremos crescer o negócio, arrumar os fundamentos, continuar nessa entrega acima do que o mercado espera e, com isso, ver uma valorização do papel e um possível follow-on
a General Atlantic vai impor sua visão e seu senso de premência
title: Raise capital vs. wait — and how to sequence it

text: **Regulatory/labor reform: the end of the "escala 6x1" work schedule.** A hedged, non-oppositional but skeptical position, repeated consistently in two independent interviews. Upside acknowledged: "é bom porque melhora a qualidade de vida das pessoas, que passam a ter uma folga a mais" [it's good because it improves people's quality of life, they get an extra day off]. Downside flagged: "Muitas delas vão pegar esse dia a mais e arrumar outro trabalho... No fundo, a semana ficou mais curta, e o nível de dedicação de muitos também. Será que a gente está preparado para isso?" [Many of them will take that extra day and get another job... deep down the week got shorter, and so did a lot of people's dedication level. Are we ready for that?] — using New Zealand's abandoned four-day-week mandate as his empirical reference case (Exame, "Escala 6x1"; syndicated with translation in Panorama Farmacêutico). text: Marques's public register is unusually therapeutic for a listed-company CEO, and he does not code-switch it away for investor audiences: the same "feedback é um presente" [feedback is a gift] language and citations to Karpman, Jung, Lacan, and Amy Edmondson that show up in a lifestyle podcast (Pause | O POVO) also show up, nearly verbatim, in earnings calls with sell-side analysts — he explicitly prizes this as authenticity ("aqui a gente faz ao vivo," no teleprompter). His sentences run long and story-shaped: he rarely states a framework abstractly without immediately attaching a small, specific, sensory anecdote (the pizzeria next door, the embroidered "broken" note on an airplane seat, the Roman slave whispering behind the triumphal chariot) — the anecdote does the argumentative work, not the label. He repeats a small set-piece stories verbatim, word-for-word close, across very different venues over roughly two years (the 178,000-hour label-cutting story; the air-conditioners and microwaves; "complacência mata"; low self-esteem "unanimous on three continents") — a sign these are deliberately rehearsed signature stories, not spontaneous color. He names his intellectual debts constantly and without anxiety of influence — Jim Collins, Simon Sinek, Bain's Founders Mentality, Michael Watkins's *The First 90 Days* (his own IMD professor), Amy Edmondson — treating management literature the way a therapist cites schools of therapy, as tools to be applied rather than proprietary insight to be guarded. He is blunt about hard numbers (leverage ratios, EBITDA percentages, the exact count of air conditioners) in the same breath as soft claims ("resultados são fumaça mental" [results are mental smoke]), and rarely resolves that tension explicitly — he holds both registers open at once rather than picking one. He is candid to the point of self-critique in long interviews (admitting he ignored his own daughter over a phone, admitting the work/life "math doesn't close"), a hedge that reads as more genuine than defensive because it is unprompted. In Portuguese-language interviews he leans on regional and cultural specificity (Macunaíma, samba schools, Ceará) to explain both his own motivation and Brazilian workplace culture; in English-mediated earnings calls the register compresses slightly but keeps the same rhetorical moves (opening greetings to "our 27 thousand giants," closing by inviting investors to visit stores "to see if we're walking the talk").

aqui a gente faz ao vivo,
unanimous on three continents
resultados são fumaça mental
math doesn't close
our 27 thousand giants,
to see if we're walking the talk

text: **Leverage remained a real, dated weak spot well into the turnaround.** Sell-side coverage flagged it directly: BTG Pactual rated the stock "Neutro" in March 2025 specifically "devido à valorização limitada e aos riscos relacionados à alavancagem da companhia" [due to limited upside and risks related to the company's leverage] even as revenue and SSS growth beat consensus, with net debt/EBITDA at 2.8x versus 0.9x for Raia Drogasil and 1.1x for Panvel, and short-term debt (R$370 million) exceeding cash on hand (R$150 million) — "tornando praticamente inevitável uma rolagem de passivos ao longo de 2025" [making a liability rollover in 2025 practically inevitable] (Exame). BTG upgraded to "Compra" by September 2025 as deleveraging progressed, but the same research note's own financial table shows net debt continuing to *rise in absolute terms* (R$3.1–3.5 billion, 2025E–2027E) even as the debt/EBITDA ratio falls — the improvement is relative (EBITDA outgrowing debt), not an absolute paydown, a nuance the promotional coverage of him tends to elide.

tornando praticamente inevitável uma rolagem de passivos ao longo de 2025

text: **Independent research also flagged the growth itself as partly flattered by weak comparables — not only the leverage.** Genial Analisa's 4T24 note (rating the stock **MANTER**/Hold at a R$3.60 target vs. a R$3.10 price, analysts Iago Souza and Nina Mirazon) is a third sell-side voice alongside Safra's "compra" and BTG's "neutro," and it lands the sharpest analytical caveat in the corpus: "A base de comparação distorcida. O crescimento expressivo precisa ser analisado dentro do contexto. The best-supported date, corroborated by the original Brazil Journal breaking-news announcement and by Brazil Journal Play, is January 4, 2024, with a 90-day transition running to early April — the "abril"/"fevereiro" references in secondary profiles likely conflate the transition's end with the effective start.
