text: **vs. valuation-maximizers (and many VCs).** Against treating a high valuation/large round as the win, he treats fast-close-then-build as the win and a fat round as a self-deception risk, and generalizes it into a counterintuitive claim that over-raising *reduces* the odds of success. He rejects the premise at its root — "raising a round should be a byproduct of success," not success itself, and treating it as a milestone breeds "short term showmanship instead of making something people want" — which sets him against the fundraise-announcement culture of much of the VC/press ecosystem, not just individual over-raisers. ([Fundraising Rounds Are Not Milestones](https://www.michaelseibel.com/blog/fundraising-rounds-are-not-milestones); [Why Does Your Company Deserve More Money?](https://www.michaelseibel.com/blog/why-does-your-company-deserve-more-money); [5 Things That Kill Startups Post-Seed](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/8a-the-5-things-that-kill-startups-post-seed-rounds))

([Dalton & Michael: The Truth About Y Combinator](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/IU-dalton-michael-the-truth-about-y-combinator))

text: **vs. Ryan Bethencourt / IndieBio (institutional, on regulated industries).** Bethencourt's on-record critique — "YC wants to fund tech people that do biotech, rather than embracing what it takes to do biotech... YC doesn't have the expertise to tackle an established industry with regulatory hurdles" — targets the YC model under Sam Altman's presidency (2017), not Seibel by name; but it lands inside his tenure as the core accelerator's CEO and is the sharpest named external counter-position to his "launch fast" doctrine as applied to regulated markets. ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2017/06/30/yccombinator-biotech-partner-added.html)) Seibel's own later carve-out (regulated industries as an explicit exception, see Blind spots) is a partial, unprompted concession to exactly this critique.

title: vs. Ryan Bethencourt / IndieBio (institutional, on regulated industries)

text: **Survivorship bias is structural to the YC canon.** His advice is distilled from a YC-pre-selected sample dominated by winners; critics note YC "glamorize[s] and romanticize[s] the journey" and can "distort founders' sense of natural development timelines," creating pressure to match peers' "rocketship metrics" ([critique compilation](https://medium.com/@markeeters/what-are-some-negatives-with-y-combinator-db367de884ae)). He pre-empts this himself repeatedly — "we broke many, if not all of the rules" and, more precisely, "I bet you can name a startup that has made every one of these mistakes and has still been successful... those tend to be exceptions" ([Biggest Mistakes First-Time Founders Make](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/66-biggest-mistakes-first-time-founders-make)) — cite his own disclaimers as the honest framing.

distort founders' sense of natural development timelines,
we broke many, if not all of the rules

title: Survivorship bias is structural to the YC canon

text: **One-size-fits-all, though he now names the boundary himself.** The same external critique notes YC's curriculum is "geared toward the widest applicability rather than solving specific company problems," weakest for biotech, deep tech, and regulated/enterprise hardware, where "launch something bad quickly" can be illegal, unsafe, or impossible ([critique compilation](https://medium.com/@markeeters/what-are-some-negatives-with-y-combinator-db367de884ae)). This is corroborated by a named, on-record competing-accelerator critique: Ryan Bethencourt (IndieBio) argued in 2017 that "YC doesn't have the expertise to tackle an established industry with regulatory hurdles, pricing and reimbursement complexities," and that the model "haven't changed... enough to reliably build therapeutics companies" — aimed at YC's institutional strategy under Sam Altman's presidency, not at Seibel by name, though it falls inside his tenure as accelerator CEO ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2017/06/30/yccombinator-biotech-partner-added.html)). What upgrades this from an inferred to a partly self-acknowledged limit: Seibel himself now names the exception plainly — "in some extremely regulated markets like banking or lending, it's just really hard to launch. You actually have to get approval done before you're even allowed to get customers" ([Biggest Mistakes First-Time Founders Make](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/66-biggest-mistakes-first-time-founders-make)). His frameworks were still forged in, and generalize best to, consumer/mobile (Socialcam, Twitch).

No" ([Wharton FinTech](https://medium.com/wharton-fintech/y-combinators-michael-seibel-dalton-caldwell-lessons-from-5000-entrepreneurs-be77ba6a6970)) sits in tension with his own "access not talent" thesis — readable as downplaying structural barriers even while championing access. He also notes the real cost some carry ("Imagine being a 25 year old and being the safety net for your family?"), which complicates his "go all-in in your 20s" default. Surface as internal tension, not external scandal.

text: **Batch-size critique falls inside his tenure but is not attributed to him by name.** Reporting on YC's "identity crisis" documents batch sizes growing from a combined 42 companies across both 2009 cohorts to 400 in the single Winter 2022 batch, with named critics (Arpita Agnihotri; Masha Bucher of Day One Ventures) saying "the core base of Y Combinator has diluted" and batches feel "overwhelming." The reporting credits the *fix* to Garry Tan as the incoming CEO and never quotes or names Seibel — the Winter 2022 run-up falls within his 2016–2024 tenure as accelerator CEO by outside dating only; treat any link to Seibel personally as inference, not a documented critique of him. His teaching material reads as post-hoc correction of his own lived failure, not abstract theory. ([Twitch Co-Founders Reunion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2vG-Sxk-c2k))

text: Miguel Krigsner turned a US$3,000 compounding pharmacy in 1977 Curitiba into Grupo Boticário (R$38.1bn GMV, the world's #1 specialized beauty retailer by store count in 2025) by pioneering Brazilian franchising before a legal framework for it existed — and his lens is relationship-as-collateral: the conviction that a business survives decades only if "the other person's capital" (the franchisee betting a lifetime's savings) is protected and every deal is ganha-ganha, because "as franquias que querem favorecer só um dos lados morrem na praia." He pairs a fearless-leap ethic ("saltar do precipício sem saber como vai cair") with a strict downside test ("e se der tudo errado?"), treats culture and transmissible values as what outlasts the founder (a deliberate, years-long professionalization to non-family CEOs — he left the executive presidency in 2008 — while daughters sit on the board, not in operations), and funds conservation structurally precisely because it is "séria demais para ser tratada como problema de marketing." He opposes lean-startup "test-before-you-bet" orthodoxy (he bought tens of thousands of bottles he couldn't store), Buffett-style margin-of-safety caution on the leap, and founder-as-brand exit plays like Rony Meisler's; his blind spots are survivorship framing and a handshake-trust ethic that frays at scale — documented not just in reseller commission complaints but in multiple franchise-termination disputes (Hannan, João Pessoa) where the same relational language ("olho no olho") gave way to institutional rigidity once the company grew past what he could personally manage.
quotes: the other person's capital

text: Miguel Krigsner (b. La Paz, Bolivia, **1950**; arrived in Brazil at age 11 in 1961, son of Polish-and-German Jewish parents who fled Nazism and settled in Curitiba) is founder and chairman of **Grupo Boticário**, the holding behind O Boticário, Eudora, quem disse, berenice? and The Beauty Box. A pharmacist-biochemist by training (UFPR), in **1977** he opened a small *farmácia de manipulação* on Rua Saldanha Marinho in downtown Curitiba with roughly US$3,000 borrowed from an uncle. Noticing his clientele skewed female, he turned to cosmetics and perfume; a second store at the Curitiba airport (1979) — which, per co-builder Artur Grynbaum, "nos colocou em contato com o Brasil inteiro" [put us in contact with all of Brazil] — gave the brand national exposure, and the **first franchise opened in Brasília in 1980**, pioneering a model that did not yet legally exist in Brazil. From that base he built one of the world's largest franchised cosmetics networks: by 2025-2026, Euromonitor ranks Grupo Boticário the **world's #1 specialized beauty retailer by store count**, with roughly 4,000 O Boticário stores across 16 countries, 1,655+ Brazilian cities, 21,000+ direct employees, and **R$38.1 billion in consumer sales (GMV) in 2025** (Exame; Forbes BR; WSCOM). He **left the company's executive presidency in 2008** (Google Books author note; Forbes), handing operations first to his brother-in-law **Artur Grynbaum** (later non-family executive **Fernando Modé** in 2021) while moving to chairman of the board — a deliberate, multi-stage professionalization. Forbes estimates his personal net worth at **~US$6.8 billion (#592 globally, 2026 list)** and reports he holds roughly **80% of the group individually**, with Grynbaum holding the remaining ~20% as his historic financial partner. His other signature institutions are the **Fundação Grupo Boticário de Proteção à Natureza** (founded 1990, funded at ~1% of net revenue/profit annually) and the **Museu do Holocausto de Curitiba** (2011, Brazil's first, which he idealized as the son of survivors). His 2024 memoir ***A Essência de Empreender*** (Portfolio-Penguin, 144 pages) won the **Prêmio Jabuti 2025** in the Business category; its table of contents opens with dated sections running 1931–1975 before the 1977 founding — a structural signal (unconfirmed against the actual text — see Provenance) that the book frames the company's origin inside his family's earlier history, not just the entrepreneurial leap itself. He is worth borrowing on one hard problem: building a *multi-decade, multi-channel, relationship-dense* business on third-party capital (franchisees and resellers) without burning the people who carry it — and on what happens to that ethic once the founder can no longer personally hold every relationship.

(MAGG; Brazil Journal)

Como é que eu fico?"* The leap is irrational only if the worst case is unsurvivable — this is what makes "jump off the cliff" *bounded* risk, not recklessness. *Worked example:* when he committed the company's scarce capital to the 1977–80 expansion, the gate was always survivability, not certainty. (MAGG)

Ownership stays concentrated with Krigsner (~80%) and Grynbaum (~20%); *operation* is professionalized in deliberate stages — *"Você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia."* (Hospital INC; gonext; Brazil Journal; Forbes)

Era um outro universo, totalmente diferente. E eu decidi sair."* [I did invest in a shopping mall in Curitiba, but there was a moment when it clicked for me that it wasn't for me. It was a different universe entirely. So I decided to get out.] He hardens the rule generally: *"Tem gente que investe em várias coisas, mas não entra com a alma. Isso não serve para mim."* (Exame; Exame abr/2026; book coverage)

text: **Absorb bottom-up tools instead of competing with your own franchisees.** *Worked example (institutional continuation under CEO Modé, descended from Krigsner's franchisee-first ethic):* a franchisee built its own financial-management tool (F360) to solve its own operating pain; rather than build a competing top-down system, the group *bought the data from that franchisee's store base and folded the tool into its own ecosystem*, leaving it to keep operating independently for other retailers too. Per Exame's reporting — journalist narrative describing the deal, not a quote spoken by Modé or Krigsner: o grupo enxergou o valor da solução, comprou os dados da sua base de lojas e incorporou ao seu ecossistema, transformando uma iniciativa de base em ferramenta estratégica de gestão da rede [the group saw the solution's value, bought the data from its store base, and folded it into its ecosystem, turning a grassroots initiative into a strategic network-management tool]. A clean example of the "don't compete with your franchisee" principle surviving into the professional-CEO era — company-voice reporting, not Krigsner's own words. (Exame — "sem tecnologia")

text: **Bootstrap vs. raise / scale on whose capital.** He scaled on *franchisees'* capital, not equity dilution or heavy debt — franchising turned a Curitiba pharmacy into a national network — with the corollary obligation (respect for the franchisee's capital) treated as non-negotiable. (euqueroinvestir; Consumidor Moderno)

text: **Expand a channel without cannibalizing partners.** Multichannel (stores, direct sales/resellers, e-commerce, B2B in pharmacies/supermarkets, B2P in salons) is pursued aggressively, but the founding rule is *don't compete with your franchisee*. Exame's reporting (journalist Isabela Rovaroto's framing, not a quote spoken by Modé or Krigsner) dates the strategic shift to roughly 15 years ago: the group made a decision that "parecia óbvia na teoria e era extremamente complexa na prática: seguir o consumidor, não o canal" [seemed obvious in theory and extremely complex in practice: follow the consumer, not the channel]. The mechanism, per the same journalist narrative (also descriptive text, not a direct quote): o franqueado é o beneficiário final de todas as transações que passam pelo seu território, independentemente do canal — quando o consumidor compra pelo e-commerce, pela revendedora ou na loja física, o franqueado fatura em todos os casos [the franchisee is the final beneficiary of every transaction in their territory, whatever the channel — the franchisee earns revenue whether the sale happens via e-commerce, a reseller, or the physical store]. Channel conflict itself is treated as permanent, not solvable — this part **is** a direct, on-the-record Modé quote: *"Esse conflito não tem solução, é insolúvel, mas é gerenciável"* [This conflict has no solution, it's unsolvable, but it's manageable] — and a 2025 execution of the same logic put the quem disse, berenice? brand inside 1,300+ O Boticário stores as reinforcement, not cannibalization. (Exame — reporting + Modé, "conflito entre canais")

Grandchildren's involvement is their free choice. (Hospital INC; Exame; MAGG; Forbes)

Relationship as collateral. (MAGG; Consumidor Moderno) — *Contrast:* in later, company-level supply disputes with franchisees themselves (see Blind spots), the same "protect the relationship" instinct is not what the institution did.

text: Warm, plainspoken, and self-effacing — a founder who talks in lived anecdote (the homemade mixer, the borrowed US$3,000, the Silvio Santos bottles, the Curitiba mall he walked away from at "um clique," his father's maxims) rather than abstraction or jargon. He reaches for vivid physical metaphors: the cliff jump, "morrem na praia," the captain who must descend to the mechanic, "olho no olho." He credits others constantly ("você não faz nada sozinho") and downplays himself — still "um farmacêutico que gosta de perfumes," the "velhinho que construiu o Boticário." His register is moral and relational before financial: profit is real but "muito pouco" next to transformation and trust, "o negócio é ganhar dinheiro, mas não pelo dinheiro," and "jamais queria causar prejuízo para outra pessoa" is closer to a creed than a tactic. He's blunt about risk being unavoidable ("tem um momento em que temos de arriscar mesmo") and the limits of planning, almost tender about obligations to people who staked their savings on him, and unusually willing to admit weakness ("não precisamos mostrar que somos fortes o tempo todo"). He borrows wisdom rather than claiming it — Antonio Machado's *"Caminante, no hay camino. Se hace camino, al andar"*; Drucker's "culture eats strategy." One documented outlier breaks the pattern: a single English-language Forbes quote ("Everything will make sense when you look back...") is more abstract and reflective than his usual concrete, Portuguese, anecdote-first register — worth flagging as an exception rather than the baseline voice, possibly an artifact of translation or a different interview context. Recognize a paraphrase as "sounds like Krigsner" by the combination of folksy anecdote + relationship-as-asset moral + understated bigness ("você não faz uma empresa dessas da noite para o dia").

text: **vs. Rony Meisler — build a dynasty to transmit vs. build a brand to (eventually) sell.** Krigsner kept ownership concentrated in himself and his brother-in-law across two professional-CEO handoffs (leaving the executive presidency himself in 2008) and frames the whole point as a *transmittable, multi-generational legacy* (Drucker's "culture eats strategy"; daughters on the board). Meisler's arc is the opposite: he built Reserva on his own founder-rebel charisma and *sold it to Arezzo&Co* (2020), then exited turbulently. Where Meisler fuses brand to founder, Krigsner treats the founder as something the company must outgrow — and would flag the "soul leaves with the founder" risk as the exact failure his succession architecture is built to prevent.

text:
**The franchisee/reseller relationship he idealizes has repeated, escalating documentation of friction — not just a single complaints channel.** Beyond Reclame Aqui commission disputes ("uma mixaria" at ~15% vs. ~30% at competitors, freight, stockouts, abusive collection calls), three separate, independently reported franchise-termination disputes surface the same pattern at larger scale:
- **João Pessoa, 2017** (Portal Correio, two articles): a franchisee sought to return his franchise; when negotiations over the buy-back value stalled, **the group cut off product supply**. The franchisee won a court injunction to buy stock, but only cash-upfront. Result: 7 of 10 stores closed, the direct-sales unit shut down, 50+ layoffs (many without severance per ex-employees), delayed December salary/13th-month/vacation pay, and a labor protest. The company's only public response was a refusal to comment ("situação pontual que está sob análise do Poder Judiciário... o grupo não comenta casos que estejam em discussão na Justiça") — leaving unanswered whether the supply cutoff (not just the civil dispute) caused the labor cascade onto third parties (the franchisee's own employees).
- **Hannan franchise, ~2015–2016** (dcomercio, via reader-proxy fetch): a 33-year franchise partner, Izabel Cristina Litieri, went from R$55m/year in sales across 14 stores and direct-sales channels to insolvency after a debt-financed real-estate expansion (R$16m) collided with Brazil's credit crisis; when she asked the group to restructure or accept her property in lieu of payment, it refused, began demanding cash-upfront for product (ending historical credit terms), and — per her account — became inaccessible ("Cheguei a ir quatro vezes para Curitiba, mas não consegui falar com o Grynbaum, só com diretores da empresa"). Her lawsuit alleges the group moved to "asfixiar financeiramente" [financially suffocate] the franchise to reclaim the territory she'd built. She explicitly contrasts this with the founder era: *"Comecei quando o Miguel Krigsner vinha para São Paulo e fazia reuniões na casa da minha irmã... mas o grupo poderia ter sido mais flexível em nosso caso."* [I started when Miguel Krigsner used to come to São Paulo and hold meetings at my sister's house... but the group could have been more flexible in our case.] This is the sharpest documented seam between the founder's personal "olho no olho" ethic and the institution he handed off to.
- **Polêmica Paraíba (undated critique, lightly sourced, re-quoting Exame):** alleges the group's ~2011 pivot into direct-sales-style distribution forced franchisees to build their own distribution centers at their own cost, while giving resellers better effective pricing than franchisees buying direct — then had a related entity, Interbelle, acquire distressed franchises "below market." Retail consultant **Adir Ribeiro (Praxis)** is quoted (originally to Exame) warning precisely of this risk: *"O maior risco na hora de uma empresa diversificar o modelo de vendas é prejudicar o relacionamento com aqueles que a fizeram crescer."* [The biggest risk when a company diversifies its sales model is damaging the relationship with those who made it grow.] Treat this source as an allegation from a lightly-sourced outlet, not an adjudicated finding — but it names the exact risk his own "ganha-ganha" rhetoric claims to guard against.
*All three are sourced complaints/allegations and one company non-denial, not adjudicated findings of wrongdoing.*

text: **A figure of his era and class.** The "olho no olho," handshake-trust, captain-and-mechanic register is the wisdom of a specific Brazilian mid-century founder context. It can read as paternalistic, and assumes personal access and goodwill that don't scale cleanly to a network of thousands of franchised/reseller points of sale — which is exactly what the Hannan and João Pessoa cases document happening once he was no longer the one picking up the phone.

text: **Sustainability framing invites the "is it really not marketing?" question — now with self-reported numbers to weigh.** He insists the Fundação isn't marketing, and the separate-entity / ~1%-of-revenue-or-profit structure and ESG-linked bond financing (R$5.775bn across four issuances) are genuine — but the company's own 2025 Relato Integrado admits real shortfalls (Scope 3 emissions cut only 2% against a 17%-by-2030 target; recycled content at 6% against a 30% goal), which cuts both ways: real self-disclosure of gaps (not pure PR), but also evidence the "not marketing" claim still has ground to cover operationally.

title: Sustainability framing invites the "is it really not marketing?" question — now with self-reported numbers to weigh

text: **Practical implication for a council.** A sharp lens for *franchising and channel design, partner/stakeholder trust, family-business succession and professionalization, building patiently over decades, decisive bets under uncertainty, and purpose-as-structure*. Weaker for *operational/financial mechanics at scale, risk accounting beyond a survivability check, fast-iteration product cultures, and any situation where partner-trust must be enforced by systems rather than personal relationship* — which the documented franchise disputes suggest is precisely where his own model has been tested hardest and where the institution, without him personally in the room, has not always held to his stated ethic.
title: Practical implication for a council

text: Naval Ravikant, AngelList co-founder, prolific angel (Twitter, Uber, Notion), and the most quotable aphorist on wealth and happiness, is the council's lens for **leverage, autonomy, judgment, and desire-management**: wealth is "assets that earn while you sleep" built on *specific knowledge + accountability + permissionless leverage* (code/media) multiplied by *judgment*, the whole stack reduced to two words, "productize yourself", and happiness is a learned skill whose engine is desire ("a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want"), whose real target is *peace*, and whose enemy is envy. His sharpest contrarian moves: "you're not going to get rich renting out your time"; "hard work is really overrated" (yet "work as hard as you can" if wealth is the goal, ordered what, who, how hard); labor is the *worst* leverage and capital the touchier one; "if you can't decide, the answer is no"; "escape competition through authenticity"; "valuation is temporary, control is forever" (he watched Epinions get zeroed); "Angel investing is the opposite of value investing", where "The best deals are weird", dealflow is not access, and judgment must be calibrated because "If you have poor judgment, you won’t know it"; set an "absurdly high" hourly rate and outsource below it; treat news as adversarial; route around captured regulators; and raise children "disobedient and free and uneducated". His late revisions matter for any consult: wealth is knowledge (he adopts Deutsch's definition and says Marx was "completely wrong"), judgment ends in taste ("I hate articulating it"), AI is a zero-alpha baseline that rewards entrepreneurs who use it better, and by 2025 he says "there's no such thing as happiness" and sells credibility instead of sales. He opposes AI doomers (his fear is *unaligned humans with AI*), splits from libertarian allies on targeted tariffs, parts from Buffett on leverage and on how to bet on startups, and out-radicalizes Paul Graham on schooling and on raising capital at all. Use him for long-horizon, ownership, control, judgment-calibration, and AI-as-leverage framing; distrust him on operational how-to in the late-aphorist register, clinical well-being (he calls depression "really a choice"), and advice that must hold for people without capital or a safety net; serious critics (Sandel via meritocracy, Bourdieu via cultural capital, the "luck paradox") argue "without getting lucky" generalizes from a survivor in Silicon Valley's Extremistan, and he names several of his own gaps ("post-wealth taste," a "fraudulent" book, anger).

text: Naval Ravikant is an Indian-American entrepreneur and angel investor, co-founder and chairman of AngelList. As an angel he made early bets on Twitter, Uber, Notion, Opendoor, Postmates, and Wish, and earlier co-founded Epinions (an online product-review site) and the Venture Hacks blog, term-sheet advice that became AngelList. The Epinions arc is load-bearing for his worldview: ~$45M raised, the founders' common stock zeroed in the 2003 DealTime merger that formed Shopping.com, then a 2005 lawsuit against Benchmark and August Capital after Shopping.com's IPO and eBay sale showed the founders had been told their stock was worthless while insiders profited (see *Positions* and *Provenance*). That experience, "I basically got cheated by my business partners", is the root of "control is forever," "judge investors by behavior, not words," and the founding of Venture Hacks (2007) and AngelList. He also names a deeper wound: he started AngelList "partially because I was cut out of some very big deals early on." Beyond investing he is best known as a writer and aphorist on wealth, happiness, and decision-making, crystallized in the 2018 "How to Get Rich (without getting lucky)" tweetstorm (expanded into a full Naval-and-Nivi interview series) and *The Almanack of Naval Ravikant* (2020), compiled by Eric Jorgenson and released free online. He is a recurring long-form guest (Tim Ferriss since 2015, the Knowledge Project, Joe Rogan, Modern Wisdom, All-In). Note the two phases: the earlier Naval (the Epinions/Venture Hacks/Elad Gil operator, term sheets, option-pool shuffles, founder-investor power dynamics) is sharper and more combative; the later aphorist is more serene and philosophical. Since ~2024 his attention has shifted heavily toward AI, crypto, longevity, and network-state themes, and in 2025 he became a heavy hands-on "vibe coder," declaring "pure software is uninvestable." The Almanack's own landing page lists him as founder of "Angellist, Epinions, and Vast.com" and as an angel in "Twitter, Uber, Yammer, and 100+ more." In 2025 and 2026 he is building a self-funded company in stealth, Impossible, Inc. ("we're burning a million and a half dollars a month of my money"), which runs on a small elite team with no Slack and no PM software, and his latest writing (sales, org design, AI, drones) shows a third register: more hedged ("I don't know"), more Deutsch and Advaita than Almanack.

text: **Seek wealth, not money or status.** "Wealth is having assets that earn while you sleep. Money is how we transfer time and wealth. Status is your place in the social hierarchy." Wealth is positive-sum ("We create things together"); status is "an old zero-sum game," and "those attacking wealth creation are often just seeking status." Money's precise nature: "social credits… the ability to have credits and debits of other people's time." (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; nav.al/rich; prioritize-and-focus)

text: **You will not get rich renting out your time.** "You're not going to get rich renting out your time. You must own equity—a piece of a business—to gain your financial freedom," because without ownership "when you're sleeping, you're not earning… and you can't earn nonlinearly." Renting time is acceptable *only* "when you are learning and saving," ideally in a field where "apprenticeship is the only model." (angel; finding-time)

"In 1,000 parallel universes, you want to be wealthy in 999 of them"; "It's about becoming the kind of person that makes money." His confidence statement: dropped penniless on a random English-speaking street, "within five or ten years I'd be wealthy again." (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; money-luck)

text: **The wealth equation: specific knowledge + accountability + leverage, multiplied by judgment, compounded over time.** Compressed: "why you, that's accountability, at scale, that's leverage, and just you getting paid… that's specific knowledge." *Specific knowledge* is "knowledge you cannot be trained for," found "by pursuing your innate talents, your genuine curiosity, and your passion," learned through apprenticeship not classrooms, and split into *timely* (e.g. ML now) and *timeless* (e.g. persuasion). *Accountability* is reputational skin in the game. *Leverage* = labor + capital + code/media. *Judgment* is the multiplier. The stack reduces to "productize yourself." (specific-knowledge; finding-time; accountability-leverage; nav.al/rich)

text: **Play long-term games with long-term people, all returns compound.** His most load-bearing principle: "Pick an industry where you can play long-term games with long-term people," because "Play iterated games. All the returns in life, whether in wealth, relationships, or knowledge, come from compound interest." The mechanism is game structure: "In a long-term game, it's positive sum. We're all baking the pie together… And in a short-term game, we're cutting up the pie." This is why he avoids cynics and one-shot deals and reuses the same partners for decades. (understanding-how-wealth-is-created; how-to-get-lucky; play-long-term-games-with-long-term-people)

You get rich by saving your time to make money." The endgame: "I would love to be paid purely for my judgment, not for any work." (judgment; nav.al/rich; get-paid-for-your-judgment)

Today one decision "can make a company $10 million or $100 million." "Companies don't know how to measure outputs, so they measure inputs instead. Work in a way that your outputs are visible and measurable." (finding-time)

Power that exists *will* be abused, so structure your life so nobody holds it over you. Forged at Epinions; unifies term sheets, permissionless leverage, parenting, and routing around regulators. text: **Happiness is a learned skill, and its mechanism is desire.** "Happiness is what's there when you remove the sense that something is missing in your life." Real happiness is a side-effect of *peace*, which comes from acceptance: "Peace is happiness at rest, and happiness is peace in motion." Its structural enemy is envy/comparison. So the real currency of life is attention. It's what you choose to pay attention to and what you do about it." Corollary on wasted time: "the true wasted time is time that you're not present for... If you're not immersed in this moment then you're wasting your time." (Modern Wisdom @03:10:55 / @01:25:31, auto-caption)

text: **Pathogens are humanity's real predators, and much of biology, hygiene and culture is downstream of that war.** "We are top of the well-known food chain, but bacteria and viruses eat us. Fungus eats us. So these microscopic predators are our natural predators. And so a lot of aging, societal structure, hygiene, religious strictures against pork, circumcision — all of these things are designed to resist bacteria and viruses." Mechanism aside: "The body releases its own hormones in pulses rather than steady state... because enemy bacteria... can't pulse. They can't coordinate to pulse." (Modern Wisdom @02:47:34 / @02:46:38, auto-caption)

text: **Wealth is knowledge, not stored capital (a late self-revision).** In the Megasode he demotes his own signature definition: "Deutsch had a better definition of wealth than I did. My definition of wealth was very focused by my desire to make money." Deutsch's version: "his definition of wealth is the set of physical transformations that you can affect." The consequence is anti-Marxist: "the value is not in the capital. It's not in the factories. It's in the knowledge," so "If you removed Elon Musk from SpaceX, you can't capture his wealth" and "It is not a pie to be divided up." He adds "this is one thing where Marx was completely wrong," and "Gold is a pointer to actual value." His own earning power follows the same logic: the highest it has been, "Because I have tremendous knowledge." (Megasode @00:01:04 to @00:05:19, auto-caption)

text: **Money is a social IOU that gets debased; status is the older game, wealth the newer.** "If I do my job right, if I create value for society, society says, 'Oh, thank you. We owe you something in the future for the work that you did in the past. Here's a little IOU. Let's call that money.'" The failure modes are theft and printing: "That money gets debased because people steal the IOUs. The government prints extra IOUs. People renege on their IOUs." Its purpose (see the signature line) is "so that you are your own sovereign individual." His history of the two games: before farming "You couldn't have wealth before the farming age because you couldn't store things. Hunter-gatherers carried everything on their backs," so status, not wealth, predicted survival. Even a house counts as wealth because it can be rented, "although that's probably a lower use of productivity of land than doing some commercial enterprise." (seek-wealth)

text: **Wealth does not change the person; inner state is the real bottleneck.** "When you’re finally wealthy, you’ll realize it wasn’t what you were seeking in the first place." "The first thing you realize when you’ve made a bunch of money is that you’re still the same person. If you’re happy, you’re happy. If you’re unhappy, you’re unhappy." Money removes one channel of conflict ("A lot of divorces happen over money") but not the rest ("A lot of external battles happen because your internal state is not good"). His stated ultimate purpose of money: "so you don’t have to be in a specific place, at a specific time, doing anything you don’t want to do." (finally-wealthy)

text: **Happiness is trainable because the set point is only about half genetic.** "The first step to increasing your level of happiness is realizing you can." "your genetic set point is only about half of it. And happiness, or general contentment, is much more malleable than the other things." His own contrast: workouts could not change his athletic ceiling much, but "things like my temperament, outlook on life, how peaceful I am, how angry I get—these are much more in my control." The obstacle is disbelief: "Many people believe that happiness cannot be developed or changed, so they devalue it. They say, “Well, I don’t want to be happy.”" ("roughly half" is his gloss, uncited on the page.) (skill)

text: **Smart people can be happy; cynicism is the intelligence signal that blocks it.** He grants the objection ("Happiness is for stupid people" is "a common complaint I hear from smart overachievers"), then inverts it: "You’re not smart because you’re unhappy; you’re unhappy because you’re smart. You can be happy and smart—it’s just going to take more work." The mechanism: "You become cynical, and you signal your intelligence through cynicism." The founder's fear that contentment kills drive gets a pragmatic answer: "being unhappy is very inefficient" and "Unhappy people don’t have good judgment." The honest cost: "If you become the Buddha tomorrow, it’s unlikely you’ll also launch rockets to the moon like Elon Musk." And the permission slip: "It’s OK to not want to be happy." (smart; inefficient)

text: **Desire runs a three-step loop that never ends in lasting bliss.** "You become disturbed because you want something. Then you work really hard to get it and are miserable in the meantime. Finally, when you get it, you revert to the state you were in before you had it." The reductio: "If obtaining things made us permanently happy, then the cavemen would have been miserable, and we would all be deliriously happy." So "There’s no single permanent solution to happiness. Rather, achieving happiness requires a process of understanding and self-discovery. It is a process of training yourself to see certain truths." He scopes the claim: "Enlightenment is something different... We’re just talking about common sense happiness." Later, "The search for peace is really the search for truth." (desire; truth)

text: **The mind evolved paranoid, and peak pleasure is a quiet mind.** "Our mind evolved to be paranoid, fearful and angry," because "The optimist would catch a rabbit nine out of 10 times and get eaten by a tiger the 10th. The pessimist survives every time." But "The threat level is not as high as our genes think," so the payoff matrix has changed. What people chase in "your moments of greatest pleasure" (a drug, an orgasm, kite-surfing, a sunset) is the silence: "your mind goes quiet." The mind is not an enemy ("It’s a very useful tool") but "The mind became the master rather than a servant." (peace)

text: **Accountability = reputational skin in the game.** *Gist:* take public risk under your own name and society routes responsibility, equity, and leverage to you. *Worked example:* "Embrace accountability and take business risks under your own name. text: **Net present value.** *Gist:* discount future cash to today so founders can't dazzle you with future-value equity. "Net present value is when you say, 'That stream of payments I'm going to get in the future—what's it worth today?'" *Worked example:* a founder offers 0.1% of a company that "is going to be worth $1 billion," pitching it as $1 million of stock. Discount at a rate "that accounts for the massive risk startups face" and use the last round as the market's verdict: "If the founder recently raised a round at a $10 million valuation, then the company’s only worth 1% of what the founder says it will be worth. So your $1 million package is actually worth $10,000." Hence "You should get very comfortable doing rough net present value calculations in your head." (npv)

title: Net present value

text: **Power-law portfolio math (angel investing).** *Gist:* one extreme winner pays for all the zeros, so access beats judgment. *Worked example:* "If you invest in 100 companies and one of them produces a 1,000x return… the other 99 investments could go to zero and you would still see an overall return of 10x." Corollary: "the top deal in a good portfolio returns as much as deals 2 through N combined," so "It's okay to pass on investments—you just don't want them to pass on you." His own Twitter (~400x) and Uber (~4,000x) realized this. (angel; 11-lessons; Tim Ferriss #97)

text: **Work like a lion, not an ox, a marathon of sprints.** *Gist:* knowledge work is bursts at high output, then rest. *Worked example:* "Forty hour work weeks are a relic of the Industrial Age. Knowledge workers function like athletes—train and sprint, then rest and reassess." He owns it personally: "I'm actually a lazy person. I work through bursts of energy where I'm really motivated." text: **The four kinds of luck (luck as a designable surface).** *Gist:* (1) *blind luck*; (2) *hustle luck*; (3) *opportunity-spotting luck* (skilled enough to notice); (4) *character/brand luck*, "you build a unique character, a unique brand, a unique mindset, which causes luck to find you." *Worked example:* the best deep-sea diver gets the call about the sunken treasure, "their luck just became your luck." Ported from Disraeli: "we make our fortunes and we call them fate." (how-to-get-lucky; money-luck)
quotes: you build a unique character, a unique brand, a unique mindset, which causes luck to find you.
their luck just became your luck.
we make our fortunes and we call them fate.

text: **Only markets and nature give real feedback.** *Gist:* the learning loop (see the 10,000-iterations entries below) only works if the signal is real. *Worked example:* real feedback "comes from free markets and nature… It is impossible to fool Mother Nature"; awards and friends are "fake." Run "your own lemonade stand." (in-the-arena; nav.al/rich)

(in-the-arena)

text: **Read what you love until you love to read.** *Gist:* the *love* of reading is the asset; the specific books matter less. *Worked example:* "Read what you love until you love to read." Don't begin with Richard Dawkins… Read Darwin first." (The "best 100 books over and over" line is him *quoting* @illacertus, see *Provenance*.) (learn-to-love-to-read; read)

text: **Lindy / minority rule, ported from Taleb into crypto.** *Gist:* survival predicts survival; a committed non-compromising minority drags the system. *Worked example:* "In crypto, Bitcoin is the Lindy currency. The longer it's survived, the longer it will survive." (BlockCon 2018)

text: **Social consistency as a forcing function.** *Gist:* a public commitment binds your future self. *Worked example:* "if you want to quit smoking, all you have to do is go to everybody you know and say, 'I quit smoking… I give you my word.'" He told colleagues he was leaving to start a company; months later the public commitment forced him through. (choosing-to-build-yourself; JRE)

text: **Consumer surplus.** *Gist:* a free-market transaction nets the buyer more value than they paid, so business is a net value-creator rather than extraction. *Worked example:* "Consumer surplus is the excess value you get from something when you pay less than you were willing to pay." His illustration: you'd pay $20 for the Starbucks coffee that keeps you alert at work, but you only pay a few dollars, the gap is surplus the seller hands you for free. (surplus)
quotes: Consumer surplus is the excess value you get from something when you pay less than you were willing to pay.
title: Consumer surplus

text: **Tit-for-tat / iterated prisoner's dilemma.** *Gist:* the single most worth-knowing piece of game theory, cooperation and trust only emerge in repeated games, where defecting once poisons every future round. *Worked example:* "I've learned that tit-for-tat iterated prisoner's dilemma is the piece of game theory that is worth knowing the most. You can almost put down the game theory book after that." It's the formal engine under "play long-term games with long-term people." (nav.al/rich)
quotes: I've learned that tit-for-tat iterated prisoner's dilemma is the piece of game theory that is worth knowing the most. You can almost put down the game theory book after that.
play long-term games with long-term people.

text: **Coase theorem, firm size is set by internal vs. external transaction costs.** *Gist:* a company is exactly as big as the point where doing things in-house gets more expensive than buying them outside; tech is collapsing external costs and shrinking the firm. *Worked example:* "Ronald Coase is an economist who has this... very famous theorem, but he basically just talks about why is a company the size that it is... and it has to do with the internal transaction costs versus the external transaction costs." (JRE #1309 @00:25:33), he uses it to predict the "atomization of the firm" and the rise of individual/gig work (Airbnb).
quotes: Ronald Coase is an economist who has this... very famous theorem, but he basically just talks about why is a company the size that it is... and it has to do with the internal transaction costs versus the external transaction costs.
atomization of the firm
title: Coase theorem, firm size is set by internal vs. external transaction costs

text: **Agrippa's trilemma, every "why" chain dead-ends in three places.** *Gist:* any "why?" regress terminates in infinite regress, circular reasoning, or an axiom, so ultimate-meaning questions have no terminal answer. *Worked example:* "There's a thing called [Agrippa's trilemma]... it says that any questioning like this, why, will always end in one of three places. First is infinite regress... The second is circular reasoning... Or the third is an axiom, and the most popular axiom is god." (JRE #1309 @01:36:43), "saying we're in a simulation, or saying it's the big bang, is just another way of saying god." title: Agrippa's trilemma, every "why" chain dead-ends in three places

text: **Hand the system to your enemies to run for a decade.** *Gist:* a system is only good if you'd trust the other side to operate it; if it only works when your team holds it, it's not a good system. *Worked example:* "The test of any good system is, you build a system, hand it over to your enemies to run for the next decade. So for example, if you want censorship on Twitter or Facebook, you should build that system, and then hand it over to the other side to run." (JRE #1309 @01:13:51), he applies it to censorship and immigration policy.

text: **Taleb's nested politics, scale of the group sets where you fall on the spectrum.** *Gist:* the bigger and lower-trust the group, the more you must lean capitalist; socialism is right with your tribe, capitalism with strangers. *Worked example:* "I always liked Nassim Taleb['s framing] on this, where he said, 'With my family, I'm a communist. With my close friends, I'm a socialist. At my state level politics, I'm a Democrat. At higher levels, I'm a Republican. And at the federal level, I'm a libertarian.' So basically the larger the group of people you have mass[ed] together who have different interests, the less trust there is, the more cheating there is... the more you go towards capitalism." (JRE #1309 @00:44:21) (attributes the frame to Nassim Taleb)
quotes: I always liked Nassim Taleb['s framing] on this, where he said, 'With my family, I'm a communist. With my close friends, I'm a socialist. At my state level politics, I'm a Democrat. At higher levels, I'm a Republican. And at the federal level, I'm a libertarian.' So basically the larger the group of people you have mass[ed] together who have different interests, the less trust there is, the more cheating there is... the more you go towards capitalism.
title: Taleb's nested politics, scale of the group sets where you fall on the spectrum

text: **The internet: one hegemon plus a long tail, with the middle killed.** *Gist:* aggregation creates a single giant winner and millions of atomized individuals, and destroys everything medium-sized in between. *Worked example:* "The internet is this giant aggregator where it creates one big [hegemon] for everything, and it creates an atomized long tail of millions and millions of individuals. What it gets rid of is the medium-sized ones in the middle." (JRE #1309 @00:58:47), applied to media/commerce (Netflix, Amazon) and to predict "everyone's a journalist." The robots are already here and there are way more robots than there are humans, it's just that we packed them in data centers for heat and efficiency reasons... every great software developer now has an army of robots working for him at nighttime while he or she sleeps." text: **The outcome "equation", and the warning not to treat it as math.** *Gist:* the pieces multiply (specific knowledge × leverage × judgment × accountability × what society values, compounded over time), but treating it numerically is false precision. *Worked example:* "Your eventual outcome will be equal to something like the distinctiveness of your specific knowledge times how much leverage you can apply to that knowledge times how often your judgment is correct times how singularly accountable you are for the outcome times how much society values what you're doing — and then you compound all of that with how long you can keep doing it." text: **Two tells that you've found specific knowledge.** *Gist:* if a skill can only be learned by doing it, and the practitioner can't describe a typical day, it's specific knowledge. *Worked example:* "When you find a skill that can only be learned on the job by doing it, that is a good indicator... Another good indicator is when you ask the person doing it 'what do you do every day' and they can't give you a straight answer... 'every day is different based on what's going on.'" text: **Principal-agent, operator version: "if you want it done then go; if not then send."** *Gist:* deal with the smallest possible firm so there's "one throat to choke," and as an agent, act like the owner. *Worked example:* "my ideal law firm to work with is a law firm of one, my ideal banker to work with is a solo banker... you've got one throat to choke, there's no one else to point fingers to... text: **Turn a single-move game into a repeat game (the contractor trick).** *Gist:* high-cost, low-information one-shot deals invite defection; manufacture future rounds to align the counterparty. *Worked example:* "An example of a very high cost, low information single-move game is having your house renovated... one way to [fix it]: 'actually I need two different projects done, so the first project we'll do together and then based on that I'll decide if we do the second'... or 'I have three friends who want projects done and they're waiting to see the outcome'... these are all ways of turning a single-move game into a longer-term game." Why nearly everyone is anxious. (TF #473)

text: **Non-dual activities, the free-lunch pursuits that don't create their own opposite.** *Gist:* chasing money/fame manufactures future anxiety; some activities are intrinsically true and carry no downside later. *Worked example:* "What activities are intrinsically true in and of themselves and kind of are a free lunch? text: **Bitcoin as a finite-shelf-space Swiss bank account.** *Gist:* the speculative price mechanism is demand to enter a fixed-supply vault versus supply trying to exit. *Worked example:* "one way to think about a Bitcoin... is it's a Swiss bank account but it's a Swiss bank account with finite space and if you want shelf space in that Swiss bank account with finite space, you have to buy out one of the existing holders in that space." text: **Answer questions at the level they were asked.** *Gist:* most philosophical paradoxes are a level-switching trick, posing a question as a human here-and-now but answering it from the universe's view over infinite time. *Worked example:* "The reason it seems paradoxical is because you're asking the question of a human here and now... and then answering it from the viewpoint of the universe over infinite time. text: **The secretary problem is iteration-based, not time-based.** *Gist:* a correction of the common misreading, the stopping rule depends on the number of shots taken, not elapsed time, so bail and decide quickly. *Worked example:* "The interesting thing about the secretary theorem is that it's actually not time based... It's iteration based. The number of shots you took on goal... so you need to bail out quickly and you need to be decisive quickly." (Modern Wisdom @00:59:40, auto-caption)

text: **Iteration ≠ repetition, 10,000 error-corrections to mastery.** *Gist:* a refinement of "10,000 iterations": only iterations that *modify based on a learning* count; doing the same thing over is repetition and teaches little. *Worked example:* "I would say it's actually 10,000 iterations to mastery... Iteration is not repetition. Repeating is doing the same thing over and over. Iteration is modifying it with a learning and then doing another version. So that's error correction. If you get 10,000 error corrections in anything, you will be an expert at it." The spoken lemonade-stand/retail framing: stocking shelves the same way daily teaches nothing, "whereas if I was putting in thousands of iterations that would be different... the more shots on goal you can have the faster you're going to learn." text: **Barbell strategy for life, skeptical on specifics, optimistic in the general.** *Gist:* almost every specific opportunity fails, yet the aggregate is worth betting on; live at the extremes, not the gray middle. *Worked example:* "Every specific opportunity is probably a fail. text: **The Red Queen race, humans and pathogens evolve at the same speed by different strategies.** *Gist:* sexual selection (slow, every ~20 yrs) versus asexual mutation (fast, over thousands of generations) keep the two sides running in place against each other. *Worked example:* "We're in a red queen race where we're both running at roughly the same speed using very different strategies." (Modern Wisdom @02:44:36, auto-caption)
quotes: We're in a red queen race where we're both running at roughly the same speed using very different strategies.
title: The Red Queen race, humans and pathogens evolve at the same speed by different strategies

text: **Adams' Law of Slow-Moving Disasters.** *Gist:* visible, slow-moving problems get solved by markets and individual incentives before they become catastrophes. *Worked example:* "When disasters are very slow moving like peak oil or global warming or population collapse, and everyone can see them coming, economics and society as a force solve them because enough individual people have incentives to go solve them." (attributed to Scott Adams; used to dismiss fertility-collapse panic.) (Modern Wisdom @02:32:49, auto-caption)
quotes: When disasters are very slow moving like peak oil or global warming or population collapse, and everyone can see them coming, economics and society as a force solve them because enough individual people have incentives to go solve them.
title: Adams' Law of Slow-Moving Disasters

text: **The Schelling point, coordinating with no communication.** *Gist:* people converge on a focal answer without talking, by reasoning about what the other will reason. *Worked example:* "Suppose that I want to meet with you but I don't tell you where and I don't tell you when... we cannot communicate... we're probably gonna pick New Years, and what time, midnight... and where would we meet... probably in New York City... probably Grand Central Station under the clock." (How to Get Rich pod @03:12:01, auto-caption)

title: The Schelling point, coordinating with no communication

text: **Russian roulette, ergodicity made concrete.** *Gist:* a population average is not one person's repeated bet; what works across many people once can ruin one person who repeats it. *Worked example:* "Six people who play Russian roulette once each and then each winner gets a billion dollars — one person ends up dead, five people have a billion dollars — versus one person who plays Russian roulette with the same one gun six times is never gonna end up a billionaire, is gonna end up worth zero." (via Taleb.) (How to Get Rich pod @03:11:14, auto-caption)

title: Russian roulette, ergodicity made concrete

text: **Price discrimination, charge by willingness-to-pay, not by cost.** *Gist:* the same good is priced far above cost to those who'll pay, using small signals of comfort/status to segment them. *Worked example:* "Business class seats will routinely cost five or ten times what an economy class seat does, but it probably costs the airline just two, maybe three x to provide that — it's just the rich person is more willing to pay, so you have to give them the little things... to either signal they're rich or that little bit of comfort." (How to Get Rich pod @03:19:00, auto-caption)

title: Price discrimination, charge by willingness-to-pay, not by cost

text: **Externalities are best fixed by pricing, not exhortation.** *Gist:* moralizing campaigns waste effort; pricing the externality routes the cut to whoever consumes most. *Worked example:* "California likes to run declarations and ads to scare you into not taking showers... when it would be just much better to raise the price of fresh water. Your average consumer might pay a few pennies more for a shower, but then the almond farmers who consume a lot of the water will cut back... properly pricing externalities can save resources in a tremendous way." (How to Get Rich pod @03:22:39, auto-caption)

Your average consumer might pay a few pennies more for a shower, but then the almond farmers who consume a lot of the water will cut back... properly pricing externalities can save resources in a tremendous way.
title: Externalities are best fixed by pricing, not exhortation

text: **Steel frame vs. scaffolding, understand from the basics up, don't memorize.** *Gist:* a ground-up foundation you can re-derive beats a scaffolding of memorized advanced concepts; memorizing is the tell that you don't understand. *Worked example:* "[Know] the basics from the ground up [—] solid foundation of understanding, a steel frame of understanding, than it is to just have a scaffolding [where you're] just memorizing advanced concepts." (JRE #1309 @01:33:30), cites Feynman taking you "from counting numbers on your hand, all the way to calculus in four pages of text"; the tell of not understanding is heavy jargon you can't follow.

title: Steel frame vs. scaffolding, understand from the basics up, don't memorize

text: **The leverage ladder by evolutionary legibility: labor, then capital, then products.** *Gist:* we are evolved to understand labor, so society overvalues it; capital is more surgical; zero-marginal-cost products are the newest and least understood. *Worked example:* "Everybody understands this because we’re evolved to understand the labor form of leverage, so what happens is society overvalues labor as a form of leverage." The tell is the headcount question ("How many people work there?"), which naive listeners ask about your company. Capital's case: "If you are a brilliant investor and give $1 billion and you can make a 30% return with it, whereas anybody else can only make a 20% return, you’re going to get all the money and you’re going to get paid very handsomely for it." It scales better than people: "If you get good at managing capital, you can manage more and more capital much more easily than you can manage more and more people." He concedes the resentment is rational ("deep down, I think we all dislike capital as a form of leverage because it feels unfair"), and gives the ordering: "If you have specific knowledge in a domain and if you’re accountable and you have a good name in that domain, then people are going to give you capital as a form of leverage that you can use to then go get more capital." The Marxist fight between capital and labor is "kind of a trap." Staffing rule: "You want the minimum amount of people working with you that are going to allow you to use the other forms of leverage, which I would argue are much more interesting." (labor-capital)

text: **Ask whose permission and whose economics sit between you and your audience.** *Gist:* the history of reach is lecture hall, then TV, then your own microphone. *Worked example:* decades ago he would have lectured a few hundred people; TV was "somebody else’s leverage" that distorts the message and takes the economics; today "I can buy a cheap microphone, hook it up to a laptop or an iPad, and there you are all listening." For the startup recipe he calls the combination of minimum top-end labor, capital, and code or media "a magic combination, and that’s why you see technology startups explode out of nowhere, use massive leverage and just make huge outsize returns." The contrast with the old pattern: "The last generation, fortunes were made by capital. That was the Warren Buffets of the world... But the new generation’s fortunes are all made through code or media." Platform gripes (Facebook, YouTube, the closed iPhone) are secondary to access because "permissionless leverage, where everyone can be a broadcaster, is just too good" (paraphrase of the passage). The robots are literal: "These robots aren’t very smart. They have to be told very precisely what to do and how to do it," so "The bottleneck is just figuring out intelligent and interesting things to do to them." (product-media)

text: **Egalitarian-output test: the more human labor in a good, the less equal its consumption; ethics follows.** *Gist:* labor and capital stratify outputs, code and media equalize them. *Worked example:* "The more of a human element there is in providing that service, the less egalitarian it is. Jeff Bezos probably has much better vacations than most of us because he has lots of humans running around doing whatever he needs to do," whereas "Google doesn’t give him some premium, special Google account where his searches are better." Signaling goods invert this: "If you look at something like buying a Rolex, which is no longer about telling time. It’s a signaling good. ... That’s a zero sum game," and "Rich people don’t have better cars. They just have weirder cars." The scale-economy ladder: the most-used product gets the biggest budget at no marginal cost per user, "and so with the largest budget, you get the highest quality." The moral conclusion: "If you care about ethics in wealth creation, it is better to create your wealth using code and media as leverage because then those products are equally available to everybody as opposed to trying to create your wealth through labor or capital." Qualifier: labor and capital are getting diffuse permissioning ("community" for labor, crowdfunding for capital). (egalitarian-leverage)

text: **Input/output coupling diagnoses a career, and ownership is the escape hatch.** *Gist:* "You really just want a job, or a career, or a profession where your inputs don’t match your outputs." *Worked example:* "Tools and leverage are what create this disconnection between inputs and outputs," and by leverage "I don’t mean financial leveraged alone, like Wall Street uses, and that has a bad name. I’m just talking about tools." Even high-hourly professionals only get rich by turning time into an asset (a doctor who opens a practice and builds a brand). The employer holds the risk, so "They’re gonna pay you the bare minimum that they have to, to get you to do their job"; options at a tech company are "a fine way to start" with founding or investing as the real wealth. He retitles his own tweetstorm: "this tweetstorm should have been called “How to Create Wealth.” It’s just “How to Get Rich” was a more catchy title." (renting-time)

text: **Accountability as a position in the capital stack.** *Gist:* every piece of work sits on a ladder of claims; taking accountability moves you from salary to equity. *Worked example:* employees are paid first and have the most security, debt holders get a capped coupon, equity gets what remains ("The equity holders take on greater risk, but in exchange, they get nearly unlimited upside"; "The employees get the most security, but in exchange for that security, they don’t have as much upside."). So "Essentially, taking accountability for your actions is the same as taking an equity position in all of your work. You’re taking greater downside risk for greater upside." The pricing lever is replaceability: "If you have high accountability, that makes you less replaceable. Then they have to give you equity, which is a piece of the upside." The captain test: an airline captain cannot blame the copilot ("You can’t later blame it on anyone else"). Economic failure is survivable, integrity failure is not: "generally people will forgive failures as long as you were honest and made a high integrity effort," but a Madoff surname follows descendants. Nivi presses on whether accountability is fragile and Naval concedes "I think it could actually be fragile." (accountability-equity)

text: **Large-to-small career glide path and the peer-only hierarchy.** *Gist:* start in a big firm for training, move to smaller ones where work is visible, and let every vertical relationship justify itself as teaching. *Worked example:* "In general, ceteris paribus... you ’ll do better in a smaller organization than a larger one," and "Here is a good progression for a career: Start in a large company and progressively move to smaller and smaller ones. It’s very hard to go from a small company to a larger company." Why: "Larger companies tend to be more about politics than merit; they’re more stable but less innovative." On hierarchy: "If there’s someone above you, that’s someone to learn from. If you’re not learning from them and improving, nobody should be above you," and "If there’s somebody below you, it’s because you’re teaching them and enabling them. If you’re not doing that, then get a robot." Midlife protocol: apply the stack piecemeal through weekend projects, an evening course, and role choices at your current employer. He flags it himself: "This is utopian and still a long way off." (working-ourselves)

text: **Hustle to get leverage, then slow down to steer (sailboat to ocean liner).** *Gist:* the right tempo flips once leverage arrives. *Worked example:* "It’s like you’ve gone from  steering your sailboat around to now you’re steering an ocean liner or a tanker," so "Once you have the leverage, then you wanna slow down a bit, because your judgment really matters." A CEO whose judgment is 10 or 20 percent better on a $100 billion hull earns hundreds of millions more, which is why CEO pay is not all crony capitalism (paraphrase). Buffett is the exemplar of demonstrated judgment: "Nobody asks him how hard he works; nobody asks him when he wakes up or when he goes to sleep." His thought experiment (paraphrase) is that investors would hand Buffett $100 billion again even if he lost everything tomorrow. (judgment)

title: Hustle to get leverage, then slow down to steer (sailboat to ocean liner)

text: **Judgment needs skin in the game, and the best judges are the least emotional.** *Gist:* experience with accountability is what turns intellect into judgment. *Worked example:* "Intellect without any experience is often worse than useless because you get the confidence that the intellect gives you, and you get some of the credibility, but because you had no skin in the game, and you had no real experience, and no real accountability, you’re just throwing darts." Hence "Investment books are the worst place to learn about investment, because investment is a real-world activity that is highly multi-variate, all the advantages are always being competed away." He reads history, science and philosophy instead, since "Philosophy also makes you more stoic, makes you less emotional, and so you make better decisions; you have better judgment." As a vetting proxy: "The more outraged somebody is, I guarantee you, the worse their judgment is," and "you don’t want to hand this person the keys to your car, let alone the keys to your company." (judgment)

text: **Judgment is self-blind, so calibrate it with proxies.** *Gist:* the faculty you are assessing is the faculty doing the assessing. *Worked example:* "If you have poor judgment, you won’t know it," because "your ability to assess your own judgment is subject to your level of judgment," and "it takes five to 15 years to figure out if you have good judgment." Three proxy tests: later-round markups (which he calls "a Keynesian beauty contest where each judge is rewarded based on what the judge in the next round thinks," and which fails for Bitcoin because there is no subsequent VC round), who piles in after you (not before, "you’re probably keying off of them"), and "Don’t ask them if you have good judgment or not, because polite people will always tell you yes. Rather, ask them about your weaknesses." Cultivating it is preparation, not diligence: "Judgment isn’t necessarily due diligence or even thinking. Judgment is the preparation you do before a deal arrives so that your subconscious can process it quickly." (angel-2)

text: **The judgment ladder ends in taste, and it is loaded in sprints then left to percolate.** *Gist:* reasoning becomes intuition becomes taste; the work is getting the problem into your head and then resting against it. *Worked example:* "You start with reasoning and then you build up your judgment. And then when your judgment is sufficiently refined, it just becomes taste or intuition or gut feel, and that’s what you operate on." "Judgment comes through experience and reflection," and "there comes a point where your judgment is so good that you can't even articulate it. And that's when it's called taste, right?" (Megasode @00:51:11). His own investing is now taste "Almost entirely. I hate articulating it." Process: writing a compiler took "24 to 36 hour sessions where I wouldn't sleep," then "I want to load it into my background subconscious. I want my intuition working on it so I can have that shower breakthrough 48 hours later," and John Cleese's version, "you simply have to let your mind rest against the problem in a friendly, persistent way." Examples of taste at work: Rick Rubin, Jobs, and AI lab researchers choosing which GPU experiments to run. (arena; Megasode @00:54:18 to @01:01:32, auto-caption)

title: Angel investing and founder selection (expansion)

text: **Dealflow is not access, and a brand is how access is earned.** *Gist:* seeing deals is cheap; investing when you want and on your terms is the scarce thing. *Worked example:* "Dealflow and access are not the same thing," and "The three things it takes to get into investing are capital, judgment and dealflow." A brand is "an authentic reputation you have with founders and investors," circular at the root ("Invest in the winning companies, and you’ll develop a brand that lets you invest in winning companies") and not purchasable ("You’re not going to build a brand simply because you want to"). The build menu (paraphrase): content (Elad Gil, Fred Wilson, Brad Feld), platforms (YC, AngelList, Product Hunt, SaaStr), a stance (a16z founder-friendly), unusual LPs, software for startups, a niche capability. His own entry: a Facebook app with 20 million installs as a calling card, then a half-hour whiteboard on growth hacking for Evan Williams; Twitter declined to adopt any of it ("it’s against our ethos") but let him invest, his first major angel win. Anchor the brand on capabilities, not verticals: a cleantech-only brand dies if solar is late (Kleiner), and where top firms specialize it is "being weird" (Founders Fund). (angel-1)

text: **Shadow co-founder at pre-seed, and the pro-rata math.** *Gist:* put in the first money, help assemble the company, recruit a "seller" for 5 to 10 percent rather than the half or two-thirds technical founders often give up, and keep pro-rata rights. *Worked example:* own 5 percent and hold the right to fund 5 percent of future rounds, and you might later deploy "$30 million in the pro rata, instead of your initial $3,000"; LPs will pay carry and fees to access that, with liquidity closer than a ten-year hold. (angel-1)
quotes: $30 million in the pro rata, instead of your initial $3,000
title: Shadow co-founder at pre-seed, and the pro-rata math

text: **Market efficiency times wealth creation tells you where to invest.** *Gist:* prefer an inefficient market where the asset actually creates wealth. *Worked example (paraphrase):* art and wine are inefficient but create little wealth; gambling destroys wealth "unless you own the casino"; tech angel investing combines inefficiency with real wealth creation. Hub hierarchy follows: SF, New York, Beijing, Shanghai and Bengaluru safer; "Unfortunately, it’s exits" is the best indicator that a hub works; angels who invest locally in a weak city eventually "surrender" and buy Bay Area startups. (angel-1)
quotes: unless you own the casino

title: Market efficiency times wealth creation tells you where to invest

text: **Soft pivot versus jump (a taxonomy for pricing pivot risk).** *Gist:* "A pivot means keeping one leg in place and moving the other one around. It’s not a jump or a leap into a completely different industry." *Worked example:* Uber from black cars to shared rides "wasn’t a pivot; it was an extension"; Odeo to Twitter was a pivot by "the person who popularized blogging"; Burbn to Instagram was "barely a pivot"; Geni to Yammer and Glitch to Slack were jumps that were bets on the person ("But for every one of those, there’s 10 failures."). When pivots are likely, weight team and execution over the exact product and let valuation reflect pivot risk. (angel-2)

text: **One fatal flaw per deal, and the best deals are weird.** *Gist:* the flaw is the excuse conventional VCs use to pass. *Worked example:* "The best deals are weird. They always have something broken, strange or different about them." "You can give every deal one fatal flaw: the thing that traditional venture capitalists will use as their excuse to pass on the deal. If there’s more than one flaw, you have to worry." Uber looked like a taxi business; Google arrived after "the search wars had already been won" (paraphrase). Counterbalance: "A startup that follows all the rules probably won’t be interesting. A startup that breaks all the rules won’t get anywhere, because they have to reinvent everything from scratch." Promonos Capital's governance experiments are the extreme case, with the guardrail "One out of 100 turns out to be a genius; the other 99 turn out to be crazy." (angel-2)

text: **Standard bite and the hot-market trap.** *Gist:* sizing and sector timing are where angels bleed. *Worked example:* if you put big money in some deals and little in others, "your winners tend to come disproportionately out of the deals with little money invested," so keep your standard bite or demand a lower price. On hot sectors: "Anyone in this business who’s chasing hot markets gets killed," with consumer social, food delivery after Uber and 2017 crypto as cases, and the tell "By the time you see conferences about it and read TechCrunch articles about it, it’s probably too late." (angel-2)

Repeat founders suit enterprise execution but "tend to be less passionate" and pricier (paraphrase); the sweet spot is a repeat founder whose prior win "wasn’t so big that they lost their first-time founder mentality." (angel-2)

text: **Specific knowledge can be a temperament, not a skill (the courage case).** *Gist:* what you can do that others find hard counts. *Worked example:* a friend who "may not necessarily be the most clever or the most technical" and is "super hardworking," but "what I do notice is he’s the most courageous." In sales "he’ll call 400 people and get 399 nos. And he’s fine with one “Yes.” And that’s enough." Naval: "It is knowledge. It’s a capability that he knows that he’s okay with it." Detection: "You are not going to know your own specific knowledge until you act and until you act in a variety of difficult situations," validated by yourself or a stranger telling you "Hey, your superpower seems to be X." Family and past work also reveal it: "Our friends and family are actually better at telling us who we are. Looking back at what we’ve done is a better indicator of who we are." text: **Mimetic desire manufactures competition; authenticity exits it, with a market-fit off-ramp.** *Gist:* "We’re highly memetic creatures. We copy everybody around us. We copy our desires from them," so "Competition leads to copy-catting and playing the completely wrong game." *Worked example:* Thiel wanted to clerk for a Supreme Court justice because everyone at law school did, was rejected, and moved into business, "a lesser game" traded for "a greater game" (paraphrase). The guardrail: "It may turn out that you’re the best juggler on a unicycle. But maybe there isn’t much of a market for that, even with YouTube videos. So you have to adjust until you find product-market fit." Competition density is a signal in both directions: "When you see a lot of competition, sometimes that indicates the masses have already arrived," while an empty market means "you’ve gone too authentic" (paraphrase). The unfazed founder: "If somebody else came along and started launching rockets, I don’t think it would faze Elon one bit." (competition-authenticity)

text: **Product-market-founder fit, and the what, who, how-hard ordering.** *Gist:* extend Andreessen's PMF to include how well the founder is personally suited to the business. *Worked example:* the DHH versus Rabois fight about hours: "They’re talking past each other," because "Keith is talking about the Olympics of startups." His synthesis: "If getting wealthy is your goal, you’re going to have to work as hard as you can. But hard work is no substitute for who you work with and what you work on." Order: "You can save a lot of time by picking the right area to work in. Picking the right people to work with is the next most important piece. Third comes how hard you work." Choosing among startups: "Pick the one that’s going to have the best alumni network for you in the future" (the PayPal mafia, "a bunch of geniuses, so they all got rich"). The 80-hour week is mostly signaling: "Nobody really works 80 to 120 hours a week at high output, with mental clarity. Your brain breaks down." (work-hard; redefining)

text: **The aspirational hourly rate, extended into a time-cost filter.** *Gist:* "No one is going to value you more than you value you. Set a high personal hourly rate, and stick to it." It "should seem and feel absurdly high. If it doesn't, it's not high enough"; he used $5,000 an hour *before* he had money (prioritize-and-focus). *Worked example:* "If you decide to spend an hour driving across town to get something, you’re effectively throwing away $100" at a $100 rate; returning a broken Amazon item costs mental hassle that also drains high-output hours. Rule: "If you can outsource something—or not do something—for less than your hourly rate, outsource it or don’t do it," even home cooking. The interpersonal script he used even when broke: "I would argue with girlfriends, 'I don't do that. That's not a problem that I solve'" (prioritize-and-focus), plus an offer to hire an assistant instead (paraphrase). The distinction from frugality: "If you’re going to create wealth, it has to be your number-one, overwhelming priority." (hourly-rate)

text: **Intelligence as a tradeable asset across three constraint sets.** *Gist:* the problem-solving that works on health and wealth works on happiness. *Worked example:* "The beauty of being mentally high functioning in our society is that you can trade it for almost anything. If you’re smart, you can figure out how to be healthy within your genetic constraints and how to be wealthy within your environmental constraints."
