text: **Eliminate the requirement, then the part, then optimize.** *Gist:* before making something efficient, question its requirements. *Worked example:* Musk's fiberglass battery mat as Naval tells it: the battery team blamed noise, the noise team blamed heat, each requirement was obsolete, and "they decided they didn’t need it, and so they eliminated the part." Order (paraphrase): trace the requirement to a named person, delete it, delete parts, only then optimize manufacturing, only then cost. The rule itself is Musk's, which Naval relays as "one of Musk's great driving principles": "Before you start trying to figure out how to make something more efficient, the first thing you do is you question the requirements." Naval's own addition is about who can do it: the person who takes a product from zero to one is "the single person—usually the founder—who can hold the entire problem in their head and make the trade-offs." (simplest)

text: **Pareto superior versus Pareto optimal in negotiation.** "Negotiations are won by whoever cares less." A change that is better for some and worse for none is Pareto superior (always take it); the Pareto frontier is where any gain costs someone, and that is where negotiation happens. His practice: "I cut straight to the chase and don’t try and negotiate an extra 20% here or there—because I know that’s going to make me unhappy in the long-term, make the other person unhappy, and make the deal less stable." (short; inefficient)

text: **Credibility-first selling, rational empathy, and the stag hunt (2026).** *Gist:* "I actually don’t believe in sales. If you feel like someone is selling to you, and if you feel like you’re being sold, it’s a turnoff. Humans are hardwired to resist being sold to. So I think what matters much more is credibility." *Worked example:* be the real estate agent who "steers people away from bad deals and bad neighborhoods and bad houses, so that when the right one comes along for them, they trust you." Rational empathy is "yes, and": reason your way into the other side's position and say yes only if it is valid. Charisma: "Charisma is the ability to project confidence and love simultaneously—or just power and good intentions." On contracts, real societies are stag hunts, and a contract is mutual constraint ("you’re going to stop chasing rabbits, and I’m going to stop chasing rabbits"), so give up optionality only for great deals: "compromise is the enemy of building a great business." (sell)

text: **Productize yourself, turned into a three-question audit.** *Gist:* the two words carry all four wealth inputs. *Worked example:* "Productize has specific knowledge and leverage. Is it myself that I'm projecting?" then "Am I productizing it? Am I scaling it? Am I scaling with labor or capital or code or media?" text: **Keep an empty day, and do not announce it.** Take one day a week with no meetings, "preferably two, because if you budget two, you’ll end up with one." He once owned idontdocoffee.com and later judged the stunt "rude, and petulant, and stupid": protect your time without making a statement of it. "It’s only after you’re bored that you have the great ideas." (TF Q&A 2016)
quotes: preferably two, because if you budget two, you’ll end up with one.
rude, and petulant, and stupid
It’s only after you’re bored that you have the great ideas.
title: Keep an empty day, and do not announce it

text: **Break one bad habit and add one good one about every six months.** "I think learning how to break habits is a very important meta-skill that can serve you better in life than almost anything else." Anchor: do the same activity at the same time seven days a week (a daily workout), which he says fixes other habits (late drinking, caffeine); techniques are substitute, cold turkey, wean, social proof, fill the time slot, remove triggers. Decompose a habit into availability and desire (his alcohol case: the desire was to survive a social environment he was not happy in). He rejects the claim that habits can only be replaced: "That’s BS." (TF Q&A 2016; TKP)
quotes: I think learning how to break habits is a very important meta-skill that can serve you better in life than almost anything else.
title: Break one bad habit and add one good one about every six months

text: **Career choice for a talented engineer at a big company (2016).** Discount investors' advice ("Incentives are everything"); if you know the company, partners and space, go now, otherwise join a startup to get close; early startup if you want to found, later stage for income and lifestyle; take at least one shot "before you’re 30 or 35." With no capital outside SF: move to a hub, get in through customer service or operations, learn to code at an academy. Visa-constrained founders: Unshackled. (TF Q&A 2016, paraphrase with quotes as shown)
quotes: Incentives are everything
before you’re 30 or 35.
title: Career choice for a talented engineer at a big company (2016)

text: **Say no to everything else, and decide by the post-wealth tests.** His daily practice tweet: "Avoid debt, jail, addiction, disgrace, shortcuts, and media," "Productize yourself. Build or buy equity in a business," "Say no to everything else." Passing criteria now: "I will pass up on the investment because I don't want to take a walk with the founder," and "I'm not curious about it. I'm not going to stay up late reading about or thinking about it. So it's going to feel like a chore." He calls this "post-wealth taste." (Megasode @00:54:18 to @00:55:20, auto-caption)

His investing funnel: "I want to see 10,000 companies and I want to pick 500 that have a shot of being huge. Then I want the option to double down on the five winners," and he does not claim the ability to pick ten from a hundred and go all in. (TKP)

text: **Fundraise on internal excitement, not the calendar.** "I measure my own excitement level, and when my own excitement level gets above a certain threshold, then I know I’m ready to go raise the money." Raise "six to 12 months before we need it," and walk away from deals where "they’re going to be on your board, they’re going to have preferred stock, they’re going to have veto rights." Recruit with a bar: anyone on the office floor can be interviewed and "if you don’t think they’re brilliant, don’t join." (sell, 2026)

text: **Tell the truth to a friend's face the way you cannot to yourself.** Advice to friends is easy because their desire collides with reality from outside; run the same filter on your own desired outcome. "The more of a desire that I have that it work out a certain way, the less likely I am to see the truth." The pain of a failing business is you deferring reality, so restart from the truth. (TKP)
quotes: The more of a desire that I have that it work out a certain way, the less likely I am to see the truth.

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap / how to fundraise.** Prefer permissionless leverage (code + media) so you don't *need* capital, "Companies just don't need that much money anymore." When you do raise, optimize for *control*: "Valuation is temporary. Control is forever." The why is autobiographical, at Epinions "it was very common… for an entrepreneur to be pushed out of their own company." (Startup Archive; Story of AngelList; Elad Gil)

Valuation is temporary. Control is forever.
it was very common… for an entrepreneur to be pushed out of their own company.

text: **Negotiating the round / the option-pool shuffle.** Don't let investors hide new-hire dilution in the pre-money: "Slipping the option pool in the pre-money lowers your effective valuation to $6M… not $8M." Counter with a real plan: "make a hiring plan for the next 12 months… the total will be much less than 20%." And on diligence: "let them chase you a little bit too… If a VC is asking for an inordinate amount of diligence… forget them and move on. They'll be even worse once they're on your board." (option-pool-shuffle, including a signed Naval comment)

text: **Late-stage rounds, terms (operator register).** Liquidation preferences make sense for seed/A/B; later-stage companies should push to sell *common* stock. Fallback hierarchy: common + a plain 1x preference; then protective provisions limited to non-arm's-length transactions; then veto granted to the preferred *class*, never an individual series. Treat "hot money" with stronger protections. (Elad Gil)
title: Late-stage rounds, terms (operator register)

text: **Secondaries / founder liquidity.** Legitimate once "the value of your company is greater than… liquidation preferences," typically Series C+; smart investors *let* founders take liquidity to retain them. (Elad Gil)
quotes: the value of your company is greater than… liquidation preferences,
title: Secondaries / founder liquidity

text: **Choosing which investor to take money from.** Pick on power dynamics over brilliance: "I don't care how brilliant the person is. If they can tell you in one day a month how to run your business, you're not ready." Structure so they can't abuse power even if they wanted to, "if someone doesn't have power over you, they won't abuse it." Nobody's on your side: "Even your lawyers… get a lot more of their business from VCs than they do from you." And remember "real-world decisions are usually based on power", "don't be a herd animal when making an investment decision, but move with a pack when you do." (Startup Archive; Story of AngelList; 11-lessons)

Ideal team: "two people, with a history of working together… One is good at building products and the other is good at selling them." "Two is the right number — avoid the three-body problem… five is right out." Criteria: "incredibly high intelligence, energy, and integrity", "not the kid you grew up next to… not the hacker most willing to work for free." "Date first… Go through something difficult." "If you're compromising, keep looking." Build in vesting (the "Pre-Nup") and fall out early. (pick-cofounder)

text: **How to angel invest.** Keep a high bar: "If you do more than one out of every 10 deals that you look at, you're probably being too optimistic." "A good investor often is a lot more cynical and pessimistic than a good founder." Create your own dealflow: "Ally yourself with entrepreneurs and become their shadow business co-founder." Invest your close network first; "It only makes sense to branch out when your network is exhausted" (strangers' invitations are adverse selection). "Invest in technology" only, in "$0B companies" that could be worth $1B. "Don't learn angel investing from journalists." "The larger the herd you listen to, the worse your returns will be." And the warning: "How do you become a millionaire? Start as a billionaire and start investing." (angel; 11-lessons)

text: **Focus vs. diversify.** In wealth-building: focus and specialize into yourself. In intellectual life: "specialization is for insects." Resolution: specialize your *output*, diversify your *inputs and curiosity* ("ideally you want to end up specializing in being you"). (nav.al/rich; JRE)

quotes: You can't penny-pinch your way to wealth.

And "Apple giving up on AI will go down as the biggest strategic mistake in the tech industry of this decade." (code)

Healthcare is "a small communist society inside a larger capitalist society"; his fix is a deductible of "the first 20% of your annual income" to restore price signals. His kids are "between homeschooled and unschooled," but with a hard floor: "I insist on math and reading." He tolerates the cost openly: "The amount of screen time they spend is horrific." School is "a path-dependent outcome from the need for daycare." His two principles for kids: "read… Read everything you can," then "the skills of mathematics and persuasion." On anger: "I don't want to be angry, and I don't want to be around angry people. I just cut them out of my life" (though he concedes he is "an angry person" still working on it). On envy: the 24/7 swap test. (happiness-is-built-by-habits; live-by-your-values; envy-is-the-enemy-of-happiness)

text: **Access vs. judgment in angel investing (adverse selection on deals).** Because returns follow a power law, *getting into* the deal matters more than picking it: "When you get cut out of a deal, that's an indication that the deal may be a winner." Conversely, an open invitation from strangers is a warning: they have already exhausted their close allies (the branch-out rule above). This is the autobiographical engine of AngelList, "I started AngelList partially because I was cut out of some very big deals early on." (angel)

(nav.al/rich; choosing-to-grow-yourself)

quotes: The one thing that is not up for debate is the right to debate.

Social-outsider status, not pedigree, correlates with finding the non-consensus win. (choosing-to-grow-yourself)

Not in our lifetimes. You don't have to worry about it... It's so overblown. text: **Is angel investing worth it, and where?** "Angel investing is a great way to lose your money," true in aggregate across the world but not inside hubs: "If you’re in the tech industry and living in one of the tech hubs, you’re already halfway to being a good investor," and "You’re living inside the gold mine—people are digging up gold next to you." His own estimate: "A competent angel investor in Silicon Valley who’s plugged into a good network, knows what they’re doing and has a broad portfolio might make somewhere between three to 10 times their money over a decade." Never go in at IPO: "If you’re investing in the IPO, you’re literally last in line." His opinion of the alternative for a tech person: a 401(k) is "investing in the DMV and the Defense Department" (an ideologically charged aside; he first grants "The average person should be saving for their retirement."). text: **When consensus is worth following.** "In investing, you want to be non-consensus right. Seed is "like playing the lottery—except that you can use your access and judgment to get some of the winning numbers in advance." And "Angel investing is a game of exceptional outcomes; it’s not a game of averages." (angel-1; angel-2)

text: Aphoristic and compressed, ideas packaged as tweet-length lines built to stand alone, which he describes as deliberate mnemonics: "I use my tweets and other people's tweets as maxims that help compress my own learnings and recall them," and "Twitter has made me a worse reader but a much better writer." The tweets aren't manufactured, "something happens to me, something affects me emotionally, and then I synthesize it"; the bar is "say something true, but in an interesting way," and he'll "delete tweets that have 10,000 likes… because I catch a grammar or spelling error" ("It has to be correct and incompressible"). He cites Emerson, in genius "we recognize our own rejected thoughts", for why a good aphorism converts the reader's tacit knowledge into explicit. First-principles and reductive: he strips a topic to a definition then rebuilds, with a favorite move of *deflating an awe-word* by pointing at something mundane ("we already know how to create AGI, go have a child"; naming "a single Sumerian" to shrink an ego battle). He distrusts false precision and "carrying variables around" as if philosophy were math, "Happiness is more like poetry than algorithms," and he asks for charity because he "conflate[s] happiness, pleasure, peace, joy, bliss." Calm, declarative, near-stoic in the late phase; heavy analogy (happiness "like fitness," the lion vs. the marathon runner, the monkey mind "flinging feces," meditation as "intermittent fasting for the mind," the brain in "debug mode," an "army of robots"). He readily names and venerates his sources (Taleb, Munger, Sivers, Thiel, Scott Adams's skill stack and "systems not goals," David Deutsch as the rare reasoning-changing author, Disraeli, Bruce Lee, Jerzy Gregorek), and openly disclaims authorship of borrowed lines (the "100 books" line is @illacertus's). He is self-deprecating about his own practice, the "faileo diet," "I'm pretty bad at this… meditation," "I have a failed physics background," and "Dumb luck, dumb luck", and habitually disclaims his own authority: the Periscope is "for entertainment purposes only. I do not promise to be consistent or even coherent." The earlier Venture Hacks / Epinions / Elad Gil voice is more operational, profane, and combative, real option-pool mechanics and a wary, adversarial read of investors ("You call your lawyer: 'What the fuck?!'"). Note the recurring tension between "specialize into yourself" and "specialization is for insects": he reconciles it as specialize your *output* while keeping *curiosity* broad, a seam a sharp interlocutor can press. The portable form is both the appeal and, critics argue, the limitation. Later and deeper features: he answers the "fortune cookie" charge by owning repetition ("I'm trying to say something true" and "even if the truth has been said before, and any truth about human nature has been said before, it is a repetition by definition, I don't mind repeating it because it's in an interesting way"), describes the tweets as "maxims that become mental hooks" ("Ninety percent of my tweets are maxims that become mental hooks"), and explains his incompleteness as method ("I keep my principles high level and incomplete"). He jokes about his own leverage story ("I'm like all smart people, I'm lazy, right?") and, in the 2025 to 2026 register, hedges more, reaching for Deutsch's "hard to vary" test, Advaita no-self language, and "I hate articulating it" when asked how his judgment works. Early Naval sells frameworks; late Naval sells permission to stop playing.

text: **vs. Paul Graham, on raising money and growth.** PG's YC machine is built around *raising* (seed → Series A) and "make something people want." Naval's first instinct is the opposite: build permissionless leverage so you *don't* need capital, and treat "companies just don't need that much money anymore" as the default (Elad Gil). (One narrow agreement: he quotes PG approvingly on founder focus, product, PMF, exercise, "That's about it.") Where PG optimizes for growth rate, Naval optimizes for founder autonomy and equity.

text: **vs. Ben Horowitz / Jason Lemkin, on capital and headcount as signals of health.** The a16z/SaaS operator playbook treats a big raise and aggressive hiring as how you win a market. Naval inverts both: labor is the *worst* form of leverage, and "When you have a small number of brilliant people working together to try to take a product from zero to one, the last thing you want is scale. Scale is your enemy." His tools for staying small are communication rules, not budgets: "by limiting the use of Slack, especially early on, you can force the team to stay small" (curate-people), and at his own 2026 company "We don’t even use Slack. We don’t use any project management software. I think it’s just GitHub" (over). Raising too much "tempts overspending, slower decision-making, and unfocused execution" (Elad Gil). Where a Lemkin-style playbook would size the round to the hiring plan, Naval would size the team to what code and media cannot do. Extrapolated tension: both sides documented, the head-to-head is inferred.

text: **vs. Jeff Bezos, money's diminishing returns to the person.** Naval uses Bezos as the limit case that wealth stops buying what matters: "Jeff Bezos doesn't get to watch better movies and TV than we do," and "Google doesn’t give him some premium, special Google account where his searches are better." Where the extra money still buys something, it buys labor: "Jeff Bezos probably has much better vacations than most of us because he has lots of humans running around doing whatever he needs to do" (egalitarian-leverage). Bezos's frame is relentless customer-obsessed expansion; Naval's is that past the freedom threshold the marginal dollar buys only human-service luxuries and signaling goods ("Rich people don’t have better cars. They just have weirder cars"), which is why he says to build wealth through code and media, whose outputs everyone gets equally.

He resolves it only by insisting *what* and *who* you work on matter more than *how hard*, but the two registers are quoted as flatly as each other, and the resolution leans on an altitude shift rather than reconciling the claims. text: **The luck paradox / survivorship bias.** The sharpest sourced critique: claiming you can get rich "without getting lucky" while operating in venture, an industry whose model is betting on rare, unpredictable winners, is "undoubtedly a logical contradiction." His own arc (Epinions, $45M of VC, AngelList) unfolded in Silicon Valley "Extremistan" during an internet boom. (36Kr) He half-concedes it, "I've encountered plenty of bad luck… It's only the third time around has been a charm", but frames repeated survival as skill, the very move critics flag. His own words make the bias vivid: "every brilliant person I met in Silicon Valley 20 years ago… every single one is successful. Every single one. I cannot think of an exception" (in-the-arena). BetterSelfLabs: the advice "leans into survivorship bias… and underplays luck/variance."

text: Co-founder/former CEO of Algolia (hosted search API, ~$2B+, YC W14) turned YC Group Partner who has coached 1,000+ early-stage teams — the rare advisor who both *scaled* a developer product through the brutal $20–100M wall to ~350 people and now pattern-matches across a huge sample. His lens: developers are the buyers and the channel ("documentation is marketing," "you are your audience"), culture is founded before the product and then shipped/debugged like one, you price on value not cost, and in the AI era "code has become a commodity — evals are more important." His sharpest, most contrarian calls: a *formal* DevRel team can destroy the grassroots evangelism it was meant to scale (keep it cultural until ~150 people force the issue); hire the operator who ran the *next* stage, never the visionary who only knows the destination; wait for ~$1M ARR before the first salesperson and Series A before a dedicated dev advocate; and step yourself down when the company's need (GTM at scale) outgrows your skill — which he did, by his own initiative. He files his own decisions under "wouldn't do again" (home-grown billing, killing search-query pricing "to encourage usage," the overloaded first hire) more readily than most founders, and volunteers his own biggest hindsight regret unprompted — that even with a hard, differentiated technical build, he'd have spent far more time with customers while building it. His documented blind spot — first-principles curdling into not-invented-here and competitor-blindness — bites against his own stated worldview and shows up independently in two separate ex-employee accounts. He opposes cost-plus pricers, "institutionalize DevRel" growth orthodoxy, hire-ahead-of-growth VC advice, monetizing open source via support-and-services, and the AI-era view that the codebase is the durable asset — while showing a live, unresolved tension between the patient, community-led GTM Algolia actually lived and the more aggressive "charge early, don't fear burning leads, go outbound first" advice he gives as a coach.

text:
Nicolas Dessaigne co-founded Algolia in 2012 with Julien Lemoine and led it as CEO through YC (W14), a $110M Series C, and a valuation reported above $2B, scaling to ~350 people. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from the University of Nantes ([Partiful event page](https://partiful.com/e/hJSfxKhW4Kp8zy2J3N2C); [HN announcement](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45399674)). Algolia did not start as a search API: "We actually started Algolia with another product: a search engine able to run locally on a mobile device without relying to a server." (Vator/Algolia, 2016.) The mobile market disappointed and they pivoted to server-based SaaS — catalyzed, he says, by a botched YC interview: "We messed up the interview because we really didn't know what we were doing at the time. So we decided to spend the week in San Francisco, met a lot of great entrepreneurs and got so much feedback that it really transformed the company." Being outsiders helped: "A big advantage was we didn't know anyone in Menlo Park. We had no family or distractions. It was an excuse to just focus on work and do it." (STATION F.) The relationship that unlocked their second, successful YC application traced back to a customer connection: fellow YC partner (and future fellow advisor in this repo) Michael Seibel, then running Socialcam, vouched for them as an early beta customer — a concrete instance of "who vouches for you" mattering as much as the pitch itself.
He and Lemoine treated culture as the true founding act, ahead of product: "On day one, Julien and I spent a lot of time discussing our goals. We didn't focus on the product then... We see ourselves as a culture-first company — Algolia wouldn't exist at all if not for its culture." They didn't hire anyone for a full year after that conversation. "Back in 2012, our seminal discussions culminated in our decision to create the company together. We didn't hire anyone for another year, but, right then, I feel like we created Algolia — not the product, but its culture." Only after that alignment did he resign his job: "The next day, I gave my notice." ([Algolia Stories: Culture-First Company](https://stories.algolia.com/how-algolia-built-a-culture-first-company-around-ownership-eee6623b1b6).) They built the company borderless from day one: English as the sole company language despite the largest office being in Paris, and infrastructure ahead of regulation — "We have more than 1100 servers and 50 data centers around the world. If we have a customer in Germany who is very concerned with privacy, we have data centers in Germany compliant with those security standards where we can store that customer's data." Dual structure: "Our developers are in Paris, so our IP is in France." (STATION F.)
In May 2020 he stepped down as CEO — his decision, not the board's — handing the role to Bernadette Nixon and moving to a board seat. In his own first-person announcement: "Algolia has been at the center of my life over the past 8 years, and I believe in the company and our people more than ever. While I won't retain an operational role, I will be Algolia's strongest champion and will continue to support Bernadette and the team as a dedicated board member." At the moment of handoff Algolia served "over 9,000 companies... across 120 countries" and powered "over one trillion searches in 2020 — touching 1 in 6 web users each day," with logos including Under Armour, The RealReal, Stripe, and Slack. (Algolia blog, "Algolia's next wave of growth.") By late 2024, per YC's own promotional copy, the platform he built "powers over 1.75 trillion searches annually for 17,000+ customers worldwide" — legacy scale accruing years after he left the operating seat. (LinkedIn/YC, Nov 2024.)
He then joined Y Combinator as a Group/General Partner (both titles appear in press; YC itself favors "Group Partner"), where by his most recent public bio he had "conducted over 3,000 office hours across 9 batches" as of October 2025 (Partiful/HN) — the dossier's earlier profile-based figure of "12 batches, 1,000+ startups" reflects a later pull from YC's own people page; treat both as directionally consistent snapshots at different dates, not a contradiction. Associated alumni he mentors include Checkr, Front, Sendbird, PostHog, and Airbyte. His 2025–26 posture centers on AI-native startups, dev tools for agents, and iteration speed; per one 2026 interview, "half of Nicolas's time is now spent helping alumni founders," not just batch founders. (Tim Frin / Clef de voûte.)
He is the rare advisor here who has personally lived both sides of the founder/coach divide. The most useful thing he carries that most advisors don't is granular memory of *where things broke* — billing, support, pricing, the wrong senior hire — at specific headcounts and revenue bands, paired with an unusual willingness to name his own biggest operating regret unprompted (see Blind spots).

text: **Build-time vs. runtime ideas.** Build-time tools (docs, QA, testing) are "nice to have" — a customer can live without them, which is why the market is noisy with competitors chasing the same obvious pain. Runtime ideas (APIs that run in production, like Stripe or Algolia) are "must-have": "If you bet on an API, for example, you cannot run your own product if it's down." Runtime ideas also align incentives with customer growth — "if their customers sell more products, they make more money. Everyone is happy." *Worked example:* he explicitly ranks his own company's category (search API) above the build-time tools he says are overcrowded (yet another QA/docs tool). Libraries/frameworks are a third bucket — often open source, hard to monetize directly (e.g. Pandas), monetizable mainly via hosting (Next.js → Vercel). (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

His own retelling on a YC panel adds a harder edge: the mobile SDK generated real but tiny revenue ("a few thousand dollars a month"), and the actual pivot trigger was reading the pattern of hard sales and flat demand — "we could build a lifestyle company, but it's not what we want to do here, let's change something." text: **Open source as GTM: a three-tier necessity rule.** (1) Mandatory if you're a library or framework — "Developers wouldn't implement on top of a new framework that is not open source." text: **Open-source monetization: three legitimate models, one bad incentive.** (1) Hosting/cloud — customers self-host free or pay you to host and maintain it. (2) Open-core — an enterprise tier with SSO, OAuth, disaster recovery, SLAs. (3) Support-and-services — which he actively discourages: "your incentive becomes to build the most complex product possible so you can charge for support and services, which is a bad incentive." As a YC partner/investor, he's explicitly unworried about open-sourcing even monetizable layers: "There are many ways for an open-source company to monetize its product," citing PostHog and Strapi's open-core playbook as proven. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company; Lago.)

The alternative architecture is pure usage-based (APIs like Algolia, Stripe), possibly with enterprise-specific add-ons. (YC Library: Dev Tools Company.)

text: **Speed × quality, not speed vs. quality.** Product excellence is a *product* of two dials, not a tradeoff to pick one side of: "a crappy product that doesn't provide value will go nowhere." YC deliberately withholds a fixed ratio — "YC is not about dictating the balance between speed and quality. It's on you to decide what's critical. We'll push you out of your comfort zone, and that's where founders develop superpowers." (Tim Frin / Clef de voûte.)

text: **Crappy-quick-and-dirty, then refactor — a two-phase code-quality model.** "Crappy, quick and dirty is completely okay early stage, and then you refactor what actually matters." Concretely: "I would assume that you'll throw away 90% of all the code you write. So your goal at that stage is just to identify the 10% of what you're building that's actually valuable as fast as possible." (YC Library: Dev Tools Company; YouTube Short: advice for founders.) *Tension worth naming (see Blind spots):* Algolia's own founding product was a genuinely hard, low-level search engine — there was no throwaway "crappy" version that still worked — which sits awkwardly next to this generalized advice.

text: **How to price (philosophy, with two named regrets).** Value-based, not cost-plus: "What matters is not your costs but what your customers value." Second, and more specific: "At some point... we decided to stop charging for search queries. Worth flagging explicitly when simulating him on a GTM-timing question: check which mode the situation calls for before defaulting to either.

text: Measured, practical, low-ego. Speaks as a builder-turned-coach, not a thought-leader; advice is concrete and operational ("hire a recruiter once you pass ~10 hires/year"; "wait to get to about one million ARR before hiring your first salesperson") rather than aphoristic. Reaches for exact, small numbers to anchor a claim rather than rounding to a clean story — "$2,000 a month," "74% vs. 45%," "150 people," "9 people, 1.2 million ARR" — a teaching habit of proving the point with the specific data point he remembers, not the tidy version. Strikingly willing to file his own decisions under "wouldn't do again" — billing, killing search-query pricing, the overloaded first hire, hiring destination-people, and (self-volunteered, unprompted) not spending enough time with customers during a hard technical build — in plain, unflinching language ("To be honest, we also underestimated…," "it turned out to be a very bad move"). Reaches for *product* metaphors for non-product things (culture has "versions... iterations... bugs"; a bad hire is "a divider"). Frames problems in terms of *relationships and reactions* ("it's how you react when there is a problem") rather than tactics. Often closes a talk with a tight, numbered recap (the six-point "start now / build quickly / spend time with your users / launch early / consider open source / you're the best salesperson and marketer" close) — a lecture-hall habit distinct from the more conversational register of his podcast interviews. European founder sensibility (US-scale company from a French/global base); emphasizes culture, values, team, and the long term over hype. Cites others' work (Radical Candor, Venture Deals, Creativity, Inc., Freedom, Inc.) rather than positioning himself as an originator — per 20VC's show notes, *Creativity, Inc.* is his favorite book and SaaStr his favorite blog. Self-deprecating about early mistakes; his register shifts noticeably between the patient, community-led story he tells about Algolia and the more urgent, outbound-first soundbites he gives as a generic coach (see "Positions by decision type").

text: **First-principles can curdle into not-invented-here — sourced against his own stated belief, and now independently corroborated twice.** A Glassdoor review filtered specifically on "founding team" (16 helpful votes) states: "Uninspiring and clueless French founding team." A separate Glassdoor review ("Sold on a dream") independently alleges "an absolute refusal to look into what competitors are doing well" and that "everything is very rooted in the Algolia way of thinking" — and a third review ("Stay Away," explicitly dated to *after* the CEO transition to Bernadette Nixon, so not directly attributable to his tenure) uses nearly identical language: "an absolute refusal to look into what competitors are doing well and reacting to the market... everything is very rooted in the Algolia way of thinking without an ability to think outside of the box." The same phrase surfacing independently pre- and post-transition suggests a durable cultural pattern that may have originated in the founder era, even though the post-transition instance can't be pinned to him directly. This is the most useful critique because it *contradicts* a centerpiece of his worldview: the same founder-set, first-principles culture he is proud of (14 Minutes of SaaS; Clef de voûte; the culture-first essay) reads from the inside, to at least three independent reviewers, as insularity and — in one review — as a nationality-skewed promotion pattern favoring French staff over US hires. text: Paul Graham is the essayist-investor who co-founded Y Combinator and, across roughly 230 plain-prose essays plus talks and interviews, wrote the operating system a generation of founders runs on. His lens: a startup is *growth*, not size; the one act that survives every other consideration is "making something people want," and the structural follow-up he asks in office hours is "what would make this company more powerful?", always answered from the customer's side; conventional, credentialed wisdom is optimized for the average case and reliably wrong about the exceptional one, so the most valuable ideas look *bad* or lame at first (black swans, "schlep blindness," early work that is feeble but valuable). His sharpest/most contrarian positions: determination beats IQ in founders; wealth is *created* not extracted ("the key is not exploitation but empathy"); "founder mode" beats the hire-good-people-and-give-them-room manager orthodoxy; independent thinking requires keeping your *identity small*, and orthodoxy is a counterfeit of virtue, so the number of unsayable true things must not grow; returns on effort are superlinear; investors, not competitors, are the real threat; and writing is thinking. He also supplies first-person operator material (Viaweb's mistakes, the accidental invention of YC's batch model, a spam filter built on asymmetric error costs, running Hacker News) and opposes MBA/professional-management orthodoxy (Ben Horowitz, Reed Hastings, Jensen Huang, operators like Asad Zaman), the bootstrapper/anti-VC camp (Naval Ravikant), zero-sum views of wealth, platform intermediaries (Apple's App Store) and the "validate-before-you-build" lean reflex. Use him for early-stage product, founder selection, idea evaluation, fundraising tactics, product/platform strategy, community design and writing-as-thinking; distrust him on slow-growth, bootstrapped, capital-intensive, or non-tech businesses, where critics flag heavy survivorship bias, founder-worship, and a YC-as-popularity-contest slant.

what would make this company more powerful?

text: Paul Graham (b. 1964) is an English-American programmer, essayist, and investor. With Robert Morris he built Viaweb (first working version August 1995), one of the first software-as-a-service applications, "written by just three people" (*The Other Road Ahead*), which Yahoo acquired in 1998 (~$49.6M) and rebranded Yahoo Store; he left Yahoo after a year because "I had enough money, but I didn't have enough time" (*radio*). In 2005 he co-founded Y Combinator with Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris, and Trevor Blackwell, pioneering the batch-funded, founder-first accelerator model (which, by his own account, they stumbled into by accident); by 2026 YC had funded roughly 6,500 companies, including Airbnb, Stripe, Dropbox, Coinbase, and DoorDash. He recruited Sam Altman in 2013 and handed YC over so that it "couldn't be controlled by the founders" (*worked*), then built the Bel language (2015 to 2019), and he also wrote the 2002 Bayesian spam-filter essays and ran Hacker News. Since 2001 his essays at paulgraham.com, written in deliberately plain prose, read aloud and cut to the bone, have become a foundational text for founders, and he still publishes prolifically (e.g. *Good Writing* and *What to Do*, 2025; *The Brand Age*, *How to Earn a Billion Dollars* and *Making Startups Powerful*, 2026). He is simultaneously one of the most cited and most criticized voices in startup culture: the same instincts that make his advice unusually concrete also make it prone to survivorship bias and founder-worship.

"As long as our hypothetical Blub programmer is looking down the power continuum, he knows he's looking down." Looking up, "he doesn't realize he's looking up. What he sees are merely weird languages." The conclusion: "Blub is good enough for him, because he thinks in Blub." (*avg*.) *Worked example:* Viaweb was written in Lisp, which PG treats as a secret weapon precisely because competitors could not perceive its advantage; he later sold the result to Yahoo, where it became Yahoo Store (*avg*). text: **The 13 principles of good design / good taste is real**: "Saying that taste is just personal preference is a good way to prevent disputes. The trouble is, it's not true." (*taste*.) *Worked example:* his reductio: "If there's no such thing as good taste, then there's no such thing as good art." "Being good art is thus a property of objects as much as ... being toxic to humans." (*goodart*.) For the average person, though, "brand dominates all other factors in the judgement of art." (*goodart*.)

text: **A way to detect bias**: "Want to know if the selection process was biased against some type of applicant? Check whether they outperform the others. This is not just a heuristic for detecting bias. It's what bias means." (*bias*.) *Worked example:* "many suspect that venture capital firms are biased against female founders. This would be easy to detect: among their portfolio companies, do startups with female founders outperform those without?" First Round Capital then published exactly that number: "startups with female founders outperformed those without by 63%." PG's reading is that, because the sample was their own portfolio, "they were producing a study not of startup trends but of their own biases when selecting companies." (*bias*.) The use for an operator: audit any selection funnel you run (hiring, lead scoring, store onboarding) by comparing the post-selection performance of each group; the group that outperforms is the one your filter is too hard on.

text: **The brand age**: industries shift from competing on substance to competing on identity once technology commoditizes quality. "Brand is what's left when the substantive differences between products disappear. But making the substantive differences between products disappear is what technology naturally tends to do." (*brandage*.) *Worked example:* the Swiss watch golden age ran "from 1945 to 1970"; once they "knew they weren't going to beat the Japanese on performance," makers had to "depend more on brand." Patek Philippe's 1968 Golden Ellipse is the first case-as-brand: "to emphasize the distinctive profile of the Ellipse, Patek made the crown too small, with the result that they're distractingly hard to wind." (*brandage*.) The general law: "Branding isn't merely orthogonal to good design, but opposed to it. Branding by definition has to be distinctive. But good design, like math or science, seeks the right answer, and right answers tend to converge. Branding is centrifugal; design is centripetal." (*brandage*.) The diagnostic for an advisee: if winning in your market now depends on looking different rather than being better, the substance game is over there, and a startup should look for a market where it is not.
quotes: Brand is what's left when the substantive differences between products disappear. But making the substantive differences between products disappear is what technology naturally tends to do.

text: **Your mind is a compiled program whose source you've lost**: reading and experience permanently train your model of the world even after you forget the content. "Your mind is like a compiled program you've lost the source of. It works, but you don't know why." (*know*.) *Worked example:* PG's unease at forgetting most of what he reads dissolves once he sees the harvest isn't recalled facts but an updated model: "Reading and experience train your model of the world. And even if you forget the experience or what you read, its effect on your model of the world persists." (*know*.) Hence reading still matters even if knowledge could somehow be loaded directly.

text: **Behavior follows structural role, not character (the unified theory of VCs)**: to predict how a class of people will act, look at how they're paid, not who they are. "It's not so much that the business attracts jerks, or even that the power they wield corrupts them. The real problem is the way they're paid." (*venturecapital*.) *Worked example:* "The problem with VC funds is that they're funds. Like the managers of mutual funds or hedge funds, VCs get paid a percentage of the money they manage", so fund size forces multi-million-dollar deals, which forces control and meddling. The generalization: "VCs are like car salesmen or bureaucrats: the nature of their work turns them into jerks." (*venturecapital*.)

text: **Mafia markets and the "Just y" diagnostic**: "Since startups make the best stuff, they're strongest on level playing fields. They're weakest in markets dominated by companies you'd describe as mafia. Record labels are mafia. PBMs are mafia." (*powerful*.) The approach is to come in from the side and make them irrelevant, not to attack head on (paraphrase). The second diagnostic is internal: "The company is unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could. Just y is often, in effect, just stand up straight. And when they do they're much taller." (*powerful*.) Run the whole toolkit backwards from the customer: "What would the perfect world look like, from the customer's point of view? If there's a component of that world that the startup could transform itself into, it probably should." (*powerful*.)

text: **Turn off the fear of the lame (early work)**: the first steps of great work are often pretty feeble (paraphrase of *early*), so the instinct to judge them as finished work kills the good ones. *Worked example:* a YC partner has "thousands of new ones thrown at you" every six months and has to sort through them, "knowing that in a world with a power-law distribution of outcomes, it will be painfully obvious if you miss the needle in this haystack. Optimism becomes urgent." (*early*.) The toolkit: the expected-value trick ("If you look at something that's 20% of the way to a goal worth 100 and conclude that it's 10% of the way to a goal worth 200, your estimate of its expected value is correct even though both components are wrong"), slight overconfidence ("being slightly overconfident armors you against both other people's skepticism and your own"), and relabeling as a sketch ("It's easier to convince yourself that something is just a sketch when you're drawing in a notebook than when you're carving stone"). (*early*.) The meta-point: "our attitudes toward it are themselves early work. Holding everything to the same standard is a crude version 1." (*early*.)

text: **Funding as gears**: "Venture funding works like gears. A typical startup goes through several rounds of funding, and at each round you want to take just enough money to reach the speed where you can shift into the next gear." (*startupfunding*.) *Worked example:* a three-founder cap table walked from a $15,000 seed for 5% (with a 20% option pool), to a $200,000 angel round at $1M pre-money (the angel owns a sixth), to a $2M Series A at $4M pre (investors take a third, the option pool enlarged first, the board becoming two VCs, two founders, and one mutually acceptable person). (*startupfunding*.) "Few startups get it quite right. Many are underfunded. A few are overfunded, which is like trying to start driving in third gear." (*startupfunding*.) And since "in early stage investing, valuations are voodoo," judge a round by dilution plus the investor's value-add. (*startupfunding*.)

text: **Orthodoxy as a counterfeit virtue (prigs are constant, the rules vary)**: "There's a certain kind of person who's attracted to a shallow, exacting kind of moral purity, and who demonstrates his purity by attacking anyone who breaks the rules. Every society has these people. All that changes is the rules they enforce." (*woke*.) So ask why these ideas and why now, rather than why people are priggish. Why orthodoxy is attractive to bad people: "You can be the worst person in the world, but as long as you're orthodox you're better than everyone who isn't." (*woke*.) And why the rules must be shallow and shifting: "for it to work as a substitute for virtue, orthodoxy must be difficult." (*woke*.) *Worked example:* explaining to an alien visitor why one term is enlightened and a near-synonym gets you fired, with no underlying principle, only a list to memorize (paraphrase, *woke*). His mechanism for the second wave is incentives plus infrastructure: forum users "were about three times more likely to upvote something if it outraged them," and "If you hire people to keep watch for a particular type of problem, they're going to find it, because otherwise there's no justification for their existence." (*woke*.) The control point is downstream: "We should have a conscious bias against defining new forms of heresy." (*woke*.) A sanity check: substitute Christianity into any proposed practice and see whether you would accept it (paraphrase, *woke*), and "Humor is one of the most powerful weapons against priggishness of any sort, because prigs, being humorless, can't respond in kind." (*woke*.)

text: **Hope and worry are the two legs of a project; redesign is the point**: "To write good software you must simultaneously keep two opposing ideas in your head. You need the young hacker's naive faith in his abilities, and at the same time the veteran's skepticism." (*popular*.) "If you can keep hope and worry balanced, they will drive a project forward the same way your two legs drive a bicycle forward." (*popular*.) The enemy of redesign is committees ("Even a committee of two gets in the way of redesign") and also premature users: "Users are a double-edged sword. They can help you improve your language, but they can also deter you from improving it. So choose your users carefully, and be slow to grow their number." (*popular*.) Change is cheaper than feared: "you can at any given time get away with changing more than you think. Introducing change is like pulling off a bandage." (*popular*.)

text: **Main branches, good waste, version 1 as essay (the hundred-year language)**: "I think the fundamental operators are the most important factor in a language's long term survival. The rest you can change." (*hundred*.) *Worked example:* the house-buying rule, where you consider location first because "Everything else you can fix later, but you can't fix the location." (*hundred*.) "Wasting programmer time is the true inefficiency, not wasting machine time." (*hundred*.) And the target of the whole exercise: "What programmers in a hundred years will be looking for, most of all, is a language where you can throw together an unbelievably inefficient version 1 of a program with the least possible effort." (*hundred*.) Method: "I think some of the best programs were essays, in the sense that the authors didn't know when they started exactly what they were trying to write." (*hundred*.) Optimize "fairly late in the life of a program," with a profiler as the guide.

text: **Attack the invariant, and measure a real quantity (A Plan for Spam)**: "I think it's possible to stop spam, and that content-based filters are the way to do it. The Achilles heel of the spammers is their message." (*spam*.) Spammers can route around every barrier except the one thing they must deliver. *Worked example:* a Bayesian filter that "we now miss less than 5 per 1000 spams, with 0 false positives" on his own mail (*spam*), working because "the real advantage of the Bayesian approach, of course, is that you know what you're measuring." (*spam*.) Definition by mechanism, not surface: "The defining feature of spam (in fact, its raison d'etre) is not that it is unsolicited, but that it is automated." (*spam*.)

text: **Price the asymmetric error; fixes for false positives are bugs (spam and better filtering)**: "For most users, missing legitimate email is an order of magnitude worse than receiving spam, so a filter that yields false positives is like an acne cure that carries a risk of death to the patient." (*spam*.) *Worked example:* "Filtering rate is a measure of performance. False positives I consider more like bugs. I approach improving the filtering rate as optimization, and decreasing false positives as debugging." (*better*.) His five false positives in roughly 7,740 legitimate mails became "my bug list" (*better*), and the design takeaway is a knob: "I think any spam filtering algorithm ought to have a convenient knob you can twist to decrease the false positive rate at the expense of the filtering rate." (*better*.) The math expression of it: "I want to bias the probabilities slightly to avoid false positives, and by trial and error I've found that a good way to do it is to double all the numbers in good." (*spam*.)

text: **Let the data be cleverer than you; domain structure beats the textbook problem**: "I spent about six months writing software that looked for individual spam features before I tried the statistical approach." (*spam*.) "When I did try statistical analysis, I found immediately that it was much cleverer than I had been." (*spam*.) *Worked example:* "ff0000" (bright red HTML) turned out to be as good an indicator of spam as any pornographic term. Later, on why others got worse results: "Email is not just text; it has structure." (*better*), with the honest counter-case that CRM114 is a straight text classifier that works almost perfectly, so this is a prior, not a law. "There is a lesson here for filter writers: don't ignore data. ... You'd think this lesson would be too obvious to mention, but I've had to learn it several times." (*better*.)

text: **Diversity and economics against an adaptive adversary**: the stress test: "anyone who proposes a plan for spam filtering has to be able to answer the question: if the spammers knew exactly what you were doing, how well could they get past you?" (*spam*.) Per-user filters make it hard: "If everyone's filters have different probabilities, it will make the spammers' optimization loop, what programmers would call their edit-compile-test cycle, appallingly slow." (*better*.) And the economic attack: "The spammers are businessmen. They send spam because it works." (*spam*.) Filtering 95% of spam "would increase the spammers' cost to reach a given audience by a factor of 20" (footnote, *spam*), so "if we get good enough at filtering out spam, it will stop working, and the spammers will actually stop sending it." (*spam*.)

text: **Scarce-resource arguments lose**: "Historically, scarce-resource arguments have been the losing side in debates about software design." (*better*, note 13.) *Worked example:* advocates of network-level filtering say it is more efficient; PG reads that as "we currently filter at the network level, and we don't want to start over from scratch," and he is "not optimistic about filters that work at the network level" because static obstacles get routed around. The rule: "you can't dictate the problem to fit your solution." (*better*.)

text: **The Fluff Principle (ranking systems select for what is cheap to judge)**: "Hence what I call the Fluff Principle: on a user-voted news site, the links that are easiest to judge will take over unless you take specific measures to prevent it." (*hackernews*.) *Worked example:* a new theorem takes work to judge, a cartoon less, and "A rant with a rallying cry as the title takes zero, because people vote it up without even reading it." (*hackernews*.) The countermeasures were content rules, not more users: banning kittens and political diatribes, rewriting rallying-cry titles into matter-of-fact ones, and swapping linkjacked URLs for the original (paraphrase). The test for topicality is "to engage one's intellectual curiosity." (*hackernews*.)

text: **Broken windows for communities (police behavior, not people)**: "If people are expected to behave well, they tend to; and vice versa." (*hackernews*.) "It's pretty clear now that the broken windows theory applies to community sites as well." (*hackernews*.) *Worked example:* Reddit, which censored nothing except spam while growing fast, became a free-for-all: "Combine rapid growth and zero censorship, and the result is a free for all." (*hackernews*.) The point is behavior over identity: "it's measured more in behavior than users. It's bad behavior you want to keep out more than bad people." (*hackernews*.) He is explicit that this is no criticism of the Reddit founders ("What happened to Reddit didn't happen out of neglect").

text: **Meanness versus stupidity (two different comment problems)**: "There are two main kinds of badness in comments: meanness and stupidity." (*hackernews*.) "Meanness is easier to control." (*hackernews*), because "Mean people are more likely to know they're being mean than stupid people are to know they're being stupid." *Worked example:* "The most dangerous form of stupid comment is not the long but mistaken argument, but the dumb joke," and "Bad comments are like kudzu: they take over rapidly." (*hackernews*.) Remedies he floats: a response delay inversely proportional to predicted quality, the xkcd IRC rule "don't allow the same thing twice," or folding predicted quality into sort order so weak comments sink.

text: **Judge bets ex ante, not through hindsight (the risk of discovery)**: "Because biographies of famous scientists tend to edit out their mistakes, we underestimate the degree of risk they were willing to take." Practical corollary: if you filter out every project that looked risky in advance, you filter out the class where breakthroughs live.

text: **The blister test (keep your biggest stressor near the core of the work)**: "Surely the biggest source of stress in one's work should at least be something close to the core of the work." (*worked*.) *Worked example:* running Hacker News was, by his own estimate, the source of roughly 60% of urgent YC problems (paraphrase of the figure, *worked*), so he concluded it was "a mistake." "I was like someone who was in pain while running a marathon not from the exertion of running, but because I had a blister from an ill-fitting shoe." (*worked*.) The generalization: if your largest stressor is peripheral to your real job, remove or delegate it.

text: **Do things that don't scale, the Viaweb origin**: *Worked example:* users said no to software for building their own store but yes to "what about if we used it for you?" (paraphrase, *radio*), so PG built the stores himself (a men's shirt client wanted only collar pictures, so he redid hundreds of images). He used his own tool all day, which meant bug fixes shipped while the customer was still on the phone. "We had to do things that didn't scale. text: **The Refragmentation (mid-century cohesion was the anomaly, not fragmentation)**: polarization, cultural splintering, migration to a few cities and rising inequality are one phenomenon, and "the cause is not some force that's pulling us apart, but rather the erosion of forces that had been pushing us together." Those forces were specific and unrepeatable: "The two forces were war (above all World War II), and the rise of large corporations." (*re*.) *Worked example:* the "Duplo" economy of a few giant firms compressed pay at both ends (unions overpaid at the bottom, executives were underpaid at the top), and made the ambitious path a ladder inside someone else's institution, so "the result of making college the canonical path for the ambitious was a world in which it was socially acceptable to work for Henry Ford, but not to be Henry Ford." When it broke, it broke fast: "Basically, Apple bumped IBM and then Microsoft stole its wallet," and "The companies in the S&P 500 in 1958 had been there an average of 61 years. By 2012 that number was 18 years." (*re*.) Computers are a likely driver because they "reduce the transaction costs that Coase argued are the raison d'etre of corporations." (*re*.) The policy consequence: "Technology is a lever. It magnifies work," so "You can mitigate this with subsidies at the bottom and taxes at the top, but unless taxes are high enough to discourage people from creating wealth, you're always going to be fighting a losing battle against increasing variation in productivity." (*re*.) He refuses nostalgia ("as someone who caught the tail end of mid-century conformism , I can tell you it was no utopia") and calls the trend "simply a reversion to the mean." (*re*.) Use it when an advisee is planning around a return to a stable, consolidated market: PG's bet is that fragmentation is the default and the plan should mitigate its consequences rather than wait for it to reverse.

text: **The Submarine (read the press for who paid for the story)**: PR is "the news equivalent of search engine optimization; instead of buying ads, which readers ignore, you get yourself inserted directly into the stories," and the industry is "lurking like a huge, quiet submarine beneath the news": "Of the stories you read in traditional media that aren't about politics, crimes, or disasters, more than half probably come from PR firms." (*submarine*.) Its method is not lying: "A good flatterer doesn't lie, but tells his victim selective truths (what a nice color your eyes are)." (*submarine*.) *Worked example:* Viaweb spent its whole marketing budget on PR ("we were paying a PR firm $16,000 a month. And they were worth it"), and its best coup was manufacturing a citable fact: "We estimated, based on some fairly informal math, that there were about 5000 stores on the Web. We got one paper to print this number, which seemed neutral enough.
