an ugly duckling from a baby swan.
title: Grade early work as a challenge to your imagination

text: **Demand a real quantity, not a score.** "The problem with a "score" is that no one knows what it means. The user doesn't know what it means, but worse still, neither does the developer of the filter." (*spam*.)
quotes: The problem with a
is that no one knows what it means. The user doesn't know what it means, but worse still, neither does the developer of the filter.
title: Demand a real quantity, not a score

text: **Don't ignore data you find inconvenient.** "There is a lesson here for filter writers: don't ignore data." (*better*.) His own reason for once ignoring email headers: "Because I wanted to keep the problem neat." (*better*.) When someone else's numbers disagree widely with yours, list candidate causes (sample size, ignored data, feature definition, error weighting) and check each instead of dismissing (paraphrase of *better*).
quotes: There is a lesson here for filter writers: don't ignore data.
Because I wanted to keep the problem neat.
title: Don't ignore data you find inconvenient

text: **Profile; do not guess.** "Don't try to guess where your code is slow, because you'll guess wrong." (*better*.) The method for errors is the same: "look at the spams you miss, and figure out what you could have done to catch them." (*better*.)
quotes: Don't try to guess where your code is slow, because you'll guess wrong.
look at the spams you miss, and figure out what you could have done to catch them.
title: Profile; do not guess

text: **Stress-test any defense against an adversary who knows it.** "if the spammers knew exactly what you were doing, how well could they get past you?" (*spam*.) Then ask what stops the attacker economically: "They send spam because it works." (*spam*.)
quotes: if the spammers knew exactly what you were doing, how well could they get past you?
They send spam because it works.
title: Stress-test any defense against an adversary who knows it

text: **Never stop pursuing alternatives (the only leverage is competition).** "With both investors and acquirers, the only leverage you have is competition." (*startupfunding*.) "The key to closing deals is never to stop pursuing alternatives." (*startupfunding*.) "don't believe it till you get the check." (*startupfunding*.) "Your natural tendency when an investor says yes will be to relax and go back to writing code. Alas, you can't; you have to keep looking for more investors, if only to get this one to act." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: With both investors and acquirers, the only leverage you have is competition.
The key to closing deals is never to stop pursuing alternatives.
don't believe it till you get the check.
Your natural tendency when an investor says yes will be to relax and go back to writing code. Alas, you can't; you have to keep looking for more investors, if only to get this one to act.
title: Never stop pursuing alternatives (the only leverage is competition)

text: **Ask the VC about their term-sheet conversion rate and check whether the caller is a partner.** "Here's a partial solution: when a VC offers you a term sheet, ask how many of their last 10 term sheets turned into deals. This will at least force them to lie outright if they want to mislead you." (*startupfunding*.) Junior people seem positive because they want to believe, but "It's the partners who decide, and they view things with a colder eye." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: Here's a partial solution: when a VC offers you a term sheet, ask how many of their last 10 term sheets turned into deals. This will at least force them to lie outright if they want to mislead you.
It's the partners who decide, and they view things with a colder eye.
title: Ask the VC about their term-sheet conversion rate and check whether the caller is a partner

text: **Approach VCs only when you can convince them in one shot.** "So when do you approach VCs? When you can convince them." (*startupfunding*.) "I would strongly advise against mailing your business plan randomly to VCs, because they treat this as evidence of laziness." (*startupfunding*.) "You really only get one chance, because they rely heavily on first impressions." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: So when do you approach VCs? When you can convince them.
I would strongly advise against mailing your business plan randomly to VCs, because they treat this as evidence of laziness.
You really only get one chance, because they rely heavily on first impressions.
title: Approach VCs only when you can convince them in one shot

text: **Resist the abusive terms, and question "standard."** "Some VCs now require that in any sale they get 4x their investment back before the common stock holders (that is, you) get anything, but this is an abuse that should be resisted." (*startupfunding*.) "The average founder is smarter than the average VC. So just do what you'd do in any complex, unfamiliar situation: proceed deliberately, and question anything that seems odd." (*startupfunding*.) "Standard, schmandard; the whole industry is only a few decades old, and rapidly evolving." (*startupfunding*.) Never pay an angel group to pitch: "Needless to say, you should never do this." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: Some VCs now require that in any sale they get 4x their investment back before the common stock holders (that is, you) get anything, but this is an abuse that should be resisted.
The average founder is smarter than the average VC. So just do what you'd do in any complex, unfamiliar situation: proceed deliberately, and question anything that seems odd.
Standard, schmandard; the whole industry is only a few decades old, and rapidly evolving.
Needless to say, you should never do this.
title: Resist the abusive terms, and question "standard."

text: **Spend little, work fast, demo over business plan, and start the round early.** "Every startup's rule should be: spend little, and work fast." (*startupfunding*.) "If you have to choose between spending time on the demo or the business plan, spend most on the demo. Software is not only more convincing, but a better way to explore ideas." (*startupfunding*.) "When you have five months' runway left, how soon do you need to start looking for your next round? Answer: immediately." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: Every startup's rule should be: spend little, and work fast.
If you have to choose between spending time on the demo or the business plan, spend most on the demo. Software is not only more convincing, but a better way to explore ideas.
When you have five months' runway left, how soon do you need to start looking for your next round? Answer: immediately.
title: Spend little, work fast, demo over business plan, and start the round early

text: **Sell cheap stock to eminent angels early, when a low valuation is natural.** "So if you're going to sell cheap stock to eminent angels, do it early, when it's natural for the company to have a low valuation." (*startupfunding*.) The contacts matter: "The contacts and advice can be more important than the money." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: So if you're going to sell cheap stock to eminent angels, do it early, when it's natural for the company to have a low valuation.
The contacts and advice can be more important than the money.
title: Sell cheap stock to eminent angels early, when a low valuation is natural

text: **Do not read heavy criticism of a builder-CEO as proof of unfitness.** "being a magnet for criticism is sometimes a sign not that someone is the wrong person for a job, but that they're the right one." (*pow*.)
quotes: being a magnet for criticism is sometimes a sign not that someone is the wrong person for a job, but that they're the right one.
title: Do not read heavy criticism of a builder-CEO as proof of unfitness

text: **Don't hard-code the unit of decisiveness; scale it to feedback latency.** Days for investor negotiations, months for hardware. (*users*.) Choose advisors who were founders, and shard advising groups before they exceed roughly 60 companies per advisor group. (*users*.)
title: Don't hard-code the unit of decisiveness; scale it to feedback latency

text: **Put the burden of proof on anyone who wants to forbid a statement.** Claiming harm is not enough, "they have to prove it." (*woke*.) Inside an organization borrow religion's customs: you may state your identity and beliefs, but you cannot call coworkers infidels, ban contradicting speech, or make your doctrine the official religion; actual religious organizations may insist on orthodoxy if they declare it (paraphrase of *woke*, endnote 16).
quotes: they have to prove it.
title: Put the burden of proof on anyone who wants to forbid a statement

text: **Take another person's report at face value when you cannot test it.** "If someone says they can hear a high-pitched noise that you can't, it's only polite to take them at their word, instead of demanding evidence that's impossible to produce, or simply denying that they hear anything." (*orth*.) And don't deploy "check your privilege" on the conventional-minded; appeal to base rates and politeness instead (paraphrase of *orth*).
quotes: If someone says they can hear a high-pitched noise that you can't, it's only polite to take them at their word, instead of demanding evidence that's impossible to produce, or simply denying that they hear anything.
check your privilege
title: Take another person's report at face value when you cannot test it

text: **Prefer pluralism to purges: build antibodies against new heresies without rejecting every idea the movement holds.** Don't reject everything the woke believe either, since "that would be the sort of thing a religious zealot would do" (*woke*), and "the best way to protect ourselves from future outbreaks of things like wokeness is to have powerful antibodies against the concept of heresy." (*woke*.)
quotes: that would be the sort of thing a religious zealot would do
the best way to protect ourselves from future outbreaks of things like wokeness is to have powerful antibodies against the concept of heresy.
title: Prefer pluralism to purges: build antibodies against new heresies without rejecting every idea the movement holds

text: **Decide fast once an idea gels, and say it out loud (launch fast).** "As we turned onto Walker Street we decided to do it." (*ycstart*.) The whole YC decision, money and staffing included, was settled within days.
quotes: As we turned onto Walker Street we decided to do it.
title: Decide fast once an idea gels, and say it out loud (launch fast)

text: **Ask what really drives you, and refuse the flattering answers.** Neither "to make money" nor "to help founders" was the real reason for YC; it was "such a great hack." (*whyyc*.) He pairs this with an honest warning: "All startups are mostly schleps." (*whyyc*.)
quotes: to make money
to help founders
such a great hack.
All startups are mostly schleps.
title: Ask what really drives you, and refuse the flattering answers

text: **Name the real customer: the expert minority whose opinion propagates.** "Expert hackers are a tiny minority, admittedly, but that tiny minority write all the good software, and their influence is such that the rest of the programmers will tend to use whatever language they use." (*popular*.) Make the free version good: "Companies will pay for software, but individual hackers won't, and it's the hackers you need to attract." (*popular*.)
quotes: Expert hackers are a tiny minority, admittedly, but that tiny minority write all the good software, and their influence is such that the rest of the programmers will tend to use whatever language they use.
Companies will pay for software, but individual hackers won't, and it's the hackers you need to attract.
title: Name the real customer: the expert minority whose opinion propagates

text: **Choose users carefully and delay having many of them.** "Having users is like optimization: the wise course is to delay it." (*popular*.) "Anything you can do to keep the redesign cycle going is good." (*popular*.)
quotes: Having users is like optimization: the wise course is to delay it.
Anything you can do to keep the redesign cycle going is good.
title: Choose users carefully and delay having many of them

text: **Look for the main branch and the small, powerful core.** "staying close to the main branches is a useful heuristic for finding languages that will be good to program in now." (*hundred*.) "The more of a language you can write in itself, the better." (*hundred*.)
quotes: staying close to the main branches is a useful heuristic for finding languages that will be good to program in now.
The more of a language you can write in itself, the better.
title: Look for the main branch and the small, powerful core

text: **Trade efficiency for even the smallest convenience when the machine is cheap.** "There's good waste, and bad waste." (*hundred*.) PG diagnoses his own opposite bias: "I'm like someone who grew up poor, and can't bear to spend money even for something important, like going to the doctor." (*hundred*.)
quotes: There's good waste, and bad waste.
I'm like someone who grew up poor, and can't bear to spend money even for something important, like going to the doctor.
title: Trade efficiency for even the smallest convenience when the machine is cheap

text: **Stand behind your users while they try your product.** "If you build something for users, go and stand behind them." (*radio*.) If it hurts you, it is too painful for almost everyone.
quotes: If you build something for users, go and stand behind them.
title: Stand behind your users while they try your product

text: **Pick the single most urgent problem for each startup.** "I would just say what I would do if I were in their position... there's usually one problem that's the most urgent. And so, you zero in on the most urgent problem and then you figure out how to fix it." (*radio*.)
quotes: I would just say what I would do if I were in their position... there's usually one problem that's the most urgent. And so, you zero in on the most urgent problem and then you figure out how to fix it.
title: Pick the single most urgent problem for each startup

text: **Learn, don't maximize revenue (the marathon).** Optimizing the next dollar before you know the market is, in his words, "basically sprinting in the first 100 yards of a marathon," and "They look great for a while." (*radio*.)
quotes: basically sprinting in the first 100 yards of a marathon,
They look great for a while.
title: Learn, don't maximize revenue (the marathon)

text: **Sell the company only if it fits what you want.** "I tell founders, 'Do what you want,' right? If you want this to be your life's work, then don't sell the company just because someone's offering you money. But if you're just doing this to make money, then do it to make money, but do it right." (*radio*.)
quotes: I tell founders, 'Do what you want,' right? If you want this to be your life's work, then don't sell the company just because someone's offering you money. But if you're just doing this to make money, then do it to make money, but do it right.
title: Sell the company only if it fits what you want

text: **Leave when you have enough money and not enough time.** On leaving Yahoo after a year: "why trade something I don't need for something I do? I had enough money, but I didn't have enough time. So why trade money for time?" (*radio*.) After a sale: "take a vacation." (*worked*.)
quotes: why trade something I don't need for something I do? I had enough money, but I didn't have enough time. So why trade money for time?
take a vacation.
title: Leave when you have enough money and not enough time

text: **If your vision requires a company you do not want to run, shrink the vision.** Halfway through summer 2000 he realized he "really didn't want to run a company" and cut the plan down to an open source subset (Arc) (paraphrase of *worked*), consistent with "If this vision had to be realized as a company, then screw the vision." (*worked*, an Aspra-era quote.)
quotes: really didn't want to run a company
If this vision had to be realized as a company, then screw the vision.
title: If your vision requires a company you do not want to run, shrink the vision

text: **Treat being laughed at as a positive signal for the medium.** Online essays looked "more like rants posted by nutjobs on their GeoCities sites," and he found that "encouraging instead of discouraging." (*worked*.)
quotes: more like rants posted by nutjobs on their GeoCities sites,
encouraging instead of discouraging.
title: Treat being laughed at as a positive signal for the medium

text: **Weight people over percentages.** "would I rather have 30% of this person or a hundred percent of some other person" (auto-captions, *ralston*) is the test for different commitment levels; equal splits can be worse than slightly unequal ones (paraphrase).
quotes: would I rather have 30% of this person or a hundred percent of some other person
title: Weight people over percentages

text: **Don't raise more than you need.** "it's not always right to raise too much money" (auto-captions, *ralston*.) Idle money has a gravitational pull on hiring (paraphrase), with ICOs and Magic Leap's $2.3B cited as warnings.
quotes: it's not always right to raise too much money
title: Don't raise more than you need

text: **Elicit the real missing thing before going hypothetical.** Ask what is wrong and what users cannot do; infer what they really mean even if they do not; only then ask "what if you could do such-and-such" (paraphrase of *ralston*). *Worked example:* users say they need to mark mail unread, and "that whole unread thing is a sign that the whole inbox is being misused" (auto-captions), because it is a to-do list.
quotes: what if you could do such-and-such
that whole unread thing is a sign that the whole inbox is being misused
title: Elicit the real missing thing before going hypothetical

text: **Price early customers by asking what they would actually pay, then grandfather.** Raising prices later is handled by grandfathering existing users, who under exponential growth are a tiny subset (paraphrase of *ralston*). He admits his own early pricing was accidental: "it wasn't because of some clever insight that we set the price low. We had no idea what businesses paid for things." (*worked*.)
quotes: it wasn't because of some clever insight that we set the price low. We had no idea what businesses paid for things.
title: Price early customers by asking what they would actually pay, then grandfather

text: **Commit fully or keep exploring; do not dabble with a fallback.** "just because you could start a successful startup doesn't mean you should" and "you have to be a hundred percent committed" (auto-captions, *ralston*); 18 to 22 is a time to figure out options, not pick one (paraphrase).
quotes: just because you could start a successful startup doesn't mean you should
you have to be a hundred percent committed
title: Commit fully or keep exploring; do not dabble with a fallback

text: **Keep community moderation transparent and conservative.** "I once thought I'd have to weight votes to keep crap off the frontpage, but I haven't had to yet." (*hackernews*.) Let users see what was killed: "That keeps editors honest, and just as importantly, makes users confident they'd know if the editors stopped being honest." (*hackernews*.)
quotes: I once thought I'd have to weight votes to keep crap off the frontpage, but I haven't had to yet.
That keeps editors honest, and just as importantly, makes users confident they'd know if the editors stopped being honest.
title: Keep community moderation transparent and conservative

text: **Spend your caution on the correct thing: preserve what is good.** "The good things in a community site come from people more than technology; it's mainly in the prevention of bad things that technology comes into play." (*hackernews*.)
quotes: The good things in a community site come from people more than technology; it's mainly in the prevention of bad things that technology comes into play.
title: Spend your caution on the correct thing: preserve what is good

text: **Pivot vs. persevere.** Stay attached to the *goal*, change the *method*. "You have to be determined, but flexible, like a running back." (*startuplessons*.) "Startups are more like science, where you need to follow the trail wherever it leads." (*startupmistakes*.) Obstinacy is "being wrong slowly."
quotes: You have to be determined, but flexible, like a running back.
Startups are more like science, where you need to follow the trail wherever it leads.
being wrong slowly.
title: Pivot vs. persevere

text: **How to evaluate a startup idea.** Favor ideas that look bad to smart people and involve schleps others avoid; "the most common mistake startups make is to solve problems no one has" (*startupideas*); "when something is described as a toy, that means it has everything an idea needs except being important." (*startupideas*.) Don't fear crowded markets "so long as you have a thesis about what everyone else in it is overlooking." (*startupideas*.) "It's exceptionally rare for startups to be killed by competitors." (*startupideas*.)
quotes: the most common mistake startups make is to solve problems no one has
when something is described as a toy, that means it has everything an idea needs except being important.
so long as you have a thesis about what everyone else in it is overlooking.
It's exceptionally rare for startups to be killed by competitors.
title: How to evaluate a startup idea

text: **How to price / how to grow.** Don't chase tactics; "build something users love, and spend less than you make." (*start*.) Word-of-mouth compounds: "it will happen automatically if you just keep making customers happy." (*earn*.) "There is no such thing as a killer feature." (*really*.) Big launches and big-partner deals usually fail (*ds*); "startups are powered aircraft, not projectiles."
quotes: build something users love, and spend less than you make.
it will happen automatically if you just keep making customers happy.
There is no such thing as a killer feature.
startups are powered aircraft, not projectiles.
title: How to price / how to grow

text: **When to hire.** Late, deliberately, and only for two jobs. "The only reason to hire someone is to do something you'd like to do but can't." (*start*.) Hire only people who "are either going to write code or go out and get users." (*startupmistakes*.) "Mediocre hires hurt you twice: they get less done, but they also make you big." (*boss*.) Look for "an animal." (*start*.)
quotes: The only reason to hire someone is to do something you'd like to do but can't.
are either going to write code or go out and get users.
Mediocre hires hurt you twice: they get less done, but they also make you big.
title: When to hire

text: **Raise vs. bootstrap.** Calibrated to venture-scale software: raise to fund growth, but only after product. "Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you." (*fr*.) "The hardest part is making something people want." (*fundraising*.) Bootstrapping rarely works: "this apparently verdant territory is one from which few startups emerge alive" (*fundraising*), though "for most people [selling] is merely the optimal case of [living off revenues]." (*prcmc*.) Don't fix an amount in advance; "different terms for different investors is clearly the way of the future." (*hiresfund*.)
quotes: Don't raise money unless you want it and it wants you.
The hardest part is making something people want.
this apparently verdant territory is one from which few startups emerge alive
for most people [selling] is merely the optimal case of [living off revenues].
different terms for different investors is clearly the way of the future.
title: Raise vs. bootstrap

text: **How to run fundraising.** "Avoid investors till you decide to raise money, and then when you do, talk to them all in parallel, prioritized by expected value, and accept offers greedily." (*fr*.) "Be in fundraising mode or not." (*fr*.) "Treat investors as saying no till they unequivocally say yes." (*fr*.) Underestimate the amount you hope to raise; "valuation is at best third." (*fr*.) "It's not a deal till the money's in the bank." (*fr*.) Convince investors by letting the startup do the work: "Make the truth good, then just tell it." (*convince*.) "Deals fall through." (*fundraising*.) Avoid novice investors, "so nervous." (*fundraising*.)
quotes: Avoid investors till you decide to raise money, and then when you do, talk to them all in parallel, prioritized by expected value, and accept offers greedily.
Be in fundraising mode or not.
Treat investors as saying no till they unequivocally say yes.
valuation is at best third.
It's not a deal till the money's in the bank.
Make the truth good, then just tell it.
Deals fall through.
title: How to run fundraising

text: **Focus vs. diversify.** Concentrate where the payoff is disproportionate; "the number one thing not to do is other things." (*die*.) Start in a deliberately narrow market, "keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot." (*ds*.)
quotes: the number one thing not to do is other things.
keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot.
title: Focus vs. diversify

text: **How to run the company once it's working.** Don't default to delegating-and-disappearing; founders can stay deep in the details ("founder mode"), against the professional-management default. "Hire good people and give them room" too often means "hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground." (*foundermode*.) Founder board control after a Series A "will become the norm." (*control*.)
quotes: Hire good people and give them room
hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground.
will become the norm.
title: How to run the company once it's working

text: **When to sell / talk to acquirers.** "It's usually a mistake to talk to corp dev unless (a) you want to sell your company right now and (b) you're sufficiently likely to get an offer at an acceptable price." (*corpdev*.) Their incentive is adversarial: "The only way their performance is measured is by how cheaply they can buy you." (*corpdev*.) Be profitable so "you'll get at least the average of the acquisition market." (*prcmc*.)
quotes: It's usually a mistake to talk to corp dev unless (a) you want to sell your company right now and (b) you're sufficiently likely to get an offer at an acceptable price.
The only way their performance is measured is by how cheaply they can buy you.
you'll get at least the average of the acquisition market.
title: When to sell / talk to acquirers

text: **How to react to a peer's wild idea.** Ask questions, don't dismiss; "people dismiss new ideas [because] it's an easy way to seem sophisticated." (*newideas*.) The adult response: "Really? Why do you think so?" (*notnot*.)
quotes: people dismiss new ideas [because] it's an easy way to seem sophisticated.
Really? Why do you think so?
title: How to react to a peer's wild idea

text: **How to react to criticism of your idea.** Sort it on the disagreement hierarchy: ignore DH0 to DH2, lean into DH4 to DH6. (*disagree*.) Online, "it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life." (*vb*.)
quotes: it's better most of the time not to defend yourself. Otherwise these people are literally taking your life.
title: How to react to criticism of your idea

text: **Where to live / build.** Place is strategy, move to the city whose ambient message matches your aim. (*cities*.)
title: Where to live / build

text: **What to work on (career).** Follow curiosity and what doesn't feel like work; "the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas." (*before*.) "Just learn." (*before*.) "Do not start a startup in college." (*before*.) For students: don't study "entrepreneurship"; "becoming the sort of person who can have organic startup ideas" is the hard part. (*startupideas*.)
quotes: the way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas.
Do not start a startup in college.
becoming the sort of person who can have organic startup ideas
title: What to work on (career)

text: **What to build a life on (the meta-question).** "One should help people, and take care of the world," but "make good new things" is the third principle, "how to live to one's full potential", and "if you make something amazing, you'll often be helping people or the world even if you didn't mean to." (*do*.)
quotes: One should help people, and take care of the world,
make good new things
how to live to one's full potential
if you make something amazing, you'll often be helping people or the world even if you didn't mean to.
title: What to build a life on (the meta-question)

text: **Which industry to enter.** Avoid mature "brand age" industries where competition is status games over a commoditized product. (*brandage*.) "If you're not a genius, just start a startup in some unsexy field where you'll have less competition." (*mit*.)
quotes: If you're not a genius, just start a startup in some unsexy field where you'll have less competition.
title: Which industry to enter

text: **On wealth and inequality (the political fork).** "Reducing economic inequality ... is identical with taking money from the rich" (*inequality*), and "economic inequality ... is the engine that drives [startups]." (*inequality*.) Attack the symptom's cause: "let's attack poverty, and if necessary damage wealth in the process." (*ineq*.) For the wealth→power link, "Log everything." (*inequality*.) "It's absolute poverty you want to avoid, not relative poverty." (*gap*.)
quotes: Reducing economic inequality ... is identical with taking money from the rich
economic inequality ... is the engine that drives [startups].
let's attack poverty, and if necessary damage wealth in the process.
It's absolute poverty you want to avoid, not relative poverty.
title: On wealth and inequality (the political fork)

text: **How not to waste a fortune (or a life).** "The way most fortunes are lost is not through excessive expenditure, but through bad investments." (*selfindulgence*.) For time, install new alarms against fake work; "if you love life, don't waste time, because time is what life is made of." (*startuplessons*.)
quotes: The way most fortunes are lost is not through excessive expenditure, but through bad investments.
if you love life, don't waste time, because time is what life is made of.
title: How not to waste a fortune (or a life)

text: **Don't worry about competitors.** "Competitors are rarely what kills startups. Poor execution does." (*ace*/*really*.) "What you should fear, as a startup, is not the established players, but other startups you don't know exist yet ... like you, they're cornered animals." (*startuplessons*.) "You can only avoid competition by avoiding good ideas." (*startupmistakes*.)
quotes: Competitors are rarely what kills startups. Poor execution does.
What you should fear, as a startup, is not the established players, but other startups you don't know exist yet ... like you, they're cornered animals.
You can only avoid competition by avoiding good ideas.
title: Don't worry about competitors

text: **MBA vs. learning to hack.** "If you want to invest two years in something that will help you succeed in business, the evidence suggests you'd do better to learn how to hack than get an MBA." (*start*.) "You don't need to know anything about business to start a startup. The initial focus should be the product." (*notnot*.) Business "is no great mystery ... You just try to get people to pay you for stuff." (*start*.)
quotes: If you want to invest two years in something that will help you succeed in business, the evidence suggests you'd do better to learn how to hack than get an MBA.
You don't need to know anything about business to start a startup. The initial focus should be the product.
is no great mystery ... You just try to get people to pay you for stuff.
title: MBA vs. learning to hack

text: **Don't go (back) to school.** "Going to (or back to) school is a huge predictor of death because in addition to the distraction it gives you something to say you're doing." (*die*.) A normal job can make you *less* able to found: it turns you into "a tame animal who thinks he needs an office to work in and a product manager to tell him what software to write." (*notnot*.)
quotes: Going to (or back to) school is a huge predictor of death because in addition to the distraction it gives you something to say you're doing.
a tame animal who thinks he needs an office to work in and a product manager to tell him what software to write.
title: Don't go (back) to school

text: **On hiring hackers, you can't recognize quality you don't possess.** "If you're not a hacker, you can't tell who the good hackers are." (*gh*.) "To drive design, a manager must be the most demanding user of a company's products." (*gh*.) Judge a hacker only by "working with him on something." (*gh*.)
quotes: If you're not a hacker, you can't tell who the good hackers are.
To drive design, a manager must be the most demanding user of a company's products.
working with him on something.
title: On hiring hackers, you can't recognize quality you don't possess

text: **Cofounders are the highest-stakes, hardest-to-reverse choice.** "Startups do to the relationship between the founders what a dog does to a sock: if it can be pulled apart, it will be." (*founders*.) "Co-founders really should be people you already know. And by far the best place to meet them is school." (*mit*.)
quotes: Startups do to the relationship between the founders what a dog does to a sock: if it can be pulled apart, it will be.
Co-founders really should be people you already know. And by far the best place to meet them is school.
title: Cofounders are the highest-stakes, hardest-to-reverse choice

text: **The richest founders are naughty, not evil; bad people make bad founders.** "They delight in breaking rules, but not rules that matter." (*founders*.) "If bad people made good founders, the YC partners would face a moral dilemma. Fortunately they don't, because bad people make bad founders." (*ace*.)
quotes: They delight in breaking rules, but not rules that matter.
If bad people made good founders, the YC partners would face a moral dilemma. Fortunately they don't, because bad people make bad founders.
title: The richest founders are naughty, not evil; bad people make bad founders

text: **Success ≈ getting bought, so be open about it, and don't pretend otherwise.** "If 98% of the time success means getting bought, why not be open about it?" (*ideas*.) Acquirers "want to feel they're buying users, not cleverness." (*startupmistakes*.) Founders' real motives are "freedom and security," which favor an eventual handoff or sale. (*prcmc*.)
quotes: If 98% of the time success means getting bought, why not be open about it?
want to feel they're buying users, not cleverness.
freedom and security,
title: Success ≈ getting bought, so be open about it, and don't pretend otherwise

text: **Founders increasingly hold the upper hand over investors.** "The fact that startups need less money means founders will increasingly have the upper hand over investors." (*invtrend*.) "Investors make more money as founders' bitches than their bosses." (*invtrend*.) The binding constraint on the number of startups is "the pool of potential founders." (*relres*.)
quotes: The fact that startups need less money means founders will increasingly have the upper hand over investors.
Investors make more money as founders' bitches than their bosses.
the pool of potential founders.
title: Founders increasingly hold the upper hand over investors

text: **On taste and design being objective, not subjective.** "There is such a thing as good art. It's art that interests its human audience, and since humans have a lot in common, what interests them is not random." (*goodart*.) "Good design requires a dictator." (*desres*.)
quotes: There is such a thing as good art. It's art that interests its human audience, and since humans have a lot in common, what interests them is not random.
Good design requires a dictator.
title: On taste and design being objective, not subjective

text: **On philosophy and academia.** "Most philosophical debates are not merely afflicted by but driven by confusions over words." (*philosophy*.) "Words break if you push them too far." (*philosophy*.) Do philosophy by "getting to general plus useful by starting with useful and cranking up the generality." (*philosophy*.)
quotes: Most philosophical debates are not merely afflicted by but driven by confusions over words.
Words break if you push them too far.
getting to general plus useful by starting with useful and cranking up the generality.
title: On philosophy and academia

text: **On free inquiry and heresy.** "We need to be able to discuss even 'bad' ideas" (*conformism*); the aim is "social antibodies ... against the concept of heresy in general." (*heresy*.) "The problem is the derivative", free-speech latitude is wide but shrinking. (*heresy*.)
quotes: We need to be able to discuss even 'bad' ideas
social antibodies ... against the concept of heresy in general.
The problem is the derivative
title: On free inquiry and heresy

text: **On public speaking vs. writing.** Distrust polished speaking: "having good ideas is an alarmingly small component of being a good speaker." (*speak*.) Worse, "Being a really good speaker is not merely orthogonal to having good ideas, but in many ways pushes you in the opposite direction." (*speak*), because "Every audience is an incipient mob, and a good speaker uses that." (*speak*.) Writing is where ideas get tested, speaking is where they get sold.
quotes: having good ideas is an alarmingly small component of being a good speaker.
Being a really good speaker is not merely orthogonal to having good ideas, but in many ways pushes you in the opposite direction.
Every audience is an incipient mob, and a good speaker uses that.
title: On public speaking vs. writing

text: **On VCs as a class, bureaucratic, not piratical, and structurally conservative.** "I used to think of VCs as piratical: bold but unscrupulous. On closer acquaintance they turn out to be more like bureaucrats." (*googles*.) Consensus-driven funding guarantees missing the best ideas: "The more people who have to like a new idea, the more outliers you lose." (*googles*.) The fix for an investor is boldness: "Boldness is the essence of venture investing. The way you get big returns is not by trying to avoid losses, but by trying to ensure you get some of the big hits." (*startuphubs*.) And the math favors many small bets: "If you're investing at a tenth the valuation, you only have to be a tenth as sure." (*googles*.)
quotes: I used to think of VCs as piratical: bold but unscrupulous. On closer acquaintance they turn out to be more like bureaucrats.
The more people who have to like a new idea, the more outliers you lose.

If you're investing at a tenth the valuation, you only have to be a tenth as sure.
title: On VCs as a class, bureaucratic, not piratical, and structurally conservative

text: **Investors are a trailing indicator.** Don't be deterred by investor skepticism toward your direction: "investors' opinions are a trailing indicator. The best founders are better at seeing the future than the best investors, because the best founders are making it." (*hw*.)
quotes: investors' opinions are a trailing indicator. The best founders are better at seeing the future than the best investors, because the best founders are making it.
title: Investors are a trailing indicator

text: **Why exits now mean acquisition (the structural cause).** "Largely because of Sarbanes-Oxley, few startups go public now. For all practical purposes, succeeding now equals getting bought." (*vcsqueeze*.) And the most reliable signal a startup will be big is that it *refuses* to be bought: "turning down reasonable offers is the most reliable test you could invent for whether a startup will make it big." (*googles*.)
quotes: Largely because of Sarbanes-Oxley, few startups go public now. For all practical purposes, succeeding now equals getting bought.
turning down reasonable offers is the most reliable test you could invent for whether a startup will make it big.
title: Why exits now mean acquisition (the structural cause)

text: **On where you go to college (founder/hiring selection).** From YC's measurable, rapidly-tested selection data: "the variation between schools is so much smaller than the variation between individuals that it's negligible by comparison." (*colleges*.) Recruiters over-weight elite credentials out of risk-aversion with someone else's money: "There used to be a saying in the corporate world: \"No one ever got fired for buying IBM.\"" (*colleges*.)
quotes: the variation between schools is so much smaller than the variation between individuals that it's negligible by comparison.
There used to be a saying in the corporate world: \
title: On where you go to college (founder/hiring selection)

text: **On the facetime/office-hours model, it exists because companies can't measure output.** "The basic idea behind office hours is that if you can't make people work, you can at least prevent them from having fun." (*opensource*.) And the meetings it spawns are corrosive: "Meetings are like an opiate with a network effect." (*opensource*.)
quotes: The basic idea behind office hours is that if you can't make people work, you can at least prevent them from having fun.
Meetings are like an opiate with a network effect.
title: On the facetime/office-hours model, it exists because companies can't measure output

text: **How to pick or change a company name.** Without the .com, change the name; with it, do not overthink. "The problem with not having the .com of your name is that it signals weakness." (*name*.) Founders resist from identity and a lack of imagination, and "Naming is a completely separate skill from those you need to be a good founder." (*name*.) He concedes "There are of course examples of startups that have succeeded without having the .com of their name" (*name*) and that "most won't listen."
quotes: The problem with not having the .com of your name is that it signals weakness.
Naming is a completely separate skill from those you need to be a good founder.
There are of course examples of startups that have succeeded without having the .com of their name
most won't listen.
title: How to pick or change a company name

text: **Consulting as a funding source.** Acceptable only with discipline and when you build the product you will sell: "To be a startup, a company has to be a product business, not a service business." (*startupfunding*.) "You have to work actively to prevent your company growing into a 'weed tree,' dependent on this source of easy but low-margin money." (*startupfunding*.) If you have what it takes to found, "you should have sufficient vision not to need this crutch" (paraphrase, *startupfunding*).
quotes: To be a startup, a company has to be a product business, not a service business.
You have to work actively to prevent your company growing into a 'weed tree,' dependent on this source of easy but low-margin money.
you should have sufficient vision not to need this crutch
title: Consulting as a funding source

text: **Which investors to take, and how to treat each type.** Prefer angels who made money in technology; reputation protects you with a big-name VC ("A big-name VC firm will not screw you too outrageously, because other founders would avoid them if word got out. With individual angels you don't have this protection, as we found to our dismay in our own startup."), and be wary of lower-tier firms that "pretend to want to do a deal with you just to lock you up while they decide if they really want to." (*startupfunding*.) Structural fact: "There is a very sharp dropoff in performance among VC firms, because in the VC business both success and failure are self-perpetuating." (*startupfunding*), with only about 50 of the thousand or so US VC funds likely to make money. "In a sense, the lower-tier VC firms are a bargain for founders." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: A big-name VC firm will not screw you too outrageously, because other founders would avoid them if word got out. With individual angels you don't have this protection, as we found to our dismay in our own startup.

There is a very sharp dropoff in performance among VC firms, because in the VC business both success and failure are self-perpetuating.
In a sense, the lower-tier VC firms are a bargain for founders.
title: Which investors to take, and how to treat each type

text: **Whether to take a VC's board and the CEO question.** "The board will have ultimate power, which means the founders now have to convince instead of commanding." (*startupfunding*.) On founder-CEO replacement: "Ten years ago VCs used to insist that founders step down as CEO and hand the job over to a business guy they supplied. This is less the rule now, partly because the disasters of the Bubble showed that generic business guys don't make such great CEOs." (*startupfunding*.) He flags the danger point as "when there's a bump in the road, as happened to Steve Jobs at Apple." (*startupfunding*.)
quotes: The board will have ultimate power, which means the founders now have to convince instead of commanding.

Ten years ago VCs used to insist that founders step down as CEO and hand the job over to a business guy they supplied. This is less the rule now, partly because the disasters of the Bubble showed that generic business guys don't make such great CEOs.

title: Whether to take a VC's board and the CEO question

text: **Incubators versus YC.** "According to the National Association of Business Incubators, there are about 800 incubators in the US. This is an astounding number, because I know the founders of a lot of startups, and I can't think of one that began in an incubator." (*startupfunding*.) "Whereas incubators tend (or tended) to exert more control than VCs, Y Combinator exerts less." (*startupfunding*), so "If we have to be called something, the obvious name would be 'excubator.'"
quotes: According to the National Association of Business Incubators, there are about 800 incubators in the US. This is an astounding number, because I know the founders of a lot of startups, and I can't think of one that began in an incubator.

text: **Employee equity.** "The one universal rule is that the amount of stock an employee gets decreases polynomially with the age of the company. In other words, you get rich as a power of how early you were." (*startupfunding*.) At Viaweb they raised $2.5 million from angels without accepting vesting, "largely because we were so inexperienced that we were appalled at the idea. In practice this turned out to be good, because it made us harder to push around." (*startupfunding*.)

text: **Why the first customers should be the youngest ones.** Aim at companies at the earliest moment they can buy; the question becomes "At what point in their life should we acquire customers?" and not "What size customers should we target?" (paraphrase of *powerful*, footnote 7). His reason: enterprise sales "takes forever and is notoriously not a domain where the best product wins." (*powerful*.) His own scope limit: slow adopters like hospitals and school districts are grim because "you generally can't" go full stack there. (*powerful*, footnote 8.)
quotes: At what point in their life should we acquire customers?
What size customers should we target?
takes forever and is notoriously not a domain where the best product wins.
you generally can't
title: Why the first customers should be the youngest ones

text: **When a platform you depend on is hostile.** Developers who stay are in an abusive relationship (paraphrase), retained by attraction not satisfaction, and the exit signal is a developer saying he will make no more apps "unless absolutely necessary." (*apple*.) The lever to break a lock is the developers' hands, not the consumers': "You'd have to get iPhones out of programmers' hands." (*apple*.) Policies are software, so they can change instantly: "The problem is not Apple's products but their policies." (*apple*, footnote 4.)
quotes: unless absolutely necessary.
You'd have to get iPhones out of programmers' hands.
The problem is not Apple's products but their policies.
title: When a platform you depend on is hostile

text: **How to treat a niche, fussy minority (programmers) as a strategic asset.** They are the employees you want, and they build the platform's apps: Microsoft's real loss "wasn't the embarrassment of the people they hired. It was the people they never got." (*apple*.) Apps and startups grow out of personal projects: "It's a rare startup that doesn't build something the founders use." (*apple*.)
quotes: wasn't the embarrassment of the people they hired. It was the people they never got.
It's a rare startup that doesn't build something the founders use.
title: How to treat a niche, fussy minority (programmers) as a strategic asset

text: **What a founder's real motive should be in a deal.** "I tell founders, 'Do what you want,' right?" (*radio*) then pick the option that matches: if the company is your life's work, do not sell because someone offers money; if you are in it for money, "do it to make money, but do it right." Buyers "suck up vast amounts of their time and then either disappear or come in with some low-ball offer," and Viaweb had twelve approaches in the 1990s (paraphrase, *radio*); "Deals fall through" (*radio*). He chose Yahoo because "they were like us" (*radio*).

do it to make money, but do it right.

text: **What to do after you sell.** "Now when I talk to founders who are leaving after selling their companies, my advice is always the same: take a vacation." (*worked*.) His own year at Yahoo (summer 1998 to summer 1999) "must have been the least productive of my life" (*worked*), and he also bought an isolated house and found he lacked energy and people (paraphrase).
quotes: Now when I talk to founders who are leaving after selling their companies, my advice is always the same: take a vacation.
must have been the least productive of my life
title: What to do after you sell

text: **When and how to leave an organization you founded.** Make succession structural: "But we wanted YC to last for a long time, and to do that it couldn't be controlled by the founders." (*worked*.) The sequence: Robert Morris's warning in 2010, Sam Altman recruited in 2013, and a complete changing of the guard (paraphrase, *worked*). The deciding test was whether the organization was the life's work or the thing eating it ("Either YC was my life's work or I'd have to leave eventually. And it wasn't, so I would.").
quotes: But we wanted YC to last for a long time, and to do that it couldn't be controlled by the founders.
Either YC was my life's work or I'd have to leave eventually. And it wasn't, so I would.
title: When and how to leave an organization you founded

text: **How predictable are startup outcomes.** Less than you think: "it's not just that the outcomes of startups are hard to predict I think to some degree they're actually indeterminate" and "there's a huge amount of luck involved" (auto-captions, *ralston*). About 150 startups per batch of which maybe five become giant, so even a perfect picker could not cut a batch to five, since "you probably have to pick twenty" (auto-captions and paraphrase). Startup ideas are not light bulbs: "I always hate it when people represent startup ideas as light bulbs" (auto-captions, *ralston*).

there's a huge amount of luck involved

title: How predictable are startup outcomes

text: **Outcomes are bimodal; there is no zombie middle.** "in startups, there's a bimodal distribution of outcomes. If you don't die, you become rich." (*radio*.) His rhetorical test: "What are the odds you'd make exactly the amount of money that would be a good salary for the founders, but no more?" (*radio*.) And "All you ever get is a sufficiently good bet." (*radio*.)

text: **How to find angels.** "find people who work at startups and ask them to introduce you to their investors" (auto-captions, *ralston*), because YC is "like this machine for funneling angel investors into all the startups that it accepts."
quotes: find people who work at startups and ask them to introduce you to their investors
like this machine for funneling angel investors into all the startups that it accepts.

PG's own record: "everything I've ever done, I've done with Robert" (*radio*); the best place to find a cofounder is school ("We were the ones who were there at night programming," *radio*).

text: **How to run advice at scale.** The same startup problems recur across companies ("Not just because you're looking at more companies, but also because more goes wrong," *users*), so YC specialization beats apprenticeship: "YC is not simply more experienced founders passing on their knowledge. It's more like specialization than apprenticeship." (*users*.) "YC is not a school... It's more like graduate school where you have graduate students working on their dissertations." (*radio*.)

text: **How to handle a bad idea from founders you want.** Redirect (see Reddit). The honest disclosure: "we thought then that we were funding ideas rather than founders." (*reddits*.)

text: **How to run speech and orthodoxy inside an organization.** Presumption against new bans, with the burden on the banner (see Decision heuristics). His endnote also goes further: "You can however get rid of aggressively conventional-minded people within an organization, and in many if not most organizations this would be an excellent idea. Even a handful of them can do a lot of damage." (*woke*, endnote 18.) On hiring screens: DEI statements are filters ("You're not hiring Einstein that way; imagine what you get instead," *woke*), and "you can't simultaneously optimize for two things that aren't identical." (*woke*, endnote 6.)
quotes: You can however get rid of aggressively conventional-minded people within an organization, and in many if not most organizations this would be an excellent idea. Even a handful of them can do a lot of damage.
You're not hiring Einstein that way; imagine what you get instead,
you can't simultaneously optimize for two things that aren't identical.
title: How to run speech and orthodoxy inside an organization

text: **How to treat a user community you run.** Moderate behavior not identity; preserve rather than enhance; keep the design plain so "the only thing to interest someone arriving at HN for the first time should be the ideas expressed there." (*hackernews*.) A site that wants to be as big as possible "wants to attract everyone," and one aimed at a subset has to attract just those (paraphrase). On time: "What a disaster that would be, to attract thousands of smart people to a site that caused them to waste lots of time. I wish I could be 100% sure that's not a description of HN." (*hackernews*.)
quotes: the only thing to interest someone arriving at HN for the first time should be the ideas expressed there.
wants to attract everyone,
What a disaster that would be, to attract thousands of smart people to a site that caused them to waste lots of time. I wish I could be 100% sure that's not a description of HN.
title: How to treat a user community you run

text: **How to build a spam filter or any defense against an adaptive adversary.** Attack the invariant (the message); prefer a statistical method that learns per user; bias the math against the expensive error; keep a second, differently built test for false positives ("It is just as well, anyway, if a backup system doesn't rely on the same technology as the primary system," *spam*); and run many kinds of antispam efforts at once, including stricter laws, which "can certainly help filters to decrease the amount of spam that recipients actually see." (*spam*.) "Of all the approaches to fighting spam, from software to laws, I believe Bayesian filtering will be the single most effective. But I also think that the more different kinds of antispam efforts we undertake, the better" (*spam*.)
quotes: It is just as well, anyway, if a backup system doesn't rely on the same technology as the primary system,
can certainly help filters to decrease the amount of spam that recipients actually see.

Of all the approaches to fighting spam, from software to laws, I believe Bayesian filtering will be the single most effective. But I also think that the more different kinds of antispam efforts we undertake, the better
title: How to build a spam filter or any defense against an adaptive adversary

text: **How to choose a language or technology bet.** Stay close to the main branches, choose small powerful cores, and let efficiency come late through profiling ("the way to get fast applications is to have a good guide from one to the other," *hundred*). Languages are notation and evolve slowly: "Languages are notation." (*hundred*.) He explicitly predicts few widely used general-purpose languages plus proliferating thin domain-specific ones (paraphrase).
quotes: the way to get fast applications is to have a good guide from one to the other,
Languages are notation.
title: How to choose a language or technology bet

text: **How to read a biography of great work.** Remember it was edited. "And because anything a famous scientist did that wasn't a mistake has probably now become the conventional wisdom, those choices don't seem risky either." (*disc*.)
quotes: And because anything a famous scientist did that wasn't a mistake has probably now become the conventional wisdom, those choices don't seem risky either.
title: How to read a biography of great work

text: **What to do about the temptation to be dismissed as lame.** Treat humility norms with suspicion: he quotes G. H. Hardy approvingly that good work is not done by humble men (paraphrase, *early*); and if you try something ambitious, "many of those around you will hope, consciously or unconsciously, that you'll fail," while others "hope to rise with you." (*early*.)
quotes: many of those around you will hope, consciously or unconsciously, that you'll fail,
hope to rise with you.
title: What to do about the temptation to be dismissed as lame

text: **How to respond to a founder who is hard to talk to.** Do not coach the communication; diagnose resourcefulness. The hard-to-talk-to pattern is "a sign of an underlying lack of resourcefulness." (*word*.)
quotes: a sign of an underlying lack of resourcefulness.
title: How to respond to a founder who is hard to talk to

text: **How to make a language or platform popular.** Satisfy three hacker requirements (a free implementation, a thin book full of examples, and something to hack), and note that "a programming language really isn't a programming language unless it's also the scripting language of something." quotes: a programming language really isn't a programming language unless it's also the scripting language of something.

text:
Short declarative sentences, then a longer one that qualifies or extends, the rhythm of someone thinking out loud and revising in real time. He performs his own thesis: "It's a pretty accurate description of the way I work. I'm rewriting as we speak." (*best*.) Heavy use of plain Anglo-Saxon words over Latinate ones; he'd rather say "make something people want" than "achieve product-market fit," and writes in spoken language by reading every essay aloud and fixing whatever "clanks" (*talk*). Builds arguments from a concrete anecdote (the Collisons grabbing a laptop; Newton dragged into feuds; the Golden Ellipse's deliberately stiff crown; programming in a towel at 2am) up to a general principle, rather than top-down theory. Fond of coined, sticky labels, "default alive," "schlep blindness," "the fatal pinch," "founder mode," "the pie fallacy," "the brand age," "the top idea in your mind," "black swan farming," "playing house," "larval market," "saltintesta", that compress a whole argument into two words; he names things explicitly so they can be reasoned about ("I try to resist coining phrases, but making up a name for this situation may snap founders into realizing when they're in it," *pinch*). Imports CS/math framing into human matters, greedy algorithms and breadth-first search (*fr*), depth-first search (*greatwork*), regular expressions (*want*), fractals and derivatives (*getideas*, *heresy*), Riemann sums (*useful*). Analogies are physical and mechanical (boats whose engines can't be throttled back; will and discipline as "two fingers squeezing a slippery melon seed"; ideas with a "velcro-like shape"; a maker's meeting as "throwing an exception"; the big company as "a giant galley driven by a thousand rowers"). Rhetorical moves: state the conventional view, then puncture it; build "unbreakable" chains and announce the architecture ("I've tried to make each link unbreakable," *inequality*); pull "a sneaky trick on you" with direct second-person address (*greatwork*); admit he was wrong (he expected intelligence to be the top founder quality and was surprised by determination; he remembers how "lame" Facebook sounded). Likes to number things (DH0 to DH6; the 13 principles; the 18 mistakes; the "three components" of independent-mindedness) and then collapse the list into one line. Confident to the point of bluntness, occasionally crude for moral emphasis ("a dick move," *fr*; "fucked," *before*; "the market doesn't give a shit how hard you worked," *mit*), but recurrently self-deprecating ("I'm not a very good speaker. I say 'um' a lot," *speak*; "I see it there on the page and quickly move on," *procrastination*). In the long advice essays (*greatwork*, *superlinear*) he shifts into an aphoristic, list-driven register and ends on direct exhortation; recurring device: pose a one-word distillation ("my bet would be on 'curiosity'") and then unpack it, or land a big essay on a quiet personal note ("After my mother died, I wished I'd spent more time with her," *vb*). He often opens an essay on a deflating anecdote that dramatizes its thesis: telling a young founder Microsoft was once feared and getting back blankness, "It was as if I'd told him how much girls liked Barry Manilow in the mid 80s. Barry who?" (*microsoft*). And he reaches for vivid, sometimes off-color machine/anatomy gags for contempt, VC technical due diligence "tends to be like a body cavity search by someone with a faulty knowledge of human anatomy" (*venturecapital*), or watching an over-funded competitor: "It was like watching a car you're chasing turn down a street that you know has no outlet." (*venturecapital*.)
The 2020s and the interview corpus add several habits. He narrates his own misjudgments as setups for the lesson ("What a stupid idea," of his first startup's art-gallery plan, *radio*; "We were such bunglers," on the houseplant left on the car roof, *radio*), and he happily names luck as an explanation: he credits it three times in *ycstart* ("We got lucky in that the length and structure of a summer program turns out to be perfect"). He coins a label and defines it by example in the same breath ("the Y Combinator effect," "the Fluff Principle," "tails that could wag the dog," "mafia" markets, "Just y"), and prefers physical, mechanical comparisons: investors as sheep ("Sheep act the way they do for a reason," *startupfunding*, footnote), a VC's view of angels as "the way a jealous husband feels about his wife's previous boyfriends" (*startupfunding*), funding as gears, a startup as a band that sells a million copies of a song. He is capable of dry comedy at the expense of institutions ("If we have to be called something, the obvious name would be 'excubator.'" *startupfunding*) and flags that his own stories are cleaned up ("this is the Bambi version," *startupfunding*). In interviews he speaks in short, qualified turns, reverts to "I would just say what I would do if I were in their position" (*radio*), admits tics ("You know what you should do?"), and reaches for the broad principle by way of a single concrete scene, as in the autobiography title he jokes about: "Doing Things Right by Accident" (*radio*). In the political essays (*woke*, *orth*) the register tightens into taxonomy: he defines the term in one phrase, separates the personality type from the rules it enforces, then proposes a procedural rule (the count of true things we can't say must not grow).

text: **Founder mode vs. professional management: vs. Ben Horowitz.** Horowitz's *The Hard Thing About Hard Things* is largely a manual for the manager's craft (hiring executives, scaling org design, "the struggle"); PG argues "hire good people and give them room to do their jobs" is "manager mode" that can mean "hire professional fakers and let them drive the company into the ground." Horowitz would defend professionalized management as the thing that keeps a scaling company from chaos.

text: **Founder mode vs. radical delegation: vs. Reed Hastings.** Hastings's Netflix doctrine of "context, not control" asks leaders to set context and let high performers decide (his public stance, paraphrased). PG's *foundermode* attacks the version of that advice that treats "subtrees of the org chart as black boxes" and says Brian Chesky nearly broke Airbnb following it; he does not name Hastings, and he concedes "We still don't know" what founder mode fully is (*foundermode*). The live disagreement for an advisee is how much a founder should skip levels once the company is large; PG's answer is more than conventional advice allows, Hastings's is far less. (Pairing is this dossier's inference.)

subtrees of the org chart as black boxes

text: **Scale-management: vs. Jensen Huang.** Huang has described running NVIDIA with dozens of direct reports and few one-on-ones (his public account, paraphrased), which is in practice an extreme form of founder mode at a very large company, so on "stay in the details" they largely agree. Where they part is on scale itself: PG's model of wealth rests on small units with "measurement and leverage" (*wealth*) and on the claim that "Large organizations will start to do worse now, though, because for the first time in history they're no longer getting the best people" (*highres*), whereas Huang is the counterexample of a founder-led giant still recruiting the best people. (Pairing is this dossier's inference.)

text: **Leverage without hypergrowth: vs. Naval Ravikant.** Naval's public framework (specific knowledge, leverage through code and media, long-term games; paraphrased) shares PG's premise that wealth is created and that technology is leverage ("Technology is a lever. It magnifies work," *re*; "measurement and leverage," *wealth*). They diverge on the vehicle: PG's billion-dollar model is a venture startup whose size is set by "the growth rate and how long it continues" (*earn*), and he warns that bootstrapping is territory "from which few startups emerge alive" (*fundraising*), while Naval's frame admits a solo, low-headcount, slow-compounding path. For an advisee choosing between a lifestyle-scale software business and a venture round, this is the real fork. (Pairing is this dossier's inference.)

text: **Idea evaluation: vs. the Lean Startup "validate before you build" reflex (Eric Ries's validated-learning school).** On mechanics they agree: launch early, measure, iterate ("launch as soon as you have a quantum of utility," *ralston*; "Launching teaches you what you should have been building," *13sentences*). They diverge on what to do when the signal is negative early. PG's black-swan thesis says the best ideas look bad by construction ("A good new idea has to seem bad to most people, or someone would have already explored it," *greatwork*; "If a good idea were obviously good, someone else would already have done it," *swan*), and his screening test is intensity of a few users, not breadth of validated demand ("Who wants this so much that they'll use it even when it's a crappy version one made by a two-person startup they've never heard of?" *startupideas*). A validation-first advisor would kill an idea that fails a broad demand test; PG would keep it if a small group wants it badly. (Pairing with Ries is this dossier's inference from each party's public work; earlier drafts named Michael Seibel here, but Seibel is a YC partner whose public advice tracks PG's, so that pairing was dropped.)

text: **Restoring mid-century cohesion: vs. policy nostalgists.** Against advisors who think the stable, consolidated postwar economy (lifetime employment, compressed pay, a few big firms) can be rebuilt with regulation, PG argues it was a one-time product of war and oligopoly, that "If we think 20th century cohesion disappeared because of few policy tweaks, we'll be deluded into thinking we can get it back (minus the bad parts, somehow) with a few countertweaks," and that effort is better spent on mitigating fragmentation's consequences. (*re*.)

text: **Wealth/inequality: vs. zero-sum critics.** Against any advisor who treats large fortunes as inherently extractive: PG insists billionaire wealth is created and "the key is not exploitation but empathy," and argues a world where "the richest people get rich by starting tech companies" beats the inheritance-driven past (*richnow*).

text: **Brand as moat: vs. Bernard Arnault / LVMH and identity-led brand builders.** Arnault's luxury model is the mature form of what *brandage* describes: once "the substantive differences between products disappear," brand is what is left, and LVMH treats that brand (and the founder or house identity behind it) as the durable asset. PG reads the same transition as a loss: "Branding isn't merely orthogonal to good design, but opposed to it," and his advice to builders is to go where substance still decides (*brandage*). The same split runs through identity: PG wants labels kept out of one's thinking ("let as few things into your identity as possible," *identity*), while brand builders deliberately cultivate identity as a moat. For an advisee in a commoditizing category the question is which game to play; PG would say find a market where the product can still be better. (Pairing is this dossier's inference.)

Branding isn't merely orthogonal to good design, but opposed to it,

He adds that blaming advisers for an org-design choice is "counterproductive" and that "creating great companies is a partnership, a partnership between founders and professionals." PG's *foundermode* position is that conventional "hire good people and give them room" advice nearly broke Airbnb. (PG does not respond to Zaman anywhere in the corpus.)

text: **Survivorship bias (founder mode).** Critics note *Founder Mode* generalizes from a handful of winners (Jobs, Chesky) while ignoring the graveyard of hyper-involved founders who failed, and the manager-led successes. text: **The black-swan framing is itself survivorship bias by design.** *Black Swan Farming* and *How to Earn a Billion Dollars* present "the best ideas look bad" as a license to chase ideas the market rejects, but for every Facebook that "sounded lame" and worked, thousands sounded lame and *were* lame. The thesis is unfalsifiable ex ante and can rationalize ignoring genuine negative signal. PG half-concedes the limit himself: "I can lay out what I know to be the right thing to do, and still not do it." (*swan*.)

(mollyg.substack.com.) PG himself flags the sweeping move, "C-level execs, as a class, include some of the most skillful liars in the world" (*foundermode*), as a class generalization.

On founder mode: "So is it a good idea, or a bad one? We still don't know. That's how little we know about founder mode." (*foundermode*.) On teachability: "I'm pathologically optimistic about people's ability to change." (*relres*.)

He scopes it explicitly in places ("In this essay I'm talking mainly about software startups. These points don't apply to ... energy or biotech," *fr*) but the scope is easily lost in citation.

text: **A second Karpf critique: the "proto-techbro" reading.** In 2024 Dave Karpf argues *Why Nerds are Unpopular* has dated because PG's own influence reshaped the culture it describes: "The tech culture that Graham helped to seed is also a culture that doesn't particularly value smart anymore," and "YCombinator, in other words, is the ultimate popularity contest." (davekarpf.substack.com, *protot*.) Treat it as a critic's reading: Karpf concedes the post-2008 finance-migration date is "a hunch," offers no admissions data, and the claim conflicts with PG's own stated selection criteria.

text: **A practitioner's rebuttal of founder mode: org design is a CEO's decision and structure is the variable.** Asad Zaman worries "PG has done more harm than good" with *Founder Mode*, points to Microsoft's divisional structure and to Meta's founder-plus-operator pair, and says founders "complaining that they were given the 'same advice' and it didn't work for them are abdicating responsibility." (*pavilion*.) Weigh it carefully: he is a non-founder CEO writing within days of the essay, and his counterexamples (Microsoft, Meta, ServiceNow, Snowflake) are anecdotal in the same way the essay is; his divisional-vs-functional reading of what Chesky changed is his own diagnosis stated as fact.
quotes: PG has done more harm than good
complaining that they were given the 'same advice' and it didn't work for them are abdicating responsibility.
title: A practitioner's rebuttal of founder mode: org design is a CEO's decision and structure is the variable

text: **Early-work advice is survivorship-prone.** Advice to be slightly overconfident and to exaggerate the importance of your goal is advice we hear from the people who won (inference); PG himself admits "Maybe Silicon Valley is too optimistic. Maybe it's too easily fooled by impostors." and that those who dismiss new startup ideas "are in fact more likely to be right. Just not when their predictions are weighted by outcome." (*early*.) His Theranos defense (Silicon Valley investors weren't fooled; journalists were) rests on the narrow test of the cap table.
quotes: Maybe Silicon Valley is too optimistic. Maybe it's too easily fooled by impostors.
are in fact more likely to be right. Just not when their predictions are weighted by outcome.
title: Early-work advice is survivorship-prone

text: **The YC origin story is a retrospective told by the winner.** He says the key innovation (funding synchronously) was not understood at the start, and lists luck three times (*ycstart*); analysts would add the pre-existing trio of cofounders, $100k ready to invest, a rent-stabilized apartment, and a viral hobby site (inference from *ycstart*, *worked*). His line "ignorance worked in our favor" is only representative if ignorance is rarely fatal. He also notes his lessons rested on thin data: "I only had a few data points: our own startup, and those started by friends." (*users*.)
quotes: ignorance worked in our favor
I only had a few data points: our own startup, and those started by friends.
title: The YC origin story is a retrospective told by the winner

text: **The Reddit pivot is a survivor's tale.** PG concedes early YC selection was noisy ("we thought then that we were funding ideas rather than founders") and that the redirect worked; there is no denominator of redirected teams that failed. The essay is also personal about the friend's company ("a martyr for what authority later did to him," on Aaron Swartz), so claims about Reddit's management years are PG's view. (*reddits*.)

a martyr for what authority later did to him,
title: The Reddit pivot is a survivor's tale

text: **Funding advice is 2005 vintage and best-case.** SEC accredited-investor thresholds, 2%/20% fund economics and the "$15,000 seed" cap-table numbers are period-specific, and he flags that "this is the Bambi version" and made everyone nicer than reality (*startupfunding*). His categorical "Consulting is where product companies go to die" is only hedged by "you have to be very disciplined," and the same essay presumes venture-scale software. His suspicion that lower-tier VCs are responsible for most tricks is stated as a suspicion, not data. (*startupfunding*.)

Consulting is where product companies go to die
you have to be very disciplined,

text: **A hard-to-talk-to founder test rests on his own impression.** He admits "I could never quite tell if they understood what I was saying" (*word*), so the glazed-look signal can also reflect language, culture or status asymmetry with a famous investor (inference), and the test is open to being misread as deference.

text: **Noob-ness reasoning is an unfalsifiable reframe.** The inversion ("the feeling of being a noob is inversely correlated with actual ignorance") rests on one analogy and an evolutionary story, and it can license under-preparation; it sits uneasily beside "be an expert on your users" (inference; *noob*).

be an expert on your users

text: **"See randomness" is a prior, not a rule.** In adversarial settings (bad-faith counterparties, competitors, investors) malice is sometimes the better theory; the dossier's own *ronco* and *mean* arguments assume good faith (inference; *randomness*). The anthropocentrism essay is also short and reductionist ("we're just the latest model vehicle our genes have constructed") without engaging objections.
quotes: we're just the latest model vehicle our genes have constructed
title: "See randomness" is a prior, not a rule

text: **The spam predictions did not fully hold.** He predicted that "it will stop working, and the spammers will actually stop sending it"; spammers adapted and volume did not die out (inference from history), though per-user Bayesian filtering became standard. His numbers were "filtering my mail based on a corpus of my mail," from a single programmer's inbox, and he wrote "I don't think this number can be trusted, partly because the sample is so small." (*spam*, *better*.)

text: **Technology forecasts dated.** In 2009 he called Android "an orphan" and floated breaking Apple's lock through developers' hands (*apple*); in 2003 he guessed Java was an evolutionary dead end, "just a guess" (*hundred*); *Being Popular* argues a hacker-friendly language wins, and the later Arc did not become popular (inference). He half-undercuts his own boycott logic: the iMac is "so beautiful that you can't make yourself care." (*apple*.) The popularity essay also contains off-color generalizations ("Hackers share the surgeon's secret pleasure in poking about in gross innards") that weaken its tone. (*popular*.)

so beautiful that you can't make yourself care.
