text: Reid Hoffman is the "theory-of-the-firm" venture capitalist: LinkedIn co-founder, PayPal COO ("PayPal Mafia"), Greylock partner, *Masters of Scale* and *Possible* host, and the most prolific framework-author among operators (Blitzscaling, The Start-Up of You, The Alliance, Masters of Scale, Impromptu, Superagency). His lens is that **networks are the substrate of opportunity** and that in winner-take-most markets **speed under uncertainty beats efficiency**: raise *more* money than you need, ship a v1 that embarrasses you, hunt "a valuable market with bad competition," and back the bet that splits smart people into "you're out of your minds" and "I see it." He is also the most useful advisor in the set on the operating forks that follow a raise: when to pivot (and pivot *away*), how to hand off a CEO job (the "brain transplant"), what a board is for, whether to sell or IPO, how a pirate crew becomes a navy, and how to compete with a giant. Crucially he is *not* the reckless-speed caricature: blitzscaling is a costly, bounded *phase* you switch off, never applied where errors are irreversible or endanger life ("embarrassed" is not "indicted"), and he disowns "fail fast." On AI he is a "Bloomer": "superagency," iterative deployment, measurement-first regulation, and the view that society's non-participation is itself a risk. He opposes the bootstrap school (O'Reilly), activist short-termism (Icahn), AI doomers *and* pure accelerationists, the MBA as founder prep, ad-driven engagement models, and the founding-CEO purists (Horowitz); critics counter that blitzscaling socializes risk and rewards the deepest pocket (O'Reilly, Stoller, Kirkus, Berkey), that his AI optimism is "faith over proof," and that Project Birmingham exposed the governance gap his optimism glosses.
quotes: a valuable market with bad competition,
you're out of your minds
I see it.
faith over proof,

text:
Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn (2003), the professional network that became the canonical case study for his own theories, and sold it to Microsoft in 2016 for ~$26B; Satya Nadella made Jeff Weiner the day-one integration lead (MoS Hoffman Story). Trained as a philosopher (Stanford Symbolic Systems; Oxford MPhil, Marshall Scholar), he expected to become a public intellectual and professor and "more or less learned within the first three to six months that I didn't really want to be a philosophy professor" (How I Built This, machine transcript). He then learned product management at Apple's online service and at a Fujitsu software subsidiary, and founded his first company, SocialNet (1997 to about 1999), where VCs who "decided that they needed to be running the show versus the founders" removed him from the board; he found out when the financing paperwork arrived (How I Built This; MoS Hoffman Story: "finding out through the paperwork that I was no longer on the board of the company that I founded").
Peter Thiel, whom he met in a Stanford philosophy class, brought him to PayPal as COO in January 2000, where he was, by his own account, "very capable as a firefighter" ("one of the traits that I think defines me more as an adult"; How I Built This) and, in his own comparison, closer to Pulp Fiction's Winston Wolf, the cleaner, than to a good cop to Thiel's bad cop. After eBay bought PayPal (2002) he angel-invested in Facebook, Airbnb, Zynga, Aurora and many others, then built LinkedIn, handing the CEO job to Weiner in 2009. He has been a partner at Greylock since 2009, sits or sat on the boards of Microsoft, Airbnb, Aurora, Convoy and others (How I Built This; Superagency site), served five years on the OpenAI board (AI tag index), and co-founded Inflection AI (Pi). He is author or co-author of six business books and co-host of the *Masters of Scale* and *Possible* podcasts. In early 2025 he co-founded **Manas AI**, an AI-native oncology drug-discovery company, with physician-author Siddhartha Mukherjee (CNBC: a ~$24.6M seed co-led by General Catalyst and Hoffman). He frames business as questions about systems, incentives, and human nature, which is why he reaches for explicit, memetic frameworks far more than most operators, and why he argues a company strategy "should include an embedded theory of human nature" (The Philosopher Entrepreneur).
In April 2026 he started a Substack named after that habit, *Theory of the Game*, opening with "Faith in the Possible" and a series on Silicon Valley's "denominations." Asked by Dan Shipper where his sense of strategy came from, he credits childhood Dungeons & Dragons and Avalon Hill war games over chess and go, because "By having some randomness with dice rolls, it actually more closely approximated the kinds of circumstances we encounter in life. Because, life is not like chess" (Every, AGI episode).

text: **Networks are the substrate of opportunity.** Value, careers, and competitive advantage flow through relationships and network effects. LinkedIn and *The Start-Up of You* both rest on the premise that your career keeper is your network, not your employer; the New Yorker dubbed him "the Ubernode" (The Network Man, New Yorker). The concrete unit is the introduction: "Every introduction is a bet," and his reason for making many of them is network value, not favors: "The more of this kind of introduction I make, the more I build a network of this kind of people around me, and the more valuable the entire network becomes to each of its members" (Make good introductions). The operating rule is under Decision heuristics (double opt-in).
quotes: Every introduction is a bet,
The more of this kind of introduction I make, the more I build a network of this kind of people around me, and the more valuable the entire network becomes to each of its members
title: Networks are the substrate of opportunity

text: **Speed is a strategy, not a vice.** In winner-take-most markets the prize goes to whoever scales fastest, even at the cost of efficiency and certainty, the engine of *Blitzscaling* (w/ Chris Yeh): "prioritising speed over efficiency in an environment of uncertainty" (ELC). Its bounds are in Mental models.
quotes: prioritising speed over efficiency in an environment of uncertainty
title: Speed is a strategy, not a vice

text: **Contrarian-and-right is the only path to breakout returns.** Consensus deals are already priced and crowded; you want smart people split. "If I’m presenting an idea to my partners at Greylock and they all go: that’s great, we should do that! I’m like, shit. Here’s a bunch of hyper smart people and no one’s saying watch out for this, or watch out for that. It’s too easy!" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).

text: **Iterative deployment beats waiting for perfection**, true of products, careers, and AI. You learn by shipping and collecting feedback: "You don't get to an optimistic future by trying to avoid failure" (Diary of a CEO).

text: **Humans are entrepreneurs by default.** "All humans are entrepreneurs not because they should start companies but because the will to create and take control of our destiny is encoded in human DNA" (The Start-Up of You, Penguin sample chapter); run your career like a startup in permanent beta. In the same paragraph he undercuts the hustle cliche: "In fact, most people shouldn’t start companies. The odds of success are small, the emotional roller coaster constant" (Penguin sample chapter). The framing is borrowed from Muhammad Yunus, whose epigraph opens the chapter.

text: **Optimism is a tool, applied under discipline.** On AI he is a "Bloomer": overwhelmingly net-positive and insistent on braking. "Everyone, generally speaking, focuses way too much on what could go wrong, and insufficiently on what could go right" (Superagency, w/ Greg Beato; TechCrunch).

And: "Facing uncertainty with hope and confidence is the first step toward progress, because it’s only when you have hope that you see opportunities, potential first steps, a new path forward" (Impromptu intro, Greylock).

text: **Entrepreneurs are the heroes; investors are not.** The line is Greylock's house philosophy, which he quotes as the reason he joined: "One of the reasons I joined Greylock is that I shared the firm’s philosophy on investors and entrepreneurs." The quoted creed (Greylock's words, not his coinage) is "Companies succeed because of the entrepreneurs and executives, not the investors. They, not the VCs, are the heroes of the story," and he draws the board consequence himself: "Right now, our whole bet is on the CEO and the founders and making them successful" (Board Pt. 1). The corollary he took from LinkedIn's early days: "people wanted to be the hero of their own story, that that was a fundamental kind of human drive across almost everybody" (MoS Hoffman Story).

text: **Building is a faith, and the faith holds the argument.** His 2026 restatement of techno-optimism is explicitly religious: Silicon Valley's "central doctrine: no force in history has done more to improve human life than technology, and no institution is better positioned to build it for scale than the company." He grants critics the point that the Valley "has a God complex" and argues only about "which god," then names the real risk: "The risk is not that we build too boldly. The risk is that we stop believing building matters—that we trade the possible for the permissible, creation for consensus." His evidence is deployment outside the Valley (Alipay and WeChat skipping branch banking; Rwanda's blood-delivery drones; Argentina's precision agriculture), and "Those numbers are the scripture" (Faith in the Possible).

text: Cross-references Core ideas rather than restating them. Each carries at least one sourced worked example. Models are grouped: scaling and competition; pivots, organization and succession; boards, financing and exits; networks and careers; risk, ethics and AI.

[Scaling and competition] **Blitzscaling** (w/ Chris Yeh): prioritize speed over efficiency under uncertainty to win a winner-take-most market. The under-quoted half is that it is costly and bounded: "Blitzscaling means that you're willing to sacrifice efficiency for speed, but without waiting to achieve certainty on whether the sacrifice will pay off," and, on the ELC podcast, "Do you ever stop blitzscaling? And the answer is of course you do... Eventually, you want to be efficient." (ELC). The authors' own gloss: "You accept the risk of making the wrong decision and willingly pay the cost of significant operating inefficiencies in exchange for the ability to move faster" (CNN).
- *Learnable, not genius:* the authors' site presents it as practice, not talent: "Contrary to the popular narrative, it's not their superhuman founders or savvy venture capitalists. Rather, it's that they have learned how to blitzscale" (blitzscaling.com).
- *Forcing model:* the OODA loop. "Observe, Orient, Decide, Act. It's fighter pilot terminology. The faster OODA loop with a fighter pilot wins, the other one dies" (ELC); "It stands for observe, orient, decide, act. The fighter pilot who has the fastest OODA loop wins. The other one dies" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).
- *Worked example:* PayPal during the dot-com crash, accepting massive inefficiency to keep tempo. "You're standing on the roof of our building and throwing wads of hundred dollar bills over the edge of the building — we would be spending money less fast than we were spending money in fraud" (Startups.com). PayPal "was compounding at two to five percent per day in both users and transactions" (ELC), which is what made speed over efficiency rational. The near-death IPO: "It wasn't like we rolled in... It was like, 'OK, anyone got morphine?'" (Startups.com).
- *Worked example (changing the ruleset):* PayPal's customer service with about 35 people: angry-customer calls were routed to desk phones that rotated, and "we turned off all our desk phones" so the ringing phone became a demonstration of why speed mattered; the Omaha center then went to "250 reps live in six weeks" (ELC).
- *Counter-example he cites against himself:* "[WeWork] spent billions to become the biggest player in a market without true winner-take-most dynamics" (Is Blitzscaling Over?), blitzscaling misapplied where the network effects don't exist.

[Scaling and competition] **Throw out the rules, in ten domains** (w/ Yeh). "The only circumstance under which it makes sense is when, whether for offensive or defensive reasons, speed into the market is the critical success strategy" (Throw out the rules). The list covers finance, organization, culture, product, strategy, engineering, marketing, sales, and support: "Raise more money than you need." "Don't set your culture, evolve it." "Ask for forgiveness, not permission," bounded by "As long as the decision doesn't have “below the waterline” implications, have a bias towards action." "Invest in throwaway work." "Hire salespeople for now, even if they aren't scalable."

(Throw out the rules) and, in the ELC podcast, "ignore your current customer for your scale customer." Kirkus singles this rule out as the book's most obnoxious (Kirkus on Blitzscaling).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Blitzscaling is not free, and sometimes you decline it.** "Blitzscaling isn't a free option. It's costly in a variety of ways, from lower operational efficiency to higher capital expenditure and employee (and founder) burnout" (Blitzscaling Beyond Startups). The decision question is which risk is bigger: "if your competitor is blitzscaling and you're not, you're losing" (ELC).
- *Worked example (LinkedIn declined):* "we decided against this strategy; we felt that keeping our burn rate lower would allow us to wait for the market to catch up to our point of view." And: "If the market conditions aren't right for hypergrowth, premature Blitzscaling can kill a company" (Throw out the rules). Premature blitzscaling can also kill a market: "WebVan's notorious failure kept most players out of the grocery space for over a decade."
- *Worked example (compounder, not oil well):* on How I Built This he says most consumer internet products "hit the oil well" and go to the moon or never go, while "LinkedIn was one of those ones that compounded year after year." A slow-curve network can still be a blitzscaling-class outcome (How I Built This).

[Scaling and competition] **Speed is gated by reversibility and stakes.** The safety carve-out most people miss. On Theranos (ELC): "If you're gonna have... call it life impact on people, don't take those kinds of risks. Be more certain." And the decision heuristic: "What's the cost of being wrong? Is this reversible as a factor of how much should I push?" (ELC).
- *Worked example (externality that is reversible):* on Uber and Lyft congestion he says blitzscalers can live with it because congestion is reversible and the companies can build features to address it (he floats a cap on cars on the road) (CNN).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Two axes of ethical stringency: severity and scope.** "There's a big difference between being embarrassed and being indicted" (Theranos essay). Severity to the individual runs from a $1.99 app that fails to mortal risk; scope is how many people. Mortal risk at massive scale (Theranos) demands the highest standard, and "high-integrity entrepreneurs don't try to fool their audience when it comes to what is vision and what is reality" (Theranos essay).
- *Worked example:* Theranos kept a contractual Walgreens deadline while covering known problems. The alternative he describes is the do-things-that-don't-scale path: run tests on standard Siemens machines with a normal blood draw at Walgreens, truthful and still convenient, then move to the proprietary device once it worked (Theranos essay).
- *Limits restated:* "blitzscalers should never take risks that endanger their customers or pose a significant risk to the fabric of society," and no ethical or integrity risks such as the self-dealing reported under WeWork's founder (WeWork essay). "Blitzscaling founders and companies have a moral obligation to do so responsibly. You can pursue rapid growth without giving up your moral compass" (Theranos essay).

title: Two axes of ethical stringency: severity and scope

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Four growth factors, two growth limiters, and the Glengarry Glen Ross market.** Factors: market, distribution, high gross margins, network effects or other moats. Limiters: lack of product/market fit and operational scalability. "Product/Market fit doesn't guarantee long-term success, but a lack of Product/Market fit does guarantee long-term failure" (WeWork essay). A Glengarry market is winner-take-most: "First prize is a Cadillac, second prize is a set of steak knives, and third prize is, 'You're fired.'"
- *Worked example (WeWork scored):* market yes, distribution yes; gross margin fails (H1 2019 revenue $1.5B against expenses $2.9B, "gross margins of just 3%" on a generous reading, against Apple 38% and Alphabet 56%); network effects fail ("WeWork tenants can easily move"). Verdict: "blitzflailing." Subsidies "only make sense in blitzscaling if they are a temporary measure that allows you to achieve market leadership and establish a profitable and sustainable business on the other side of those subsidies." Fix direction: asset-light, as Marriott and Hilton manage branded hotels and Airbnb is "completely asset-less" (WeWork essay).
- *Why software can take bigger risks:* the ratio of risk capital required to potential economic value is low; Alphabet invented AdWords years after launch and Amazon built AWS a decade after its IPO (WeWork essay).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **First-scaler advantage** (sharper than "first-mover"). "It's important not to confuse critical mass with first-mover advantage; rather, it is a first-scaler advantage. Being first only helps if you're also able to achieve critical mass" (Throw out the rules). Growth is relative in a downturn: "What matters is that you win the race, not whether or not you set a new world record" (Is Blitzscaling Over?). Bear-market variant: "Speed is always a critical function in competition," but you sequence "defense first, then offense" (Bear Market Blitzscaling).
- *Worked example (Airbnb in Covid):* "On an absolute scale, Airbnb is in a much worse position ... But on a relative scale, Airbnb's competitive position is as strong as ever." Hotel RevPAR was down 78.4% and Airbnb cut about a quarter of staff with 14 weeks of severance, a waived equity cliff, laptops kept and 12 months of health cover, which he praises as the right way to do layoffs (Is Blitzscaling Over?). In the same essay: "Even Warren Buffett makes mistakes."

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Staged competitive playbook.** Speed as a weapon early; offense at Tribe ("raise more, hire more, scale more"); defense at Village with a self-red-team question, "If we were trying to compete with ourselves, what we would do?"; beyond Village, establish a standard or platform; then "Make financial strategy your competitive strategy," with acquisitions as the largest offensive and defensive plays (Competitive edge).
- *Worked example:* Virgin Atlantic entered a valuable market with weak competition and competed on the flying experience, not landing slots; Facebook bought Instagram and WhatsApp to defend mobile; Microsoft's desktop monopoly could not stop iOS and Android (Competitive edge). The ideal rival is locked into its model: "your ideal competitors are ones that are really locked into their business model, that are kind of traditional. It's very hard for them to change" (Blitzscaling | Competitive Strategy).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Taking on tech titans.** Ask whether the thing is in the giant's top-line priorities, not whether the giant could do it: "organizations, generally speaking, have the same number of top-line priorities, whatever their size are." "If you get so relevant that they’re paying attention, that’s a happy place." And: "Where is your contrarian thesis? That if you turn out to be right, you have something very interesting" (Taking on Tech Titans).
- *Worked example (LinkedIn's contrarian thesis):* competitors assumed a professional's address book belongs to the employer, a Salesforce-like corporate product; LinkedIn bet on individuals navigating their own lives. Counter-example: Clubhouse stayed too long in open growth without lock-in after incumbents copied social audio (Taking on Tech Titans).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Blitzscaling beyond startups.** Incumbents have scale (only if it is a 10X edge), iteration ("repeated shots on goal"), longevity, and M&A; they lack incentives, staged commitment, and public-market patience. "If you hear people talking about pursuing a 'land grab' strategy, but can't explain the source of lasting advantage, close your wallet." Three sources of lasting advantage: network effects, customer loyalty, and data/learning loops (Blitzscaling Beyond Startups).
- *Worked example:* "A classic big company mistake is to attack a new market at scale right from the beginning." Groupon fit consumers but not merchants; GM invested $500M in Lyft rather than blitzscale its own; Airbnb answered Rocket Internet's clone with ten European offices in under three months while Rocket had raised $90M and hired 400 (Blitzscaling Beyond Startups).

title: Blitzscaling beyond startups

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Distribution beats product.** "A good product with great distribution will almost always beat a great product with poor distribution" (Distribution Techniques). Two engines: leveraging an existing network as a "booster rocket," and virality (organic vs. incentivized).
- *Worked example:* PayPal automated inserting its "Pay with PayPal" button into eBay listings (unlike competitor Billpoint), and its $10/$10 double-sided referral drove "PayPal to grow 7 to 10 percent per day." Airbnb's one-click Craigslist cross-post carried the earnings-framed CTA "Reposting your listing from Airbnb to Craigslist increases your earnings by $500 a month on average." He also flags the tactic's fragility (Zynga on Facebook, Demand Media on Google): the booster rocket can be cut off (Distribution Techniques).
- *Worked example (speed as the tactic):* PayPal's payment notice reached sellers before eBay's own winning notification in "80, 90%" of cases, "Our whole trick to dominating that platform was to be faster than the eBay technology" (MoS Hoffman Story).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Do things that don't scale, to get to scale.** "In order to scale, you have to do things that don't scale," but his phrasing is his own: "Handcrafted work is essentially a kind of booster rocket that gets you out of the gravity well" (Tim Ferriss #326). The discipline is judging which feedback generalizes, and knowing scale itself breeds antibodies against handcraft.
- *Worked example (norm-setting, not just acquisition):* LinkedIn's publishing platform launched to only ~150 hand-picked leaders and stayed gated ~17 months before opening to 178M users, to set "norms and behaviors" first (Investing in Vices and Virtues).
- *Attribution:* the "do things that don't scale" advice to Chesky ("this is the only time you'll ever be small enough") is Paul Graham's; the cereal-box and "11-star / seven-star experience" stories are Brian Chesky's. Hoffman narrates them.

text:
[Scaling and competition] **Let fires burn.** Triage as a first-class scaling skill: "We're very careful to say let fires burn because part of the whole thing on scaling is you will let things burn" (Forbes/MoS). "Smart entrepreneurs don't try to fight every fire... so they can focus on the ones they absolutely have to fight."
- *Worked example (against interest):* "LinkedIn didn't have a failover database for its first six years," a deliberately un-fought fire (Why the Best Entrepreneurs Let Fires Burn).

text: [Scaling and competition] **Scale yourself: three ways.** "There are only three ways to scale yourself: delegation, amplification, and just plain making yourself better" (Scale yourself). The delegation trick is to picture the hire as a named person, not a role; the answer to "Will someone else be able to do this as well as I can?" is "No, especially not at first, but they'll probably figure it out over time, just like you did." Amplification means a chief of staff who can triage and brief (his: Ben Casnocha, then David Sanford). Learning means a personal board and feedback dinners (monthly with Brian Chesky). Attribution: "You've got to keep your personal learning curve ahead of the company's growth curve" is Drew Houston's; "I was too busy chopping wood to sharpen the axe" is Reed Hastings's.

text: [Scaling and competition] **Always Be Scaling, and hire for roles that never existed.** From Michael Dell's story (selling newspaper subscriptions from marriage-license lists, then hands-on customization on $1,000 of capital): "TO SCALE, FIRST DO THINGS THAT DON'T SCALE," "Success is a horrible teacher" and "Be pleased but never satisfied" (Dell's lines, quoted by Hoffman), and "Always Be Scaling" (Michael Dell post). From Sheryl Sandberg: open communication (her direct reports applauded when she offered to stop interviewing, because she was a bottleneck nobody had told her about), and hiring for roles that never existed, as Meg Whitman said: "No one has any experience, because no one’s ever done this before." Hoffman adds: "I’ve seen companies swap upwards of a third of their managers in 18 months" when swapping generalists for specialists (Sandberg post; Michael Dell post).

text:
[Scaling and competition] **A specific culture, evolved, not set.** "It is better to be loved by a few than liked by a multitude," and the test of specificity: "If your culture doesn't rule out 'A' players who aren't a good fit, it's not specific enough." PayPal's culture was "very individualistic ... 'structured panic'"; LinkedIn's "far more collaborative and patient ... take multiple shots on goal"; "People that fit the PayPal culture tended not to fit the LinkedIn culture, and vice versa" (Culture for Blitzscaling).
- *Hiring corollaries:* "At first, hire generalists over specialists"; "Hire for today, worry about tomorrow tomorrow" (and only two of LinkedIn's original ten employees remain). "Bad" cultures can produce good companies (Oracle, Zynga, Uber, PayPal), but the tradeoff must be made "consciously and explicitly," never at the cost of an inclusive culture (Culture for Blitzscaling). On management: "bad management is not criminal management," and on harassment and misconduct "we should not allow any of this shit to go on and you should immediately end it" (ELC).

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **Invention vs. reinvention, and the pivot as Plan B.** "Actually, startups, like all businesses, work because of a cycle of invention and reinvention." Using Mark Pincus's definition, invention adds to the business; reinvention transforms a major element and combines addition with subtraction, and invention alone ends in a "Frankenstein’s monster of mis-matched elements." A pivot is "a Plan B, not a Plan Z" in his ABZ vocabulary: "anything that leads to a rational and significant reduction of belief in your investment thesis can justify a pivot" (Startup Pivot).
- *Test:* is your confidence in the explicit, written investment thesis going up or down? If it was never stated crisply you cannot tell when to lose confidence (Startup Pivot, paraphrased).
- *Hard parts:* "Having the willpower to discard lessons that were true and valuable before, but now have to change, is one of the keys to successful reinvention," because success imprints more strongly than failure. Say explicitly what is being thrown out. "Hard does not equal valuable" and "Value is what someone else will pay" (Startup Pivot).

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **PayPal's five pivots, as a worked example.** FieldLink (Max Levchin's low-compute mobile encryption) became cash on mobile, then cash on Palm Pilot, then Palm plus email sync, then email payments for eBay sellers, then the master-merchant model. Hoffman's restaurant-tab thought experiment (at most one table per Palo Alto restaurant would have a Palm Pilot) killed the Palm use case; Max proposed email sync; he later questioned Peter Thiel's call to drop Palm ("Shouldn’t we try to sell it or something?") and Peter was right (Startup Pivot).
- *The last pivot:* growth was 2 to 5 percent per day with no business model and a public "always free" commitment. At an off-site at his grandparents' house in Gualala, Thiel, Levchin, Luke Nosek and Hoffman decided to keep individuals free but cap credit-card acceptance and force merchants to pay; six weeks after launch 88% of payments flowed through the new system with no dent in the growth curve. "All of these pivots were absolutely essential. All of them could have killed the company." Pivoting plus blitzscaling means you "execute at warp speed even though you don’t know for certain if the pivot is going to work" (Startup Pivot).

title: PayPal's five pivots, as a worked example

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **Pivot away, not only toward.** "Not only do you need to pivot towards your new business, you also need to pivot away from your old business," and "Unless you find a way to provide clear decisions and graceful closure for your team and customers, you'll be torn between old and new" (Butterfield post). Peter Thiel's version, as relayed: "You play on where your growth market lies. We’re not going to get enough money for the technology to outweigh the distraction. Just close it down" (Startup Pivot); Gates erased engineers' hard drives on Blackbird so they would move to the internet code base.
- *Worked example:* Stewart Butterfield's Slack followed 15 consecutive failed pivots over 18 money-losing months, ending in a tearful meeting and layoffs of nearly the whole team; he threw a final party for staff and the game's fans and found laid-off employees new jobs (Butterfield post). Slack's second life came out of Glitch's internal messaging tool, and Slack later sold to Salesforce for $27 billion in 2020 (False Choices).

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **The sideways path.** "A scalable idea rarely sits squarely on the path ahead. It’s always scurrying off to the left or the right" (Diane Greene post). VMware's first customers were college science professors, then bankrupt dot-bombs saving on hardware, then Linux developers needing email; Greene was a national champion sailor and tacked. The question he leaves: what scalable idea came sideways, and which did you miss "because you were too determined to keep forging straight ahead?"
quotes: A scalable idea rarely sits squarely on the path ahead. It’s always scurrying off to the left or the right

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **Pirate to Navy.** "Navies can establish nations, whereas pirate fleets eventually collapse." Early startups behave like pirates (no formal process, willing to break rules, decisive because "the default outcome is failure"); as they pass his headcount stages (Family 1 to 9, Tribe 10 to 99, Village 100 to 999, City 1,000 to 9,999, Nation 10,000+) they must become a navy: "You can't run a successful navy if what you really have is a set of pirate ships pretending to work together." Two tests: ethical pirate vs criminal pirate ("Am I a creator who is trying to improve the state of the world for everyone, or am I a thief who is just trying to grab things for myself?") and fleet design (country managers with real control plus a unified executive team) (Pirate to Navy).
- *Worked example (Uber, 2017):* Uber had the first two parts of the fleet (GMs like ship captains; surge pricing began as a Boston market experiment) but lacked a cohesive management team; eight VPs or department heads left in the first half of 2017. Counter-examples: Facebook moved from "move fast and break things" to "move fast with stable infrastructure," and Larry Page's flat Google engineering org (about 400 engineers under one manager) failed until Eric Schmidt built structure. Heuristic: "steer into" getting big and iterate structure repeatedly instead of one "someday" leap; "Any given management structure is likely to be temporary" (Pirate to Navy).
- *Caveat:* the essay was a prescription written while Uber was in crisis, and treats the structural failure as separable from the ethical one.

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **CEO succession: four conditions, brain-transplant mechanics.** "Bringing in a CEO is like performing a brain transplant—you need to wire in a whole new set of connections." Four conditions in founder/outside-CEO pairings that work: the step back is self-realization, not investor-imposed ("The decision to step back from being CEO is a function of self-realization"); the outsider comes early enough to shape product, business and culture (turnarounds like Gerstner at IBM excepted); the founding group is small (two to three); and the new CEO has run a large organization (Professional CEO essay). Pairings he cites: Yahoo (Koogle), Google (Schmidt), eBay (Whitman), Facebook (Sandberg), Twitter (Costolo).
- *Worked example (LinkedIn):* by 2005 he knew he disliked running the weekly staff meeting; Greylock's David Sze asked "Couldn’t we just hire a COO and have you stay as CEO?" and he refused because the right person "owned the ball." Search took more than a year; Dan Nye became CEO at the start of 2007, built sales and doubled the company, but Hoffman had handed him everything except product. "My mistake was thinking you could divorce product strategy from the CEO role." Weiner, introduced by Greylock's James Slavet, was named CEO mid-2009 (Professional CEO essay).
- *Mechanics:* bring the new CEO in "as a co-founder of the company, not as an “adult supervisor.”" Rewire decision flow by being absent: he travelled heavily so staff stopped double-checking ("Sorry, I’m in Rome, talk to Jeff"). The essay says six months of travel; later retellings say the first six to eight weeks, and asking callers "Is it solved or not?" (more than half the time they had already solved it with Jeff) (Professional CEO essay; MoS Hoffman Story; Bezos succession). As Executive Chairman he took the office next to the CEO and held a weekly candid-feedback meeting; "the CEO is the CEO, and makes the final decisions" (Bezos succession).

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **Founder-CEO is a state of mind.** Against Ben Horowitz's "Why We Prefer Founding CEOs" (he calls the evidence "one-sided and overwhelming"), Hoffman answers that "it’s hard to call the evidence “one-sided and overwhelming” when there are so many strong counterexamples," and cites Noam Wasserman: "the more decision-making control kept (at both the CEO and board levels), the lower the value of the entrepreneur’s equity stake," and fewer than half of founder-CEOs are still CEO after three years. He concedes the point only by redefining it: "So as it turns out, Ben was right. You always do want a Founder-CEO. But that person doesn’t always have to be the Founding CEO," because "“Founder” is a state of mind, not a job description" (Professional CEO essay; LinkedIn original, Jan 2013). The reaction he collected in his own round-up shows the unusual part of his case: TechCrunch's MG Siegler noted that founder-CEO replacements usually "happen when things are going badly," whereas at LinkedIn "it was Hoffman himself who decided he wanted to bring in a CEO to replace him. He benched himself!" (Round-up post).

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **The CEO tour of duty and looking externally.** "if a CEO isn’t committing to at least 10 years, that organization is likely unstable and in trouble." Ask which function (sales, product, engineering, finance, ops) is now the primary driver of success; the default is the original one. And look outside even when choosing inside: "I think it’s almost never the right thing to look only internally (no matter how amazing those internal candidates) because looking externally is a useful forcing function to make the company explicitly define the role of the CEO." "Ultimately, if a company only looks inward, it will become like Rome and decay" (Bezos succession). The caveat he states himself: "I have no inside information on Jeff’s decision."

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **Hero casting and the alliance of missions.** "People have this drive to be the hero of their own story. And so, when you are composing a team, but at most especially when you’re composing executives or CEOs, they also have to have the ability to play that hero narrative," and "CEO transitions are super difficult because they are brain transplants" (MoS Hoffman Story). Part of the difference between a CEO and a co-founder: a co-founder is "trying to build an institution for the ages."
- *Worked example (LinkedIn into Microsoft):* the test of the 2016 deal was whether it works for shareholders, employees and customers and whether the missions already fit: "The Microsoft mission fits very well with the LinkedIn mission." Putting the acquired CEO in charge of integration on day one is "just another tool in the tool chest that is occasionally used," not a norm (MoS Hoffman Story).

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **The Alliance / tour of duty** (w/ Casnocha & Yeh): reframe employment as a mutual, finite, renewable alliance: rotational, transformational, foundational tours. The HBR version opens: "For most of the 20th century, the compact between employers and employees in the developed world was all about stability" (HBR Tours of Duty). "Stop thinking of employees as family or free agents, and start thinking of them as allies on a tour of duty," and "The paradox is that recognizing an employee’s independence is what allows a company to rebuild the loyalty and trust that’s been missing from today’s employment relationship" (Alliance site). Recruiting is better with a concrete tour: "offering a clear tour of duty with specific benefits and success outcomes beats vague promises like “you’ll get valuable experience.”"
- *Extended into the AI era:* "AI wins by doing more, not spending less... Those who frame AI purely as a cost-cutting exercise will miss the alliance-building moments" (Moral Promises). The alliance outlasts the job: "[The] employee who leaves to start a company isn't exiting the relationship; they're changing its shape."
- *Worked example:* his own LinkedIn CEO handoff to Jeff Weiner. He knew he wanted the "150-to-500 people" job less than the large-scale one, and recruited a "later-stage co-founder," a missionary not a "hired gun" (Tim Ferriss #101; Diary of a CEO). His public view: "Some people should work with this company forever, and some people should work in this company for some time – and then go off and do other things" (MoS Hoffman Story).

text:
[Pivots, organization and succession] **Team, not family.** "In a real family, parents can’t fire their children," so a CEO who calls the company a family and then lays off hurts people "with real justification"; "a business is far more like a sports team than a family." Winning franchises stay consistent despite turnover by combining "a realistic view of the often-temporary nature of the employment relationship with a focus on shared goals and long-term personal relationships" (HBR Not a Family).
- *Worked example:* only Tom Brady remained from the Patriots' first title team, only David Ortiz from the 2004 Red Sox, only Tim Duncan from the 1999 Spurs; five of the other 29 NBA teams have a former Spurs assistant as head coach, and the Spurs' alumni still dine with the team. Alumni networks as a recruiting asset ("Do you think that current players, seeing that kind of loyalty, might want to play for the Spurs?"). The authors concede the limit: "It’s doubtful, for example, that you obtain the bulk of your employees by taking turns with your competitors as part of an organized talent draft" (HBR Not a Family).

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **Culture is hiring plus process design** (Hastings's Pure Software lesson, as narrated). "Pure Software couldn’t adapt because they had the wrong employees. And they had the wrong employees because of management decisions that explicitly selected for those employees." Processes meant to prevent error attracted people who value following process; when the market moved from C++ to Java, they could not adapt (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript). His own framing of the episode: "As CEO of Pure Software, Reed had built an organization he didn't want to work for," and the guests he paired with Hastings (Aneel Bhusri, Jeff Weiner) argue the CEO's job is teaching managers to turn down "perfect" candidates who do not share the culture (First Principles from Netflix, paraphrased except the quoted words).
quotes: Pure Software couldn’t adapt because they had the wrong employees. And they had the wrong employees because of management decisions that explicitly selected for those employees.
As CEO of Pure Software, Reed had built an organization he didn't want to work for,
title: Culture is hiring plus process design

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **Board as one of the tools of a pivot.** Do not make a pivot a committee decision: enlist the one or two key VCs as partners first, and they persuade the rest; a general board debate yields "reflexive risk-avoidance and not enough intelligent risk-taking." For a risky strategy he adds: "add someone who's the catalyst to the board. Have that be an explicit conversation with them about, 'Look, I think this needs to be going this way, do you buy in?'" and invest in board education (Startup Pivot; Nadella, LinkedIn version).
quotes: reflexive risk-avoidance and not enough intelligent risk-taking.
add someone who's the catalyst to the board. Have that be an explicit conversation with them about, 'Look, I think this needs to be going this way, do you buy in?'
title: Board as one of the tools of a pivot

text: [Pivots, organization and succession] **Team buy-in in a pivot.** Easy while team and mission stay the same; generalists adapt, specialists resist pivots away from their specialty, and an employee who joined to build a videogame may not want enterprise software, so both sides are better off parting. "Startups need coherence" (Startup Pivot, paraphrased).
quotes: Startups need coherence
title: Team buy-in in a pivot

text:
[Boards, financing and exits] **Board as passenger-seat co-navigator.** Not the driver, not the backseat driver, not the passive "yes-person" VC, but front seat "helping you navigate," including asking the hard questions. "You’ll know you’ve been a good board member based on the extent to which you helped the founders and CEO succeed." "It’s not enough to just think, I’m smart and helpful" (Board Pt. 1).
- *Worked example:* an early LinkedIn director insisted with "great vigor and certainty" that the business would be advertising and never came back to admit LinkedIn is a SaaS and subscriptions business. The healthy form: "I’ve got a question about your strategy. Let’s discuss it so that I can understand your assumptions, data, and conclusions." "We VCs are pattern matchers" is, to him, a warning sign (Board Pt. 1).

[Boards, financing and exits] **VC Hippocratic oath: first, do no harm.** For seed or Series A, replacing the CEO is almost never an option: "If you get to the point where you’re thinking of firing a CEO, you’re probably dead whatever you do," and you have "almost certainly made a bad investment." Later it flips: "If you say, “I’ll never replace a CEO,” you’re not fulfilling your fiduciary responsibility." He also rejects "I never invest in an entrepreneur that can’t be the CEO through the entire journey": "How can you know, when the entire company fits into a single compact car, that the CEO will be able to command a 10,000-person publicly-traded company? You can’t" (Board Pt. 1).
- *Origin:* at SocialNet, "experienced" board members decided he was a failure after his first go-to-market failed and ordered television advertising for an online product. His lesson was "not tracking learning curves, and thinking that they could run the company from the board" (Board Pt. 1). He also reports that hiring a CEO "usually has–at best–a .500 batting average for improving the company."

text: [Boards, financing and exits] **Board needs by stage.** Family: angel or part-time exec, more than one or two hours a week. Tribe: help place "the right concentrated bets" (asset value is near zero, so play for upside). Village: the blitzscale-or-not decision, which may mean pushing "those hard-won chips to the center of the table." City: balance reinvesting against protecting existing assets; executive recruiting dominates. Nation: public boards skew to risk management "to the exclusion of pursuing new opportunities," which is why he co-founded Reinvent Technology Partners with Mark Pincus. Director tours of duty: not under three years, with exceptions not over ten; "Hire Ms. Right Now, Not Ms. Right" (Board Pt. 1). "You don’t send a Marine to do a police officer’s job."

text: [Boards, financing and exits] **Use the board to fill gaps, not to collect names.** "Rather than treating your board as a collection of names, use it as a way to fill the critical gaps you don't have other ways to fill," and "Far too many board members are selected for their brand value." He wants skills, knowledge, and a network "mission-critical to the company, but that you cannot easily hire," such as Nancy Lublin for Change.org (too committed to her own mission to hire, available as a director) or Karen Francis for Nauto over an "industry titan" (Board post 2017). PayPal's early board: Thiel brought in friends with the most startup experience, Scott Banister and Hoffman, as independent directors before taking a VC (Board post 2017; Board Pt. 1). On directing: "The art is developing these relationships without undermining the CEO."

My employees most centrally among them, but of course also shareholders and society and all the rest." He located the failure in board competence, not structure: "there isn’t anything that you can do to particularly change the structure of boards of directors to avoid errors like the OpenAI one. It’s kind of one of the places where expertise matters" (Possible S2 wrap). Disclosure: he was an OpenAI board member and sits on Microsoft's board.

text:
[Boards, financing and exits] **Seven pitch myths, from his own Series B deck.** "Put another way, the ideal financing partner is a financing cofounder." "Open your pitch with the investment thesis." "Decide whether your pitch is a data pitch or a concept pitch." "Identify and steer into your risk factors." "Pitch by analogy," but "don’t necessarily reason by analogy." "Think also about the round after the one you’re currently raising." And on competition: "if you claim that you don’t have competition, you either believe the market is completely inefficient or no one else thinks your space is valuable" (Pitching LinkedIn).
- *Worked example:* LinkedIn's IPO was a data pitch (a multi-year track record); a concept pitch depends on "promised future data." If you cannot name one to three risks and mitigations you look dishonest or dumb. The first 60 seconds should be three to eight bullets of what an investor must believe. "Jaws with Paws" was a Hollywood pitch for a movie that "turned out to be terrible, but the pitch was excellent" (Pitching LinkedIn).

text:
[Boards, financing and exits] **Companies are bought, not sold; build strategic value first.** "The big problem with building to sell is that companies are bought, not sold," and "when you offer to sell your company, you are signaling that you as a knowledgeable insider are fundamentally worried about your company’s ability to succeed." "When you build massive strategic value, you can generally build massive economic value at some point." And: "going public is not the ultimate goal; it’s a means to achieving your goals" (M&A or IPO).
- *Worked example (PayPal's exit):* Thiel sent Hoffman to sell for $600M; VeriSign offered $550M (declined); eBay would pay only $850M against a $1B target (declined, IPO); eBay later paid $1.5B. He defends the eventual sale: eBay had been discouraging PayPal use even though PayPal handled about a quarter of eBay's transactions, and after the deal the headwind became a tailwind. He also treated LinkedIn's IPO as "essentially a marketing strategy" because users and recruiters read the business press. WeWork's S-1 is the canonical failure of storytelling (M&A or IPO).
- *Founder test:* "When a founder tells me, “There’s no chance we’ll sell; I’m not going to think about anything other than going public,” I think, “Wow, you’re either lying to yourself or lying to me because nothing in life is that certain.”"

[Boards, financing and exits] **Pitch rejection by quality, not quantity.** "You have to pay attention to the quality, not the quantity of rejections." "You want to see at least a teeny minority of investors squirm. You don’t have to get them to a yes, but you should detect some friction as they reason their way to a no" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).
- *Worked example:* Kathryn Minshew (The Muse) pitched 148 times, and the objections ("fool's errand," "doesn't scale") revealed the investor's blind spot; Tristan Walker (Bevel) found the exact slide (14) where an investor lacked context and moved on, preferring "a hard no to a comforting maybe" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).

text:
[Boards, financing and exits] **Raise more than you need, for two reasons.** His one-line thesis: "Entrepreneurs should always raise more money than they need, so they can plan for the unforeseeable," which covers "anything from a stock market crash or outlandish expenses to an opportunity you couldn’t predict in a market that didn’t exist when you started out" (Raise more money post, 2017). "Opportunities may arise later than you hope, and you want the capital to carry you in new directions," and "you should always take the money whenever and wherever you can get it. you never know when it will dry up" (transcript typo preserved; Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript). The capital "increases your optionality" and a major raise has signalling effects (Throw out the rules). "Entrepreneurs try to avoid raising more capital than they need" is the default he opposes (Throw out the rules).
- *Worked example:* Minted raised $2.5M for a branded stationery store that did not sell for a month; about $100K on a side crowd-sourced design competition became the real business, and the round closed about two weeks before Lehman failed. Mariam Naficy bought Eve.com from a five-year-old for roughly $50,000 plus Disneyland trips, the unexpected-opportunity case (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript). Ferriss's counterpoint: top angels often prefer a prototype and traction before raising.
- *The direct exchange with Tim O'Reilly:* "In these markets, time really is your enemy, not your ally." "Tim's preferred strategy of focusing on sustainable cash flow and growing at the rate that customers are willing to fund with their purchases is generally a good approach, but it isn't universal, especially when it comes to technology companies." The bootstrapped giants O'Reilly cites (Microsoft in Albuquerque, Bloomberg, ESRI, Epic, SAS, Dell) were all outside Silicon Valley: "None of them were started in Silicon Valley," and "all had the space to grow without blitzscaling competitors" (Blitzcapital). His decision checklist: actual or potential competition, capital you and rivals have, whether you need critical mass for a network product, and whether you can first prove product-market fit at limited risk. Rocket Internet's $100M attempt to beat Airbnb to Europe made "raise money and grow faster" Chesky's right play.

text: [Boards, financing and exits] **Venture capital is the least bad option.** "venture capital is the worst method for financing scaling startups except for all the others." The alternatives are government allocation (Solyndra: political risk added to financial risk) or wealthy families ("You're begging the 15 families who have the capital," Wences Casares). VC as "financial co-founder": Gates sold 5 percent for $1M to get Dave Marquardt on the board and never spent the money (Professional VC post).

text: [Boards, financing and exits] **Short-term profit-taking vs. long-term value.** Against Carl Icahn's 2014 push to spin PayPal off eBay: "Innovation comes from long-term thinking and iterative execution," and "In the end, Icahn’s stock in trade is trading stocks." and "Silicon Valley’s stock in trade is creating powerful products and platforms." His case was convergence (Amazon, Google, Apple, Square-with-Starbucks all converging on commerce plus payments) and that 30 percent of PayPal's $180B annual transactions and new users came from eBay; he disclosed he had no inside information on their vision (PayPal/Icahn post). Editor note, not from the source: PayPal was in fact separated from eBay in 2015, so the essay is a record of his stance, not a successful forecast.

[Networks, identity and careers] **Network literacy in three levels.** Apprentice (using network technology), Journeyman (establishing a network identity), Master (utilizing network intelligence). "When I walk through an office, I see networks." "make it a priority to turn connections into relationships, and relationships into alliances." Job hunting by searching listings is "the Information Age approach!" (Network Literate).
- *Worked example:* his LinkedIn headline reads "Entrepreneur. Product Strategist. Investor." because the profile targets entrepreneurs who might want financing; at Greylock he does not form a thesis and search for startups but sits "at as many key intersections in my networks as I can"; before meeting Weiner he had a "network portrait" through mutual trusted colleagues (Network Literate).

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Network intelligence in a decision.** LinkedIn pivoted to corporate subscriptions after early customer feedback, and Hoffman, who had never built a corporate product, called David Sze, who routed him to Workday CEO Aneel Bhusri and then Mike Stankey. Treat the network as a sensor network and do better reference checks (Don't Make Decisions Alone). The decision frame there: "Don’t Make Decisions Alone."

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Allies, Friendlies, Followers.** Allies: at most eight to ten strong professional alliances that you consult regularly and share first drafts with. Friendlies: weak ties with different information. Followers: attention as career capital. Strengthen ties with small, thoughtful gifts (information, articles, introductions): "An expensive gift can feel like a bribe" (Allies).

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Growth loops for careers.** "It’s a feature of a business that yields compounding value—value that multiplies over time—rather than one-off gains." LinkedIn's address-book upload raised connection density; a career loop is a relationship with a super connector, an asset that builds your brand, and an expanded network (Growth Loops).
quotes: It’s a feature of a business that yields compounding value—value that multiplies over time—rather than one-off gains.

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Why ten-year plans fail.** On Covey and Bolles: "Don’t listen to this advice. It’s not that it’s bad, per se. It’s just incomplete. And impractical." Three reasons: a static-world assumption (whitewater rafting, not a pedal boat); self-knowledge cannot be had by introspection; and a calling does not mean someone will pay. The replacement is competitive advantage plus ABZ planning (10 Year Plans).

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Pick an industry, not a job.** "A strong market can overcome almost any deficiency in a startup, at least for a time." "Pick an industry, not a job." A hallmark of an uncrested wave is that the original inventors are still alive (Zuckerberg and social; Eastman and print photography) (Make the Market Work).

On How I Built This: "these are false dichotomy questions, because the answer is massively both," about luck and work: "And so the answer is just massive quantities of both luck and work."

text: [Networks, identity and careers] **Identity: the 6 Ws.** "Identity comes from choice; choice comes from identity." Who you stand with, what you stand for, how you manifest it, where, why, and when you will take on risk: "Your identity is your vector." Network identity: a group identity is the same for every member; a network is different for each, and "You are whom you choose to befriend." He disagrees with Paul Graham's keep-your-identity-small: "I agree that challenging someone’s identity can trigger defensiveness, but the answer isn’t to pretend that identity doesn’t exist," and the difference is "being principled and self-righteous" (Shape Your Identity). Worked example: Steve Jobs was inflexible on design and user experience but chose those things "thoughtfully and with a purpose."

[Networks, identity and careers] **ABZ planning + permanent beta** (w/ Casnocha): hold Plan A (your written investment thesis), Plan B (the adjacent pivot inside the same thesis), and Plan Z (the lifeboat you invoke while you still have resources, once you no longer believe the thesis). "If Plan A isn't working, it's time to break glass... and switch to Plan B." Treat yourself as a perpetual work-in-progress: "you must think of yourself as a work-in-progress and, therefore, you must invest in yourself every single day" (ABZ Planning; The Start-Up of You). The Start-Up of You site: "We are all works in progress" and "Permanent beta is a lifelong commitment to continuous personal growth."

Evidence: an associate's degree at Foothill College (~$2,790) counts for nothing with employers requiring four-year degrees while Stanford tuition exceeds $160,000 (Disrupting the Diploma). Examples are Greylock companies (Shopkick, Wrapp, Swipely, Cardspring) plus online-to-offline (OpenTable, ZocDoc, Uber) and e-commerce going physical (Warby Parker showrooms) (Physical retail post).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **First-principles tests for a bet: contrarian-and-right / polarized reaction.** A great bet should split smart people: "What you want is some people going, “You guys are out of your minds,” and some people going, “I see it.” You want a polarized reaction." "The first truth of entrepreneurship and investing is that the very big ideas are contrarian because the contrarian is part of the reason why a bunch of large companies and competitors haven’t already done it" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript). "The best ideas make you want to say yes and no in the same breath."
- *Worked example:* the Airbnb Series A. His first reaction ("That doesn't sound interesting at all") flipped when he re-derived it himself ("I really know networks and marketplaces"), and he offered inside the meeting: "Look, I'm going to make you an offer to invest. Let's make the rest of the session a working session" (Airbnb Reflections).
- *The dissent:* his partner David Sze warned him ("Every venture capitalist has to have a deal that they can fail on. Airbnb can be yours"); Greylock led anyway. Hoffman's own words on Sze's disagreement: "If someone as smart as David disagrees with me, I worry. But I also get excited. It’s an emotional roller coaster" (Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).
- *Self-diagnosed lesson (subtler than "renting couches sounds dumb"):* "I should have realized that the first person who pitched me on Airbnb wasn't a great consumer internet investor... he might not describe the opportunity accurately." Discount the messenger, re-derive the idea yourself (Airbnb Reflections).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Choosing bad competition** vs. **escape competition.** "The great strategy is not to try to find a competition-free market. Rather, you should seek a valuable market with bad competition" because "no competition" usually signals a worthless market. Three types (lazy / overlooked / stuck-in-stasis), unified by "a fundamental inability to recognize change": "Success imprints more strongly than failure. That's how otherwise smart people end up with big blind spots and become bad competition" (Choosing Bad Competition; LinkedIn vs. Monster/CareerBuilder; Tesla vs. the Big Three).
- *The Thiel counterpoint:* he also endorses Thiel's "Competition is for losers" ("invent a new game, and then master it"), saying the same formula persuaded them to invest in Facebook despite a lackluster pitch (Thiel post). He reconciles them: avoid head-on competition, but "more likely, weak competition" rather than none, and "You don't have to make it easy for challengers to copy your playbook, but you have every right to fiercely compete and win" (Competitive edge). Use bad-competition logic when picking a market; use the escape-the-game logic when the incumbents are strong.
- *Also:* "this distaste for monopolies shouldn't lead us to conclude that dominant competitors need to be penalized" (Competitive edge).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **The five kinds of "No"** (Masters of Scale): classify a rejection by its reasoning, not its count. Lazy no (zero information; "leaving these lazy 'No's in the dust"); *squirmy* no (they want to say yes and no, the strongest buy signal); *affirmative* no (an expert's conventional-wisdom no plus your contrary data equals "being contrarian and right"); *honest* no (the expert is right; kill it); *unhelpful* no (discouragement from people you love: "An idea is at its most vulnerable in its infancy"). "My theory is that many a great entrepreneur’s journey begins with hearing “No.”" (Bad-idea post).
- *Worked example:* LinkedIn's "squirmy no," in which every segment said "It's not for us — but here's who it could be for," which drove the decision to open the network rather than stay invite-only. (The Tribe "honest no" is Mark Pincus's; the Spanx "unhelpful no" is Sara Blakely's, not Hoffman's own companies.)
- *Worked example (the open-network call):* LinkedIn debated referral-only signup and opened it to reach the fastest path to people who believe in the network and invite others, with a media-heavy early strategy; and a "Who else is here?" onboarding loop showed new users people they already knew, which created reactivation touchpoints (MoS Hoffman Story, paraphrased).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Investing in vices and virtues.** "Social networks do best when they tap into one of the Seven Deadly Sins. Facebook is [pride]. Zynga is sloth. LinkedIn is greed." text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Calculating risk: the Decision Window + the Three S's.** "Reducing risks to zero is both impossible and counterproductive." First ask what you'd decide if forced to right now, then use the remaining window to gather intelligence; "The default decision window for startups and entrepreneurs is 'right away.'" For severe risk, weigh Severity, Scope, Systematicity; all three fire at once for autonomous vehicles (Aurora), so a founder must personally own it (Calculating Risk).
- *Elaboration (provisional decisions):* after the provisional decision ask "what specifically is what I want to know? Who's specifically who I want to talk to?" and "what are the macro things that would cause me to change this decision," and weigh the cost in time and decisiveness (ELC). Ben Casnocha's account of the method: note what additional information would disprove the provisional decision and fetch only that; he tolerated "an error rate of 10 to 20 percent" from his chief of staff (Casnocha quoted in the Tim Ferriss 10 Commandments transcript).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **How to decide: sprint across the minefield.** "I describe entrepreneurial-decision making as confronting a rocky minefield (at night, inside a dense fog bank…) and deciding to sprint across." Better means faster as well as more accurate; "That instinct is almost 100% wrong for entrepreneurial decision-making," meaning the instinct to slow down and collect all information. Compounding: "after 1,000 such good decisions, that same function will have increased 147X." When evaluating repeat founders, look at their decision-making; if they have not improved it, "it’s probably not worth paying the experience premium." Own every decision, and use RACI and DACI matrices to speed them (How to Decide). SocialNet taught him he decided too slowly, badly, or both.

Philosophy's gift to a founder is "predictive anthropology," reasoning about how humans will behave with a product, and "an ability to state theses with precision" (Philosopher Versus MBA; The Philosopher Entrepreneur). At Bologna: "I’ve always believed that any new venture must have a strong theory of human nature underlying it" (Bologna speech).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Value-sculpted technology.** Neither value-neutral nor value-laden: "So, is technology value-neutral or value laden? Neither. The truth is it’s value-sculpted." "We shape it—not like clay, but like marble. It takes muscle, intention, and repetition" (LSE lecture). The sequencing rule: begin value-neutral (scientific rigor, factual verification, iterative deployment) in early development; once AI is integrated into society, ask the value-laden question of how it can be shaped to prioritize human well-being. Healthcare AI should aim not only to diagnose more accurately but to ensure equitable access (LSE lecture, paraphrased). "However, inevitability does not imply passivity."

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Small risks to navigate big risks (Minsky).** "stopping or pausing to avoid risk is a risk—and most often a more perilous one than embracing risk in the first place." "This allows us to take smaller risks with AI to better navigate any big risks." "Taking smaller risks more often is less of a risk—and allows for iteration, discussion, and continual improvement" (LSE lecture; Perugia speech). Hyman Minsky's "stability creates instability": "Too many safeguards in a financial system can actually make it more brittle." He applies it to AI regulation: over-safeguarding risks a Minsky Moment, so prefer frequent small releases to diverse users. "To maintain stability in a turn, you’ve got to accelerate through it" (Perugia speech).
- *Worked example (driving):* he raced a Dallara in Italy: brake before a turn, never in one; the cost of delay is concrete, a "personalized, digital doctor or tutor in everyone’s pocket" not arriving sooner (Perugia speech).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Iterative deployment as consent of the governed, and a golden braid of accountability.** "Iterative deployment—or companies releasing AI models to the public at a frequent cadence—has already resulted in more governance and de facto regulation than a pause or more top-down regulatory efforts" (Perugia speech). "It will take a network of human accountability to stay on course: a golden braid, if you will, that intertwines government, the private sector, the press, academia, the public—all of us." In the LSE lecture he ties it to Jefferson: citizens must play "an active and substantive role" in legitimizing AI (paraphrase), so AI works "with you and for you, rather than on you" (paraphrase). Applied to a launch: ChatGPT was the fourth major GPT model, released imperfect to a public who "could have" waited for a cadre of experts (paraphrase).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Hegelian synthesis, not dichotomy.** Roman Cato ended speeches "Carthage must be destroyed" and Corculum answered "Carthage must be saved"; Hoffman maps these to AI should be limited versus accelerated. "The challenge with dichotomies like this is we start to lose the subject at the center of the debate: Us. Humans. Humanity." "It’s not human vs. AI. It’s human with AI." "The synthesis is not a cyborg, but a better human" (Perugia speech). "Only delusional people want a dystopia." The six Latin maxims include cathedral projects ("Cathedral projects bring an ennoblement to our efforts") and the obligation to make the future better than the now (paraphrase), with Savery-Newcomen-Watt and Davy-Swan-Edison as multi-generation chains.

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Order of operations for a new technology.** Do not start with spacefaring cars (utopia) or traffic jams (dystopia): first invent the car, then modify it, only then solve congestion. "That’s why the answer is not to slow down technology, but to accelerate it." "Technology is a tool. And the faster we have it in our hands, the better we can solve the problems we have—and the problems it might create." "For AI should not be an abbreviation for artificial intelligence, but for amplification intelligence" (Bologna speech). His builder's questions from that speech (paraphrased): how to increase beauty, make better tools for fellow humans, and make work that outlasts you; the example is Brunelleschi's Dome.

[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Three lenses on disruption: view, deploy, manage.** AI as "a GPS of the mind" ("Rather than an existential threat, AI can be a GPS of the mind and usher in a new cognitive industrial revolution—if we continue to sculpt it"). GPS began as a US military system, was opened to civilians after the 1983 shootdown of a Korean airliner, and is now a free global utility; he draws three lessons: a pro-innovation government stance, converting "Big Data" into "Big Knowledge," and reinforcing individual agency (LSE lecture, paraphrased).
- *Luddite re-reading:* the power loom made cloth 40 times faster; the Luddites, per Brian Merchant, resisted "the factory system, its exploitative working conditions, and the regimentation and seeming loss of liberty" (paraphrase). Fix the system around the technology, not only the technology (LSE lecture).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Regulate by measuring.** "In short: let’s regulate first by measuring." "we find ways to measure twice, and cut once" (paraphrase of the lecture wording). He says he is "not unconditionally opposed" to regulation; "Striking the right balance between speed and deliberation is crucial, but if we err towards one, let it be speed." The checks and balances are "overlapping networks of the public and private sector, and the press and non-profits" (LSE lecture). And: "There's a way to propose a lightweight set of regulatory frameworks that enhance trust, still create the maneuverability for innovation" (Nadella, LinkedIn version).
- *His own label and his one concrete rule:* "I tend to be, call it more regulatory cautious than anti-regulation," with the instruction "when you start having the impulse that maybe there should be regulation, you should start with, well, how do we measure the questions that we're worried about as harms?" (Every, AGI episode). The one concrete rule he has proposed to lab leaders is remediation: "the ultimate regulatory thing that I’ve been suggesting has been something that’s along the lines of being able to remediate the harms from your models," ideally in "a more collective regulatory framework so that preferably everywhere in the world can sign on" (Possible, Altman and Brockman; he was then an OpenAI investor and former board member).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Superagency + Doomer/Gloomer/Zoomer/Bloomer** (w/ Greg Beato): a technology gives one person a superpower; when millions get it at once, the second-order reshaping loops back to expand everyone's agency ("superagency is when a lot of people get superpowers, I also benefit from it"). His four-attitude spectrum, verbatim from his own X post: "Doomers: Won't stop predicting an AGI-becomes-terminator future; Gloomers: Think we're worse off with AI; Zoomers: Accelerate at all costs w/o considering risk; Bloomers: Accelerate towards a bright future, manage risk." He is a Bloomer, "driving forward while tapping the brakes" (Wharton).
- *Worked example:* he wrote *Impromptu* with GPT-4, demonstrating amplification, not just arguing it: "I wanted to write a book about GPT-4, *with* GPT-4." Because AI moves faster than publishing, he reframed the artifact as a "travelog" rather than a definitive book: "Well aware of the brief half-life of this travelog’s relevance, I decided to press ahead" (Impromptu intro). He then ran the same test on the audiobook: Microsoft's research-only Vall-E text-to-speech, which can work from "as little as three seconds of a speaker’s audio," against Respeecher's speech-to-speech, which mapped "120 minutes of my voice" onto the manuscript as read by "Scott, a professional voice actor" (AI voice synthesis post).
- *Worked example (societal superagency):* everyone gains "even those who rarely or never use AI directly": your doctor's AI-assisted diagnosis, your mechanic's AI diagnosing the odd sound, multilingual ATMs (LSE lecture, paraphrased). House calls were once only for the wealthy; the doctor's car spread that agency to the middle class (Possible Beato, paraphrased).

text: [Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **AI is multiplayer, not single-player.** His least-press-covered AI thesis and a direct extension of network intelligence: "People always tend to think, because of chatbots, of AI as one to one interaction," but "we are going to be in a surrounding field of agents." Paired with a caution against anthropomorphizing: at Inflection, Pi was designed to refuse the substitute-friend role: "No, I am your AI companion, let's talk about your friendships" (Johnathan Bi; Fortune). On Possible: "your best friend should be other humans" (Possible S2 wrap). The design brief he gave for Pi, which he co-founded with Mustafa Suleyman, is "to both be, you know, the IQ helper, but also the EQ presence," because life is not only "how do I fix my lawnmower?" (Possible, Suleyman episode; co-founder's interest).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **The denominations of the lever: find your counterbalance.** Technology is "the Archimedean lever of human flourishing," capitalism is its palm ("The palm of that grip? Capitalism."), and the Valley's factions are "fingers of the same hand, which either separate or coordinate into a grip." He pairs eight denominations so each excess is checked by another's instinct: Purists and Ethicists ("something like a conscience with a deadline": "The Purist asks: can we build it? The Ethicist asks: should we, and how?"); Humanists and Missionaries (context plus reach); Venture Capitalists and Narcissists; Accelerationists and Determinists ("acceleration without direction is not progress. It is velocity"). Each gets a named failure mode: the Ethicist's is "paralysis dressed up as principle," the Missionary's is "paternalism with good branding," the Determinist's is "the abdication it licenses" (Denominations of the Lever).
- *Applied to a person or a team:* "in the moment of decision, one denomination leads. That is your primary—and it is also, usually, your blind spot." The instruction: "You have your denomination. Now find your counterbalance—inside yourself first, then in the room." Worked examples he credits to the Humanist and Missionary pairing are mobile money, drone logistics and agricultural data built for Lagos, Dhaka and Kigali, "products that found massive markets precisely because Humanists understood the context and Missionaries insisted on the reach" (Denominations of the Lever).

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Slop before the grid (Peak Pickle).** Early, frivolous uses of a general-purpose technology are not a failure signal; they fund and normalize the infrastructure. His case is electrification: the 43-foot electric Heinz pickle over Madison Square, Robert Louis Stevenson calling electric light "unearthly" and "obnoxious," and Boston's Bijou Theatre as the first customer of Edison's Boston utility, because early stations burned the same coal at partial load and a theater supplied the steady load the grid needed. "In this way, electric slop played a key role in funding and scaling the wires, underground cables, and massive dynamos that would eventually service both factories and individual homes" (In Defense of AI Slop).
- *Applied to AI:* "this view mistakes the “pickle” for the “grid.”" "The faster we get to Peak Pickle, the more likely it becomes that we will see the 21st-century equivalents of the X-ray machine and affordable bread," and "it’s exceedingly hard to ration and constrain your way to a revolution." The bounded concession on data centers: communities lack an absolute legal veto, but "it’s morally, politically, and operationally strategic for developers to heed it," with "Fair-market offers and a commitment to long-term coinvestment" as "table stakes," and "the power to say “Yes” is just as important as its right to say “No”" (In Defense of AI Slop).

title: Slop before the grid (Peak Pickle)

text:
[Risk, ethics, theory and AI] **Compass, not blueprint.** "plans that are rigid, break fast and uselessly." A compass lets you re-route when a trail is washed out; AI chatbots are "almost like it's a compass helping you with these informational decisions, hence informational GPS," which Superagency calls a "techno-humanist compass." Worked example: early car navigation, where the German system he drove repeated "return to the path" while the Japanese one offered new directions: "if you say first principle is only being Germanic, then you're going to have problems" (Every, AGI episode). The same logic as ABZ planning and "Why ten-year plans fail."
- *His own AI trial run:* he asked ChatGPT how Reid Hoffman would make money investing in AI and got "the business school professor's analysis that was completely wrong for venture capital," but in the same session its due-diligence checklist surfaced items "I would have thought of that in a few days." The lesson: use it on things "you are serious and earnest about," because many jobs will see "the human will be replaced by humans with AI" (Every, AGI episode).
