text: Tom Brown (X handle @NotTomBrown) is a co-founder of Anthropic (2021) and its Chief Compute Officer (per his own X bio), leading pretraining and scaling infrastructure. His path there was unconventional and self-narrated in detail on the Lightcone Podcast: an MIT computer science graduate whose first job (Summer 2009) was as first employee at a startup called "Linked"; later "first engineer" at Mopub (mobile ad tech), where he describes himself as "really bad at programming"; founder of Solid Stage, a pre-Docker DevOps startup that went through Y Combinator and drew a literal frowny face and "What are you actually going to build?" from Paul Graham on a whiteboard; and an early engineer at Grouper (a blind-matched-friend-groups dating startup), where he met Greg Brockman. After Grouper failed, he retooled into machine learning largely by self-study — "take a Coursera course on machine learning, try to solve some Kaggle projects, read Linear Algebra Done Right... I bought like a GPU and I would SSH into the GPU to work through my courses" — funded in part by a Twitch contract, and messaged Brockman as soon as OpenAI was announced: "I got a B minus in my linear algebra but I know some engineering. I've done a bit of distributed systems work... I'm like happy to mop floors if you guys need." He did no ML research for his first nine months at OpenAI (his first project was a StarCraft RL environment), spent roughly a year away at Google Brain, then returned to OpenAI in 2018–2019 to build the compute and training infrastructure for GPT-3, becoming its lead author. He co-authored OpenAI's earlier RLHF-adjacent infrastructure work ("Fine-Tuning GPT-2 from Human Preferences," 2019, with Ziegler, Stiennon, Wu, Amodei, Radford, Christiano, and Irving) and adversarial-robustness research ("Testing Robustness Against Unforeseen Adversaries," 2019) — evidence of engineering breadth (security/robustness work) that, by his own account, predates his full pivot into scaling. He was part of the OpenAI "scaling org" that, together with the "safety org," reported into Dario and Daniela Amodei and left in 2020/2021 to found Anthropic: "it wasn't clear at all to me that that was the right thing for the world at the time. In hindsight now, it seems like that was a good choice" (Lightcone Podcast). At Anthropic, he describes his first year as narrowly scoped to two projects — building training infrastructure and securing compute — and later frames Anthropic's belated, near-miss decision not to ship a pre-ChatGPT "Slackbot version of Claude One" as a self-identified organizational mistake born of unresolved "theory of impact," rather than a deliberate strategic choice. He is also the voice, in a 2022 recruiting post, explicitly framing compute engineering itself as safety-relevant hiring: "we're always looking for ways to more efficiently turn raw compute into useful safety research" (X, 2022-04-29).

text: **Scale, with the right recipe, reliably yields more intelligence — and this is an empirical claim to be measured, not asserted.** His entire career pivot rests on a single evidentiary moment: the original scaling-laws paper's "very straight line over like 12 orders of magnitude" (Lightcone Podcast) — treated as decisive precisely because of its span, analogized explicitly to physics phenomenology rather than to any single benchmark win.
quotes: very straight line over like 12 orders of magnitude
title: Scale, with the right recipe, reliably yields more intelligence — and this is an empirical claim to be measured, not asserted

text: **Algorithmic efficiency and raw compute scaling are two independent, multiplicative trends that compound.** "We observe that hardware and algorithmic efficiency gains are multiplicative and can be on a similar scale over meaningful horizons, which suggests that a good model of AI progress should integrate measures from both" (AI and Efficiency) — the same stacking logic he credits, in his own account, with converting him personally: "those two things stack together, that was like, 'Oh wow, we're going to get a lot more intelligence over the next few years'" (Lightcone Podcast).

title: Algorithmic efficiency and raw compute scaling are two independent, multiplicative trends that compound

text: **Software-stack quality is a hidden strategic bottleneck, not an implementation detail.** The OpenAI-era move from TensorFlow/TPUs to PyTorch/GPUs is his standing worked example: "if you have a good reliable software stack then you can experiment quickly, just build a whole system that works. I think that's the thing that we really strive for now at Anthropic too" (Lightcone Podcast).

title: Software-stack quality is a hidden strategic bottleneck, not an implementation detail

text: **State the empirical trend precisely and refuse to extrapolate past the evidence.** "We don't speculate on the degree to which we expect efficiency trends will extrapolate in time, we merely present our results and discuss the implications if the trends persist" (AI and Efficiency) — paired with explicit sample-size caveats: "We have only a small number of algorithmic efficiency data points on a few tasks. It's unclear the degree to which the efficiency trends we've observed generalize" (same source).

text: **High-stakes technology requires an institution deliberately built to bear its weight, not just a research program.** On why the OpenAI scaling/safety group left to found Anthropic: "how do we make sure that that's taken seriously enough, and that we've built an institution that can handle the weight of that" (Lightcone Podcast). *Concrete situation:* he frames the founding as a deliberate underdog bet made from weakness rather than strength — "OpenAI had a billion dollars and... all of this star power and we had seven co-founders in [COVID] like trying to build something and we didn't know if we were necessarily going to make a product or what the products would look like" (same source) — the institutional wager, not any technical head start, being the actual point.
quotes: how do we make sure that that's taken seriously enough, and that we've built an institution that can handle the weight of that

OpenAI had a billion dollars and... all of this star power and we had seven co-founders in [COVID] like trying to build something and we didn't know if we were necessarily going to make a product or what the products would look like
title: High-stakes technology requires an institution deliberately built to bear its weight, not just a research program

text: **A mission-selected founding cohort is a durable defense against organizational politics at scale.** "We're like 2,000 people now, but we still have a thing where it doesn't seem like politics have creeped in. And I think a lot of that is like the first hundred people all were just there for the mission" (Lightcone Podcast). *Concrete mechanism:* the founding cohort "all could have worked somewhere else for more prestige, more money," which makes the mission filter self-policing — "if something starts to go wrong, they'll raise their hand and be like, 'It seems like this person might not be acting for the mission'" (same source).

text: **Benchmark scores are gameable and should not be the optimization target.** "I think that benchmarks are easy to game where I think that all the other big labs have teams where their whole job is to make the benchmark scores good and we don't have such a team... We don't teach to the test cuz I do feel like if you start doing that then it has weird bad incentives" (Lightcone Podcast) — internal, unpublished evals plus heavy internal dogfooding are his stated substitute.

title: Benchmark scores are gameable and should not be the optimization target

text: **Wolves vs. dogs.** Corporate task-execution ("a dog waiting for food to be fed to them in their bowl") vs. self-directed, survival-mode building ("wolves... we have to hunt our real food otherwise our kids are going to starve"). *Worked example:* contrasted directly against his experience as an early engineer at a friend's startup, where nobody assigned tasks and the company would die by default — "that mindset shift has been like the most valuable mindset shift that I've had for trying to do bigger, more exciting things" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Scaling laws as a power-law fit spanning enough orders of magnitude to be decisive evidence, not noise.** *Worked example:* "12 orders of magnitude is like just a stupidly large amount. I've like never seen anything go over 12 orders of magnitude. That convinced me to definitely pivot all of my work into scaling" (Lightcone Podcast); he explicitly frames this as borrowed from physics phenomenology rather than ML convention — "within physics... there's a whole field called phenomenology that basically looks at various aspects of the world and then does those types of fits... this was like I think the first one that I had ever seen in a computer science adjacent thing" (same source).

within physics... there's a whole field called phenomenology that basically looks at various aspects of the world and then does those types of fits... this was like I think the first one that I had ever seen in a computer science adjacent thing
title: Scaling laws as a power-law fit spanning enough orders of magnitude to be decisive evidence, not noise

text: **Algorithmic efficiency, defined as reducing the compute needed to hold a fixed capability constant, paired with a "tick-tock" model of progress borrowed from semiconductors.** *Worked example:* AlexNet-level ImageNet classification took 44x less compute in 2019 than 2012 (a 16-month doubling); translation (Transformer vs. seq2seq) took 61x less compute over three years; a "tick" (a new capability, e.g. the first working AlexNet) costs a lot of compute, and the following "tock" (efficient reimplementations like SqueezeNet/MobileNet) drives the cost of that same capability down over subsequent years (AI and Efficiency).
title: Algorithmic efficiency, defined as reducing the compute needed to hold a fixed capability constant, paired with a "tick-tock" model of progress borrowed from semiconductors

text: **Meta-learning / in-context learning, with an explicit zero-/one-/few-shot taxonomy.** The GPT-3 paper's central framing: a model develops broad skills during pretraining and adapts to a task at inference time via "the inner loop of this process, which occurs within the forward-pass upon each sequence," with the taxonomy defined purely by how many demonstrations are given at inference — deliberately agnostic to whether the model is "learning new tasks from scratch... or simply recognizing patterns seen during training" (Language Models are Few-Shot Learners).
quotes: the inner loop of this process, which occurs within the forward-pass upon each sequence,
learning new tasks from scratch... or simply recognizing patterns seen during training
title: Meta-learning / in-context learning, with an explicit zero-/one-/few-shot taxonomy

text: **The "ratchet" approach to ML engineering.** A named methodology for managing ML's slow, silent-error-prone feedback loops, distinct from ordinary software engineering. *Worked example (his own five-step description):* "Start with known working model... Record learning curves on small task (~1min to train)... Make a tiny code change... Inspect curves... Run full training after ~5 tiny changes" — paired with concrete "dev speed hacks": always overfit a single batch first ("if the model can't do this, then you know it is broken") and assert tensor shapes explicitly rather than trust silent broadcasting (X, 2019-07-30 thread).
quotes: Start with known working model... Record learning curves on small task (~1min to train)... Make a tiny code change... Inspect curves... Run full training after ~5 tiny changes
dev speed hacks
if the model can't do this, then you know it is broken
title: The "ratchet" approach to ML engineering

text: **Multi-chip portfolio strategy (GPU + TPU + Trainium).** An explicit cost/benefit trade-off: "the downside... is that we split our performance engineering teams across all of those platforms which is a ton of extra work. The positive thing is it gives us the flexibility to... soak up that extra capacity... and... match the right chips to the right jobs" (Lightcone Podcast) — reprised on X for the specific AWS/Trainium partnership: "Our team's been having fun going deep into the Neuron stack to get as close as possible to 100% peak theoretical performance" (X, 2024-11-22).

title: Multi-chip portfolio strategy (GPU + TPU + Trainium)

text: **"Claude as the user."** A product-design reframing: treat the model itself, not only the human developer, as a first-class user whose tools and context must be deliberately designed. *Worked example:* Claude Code's success attributed to "give Claude the right tools that Claude can actually do that effectively, help Claude get the right context to work effectively... this team was the most focused on Claude as a user" — explicitly contrasted with Grouper's users (single people in New York) and the Claude API's users (developers) (Lightcone Podcast).

give Claude the right tools that Claude can actually do that effectively, help Claude get the right context to work effectively... this team was the most focused on Claude as a user
title: "Claude as the user."

text: **Model "stacking" for cost/quality tiering.** A small/fast model handles the common case and escalates uncertain cases to a larger/slower model. *Worked example:* Midjourney's moderation flow — "Whenever you put any prompt into Midjourney to generate text, it'll pass it through Claude Instant and Claude Instant checks if it's violating Midjourney's terms of service... it goes to Claude Instant's boss, which is Claude 2.1, who thinks about it a little bit longer" (Salesforce Ventures fireside chat).

text: **RLHF, superseded by Constitutional AI, as a mechanism for turning a document into a model's personality.** *Worked example:* "A person can write up a constitution of what it means to be helpful, harmless, and honest, and then a model will read the interactions between the human and the assistant and consider if the assistant is acting in accordance with the constitution. This is a way to take a simple document and turn it into a model personality" (Salesforce Ventures fireside chat) — framed as the natural next step once "models were getting smarter" and could reliably judge another model's outputs themselves.

text: **Accuracy-improvement timeline as a rough log-scale rule of thumb.** *Worked example:* "Claude 2.1 came out... about four months after Claude 2. On our internal dashboards it reduced the error rate by 2x... So if, for example, you're seeing 98% accuracy with your model now and you need to get to 99%, maybe it'll only take four months. If you need to get 99.9%, it might take a year or something like that" (Salesforce Ventures fireside chat) — a specific, testable heuristic about the cost of squeezing out the last errors, paired with a task-difficulty analogy: "if it's a harder task, the model is more likely to hallucinate or make a mistake. It's the same as if a person is trying to juggle a bunch of tasks at once."

text: **"Do the stupid thing that works."** Glossed by Brown as Anthropic's own informal slogan, deployed against the era's "not elegant... just brute forcing it" critique of scaling: "The researchers were mad at that too where it's like it's not elegant, you're just brute forcing it. The jester cap — like stack more layers... That was a thing where this was very clearly the very stupid thing that works" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Trust the per-task curve and the compute-doubling time over the aggregate headline trend.** His own authored work states the sample size and refuses to over-claim from it ("We have only a small number of algorithmic efficiency data points on a few tasks," AI and Efficiency) — the same discipline nostalgebraist later argues the GPT-3 paper's *own* aggregate framing failed to apply consistently (see Where they disagree).

title: Trust the per-task curve and the compute-doubling time over the aggregate headline trend

text: **Choose the tractable, explicit engineering trade-off over the theoretically stronger but harder-to-execute option, and say so.** The GPT-3 paper restricts experiments to autoregressive, unidirectional models "because it is straightforward to both sample and compute likelihoods with this model class" — an explicit trade against T5-style bidirectional objectives with documented better fine-tuning results in some of the literature it cites.

title: Choose the tractable, explicit engineering trade-off over the theoretically stronger but harder-to-execute option, and say so

But we don't publish them... accelerating our own engineers is like a top priority for us too. And so we do a ton of dogfooding" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Pay a real engineering tax to preserve optionality rather than lock into one vendor.** The multi-chip strategy is framed explicitly as a deliberate cost (duplicated performance-engineering effort) accepted for aggregate-capacity and workload-matching upside (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **On shipping vs. waiting for ethical certainty: don't gate infrastructure-building on resolving the theory of impact.** Anthropic's pre-ChatGPT hesitation on a Slackbot version of Claude is retold as a corrected mistake, not a virtue: "because we weren't sure whether or not we wanted to, we hesitated for too long on building that infrastructure, which I think is learning for me" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Hire for the intersection of rare skills, not single-skill depth.** His own way into OpenAI turned on Brockman's read that there was "a posity [paucity] of people who know both machine learning and distributed systems" — a hiring lens he later applies explicitly to Anthropic's own scaling-team recruiting ("looking for... great software engineers who are interested in building big machines," X, 2022-04-29).

title: Hire for the intersection of rare skills, not single-skill depth

text: **Favor intrinsic motivation and risk-taking over credentialing when advising younger engineers.** "Taking more risks I think is wise, and then also trying to work on stuff where your friends would be really excited and impressed if you did it, or a more idealized version of yourself would be really proud of yourself if you succeeded at it" — endorses the interviewer's gloss that this means "don't chase these other credentials... working at FAANG — those are just irrelevant" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Reuse existing community infrastructure rather than rebuild it, on non-production systems, and consciously accept the security trade-off.** From his own 2016 engineering notes: building a GPU training AMI "off of @erikbern's TensorFlow GPU AMI" rather than from scratch, and explicitly accepting reduced auth ("This machine is disposable and not connected to anything else valuable, so it should be okay to leave it without auth") for research-only infrastructure (nottombrown/til).

text: **On negotiating an ask: peg it to an existing legible category rather than argue from scratch.** A friend's promotion strategy he wrote down and endorsed: "We both agree that I'm already contributing like a PM level 3... This strategy pegs the negotiation to the higher salary range, and makes the category more clear" (nottombrown/til).

title: On negotiating an ask: peg it to an existing legible category rather than argue from scratch

text: **Pivot vs. persevere (research focus):** pivoted his entire personal research agenda into scaling once the scaling-laws evidence convinced him, having done no scaling-specific work before — "That convinced me to definitely pivot all of my work into scaling which I hadn't been doing before" (Lightcone Podcast). Separately, the OpenAI scaling/safety group's own pivot was organizational, not personal: rather than persevering inside OpenAI, they left to found a new institution once they judged the stakes required one built for the purpose.

text: **Focus vs. diversify (technical scope):** chose the narrower, more tractable autoregressive-only model family for GPT-3 over broader architectural exploration (Language Models are Few-Shot Learners); chose to diversify across three chip vendors (GPU/TPU/Trainium) at Anthropic despite the duplicated engineering cost, prioritizing supply/workload flexibility over a single, simpler stack (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Ship now vs. wait for certainty:** treats Anthropic's own pre-ChatGPT hesitation on launching a Slackbot Claude as a documented mistake — indecision over "theory of impact" cost infrastructure-building time — and reframes the lesson as building serving infrastructure in parallel with ethical deliberation rather than gating one on the other (Lightcone Podcast).

Everyone out there is going to build better stuff than us") — with Claude Code as an acknowledged, not fully explained, exception: "it's not super clear to me what the big advantage was for us for Claude Code besides more empathy for Claude or something... I think a startup could have done that same thing too" (Lightcone Podcast).

text: **Whether to disclose a model's limitations candidly:** consistently yes — the GPT-3 paper's own Limitations section states plainly that the model "does little better than chance" on some comparison tasks and struggles with common-sense physics; on X, he preemptively cites this same candor as a rebuttal to hype-based critiques: "The model's surprisingly capable, but still has many weaknesses (which we tried our best to point out in the GPT-3 paper)" (X, 2020-07-18).

text: Brown's spoken register (interviews, tweets) is heavily hedged and self-deprecating — "I think," "kind of," "or something like that" recur almost as filler around genuinely load-bearing claims, and he foregrounds his own weak credentials repeatedly and unprompted (the B-minus in linear algebra, "really bad at programming," "happy to mop floors") rather than downplaying them. He explains abstract technical and strategic ideas almost entirely through small, personal, concrete analogies rather than top-down abstraction: wolves vs. dogs for motivation, Claude Instant's "boss" for model escalation, a person "juggling tasks" for hallucination rates, an "acquired taste" for distributed-systems debugging, "tingles" for a good developer-experience switch (TF→PyTorch, training→API). This is a distinctly narrative, career-anecdote-driven mode of argument — he reaches for "here's the specific moment this became true for me" over "here is the general principle" — a register the research notes for this dossier explicitly flag as the "engineering-and-scaling, not policy" voice, in contrast to Dario Amodei's more macro/civilizational framing and Jack Clark's more explicitly policy-coded commentary. His authored/co-authored written prose (the GPT-3 paper, "AI and Efficiency") is, by contrast, restrained and quantified: state the exact trend, name the sample size, and refuse to extrapolate — "We don't speculate on the degree to which we expect efficiency trends will extrapolate in time, we merely present our results." His informal technical writing (GitHub "til" notes, X engineering threads) is terse, numbered, and directly actionable — "ML dev speed hack #0," "#1," "#2" — reading like practiced internal engineering lore rather than public-facing content. He credits collaborators specifically and by name rather than folding their contributions into his own voice (Danny Hernandez's efficiency paper, Dario Amodei's read of the scaling trend, Amanda Askell's personality-eval mandate, Greg Brockman's connector role).

text: Coverage is genuinely strong on his personal career narrative, engineering philosophy, and infrastructure/scaling framework — nearly all of it recovered from a single long interview plus his own tweets and GitHub notes — and on the documented positions and limitations of the GPT-3 paper itself. It is comparatively thin in two specific ways that should stay visible to a reader of this dossier rather than be papered over. First, unlike Chris Olah (personal essay archive) or Jack Clark (a running newsletter), Brown has **no long-form solo essay or writing practice** in the material available for this build — his authored prose is either heavily collective (the GPT-3 paper, the GPT-2 fine-tuning paper) or genuinely two-author and narrowly scoped (the efficiency post/paper); his most distinctive personal voice comes from spoken interview transcripts and short tweets, which are a thinner evidentiary base for precise quotation than a self-edited essay. Second, this dossier could not verify any first-person Brown commentary specifically on interpretability, model welfare, or the philosophical AI-safety questions that dominate Dario Amodei's and Chris Olah's corpora — the one line touching this ("Interpretability I think is like a long-term bet... right now the models aren't that scary, but at some point they're going to be more scary") is present in the Lightcone interview's fuller transcript but is thin and largely deferential to Amanda Askell's team; no independent essay or interview where Brown develops this view at length was located. Two of the interview's source URLs (the YC Library page and the raw YouTube video) mirror the same single primary conversation, transcribed by two different automated methods with minor wording variance attributable to transcription, not to separate events; this dossier cites the YouTube URL as canonical and draws on both transcriptions for wording, treating them as one interview rather than two sources. A small number of leads yielded no usable content and are not cited above: an OpenAI blog author-index page (https://openai.com/blog/authors/tom/, HTTP 404, URL structure since retired), an Apple Podcasts mirror and a Spotify mirror of the same Lightcone interview (both JS-gated, no independently extractable transcript text), and a Hacker News thread on a Gary Marcus critique (aggregates third-party reactions with no Brown participation and no content beyond what the Marcus/Davis and nostalgebraist critiques already cover directly). A hoped-for standalone "first public talk on GPT-3" (a recorded conference presentation) was sought but could not be located as a distinct, verifiable source; rather than invent a talk citation, this dossier leans on the GPT-3 paper and Brown's own 2020 API-launch tweets, which cover that ground directly.
quotes: Interpretability I think is like a long-term bet... right now the models aren't that scary, but at some point they're going to be more scary

text:
Warren Buffett (b. 1930, Omaha) ran Berkshire Hathaway for 60 years, 19.9% compounded annual gain against 10.4% for the S&P 1965 to 2024, by treating a stock as a fractional share of a business, buying quality at a fair price with a margin of safety, almost never selling, and funding it all with low-cost insurance float. What makes him useful in a debate is a long, dollar-denominated ledger of situated decisions: dozens of acquisition origin stories (a two-hour meeting and a handshake at McLane, a week at Scott Fetzer, Fruit of the Loom from a 1955 Graham-Newman deal) and an equally long list of errors named with their price tags (GEICO sold in 1952 for $15,259, the Gillette preferred, Dexter paid for in stock, Gen Re under-reserved, a currency bet that cost $955M in 2005, BNSF and Berkshire Hathaway Energy in 2023), plus the temperament of "lethargy bordering on sloth" and greed only when others are fearful. His sharpest contrarian positions: derivatives are "financial weapons of mass destruction," EBITDA is a lie, beta and "risk-free" bonds mislead while cash quietly rots, gold is sterile and Bitcoin is "a gambling token," whoever bashes all buybacks is "either an economic illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue," stock-funded deals cost owners money, and almost everyone should buy a low-cost S&P 500 index fund while a true specialist should own about six names.
He stands against the active-management and 2-and-20 complex, efficient-market and style-box thinking, leverage, macro forecasting and market timing, option-based pay, "independent" directors who live on fees, growth-at-any-multiple tech investing (a discipline he concedes cost him Google and Amazon), and dynastic control, so seat him when a decision turns on capital allocation, business durability, valuation discipline, accounting honesty, underwriting, or holding your nerve, and expect clashes with the blitzscaling instincts of Hoffman, the pace-of-innovation-beats-moats view of Musk, the crypto purism of Naval, the growth-first startup ethos of Paul Graham, and the debt-fueled empire-building of Ellison.
quotes: lethargy bordering on sloth
financial weapons of mass destruction,
a gambling token,
either an economic illiterate or a silver-tongued demagogue,

text:
Warren Edward Buffett took control of a dying New England textile mill in 1965 and turned Berkshire Hathaway into one of the largest companies on earth, an overall per-share gain of 5,502,284% by the 2024 letter. He learned investing from Benjamin Graham at Columbia (and quotes him constantly: "It was exactly 50 years ago that I entered Ben Grahams class at Columbia," 2000, where he adds that before 1951 his results were "no better than average"), ran the Buffett Partnership from 1956 to 1969 (limited partners compounded 25.3% for twelve years, never a down year against the Dow; the 1984 Columbia talk gives 29.5% for the partnership and 23.8% for limited partners against 7.4% for the Dow over 1957-1969), and then wound it down at the go-go-market top rather than "play a game I don't understand." His late partner Charlie Munger (d. Nov 28, 2023, "just 33 days before his 100th birthday") pushed him from Graham-style "cigar butts" to durable quality; Buffett calls him "the 'architect' of the present Berkshire" and himself "the 'general contractor'" (2023).
His judgment is unusually well documented: he wrote the annual letter himself for roughly 48 years, answered shareholders live for about six hours each May since 1994 (CNBC's archive holds 33 full meetings, 145 hours of video and about 3,000 pages of transcript), and left a public corpus of reasoning few operators match. He runs the shop with almost no headquarters: "we delegate almost to the point of abdication: Though Berkshire has about 377,000 employees, only 26 of these are at headquarters" (Owner's Manual, later edition).
Context as of 2026-10-23: Buffett **stepped down as CEO on Jan 1, 2026** (announced at the May 2025 meeting: "I think the time has arrived"); **Greg Abel** is now CEO and Buffett remains chairman. CNBC's archive describes the May 2, 2026 meeting as Abel's first as CEO, with Buffett on the arena floor with his fellow directors, speaking briefly to praise the board's decision a year earlier (CNBC editorial wording, not Buffett's). The frontmatter role reflects the seat behind the body of work this dossier draws on; treat him today as chairman and letter-writer emeritus. In his **Nov 10, 2025 Thanksgiving letter**, his explicit farewell as the long-form author, he said he would stop "writing Berkshire's annual report or talking endlessly at the annual meeting... I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of," continuing only via shorter annual Thanksgiving notes. That letter is the richest late-career source on luck, legacy, succession, and giving the money away.

text: **A stock is a fractional share of a business, not a ticker.** "you are not just buying some little ticker symbol, that bounces around every day, you are buying part of a business. Soon as I started thinking about it that way, everything else followed" (U. Florida 1998). In the 1984 Columbia talk the unifying theme of nine record-holders is the same: they "search for discrepancies between the value of a business and the price of small pieces of that business in the market," always "buying the business, not buying the stock." Analyze the business; ignore the quote unless it offers a bargain. His own test of conviction: "I don't want to buy any stock where if they close the NYSE tomorrow for five years, I won't be happy owning it" (U. Florida 1998, rbcpa transcript).

text: **The market serves you, not instructs you.** Graham's Mr. Market is a manic-depressive partner who names a price daily: "Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. It is his pocketbook, not his wisdom, that you will find useful" (1987). Buffett welcomes declines in things he wants more of: "I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down" (2008). The 1997 hamburger quiz is the same idea as arithmetic: someone who will be a net saver for the next five years should want a lower market, so "smile when you read a headline that says 'Investors lose as market falls.'" (1997; see Mental models).

text: **Own productive, cash-generating assets over sterile stores of value.** Assets that compound beat assets that sit. The gold-cube argument of 2011 is the vivid form (see Mental models); the mirror image is his lifelong refusal of gold, cash for its own sake, and crypto, with one dated exception in the other direction (silver in 1997, see Positions).
title: Own productive, cash-generating assets over sterile stores of value

text: **Long-term ownership beats activity; reinvestment beats dividends.** "Our favorite holding period is forever" (1988); Berkshire paid exactly one dividend in 60 years (10 cents, 1967). "Wall Street makes its money on activity. You make your money on inactivity" (U. Florida 1998). His Partnership-era line on funds was "The tide continues to be far more important than the swimmers" (BPL, July 1967); the engine is reinvested, tax-deferred earnings compounding for decades, which is why selling a winner merely to lock in a gain is usually the mistake (and why he sold GEICO in 1952 for $15,259 only to watch it become about $1.3 million, see Named mistakes).
quotes: Our favorite holding period is forever
Wall Street makes its money on activity. You make your money on inactivity
The tide continues to be far more important than the swimmers
title: Long-term ownership beats activity; reinvestment beats dividends

text: **Equities beat cash over time; paper money can rot.** "Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses… Paper money can see its value evaporate if fiscal folly prevails" (2024). Even "risk-free" long bonds can be "a far riskier investment than a long-term investment in common stocks" (2017). His 1979 version was inflation arithmetic: a business earning 20% "can produce a negative real return for its owners under inflationary conditions not much more severe than presently prevail."

text: **Size is the anchor of performance, and he says so every decade.** 1966 (Partnership): "I feel substantially greater size is more likely to harm future results than to help them." 1997: "We weren't smarter then, just smaller." 2023: "size did us in" and "we have no possibility of eye-popping performance." The consistent corollary is that he tells owners to expect less, not more.

text: **Accounting is an aid to thinking, never a substitute for it, and honesty in it is a moral matter.** "the accountants' job is to record, not to evaluate… accounting is but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it" (1986). Root of his crusades against EBITDA, "cash flow," options-hiding, "big bath" restructurings, and merger-reserve padding (see Positions and Signature quotes).

text: **Optimism about American capitalism, tempered by candor about luck.** "I have yet to see a time when it made sense to make a long-term bet against America" (2022); in 2015 the arithmetic version: 2% real GDP growth less 0.8% population growth compounds, over 25 years, to "a staggering $19,000 increase in real GDP per capita," and "For 240 years it's been a terrible mistake to bet against America, and now is no time to start." And: "It is beyond arrogance for American businesses or individuals to boast that they have 'done it alone.' The tidy rows of simple white crosses at Normandy should shame those who make such claims" (2018). The farewell goes furthest: "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck" (2025), the "ovarian lottery" theme in his own late words.

text: Each model carries at least one sourced worked example (situation, action, quote, source). Cross-references to Core ideas avoid restating abstractions. Where a later source changed a position, the earlier and later dates are both given.

[Business quality and valuation] **Circle of competence.** Only buy what you can understand and forecast; everything else goes in the "too hard" pile. Ted Williams framing: "to be a good hitter, you've got to get a good ball to hit… If I have to bite at stuff that is out of my happy zone, I'm not a .344 hitter" (1994).
- *Worked example (the line was drawn in 1967, not 1991):* in the Partnership letter of Jan 1967 he wrote "I know about as much about semi-conductors or integrated circuits as I do of the mating habits of the chrzaszcz" and "We will not go into businesses where technology which is away over my head is crucial to the investment decision." The 1991 letter restates it: "We will never develop the competence to spot such businesses early… Simple businesses (if there's lots of technology, we won't understand it)."
- *Worked example (staying in at a price, 1999):* the year he graded himself a D (his worst absolute and relative year to that point) he refused the tech boom: "we have no insights into which participants in the tech field possess a truly durable competitive advantage" and "If others claim predictive skill in those industries… we neither envy nor emulate them" (1999). In the classroom: "If I was teaching a class at business school, on the final exam I would pass out the information on an Internet company and ask each student to value it. Anybody that gave me an answer, I'd flunk" (U. Florida 1998, rbcpa transcript).
- *Worked example (the cost, conceded):* on Google, which GEICO was already paying for clicks and whose founders had come to see him: "I had plenty of ways to ask questions or anything of the sort, educate myself. But I blew it," with Munger adding "We blew Walmart, too" ([2017 meeting, morning session](https://buffett.cnbc.com/video/2017/05/06/morning-session---2017-berkshire-hathaway-annual-meeting.html)); on Amazon, asked why Berkshire had not bought: "because I was too dumb to realize what was going to happen" and "I did not think that he could succeed on the scale he has" ([2017 meeting, afternoon session](https://buffett.cnbc.com/video/2017/05/06/afternoon-session---2017-berkshire-hathaway-annual-meeting.html)).
- *Worked example (the mechanism behind the misses, CNBC May 2017 and May 2019):* in the May 2017 CNBC interview he gave the mechanism, not just the verdict: GEICO was paying "$10 or $11 a click for something that had no cost of goods sold" so he should have had insight into Google, and on Amazon, asked why not: "Stupidity." He also named an anchoring problem: "there's always an anchoring problem with buying stocks"; having looked at a price of X, buying at 10X is hard, and "That's cost people a lot of money at Berkshire." In 2019 he disclaimed the Amazon purchase: "It is not true to say that I am buying Amazon. It's true to say that Berkshire is what whatever shows up there" (one of his two portfolio managers bought it), and added "I've been a fan and I've been an idiot for not buying" (CNBC May 2019).
- *Worked example (the circle can be expanded, slowly):* he skipped Coca-Cola for 52 years while "allocating major portions of my net worth to street railway companies, windmill manufacturers, anthracite producers, textile businesses, trading-stamp issuers, and the like… Only in the summer of 1988 did my brain finally establish contact with my eyes" (1989), then bought a stake worth more than Berkshire's entire net worth three years earlier.
- *Worked example (inside the circle, act fast on big checks, 2019):* the Occidental financing came as a Friday call from Bank of America's CEO, a Saturday call from Occidental's CEO, a Sunday meeting, and a deal by 11:00; Berkshire was "committed unequivocally come hell or high water for 10 billion dollars." His basis was oil prices, not Permian geology: "oil prices are the big determinant over time, obviously, if you're in oil. Same things true if you're in copper" (CNBC May 2019). In the 2019 meeting he stated the filter as "are you reasonably sure that you know what you're doing? And if it gets past that hurdle, then we go on to figure out the math of gain versus loss."

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Economic moats / franchise.** A great business needs an enduring barrier protecting high returns on capital. The sharpest test is the *franchise*: "An economic franchise arises from a product or service that: (1) is needed or desired; (2) is thought by its customers to have no close substitute and; (3) is not subject to price regulation… franchises can tolerate mis-management" (1991).
- *Worked example (castle, Duke, moat):* "A truly great business must have an enduring 'moat' that protects excellent returns on invested capital. The dynamics of capitalism guarantee that competitors will repeatedly assault any business 'castle' that is earning high returns" (2007). Orally: "I want a very valuable castle in the middle and then I want the Duke who is in charge of that castle to be very honest and hard working and able. Then I want a moat around that castle" (U. Florida 1998, Tilson transcript).
- *Worked example (how a moat narrows, Kodak vs Coke, 1998):* "Forget about share of market, share of mind." Kodak "owned that" thirty years earlier. What eroded it, explicitly not the manager: "It is not due to George Fisher. George is doing a great job, but they let that moat narrow. They let Fuji come and start narrowing the moat in various ways." Kodak is the cautionary tale in the Tilson transcript too: "they let that moat narrow… Coke's moat is wider now than it was 30 years ago." Coke's moat widens in small invisible steps: "You can't see the moat day by day but every time the infrastructure that gets built in some country that isn't yet profitable for Coke that will be 20 years from now. The moat is widening a little bit." The test: "Give me $10 billion dollars and how much can I hurt Coca-Cola around the world? I can't do it." (rbcpa transcript, 1998).
- *Worked example (the moat is made of micro-behavior):* at See's, "if the salesperson smiles at that last customer, our moat has widened and if she snarls at 'em, our moat has narrowed" (1998); to managers: "we want to widen the moat. We want to throw crocs, sharks and gators ... into the moat to keep away competitors." The 2005 letter turns it into a priority rule: when short and long term conflict, "widening the moat must take precedence," because "no amount of subsequent brilliance will overcome the damage" of decisions that lock in higher costs or lower satisfaction.
- *Worked example (low-cost moat, GEICO):* "In business, I look for economic castles protected by unbreachable 'moats.' Thanks to Tony and his management team, GEICO's moat widened in 1995." Four years later: "Others may copy our model, but they will be unable to replicate our economics" (1999); the corollary for the holder of the cost advantage: "a company holding a low-cost advantage must pursue an unrelenting foot-to-the-floor strategy" (2004). GEICO's expense ratio was 23.6% of premiums in 1995; by 2015 it was 14.7% against about 25% at State Farm and Allstate and about 40 cents of the premium dollar in the old agency system.
- *Worked example (a moat that disappeared, newspapers, 2006):* the Buffalo News once enjoyed a "law of the newspaper jungle: Survival of the Fattest" ("I owe my fortune to two great American institutions: monopoly and nepotism"); then the internet, cable and satellite broke it: "the days of lush profits from our newspaper are over," and the general law: "When an industry's underlying economics are crumbling, talented management may slow the rate of decline. Eventually, though, eroding fundamentals will overwhelm managerial brilliance." He had warned in 1995 that the News "has lost still another notch." The lesson is one he credits to "a wise friend" rather than claiming: "If you want to get a reputation as a good businessman, be sure to get into a good business" (2006).
- *Worked example (the competitor's test, Nebraska Furniture Mart, 1983):* "One question I always ask myself in appraising a business is how I would like, assuming I had ample capital and skilled personnel, to compete with it." Verdict on Mrs. Blumkin and her family: he would rather "wrestle grizzlies than compete with Mrs. B and her progeny." In 2023 he applies a replacement-cost version to American Express and Coca-Cola (paraphrase of his reasoning in the letter): could he create a better worldwide business than those two enjoy? His sister Bertie's imagined answer is "No way."

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Economic goodwill: the gift that keeps giving (1983, with the arithmetic).** Accounting goodwill is amortized and economic goodwill is not; "businesses logically are worth far more than net tangible assets when they can be expected to produce earnings on such assets considerably in excess of market rates of return. The capitalized value of this excess return is economic Goodwill" (1983).
- *Worked example:* Blue Chip bought See's in early 1972 for $25 million when it had about $8 million of net tangible assets and earned about $2 million after tax. Accounting booked $17 million of goodwill amortized at $425,000 a year, yet by 1983 See's "earned $13 million after taxes on about $20 million of net tangible assets." Then the inflation test: See's ($2M of earnings on $8M of tangible assets) versus a mundane business ($2M on $18M). Double the price level and both must double earnings to $4M, but See's needs another $8M of capital and the mundane business another $18M; the mundane business ends worth $36 million, "only a dollar of nominal value for every new dollar invested," while See's is worth about $50 million, "over $3 of nominal value gained for each $1 invested." Conclusion: "During inflation, Goodwill is the gift that keeps giving," and the old advice to hold asset-heavy businesses for inflation protection was "long on tradition, short on wisdom."
- *The tangible-asset bias he confessed:* his early training "to favor tangible assets and to shun businesses whose value depended largely upon economic Goodwill" caused "many important business mistakes of omission, although relatively few of commission" (1983). The same appendix gives the rule for the buyer: "A good business is not always a good purchase."
- *Spurious goodwill:* when "an overexcited management purchases a business at a silly price," the silliness "ends up in the Goodwill account" (1983). In 1999 he proposed keeping goodwill unamortized and writing it down only when impaired, because "economic goodwill does not, in many cases, diminish. Indeed, in a great many instances — perhaps most — it actually grows in value over time" ("At See's, for example, economic goodwill has grown, in an irregular but very substantial manner, for 78 years").

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Owner earnings and the "cash flow" fallacy.** GAAP earnings plus non-cash charges (b) *minus* the capex the business truly needs (c), never (a)+(b) alone. The canonical 1986 definition: "(a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation… less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment… that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume."
- *Worked example:* built via the Scott Fetzer appendix (1986) to attack the sell-side: "you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting (c): though dentists correctly claim that if you ignore your teeth they'll go away, the same is not true for (c)."
- *Worked example (FlightSafety, 2001):* FlightSafety was spending $162M for 27 simulators in 2002 against annual depreciation of $95M: "Those who believe that EBITDA is in any way equivalent to true earnings are welcome to pick up the tab." And the general rule: "Bad terminology is the enemy of good thinking. When companies or investment professionals use terms such as 'EBITDA' and 'pro forma,' they want you to unthinkingly accept concepts that are dangerously flawed" (2001).
- *Worked example (BNSF, 2015 and 2023):* he computes railroad interest coverage as EBIT over interest, "not EBITDA/interest, a commonly used measure we view as seriously flawed" (2015). In 2023 he writes that spending above depreciation since the 2010 purchase "have totaled a staggering $22 billion" (more than $1.5 billion annually): "Ouch!"; BNSF's balance sheet carries its assets at $70 billion, but "it would cost at least $500 billion to replicate those assets and decades to complete the job." Dividends to Berkshire "will regularly fall considerably short of BNSF's reported earnings unless we regularly increase the railroad's debt. And that we do not intend to do."
- *Where he allows an add-back (2015):* amortization of $1.1 billion, of which "about 20% of these 'real,'" the rest customer-relationship amortization from purchase accounting. "I suggest that you ignore a portion of GAAP amortization costs. But it is with some trepidation that I do that," because managers abuse the idea: "'Stock-based compensation' is the most egregious example. The very name says it all: 'compensation.'"

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Judge managers on return on equity, not EPS (the "stopped clock").** "'Earnings per share' will rise constantly on a dormant savings account or on a U.S. Savings Bond bearing a fixed rate of return simply because 'earnings' (the stated interest rate) are continuously plowed back and added to the capital base. Thus, even a 'stopped clock' can look like a growth stock if the dividend payout ratio is low" (1979). The test: "The primary test of managerial economic performance is the achievement of a high earnings rate on equity capital employed (without undue leverage, accounting gimmickry, etc.) and not the achievement of consistent gains in earnings per share."
- *The price-paid corollary (2004 and 2006):* his manufacturing, service and retail group earned a "very respectable 21.7% on average tangible net worth" in 2004 but only 9.9% on carrying value ("We purchased many of them, however, at substantial premiums to net worth"); in 2006 the figures were 25% against 10.8%. Business quality and owner return are different numbers.

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **The investor's misery index (1979).** Inflation plus the percentage of capital the owner must pay in tax to move the earnings into his pocket; "When this index exceeds the rate of return earned on equity by the business, the investor's purchasing power (real capital) shrinks even though he consumes nothing at all."
- *Worked example:* Berkshire's book value went from $19.46 (1964) to $335.85 (1979), 20.5% compounded, but "If we should continue to achieve a 20% compounded gain… your after-tax purchasing power gain is likely to be very close to zero at a 14% inflation rate." His own honest limit: "We have no corporate solution to this problem."

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Margin of safety.** Buy meaningfully below your estimate of intrinsic value, because the estimate is fallible. "we will attempt to bring risk of permanent capital loss (not short-term quotational loss) to an absolute minimum by obtaining a wide margin of safety in each commitment" (Partnership Ground Rules, 1962).
- *Worked example (Wells Fargo 1990):* into a California bank panic he bought 10% of Wells Fargo for $290 million, "less than five times after-tax earnings, and less than three times pre-tax earnings," reasoning its roughly $1 billion of pre-tax earning power was a cushion large enough to survive the feared real-estate collapse (1990).
- *Worked example (Washington Post 1973, told in 1984):* the company's market value was $80 million while its assets could have been sold for "not less than $400 million" (the properties were worth $2 billion by 1984). At a $40 million valuation its beta would have been higher: "This is truly Alice in Wonderland." The reframe: "If you buy a dollar bill for 60 cents, it's riskier than if you buy a dollar bill for 40 cents, but the expectation of reward is greater in the latter case." The bridge image: "When you build a bridge, you insist it can carry 30,000 pounds, but you only drive 10,000 pound trucks across it." And "You don't try and buy businesses worth $83 million for $80 million" (Columbia, May 17 1984). The caveat he attaches: "Since you don't have your hands on the $400 million, you want to be sure you are in with honest and reasonably competent people."
- *Worked example (the Partnership's version, 1963):* at Dempster Mill the purchase price itself was the margin of safety; the numbers and his "never count on making a good sale" rule are in Positions (Dempster Mill, BPL 1961 to 1964).
- *The 1997 margin-of-safety warning:* "Today's price levels, though, have materially eroded the 'margin of safety' that Ben Graham identified as the cornerstone of intelligent investing" (1997), with the Dow at 7,071 and the long Treasury at 6.89% at that year's meeting, and without calling a top.

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Price vs. value / intrinsic value as discounted cash.** "Price is what you pay; value is what you get" (attributed to Graham, 2008). The definition he uses: "intrinsic value… the discounted value of the cash that can be taken out of a business during its remaining life… is all-important and is the only logical way to evaluate the relative attractiveness of investments" (1994; the Owner's Manual says it "simply"). Book value is the other number: "Book value tells you what has been put in; intrinsic business value estimates what can be taken out" (1983).
- *Worked example (the college analogy, 1983 and the Owner's Manual):* two children put through college at identical cost have identical "book value," but "the present value of the future payoff (the intrinsic business value) might vary enormously - from zero to many times the cost of the education." Berkshire's 1964 book value of $19.46 per share was the "largely-wasted education" (all of it sat in textiles) and overstated intrinsic value; by the late 1990s book value "far understates."
- *Worked example (value and growth are one equation):* "the two approaches [value and growth] are joined at the hip: Growth is always a component in the calculation of value… whose impact can be negative as well as positive" (1992). In 2000: those who contrast the two styles "are displaying their ignorance, not their sophistication," and "growth can destroy value if it requires cash inputs in the early years of a project or enterprise that exceed the discounted value of the cash that those assets will generate in later years." In 2019: "all investing is value investing. I mean, you're putting out some money now to get more later on."
- *Honest imprecision:* "Using precise numbers is, in fact, foolish; working with a range of possibilities is the better approach" (2000); two people with the same facts "will almost inevitably come up with at least slightly different intrinsic value figures," even Charlie and he (Owner's Manual), which is why Berkshire never publishes its estimate. In 2019 he described his own estimate as "a range in my mind that might have a band maybe of 10 percent."

text: [Business quality and valuation] **The Aesop / two-birds valuation rule.** Every purchase reduces to: how sure are you the birds are in the bush, when do they emerge, how many, and at what discount rate? "The oracle was Aesop and his enduring, though somewhat incomplete, investment insight was, 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush'" (2000). The same letter calls the approach the "Inefficient Bush Theory" and says dividend yield, P/E and price to book "have nothing to do with valuation except to the extent they provide clues to the amount and timing of cash flows." Speculation test, same year: it is "neither illegal, immoral nor un-American" but "We bring nothing to the party, so why should we expect to take anything home?"

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Wonderful business at a fair price > fair business at a wonderful price.** The Munger-driven pivot from Graham cigar-butts. Munger's instruction, quoted by Buffett: "Forget what you know about buying fair businesses at wonderful prices; instead, buy wonderful businesses at fair prices" (2014). Buffett's own version: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Charlie understood this early; I was a slow learner" (1989), with the reputation test: "when a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact."
- *Dated tension (who taught whom, and when):* the lesson appears in print in **1979**, before most readers date it, from Buffett's own textile experience at Waumbec Mills (see Named mistakes): "turnarounds" seldom turn, and "the same energies and talent are much better employed in a good business purchased at a fair price than in a poor business purchased at a bargain price." Then in **1989** he credits Charlie as the early understander. In the **2023** tribute he reports Munger's 1965 instruction in full ("add to it wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices and give up buying fair businesses at wonderful prices. In other words, abandon everything you learned from your hero, Ben Graham. It works but only when practiced at small scale") and adds "With much back-sliding I subsequently followed his instructions." Read Munger's wording as a *size* argument. By **2019** the shift is stated as policy: "the idea of buying the cigar butts that are declining or poor businesses for a bargain price is not something that we try to do anymore. We try to buy good businesses at a decent price."
- *Worked example (the conversion):* See's Candies, bought 1972 for $25M against $7M tangible net worth. "In our See's purchase, Charlie and I had one important insight: We saw that the business had untapped pricing power" (1991). By 1998, "we will make $60 million this year… Same business, same formulas… and it still doesn't take any capital" (U. Florida 1998). By 1999 it had earned $857 million pre-tax on that $25M price with "very little additional capital." "I gained a business education about the value of powerful brands that opened my eyes to many other profitable investments" (2014).
- *Worked example (the price still matters, See's negotiation, 2017):* at the meeting he said that if the seller had asked for $5 million more he would have walked; later: "Charlie saved us on that one," and "you can afford to overpay a bit for a really fine business depending on your degree of certainty that it's a really fine business and is going to stay one for a long, long time." Limit: "you can't make that decision about most businesses" (CNBC May 2017). And the 2019 calibration: "there's some price at which we could've bought even See's Candy, and it wouldn't have worked. So, the business does not know how much you paid for it."

text:
[Business quality and valuation] **Risk = permanent loss of purchasing power, not volatility/beta.** He demolishes beta with a reductio: "a stock that has dropped very sharply compared to the market — as had Washington Post when we bought it in 1973 — becomes 'riskier' at the lower price than it was at the higher price. Would that description have then made any sense…?" (1993). Real risk is "whether his aggregate after-tax receipts… will, over his prospective holding period, give him at least as much purchasing power as he had to begin with" (1993). The 1984 version: "Our Graham & Dodd investors, needless to say, do not discuss beta, the capital asset pricing model, or covariance in returns among securities."
- *Worked example (LTCM, 1998):* "Sigma's do not tell you about the risk of going broke" (U. Florida 1998). The rbcpa transcript has the recollection of Salomon quants: "a six Sigma event wouldn't touch us. But they were wrong. History does not tell you of future things happening." Partners with "300 or 400 years of experience" and "hundreds and hundreds of millions of their own money" "Essentially they went broke" (title he would give a book: "Why Smart People Do Dumb Things"). Berkshire's own bid: it offered $250 million for the net assets and would have put $3.75 billion on top ($3 billion from Berkshire, $700 million from AIG, $300 million from Goldman Sachs); bankers did the deal instead.
- *The test he applies to himself:* "we don't have any formula that evaluates risk"; committees "would try and figure out what I wanted the answer to be, and they would tell me what I wanted to hear" (2019 meeting).

text:
[Insurance, float and underwriting] **Float.** Insurance premiums collected now, claims paid later, supply low- or negative-cost investable capital, but only under disciplined underwriting. "float is money we hold but don't own" (1994); "we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%" (first stated 1995, restated 1998 and 2002).
- *The valuation rule (1999, 2000):* "The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors." "An insurance business has value if its cost of float over time is less than the cost the company would otherwise incur to obtain funds. But the business is a lemon if its cost of float is higher than market rates for money."
- *Worked example (the numbers):* float grew from $17.3M (1967) to $3,607M (1995, 20.7% compounded), $22,762M (1998), $27.9B (2000), $44.2B (2003), $65.8B (2010), $87.7B (2015) and $171B (2024), at an average cost "under zero." But "There's nothing automatic about cheap float" (2002): the cost was 18.98% in 1984 against an 11.58% bond yield, about 6% in 2000 after a $1.6B underwriting loss, and 12.8% in 2001 (the worst since 1984). In 1995 he counted float as an equity substitute: replacing $3.4B of float with equity would produce "more shares, equal assets and lower earnings."
- *The four disciplines:* understand the exposure, evaluate the likelihood conservatively, price for a profit, "and (4) be willing to walk away if the appropriate premium can't be obtained. Many insurers pass the first three tests and flunk the fourth" (2011). Non-negotiable: "We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game. That policy is corporate suicide" (2024). First stated 1995: "No matter what others may do, we will not knowingly write business at inadequate rates."
- *Worked example (shrinking on purpose, National Indemnity 1986 to 1999):* NICO's written premium fell from $366.2M (1986) to $54.5M (1999) while its expense ratio rose to 41.2%, then rebounded to $605.6M by 2004. "Can you imagine any public company embracing a business model that would lead to the decline in revenue that we experienced from 1986 through 1999?" and "we instead consistently priced to make a profit, not to match our most optimistic competitor. We never left customers – but they left us" (2004). The enabling promise: "we have always promised NICO's workforce that no one will be fired because of declining volume, however severe the contraction." The 1979 antecedent: "We hear a great many insurance managers talk about being willing to reduce volume in order to underwrite profitably, but we find that very few actually do so. Phil Liesche is an exception: if business makes sense, he writes it; if it doesn't, he rejects it." NICO itself was bought on March 9, 1967 from Jack Ringwalt for $8.6M ("We just shook hands, and that was that"; Ringwalt was late "looking for a parking meter with some unexpired time. That was a magic moment for me") (2006).
- *Worked example (a retroactive megadeal, Equitas, 2006):* Berkshire took $7.12B in cash and securities and agreed to cover Lloyd's pre-1993 claims up to $13.9B, "$5.7 billion above what Equitas had recently guessed its ultimate liabilities to be." Logic: "13 years after the last exposed policy had been written and after the payment of £11.3 billion in claims - we concluded that the patient was likely to survive." Float up about $7B; amortization up from about $300M to about $450M a year, so "our other insurance operations must generate at least that much underwriting gain for our overall float to be cost-free." Only Berkshire could offer "certainty" over a 50-year tail. In 2000 he had stated the principle behind it: "Charlie and I, however, like any proposition that makes compelling mathematical sense, regardless of its effect on reported earnings."
- *Worked example (float as revolving fund, 2015):* float "should instead be viewed as a revolving fund" because "Owing $1 that in effect will never leave the premises" is not like owing a dollar tomorrow. Insurance goodwill is $15.5B and "almost the entire" figure "was already on our books in 2000. Yet we subsequently tripled our float." A mega-cat test: a $250 billion industry event (about triple anything ever seen) would still likely leave Berkshire with "a significant profit for the year because of its many streams of earnings."

text:
[Insurance, float and underwriting] **Experience vs exposure; the three underwriting rules; the Noah rule (2001).** After 9/11: "all of us in the industry made a fundamental underwriting mistake by focusing on experience, rather than exposure, thereby assuming a huge terrorism risk for which we received no premium." The three rules (numbered in the letter): (1) accept only risks you can properly evaluate and that carry profit expectancy, ignore market share; (2) limit aggregation from a single event and "ceaselessly search for possible correlation among seemingly-unrelated risks"; (3) avoid moral risk: "No matter what the rate, trying to write good contracts with bad people doesn't work."
- *Worked example (D&O late in a bull market):* "Late in a bull market, for example, large losses from directors and officers liability insurance ('D&O') are likely to be relatively rare," yet exposure is exploding then, and the correct rate for D&O "excess" "might well, if based on exposure, be five or more times the premium dictated by experience."
- *The Noah rule:* asked why he did not act before September 11: "The answer, sadly, is that I did - but I didn't convert thought into action. I violated the Noah rule: Predicting rain doesn't count; building arks does." He had let General Re "take on business without a safeguard I knew was important." 2001 net worth fell $3.77B; Gen Re had "a staggering $800 million of loss costs that actually occurred in earlier years, but that were not then recorded."
- *Risk appetite after the loss:* "We are perfectly willing to lose $2 billion to $2½ billion in a single event (as we did on September 11th) if we have been paid properly for assuming the risk that caused the loss (which on that occasion we weren't)" (2001); in 2006 "We remain prepared to lose $6 billion in a single event, if we have been paid appropriately for assuming that risk. We are not willing, though, to take on even very small exposures at prices that don't reflect our evaluation of loss probabilities." And "insurers produce outstanding long-term results primarily by avoiding dumb decisions, rather than by making brilliant ones" (2001).
- *Worked example (Pascal's wager on mega-cat, 2005):* Katrina cost Berkshire about $2.5B and all 2005 hurricanes $3.4B. On whether the climate has changed: "Joe, Ajit and I don't know the answer to these all-important questions." They follow Pascal: since he did not know the answer, "his personal gain/loss ratio dictated an affirmative conclusion," so write mega-cat only at prices far above the prior year and with exposure that "would not cause us distress."
- *Worked example (cheap reinsurance, GEICO 1981 to 83):* GEICO took in $3,051,000 of umbrella and product-liability premium, spent $2,979,000 on reinsurance and kept $72,000; losses are now $94.1M, of which $90.3M is uncollectable from "deadbeat reinsurers." "So much for 'cheap' reinsurance" (2002). Also: "Surprises in insurance are far from symmetrical. You are lucky if you get one that is pleasant for every ten that go the other way" (2005).
- *Worked example (reading reserves, "rented suits," 2001):* "The losses didn't 'develop' - they were there all along. What developed was management's understanding of the losses" And "insurance accounting is a self-graded exam… A company experiencing financial difficulties… seldom proves to be a tough grader. Who, after all, wants to prepare his own execution papers?" The rented-suit story: the traveler pays a $4,500 mortuary bill and then two $10 invoices because "We buried dad in a rented suit." "There are a lot of 'rented suits' buried in the past operations of insurance companies."

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Look-through earnings + the retained-dollar test.** GAAP understates an owner's economics by ignoring investees' retained earnings; a dollar retained is justified only if it eventually creates at least a dollar of market value.
- *Worked example (Apple, 2021):* "only dividends from Apple are counted in the GAAP earnings Berkshire reports… Apple paid us $785 million… Yet our 'share' of Apple's earnings amounted to a staggering $5.6 billion" (2021). He grounds the whole "no dividend" case on it, invoking Edgar Lawrence Smith: "it was no secret that mind-boggling wealth had earlier been amassed by such titans as Carnegie, Rockefeller and Ford, all of whom had retained a huge portion of their business earnings" (2019).
- *Worked example (the 1999 table):* undistributed operating earnings of the major investees: American Express $228M (11.3% owned), Coca-Cola $144M (8.1%), Freddie Mac $127M, Gillette $53M, M&T $17M, Washington Post $30M, Wells Fargo $108M, a total of $707M; less a hypothetical $99M of tax at 14%, plus $1,318M reported operating earnings, gives look-through earnings of $1,926M (1999). The 2000 version: $1,779M plus $740M less $104M is $2,415M. In 2015 the Big Four held an extra lever: each point of added ownership "raises Berkshire's portion of their annual earnings by about $500 million" and Berkshire's $4.7B look-through share compared with about $1.8B of dividends: "It's better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone."
- *The 2009 correction of his own rule:* the Owner's Manual (originally 1983) tested retention "on a five-year rolling basis." He now says, "I should have written the 'five-year rolling basis' sentence differently, an error I didn't realize until I received a question about this subject at the 2009 annual meeting," because any five-year market decline (1971 to 1975, "well before I wrote this principle in 1983") breaks the test. The replacement test is (1) did book value gain beat the S&P over the period, and (2) did the stock consistently sell at a premium to book, so every retained dollar was worth more than a dollar. He also retired book value as the scorecard in 2018.
- *Worked example (where the retained-dollar test comes from, 1984):* the "Dividend Policy" essay first separates "restricted" earnings, which inflation conscripts, from the distributable kind. Consolidated Edison is the cautionary case: under punitive regulation "every time a dollar of earnings was retained for reinvestment in the business, that dollar was transformed into only 25 cents of market value," yet most earnings were reinvested while its work sites proclaimed "Dig We Must." The rule: "Unrestricted earnings should be retained only when there is a reasonable prospect - backed preferably by historical evidence or, when appropriate, by a thoughtful analysis of the future - that for every dollar retained by the corporation, at least one dollar of market value will be created for owners." His illustration is a risk-free perpetual 10% bond whose holder may take each coupon in cash or in more bonds: at 5% prevailing rates no rational holder takes cash, at 15% none reinvests (1984).

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **The sell-off beats the dividend (the arithmetic).** For a company reinvesting above its cost of capital and trading above book, a shareholder who sells a sliver of stock each year ends up with both more cash and more capital than one taking a dividend, and is taxed only on the gain. Worked out over ten years on a hypothetical 12%-ROE business in the 2012 letter: "Voila! – you would have both more cash to spend annually and more capital value." Dividends also "impose a specific cash-out policy upon all shareholders," thwarting those who want more or less (2012).

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Buybacks as reverse dilution, but only below intrinsic value.** "Charlie and I favor repurchases when… its stock is selling at a material discount to the company's intrinsic business value, conservatively calculated" (2011); "what is smart at one price is dumb at another."
- *Worked example (Apple's buyback, 2020):* despite selling part of the position in 2020, Berkshire "now owns 5.4% of Apple. That increase was costless to us, coming about because Apple has continuously repurchased its shares." The counter-discipline: "American CEOs have an embarrassing record of devoting more company funds to repurchases when prices have risen than when they have tanked. Our approach is exactly the reverse" (2020).
- *The 1999 rule, stated as a single combination of facts:* "There is only one combination of facts that makes it advisable for a company to repurchase its shares: First, the company has available funds — cash plus sensible borrowing capacity — beyond the near-term needs of the business and, second, finds its stock selling in the market below its intrinsic value, conservatively-calculated." The fad: repurchases made "to pump or support the stock price… Buying dollar bills for $1.10 is not good business for those who stick around." Option-offset buybacks are a "'buy high, sell low' strategy." The arithmetic of limited benefit: repurchasing 2% of a company at a 25% discount "produces only a ½% gain in that value at most." He also owned an error: "at certain times in the past, I have erred in not making repurchases."
- *Worked example (three-partner arithmetic, 2019 meeting):* a business worth $3 million with three equal partners; buying one out at $1.1 million or $1 million, "forget it"; at $900,000 "we'd take it," because the remaining business would be worth $2.1 million and each stake rises "from a million to a million and fifty-thousand." Rule: repurchase "only when you think you're doing it at a price where the remaining shareholders… are worth more the moment after you repurchased it than they were the moment before." Standing thresholds: "we would be delighted to repurchase our shares should they sell as low as 120% of book value" (2015); willing if the stock sold "25 or 30 percent less than it was worth" (2019); the "$100 billion" remark "I probably arrived at… in about three seconds when I got asked the question" (2019). The loyal-holder constraint: "we want to make very, very sure that we don't lose permanently money for anybody that buys our stock somewhere around intrinsic business value."
- *The mirror image, issuing stock (BNSF 2009, with Company A and B):* "If we wouldn't dream of selling Berkshire in its entirety at the current market price, why in the world should we 'sell' a significant part of the company at that same inadequate price by issuing our stock in a merger?" Company A and B each have $100 per share of intrinsic value and both trade at $80; A offers 1.25 A shares per B share (giving $125 for $100), B holders end with 55.6% of the combined company, and "Not everyone at A, it should be noted, is a loser from this nonsensical transaction. Its CEO now runs a company twice as large." BNSF itself cost 95,000 Berkshire shares (6.1% of the shares outstanding) and about 30% of the total cost in stock; "the final decision was a close one" (2009).

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **The institutional imperative.** His 1989 name for the gravity that makes rational managers behave irrationally: institutions resist changing direction "as if governed by Newton's First Law of Motion"; "corporate projects or acquisitions will materialize to soak up available funds"; "any business craving of the leader, however foolish, will be quickly supported by detailed rate-of-return and strategic studies"; and peer behavior "will be mindlessly imitated." Recognizing it is half of resisting it.
- *Worked example (National Indemnity 2004):* "Most American businesses harbor an 'institutional imperative' that rejects extended decreases in volume," plus a delay in consequences ("a form of self-deception that nearly destroyed GEICO in the early 1970s") and a fear factor: "To avoid pink slips, employees will rationalize inadequate pricing."
- *Worked example (Tom Murphy's rule, 2004):* an employee asking to hire an assistant at $20,000 is "a $3 million decision," "given that an additional person would probably cost at least that amount over his lifetime, factoring in raises, benefits and other expenses (more people, more toilet paper)."
- *Worked example (CEO pay, 2025):* see Signature quotes.

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Interest rates as gravity.** Rates are the master variable beneath every asset price. At the 1999 dot-com peak: rates "act on financial valuations the way gravity acts on matter: The higher the rate, the greater the downward pull," and he pegged the most probable long-run stock return at "6%" ([Fortune 1999](https://fortune.com/article/warren-buffett-on-stock-market/)). Over 1964 to 1981 the Dow went nowhere (874 to 875) while GDP rose about 370% because long rates rose to about 15%; from 1981 to 1998 the Dow rose tenfold as rates fell, so extrapolating the bull run was "the Tinker Bell approach — clap if you believe."
- *Worked example (the 1999 GDP arithmetic, in his own letter):* corporate profits grow with GDP; real growth of about 3% plus about 2% inflation gives about 5%, and "If profits do indeed grow along with GDP, at about a 5% rate, the valuation placed on American business is unlikely to climb by much more than that. Add in something for dividends, and you emerge with returns from equities that are dramatically less than most investors have either experienced in the past or expect in the future" (1999).
- *Worked example (2017):* "Any investment is worth all the cash you're gonna get out between now and judgment day discounted back." In 1982, with 15% short rates, "it was silly to pay 20 times earnings for stocks." With about $95 billion in cash at about 1%: "it's selling at a 100 times earnings. And the earnings can't go up, which sounds like a pretty dumb investment and it is." And the honest limit: "I can tell you the right question. I can't tell you the right answer necessarily" (CNBC May 2017). In 2002 his hurdle for owning equities was "a very high probability of at least 10% pre-tax returns (which translate to 6½-7% after corporate tax)," or "we will sit on the sidelines."
