text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **"The Secret Sauce": a few huge winners carry everything.** The record came not from a high batting average but a handful of decades-long compounders. "The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom. Over time, it takes just a few winners to work wonders" (2022). Coca-Cola and Amex (bought about 1994 to 1995): Coke dividends grew from $75M (1994) to $704M (2022), Amex $41M to $302M, on a fixed cost basis. "Our satisfactory results have been the product of about a dozen truly good decisions — that would be about one every five years" (2022). 2023: "By both luck and pluck, a few huge winners have emerged from a great many dozens of decisions." The Rip Van Winkle version: Berkshire bought or sold neither stock in 2023, "extending our own Rip Van Winkle slumber that has now lasted well over two decades," and "our share of AMEX earnings in 2023 considerably exceeded the $1.3 billion cost of our long-ago purchase."

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **The friction tax: the Gotrocks family and the "chair-changing" cost.** "the most that owners in aggregate can earn between now and Judgment Day is what their businesses in aggregate earn" (2005).
- *Worked example (Gotrocks, 2005):* the Gotrocks family owns all of corporate America (about $700 billion a year of earnings); "Helpers" arrive in layers (brokers, managers, consultants, then "hyper-Helpers" charging performance fees), turning the family into "the Hadrocks," so frictional costs may take about "20% of the earnings of American business." Law: "For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases." Check: the Dow rose from 65.73 to 11,497.12 in the 20th century, "a gain of 5.3% compounded annually," so an equal 21st-century rate implies a Dow of 2,011,011.23 by the end of 2099.
- *Worked example (1983, the chair-changing tax):* a company earning 12% on equity with 100% annual share turnover and 1% commissions each way forfeits 2% of net worth a year, one-sixth of its earnings; 100-million-share days at 15 cents a side cost "about $7.5 billion" a year (roughly the combined 1982 profits of Exxon, GM, Mobil and Texaco). "what is good for the croupier is not good for the customer. A hyperactive stock market is the pickpocket of enterprise." He rejects the Adam Smith defense: "casino-type markets and hair-trigger investment management act as an invisible foot that trips up and slows down a forward-moving economy." Hence no stock split (then about $1,300 a share): "People who buy for non-value reasons are likely to sell for non-value reasons," with more than 90 to 95% of shares held by people who owned five years earlier.
- *Worked example (2-and-20, 2006):* gross return 10%; the manager keeps 2 points plus 20% of the remaining 8, "leaving only 6.4 percentage points for his investors. On a $3 billion fund, this 6.4% net 'performance' will deliver the manager a cool $108 million. He will receive this bonanza even though an index fund might have returned 15% to investors." He closes with "the old adage" rather than a coinage of his own: "When someone with experience proposes a deal to someone with money, too often the fellow with money ends up with the experience, and the fellow with experience ends up with the money." In 2019 he added: "If you can raise $10 billion in a fund" at a 1 1/2 percent fee with ten-year lockups, "you and your children and your grandchildren will never have to do a thing"; a manager who was told about "2-and-20" replied "I can't get 3-and-30"; private equity returns "are not calculated in a manner that I would regard as honest."

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Productive vs. unproductive capital (the gold-cube).** Compare what an asset *produces* over decades, not what it might be resold for. In 2011 he pits "pile A," all the world's gold, a 68-foot cube worth about $9.6T, against "pile B" of equal cost: all U.S. cropland plus "16 Exxon Mobils," with about $1T left over. "You can fondle the cube, but it will not respond" (2011). Generalized in 2018: a 1942 investment of $114.75 in an index would be "$606,811," but in gold "about $4,200, less than 1%… The magical metal was no match for the American mettle."
- *Dated evolution (1979, 1997, 2011):* in 1979 he reported without endorsing a commentator's finding that 1964 book value "would have bought about one-half ounce of gold" and fifteen years later the same half ounce; his reading was that government "is unable to print gold or create oil." In 1997 he disclosed 111.2 million ounces of silver (pre-tax gain $97.4M, first bought 30 years earlier "because I anticipated its demonetization by the U.S. Government") and added "Inflation expectations, it should be noted, play no part in our calculation of silver's value." The 2011 letter is the settled position against unproductive stores of value; the 1997 silver was a supply and demand bet, which is why the two do not contradict.

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Look for the important and knowable; what vs. when.** "What you really want to in investments is figure out what is important and knowable. If it is unimportant and unknowable, you forget about it" (U. Florida 1998, rbcpa). "You can figure what will happen, you can't figure out when it will happen. You don't want to focus too much on when but you want to focus on what." The Partnership said the same in 1966: "we tend to concentrate on what should happen, not when it should happen."
- *Worked example (Coke's 1919 IPO):* Coca-Cola IPO'd at $40 in 1919 and fell about 50% within a year; $40 compounding at 14.63% for 86 years with reinvested dividends was "$5 million now." "You can always find reasons that weren't the ideal moment to buy it" (rbcpa 1998).

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Generals, workouts and controls (the Partnership's three-way toolkit).** Generals are "undervalued situations"; workouts are "dependent on a specific corporate action for its profit rather than a general advance in the price of the stock"; controls are businesses he can steer. In 1957 the mix was about 85/15 generals to workouts (70/30 a year earlier). He also set yardsticks in advance ("A Word About Par," Jan 1962): "I believe in establishing yardsticks prior to the act; retrospectively, almost anything can be made to look good in relation to something or other." Worked examples are in Positions (Commonwealth Trust, Sanborn Map, Dempster Mill, Texas National Petroleum, Berkshire, Hochschild Kohn). Category returns, for scale: 1962 generals -1.0%, workouts 14.6%, Dow -8.6%; 1963 generals 20.5%, workouts 30.6%, Dow 18.4%; 1964 generals 27.8%, workouts 10.3%, Dow 16.7%.

text:
[Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Mono-linked chains (2004).** "If only one variable is key to a decision, and the variable has a 90% chance of going your way, the chance for a successful outcome is obviously 90%. But if ten independent variables need to break favorably for a successful result, and each has a 90% probability of success, the likelihood of having a winner is only 35%." So "it makes sense to look for – if you'll excuse an oxymoron – mono-linked chains."
- *Worked example (zinc, 2004):* MidAmerican's zinc-recovery project from California geothermal brine (started 1998, operational 2002) was abandoned with a pre-tax loss of $579M ("In September, we threw in the towel"): "prospects have a way of 'teasing' their developers, and every time one problem was solved, another popped up." "In our zinc venture, we solved most of the problems. But one proved intractable, and that was one too many." Guideline: "stay with simple propositions."
- *Second case (utilities, 2023):* the pact of "fixed-but-satisfactory" regulated returns "has been broken in a few states" and he did not "anticipate or even consider the adverse developments in regulatory returns" (see Named mistakes).

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Have-to-be-smart-once vs. have-to-be-smart-every-day (1995).** In retailing "a retailer must stay smart, day after day"; "In retailing, to coast is to fail." The contrast: "if you were smart enough to buy a network TV station very early in the game, you could put in a shiftless and backward nephew to run things, and the business would still do well for decades." It tells him how much to pay for management in each type of business: R.C. Willey and Helzberg's were bought only because the managers "love to compete and have done so successfully for decades." In 1979 he put the same point in price terms: a network TV station sells "one thousand cents or more on the dollar… Despite a fancy price tag, the 'easy' business may be the better route to go."

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Inversion and "What We Don't Do" (2009).** Munger's "All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there" (via Jacobi, "Invert, always invert"). Four applications: avoid businesses whose futures you cannot judge, however exciting (autos in 1910, aircraft in 1930, TV sets in 1950: the growth was foreseeable, the profit margins were not; "Even the survivors tended to come away bleeding"); "We will never become dependent on the kindness of strangers" (in September 2008 Berkshire "was a supplier of liquidity and capital to the system, not a supplicant," with $15.5B committed, $9B to three businesses and $6.5B for the Wrigley deal, at the cost of $20B+ in cash earning "a pittance": "But we sleep well"); tolerate "a few bad decisions" by autonomous managers over "the many invisible costs that come from decisions made too slowly"; and no wooing of Wall Street.

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Fat pitch (Ted Williams, 1997).** From Williams's *The Science of Hitting*: the strike zone is 77 baseball-sized cells; the best cell yields .400 and the worst (low outside corner) .230. "waiting for the fat pitch would mean a trip to the Hall of Fame; swinging indiscriminately would mean a ticket to the minors." The honest cost: "just standing there, day after day, with my bat on my shoulder is not my idea of fun." The asymmetry (my paraphrase of the passage) is that an investor, unlike a hitter, is not called out on strikes, which is why waiting is possible at all.

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **The orangutan test and Graham-and-Doddsville (1984).** Imagine a national coin-flipping contest: of 225 million Americans, after ten flips "approximately 220,000 people" have called ten in a row, and after twenty flips "215 people" have turned a dollar into "a little over $1 million." The key move: if 40 of the 215 winning orangutans came "from a particular zoo in Omaha, you would be pretty sure you were on to something." The Columbia talk then names nine records (see Positions for the table). The epistemic rule: the exercise only works because the winners were "well known to me and pre-identified as superior investors"; chosen after the fact it fails. Observation across them: "it is extraordinary to me that the idea of buying dollar bills for 40 cents takes immediately to people or it doesn't take at all. It's like an inoculation."

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **The hamburger quiz (1997).** "If you expect to be a net saver during the next five years, should you hope for a higher or lower stock market during that period? Many investors get this one wrong." Net eaters of hamburger want cheaper beef. "there is a buyer for every seller and what hurts one necessarily helps the other." He applies it to Berkshire's own investees: 97% of Berkshire's shares are held by the same investors year to year, so owners are savers, and Coca-Cola, Washington Post and Wells Fargo bought back more ownership when prices were low.

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Relative to a yardstick you set in advance (Partnership, 2001).** "Whether we do a good job or a poor job is to be measured against the general experience in securities" (Ground Rules, quoted in 2001). Defense against "you can't eat relative performance": See's loses money in summer yet you "can eat well throughout the year"; gaining small advantages annually must prove rewarding. His scorecard history: bogey the S&P with dividends, proxy per-share book value (45-year numbers: book value +20.3% a year, $19 to $84,487; market +22%), "That keeps us from the temptation of seeing where the arrow of performance lands and then painting the bull's eye around it" (2009).

text: [Capital allocation, payout and the cost of activity] **Two-column intrinsic value (1999 and after).** Value Berkshire as per-share investments plus pre-tax operating earnings with investment income excluded. 1999: investments $45 (1969), $577 (1979), $7,200 (1989), $47,339 (1999); operating earnings $4.39, $13.07, $108.86, and $(458.55) in 1999 (a General Re underwriting loss). Later: $4 to $74,129 (2005, 28.0%) and $80,636 (2006, 27.5% since 1965 but 12.6% from 1995 to 2006); operating earnings $4 to $3,625 (17.9%, 31.7% for 1995 to 2006); 2015: $159,794 of investments per share and $12,304 of pre-tax operating earnings. The 2003 warning on base years: "growth-rate presentations can be significantly distorted by a calculated selection of either initial or terminal dates," so his table starts at 1968 (1964 earnings were $175,586, or 15 cents a share).

text: [Screening and buying] **Four-filter buy test (1977):** a business "(1) one that we can understand, (2) with favorable long-term prospects, (3) operated by honest and competent people, and (4) available at a very attractive price." Restated in 2003 as three parts: businesses that "(1) have favorable and enduring economic characteristics; (2) are run by talented and honest managers and (3) are available at a sensible price." Later compressed into the **four building blocks of value** (2017): sizable stand-alone acquisitions; bolt-ons; internal sales growth and margin improvement; investment earnings from the portfolio. The 2015 five-point successor blueprint adds repurchases at a meaningful discount and "rarely, if ever, issuing Berkshire shares."

text: [Screening and buying] **Be in businesses with tailwinds, not headwinds.** Even good management "can average only modest results" in a bad business (1977); "time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre" (1989). In 1998: "But time is the friend of the wonderful business; it is the enemy of the lousy business. If you are in a lousy business for a long time, you will get a lousy result even if you buy it cheap." Textiles, shoes and USAir were the cautionary tales; the 1983 warning on turnaround capex is the cost side: "The projections will be dazzling and the advocates sincere, but, in the end, major additional investment in a terrible industry usually is about as rewarding as struggling in quicksand" (Owner's Manual; originally 1983).

text: [Screening and buying] **Price, don't time; but do hold the price discipline hard.** "We try to price, rather than time, purchases… Why scrap an informed decision because of an uninformed guess?" (1994). "Fear is the foe of the faddist, but the friend of the fundamentalist" (1994). The choice between a questionable business at a comfortable price and a comfortable business at a questionable price: "we much prefer the latter. What really gets our attention, however, is a comfortable business at a comfortable price" (1999). The 2019 calibration after Kraft: "You can turn any investment into a bad deal by paying too much. What you can't do is turn any investment into a good deal by paying little, which is sort of how I started out in this world."

text: [Screening and buying] **Five-minute analysis, then no haggling.** "General Re is a $18 billion deal. I have never been to their home office. I hope it is there." "Almost every business we have bought has taken five or ten minutes in terms of analysis." On negotiation: "I don't fool a lot around with negotiations. text: [Screening and buying] **How the seller treats his people predicts how he treats you.** Helzberg: "Though he was certainly under no obligation to do so, Barnett shared a meaningful part of his proceeds from the sale with a large number of his associates. When someone behaves that generously, you know you are going to be treated right as a buyer" (1995). The Tatelmans paid their employees about $9 million of their own money at the Jordan's sale (1999); the Star owners did the same (1997).
quotes: Though he was certainly under no obligation to do so, Barnett shared a meaningful part of his proceeds from the sale with a large number of his associates. When someone behaves that generously, you know you are going to be treated right as a buyer
title: How the seller treats his people predicts how he treats you

text: [Screening and buying] **Sellers who love the company, not only the money.** "We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him"; a business auctioned with "a total lack of interest in what follows" has often "been dressed up for sale" (2000). A late-1960s counterpart: "Even if the price had been cheaper but the management had been run-of-the-mill, we would not have bought the business" (Hochschild Kohn, BPL 1966).
quotes: We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him
a total lack of interest in what follows
been dressed up for sale
Even if the price had been cheaper but the management had been run-of-the-mill, we would not have bought the business
title: Sellers who love the company, not only the money

text: [Screening and buying] **Buying what a manager has skin in:** R.C. Willey's Bill Child offered to buy the land, build the Boise store and sell it to Berkshire at cost "(without interest!)" if it worked, and "eat the loss" if it did not (2001). Buffett was "highly skeptical" of a no-Sunday format and turned out wrong three times (see Named mistakes); "the opinion of someone who is always wrong has its own special utility to decisionmakers" (2004).
quotes: eat the loss
the opinion of someone who is always wrong has its own special utility to decisionmakers
title: Buying what a manager has skin in

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Fix mistakes fast; the costliest errors are inaction.** The "cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes" (2024). His self-scored worst losses are "errors of omission, sucking my thumb when new facts came in that should have caused me to re-examine my thinking" (2008). The 2005 Gen Re Securities rule on acting now is under Named mistakes. On Wells Fargo: "if you're in the top job, you've got to take action fast" (2019 meeting); "The big mistake was whatever sufficient information had come back that this is producing a counterproductive effect... That's the moment of truth" (CNBC May 2017).
quotes: cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes
errors of omission, sucking my thumb when new facts came in that should have caused me to re-examine my thinking
if you're in the top job, you've got to take action fast
The big mistake was whatever sufficient information had come back that this is producing a counterproductive effect... That's the moment of truth
title: Fix mistakes fast; the costliest errors are inaction

text: [Avoiding the big error] **I make mistakes when I get cash.** "I make mistakes when I get cash. Charlie tells me to go to a bar instead" (U. Florida 1998, rbcpa), about buying Salomon and USAir preferreds when he "had a lot of money around" and "it looked to me like we would never get to do anything." The pattern he names: "Buying something because you like the terms, but you don't like the business that well."

had a lot of money around
it looked to me like we would never get to do anything.
Buying something because you like the terms, but you don't like the business that well.
title: I make mistakes when I get cash

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Never mix what should happen with what will happen.** "I never believe in mixing what I think should happen (socially) with what I think will happen in making decisions" (Partnership letter, May 1969, after workouts lost money: "in this case, we would be some millions better off if I had").
quotes: I never believe in mixing what I think should happen (socially) with what I think will happen in making decisions
in this case, we would be some millions better off if I had
title: Never mix what should happen with what will happen

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Never risk what you have and need for what you don't have and don't need.** "it is insane to risk what you have and need in order to obtain what you don't need" (2017); "anything times zero is zero" (Charlie Rose 2008). The 1998 form is expected-utility, not odds: "If you risk something that is important to you for something that is unimportant to you it just doesn't make sense. I don't care if the odds you succeed are 99 to 1 or 1000 to 1." And the million-chamber gun: "If you hand me a gun with a million chambers with one bullet in a chamber and put it up to your temple and I am paid to pull the trigger, it doesn't matter how much I would be paid." Also: "If you have $100 million at the beginning of the year and you will make 10% if you are unleveraged and 20% if you are leveraged 99 times out of a 100, what difference if at the end of the year, you have $110 million or $120 million?" (rbcpa 1998).

anything times zero is zero

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Probabilities of long chains and small chances.** The mono-linked chain (see Mental models); and from 2015: "what's a small probability in a short period approaches certainty in the longer run" (a one-in-thirty annual chance gives 96.6% over a century). The one risk he says he cannot hedge: a cyber, biological, nuclear or chemical attack on the United States.
quotes: what's a small probability in a short period approaches certainty in the longer run
title: Probabilities of long chains and small chances

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Read a 10-K's risk section for three things only.** "I can't remember, however, an instance when reading a 10-K's 'risk' section has helped me in evaluating a business." He wants probability, range of costs, and timing: "A threat that will only surface 50 years from now may be a problem for society, but it is not a financial problem for today's investor" (2015).
quotes: I can't remember, however, an instance when reading a 10-K's 'risk' section has helped me in evaluating a business.
A threat that will only surface 50 years from now may be a problem for society, but it is not a financial problem for today's investor
title: Read a 10-K's risk section for three things only

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Red flags in other people's accounts (2002).** "There is seldom just one cockroach in the kitchen" (the footnote rule is under Accounting); "Managers that always promise to 'make the numbers' will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers."
quotes: There is seldom just one cockroach in the kitchen
Managers that always promise to 'make the numbers' will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers.
title: Red flags in other people's accounts (2002)

text: [Avoiding the big error] **Sizing for survival: be the last man standing.** "We run it so that we will be the last man standing" (CNBC 2023). Berkshire's four-drawdown table (falls of 59%, 37%, 49%, 51%) is "the strongest argument… against ever using borrowed money to own stocks" (2017). The 2005 risk law: "a long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero." On promises of safety: "We are quite willing to accept huge risks" if sized to survive.
quotes: We run it so that we will be the last man standing
the strongest argument… against ever using borrowed money to own stocks
a long string of impressive numbers multiplied by a single zero always equals zero.

title: Sizing for survival: be the last man standing

text: [Process, people and communication] **Ignore macro forecasts (with a documented exception pattern).** "We will continue to ignore political and economic forecasts, which are an expensive distraction" (1994); "I've been in business, running Berkshire for 58 years, and I've never opined an economic forecast of any use to the company" (CNBC 2023).

I've been in business, running Berkshire for 58 years, and I've never opined an economic forecast of any use to the company
title: Ignore macro forecasts (with a documented exception pattern)

text: [Process, people and communication] **Ignore macro forecasts: the Partnership version (Ground Rule 6, BPL 1963 and 1966).** "I am not in the business of predicting general stock market or business fluctuations. If you think I can do this, or think it is essential to an investment program, you should not be in the partnership" (Ground Rule 6, 1963 and 1966), and the 1966 test: "(1) if they knew in February that the Dow was going to 865 in May, why didn't they let me in on it then; and, (2) if they didn't know what was going to happen during the ensuing three months back in February, how do they know in May?" Go "to where the puck is going to be, not to where it is" (Gretzky, quoted 1994), but the puck is business economics, not the Fed.
quotes: I am not in the business of predicting general stock market or business fluctuations. If you think I can do this, or think it is essential to an investment program, you should not be in the partnership

(1) if they knew in February that the Dow was going to 865 in May, why didn't they let me in on it then; and, (2) if they didn't know what was going to happen during the ensuing three months back in February, how do they know in May?
to where the puck is going to be, not to where it is
title: Ignore macro forecasts: the Partnership version (Ground Rule 6, BPL 1963 and 1966)

text: [Process, people and communication] **Dated exceptions to the no-forecast rule (2002 to 2006, 2019).** The exceptions: the 2002 to 2006 currency position (see Positions) and the 2019 remark "I don't think they can coexist with really low inflation rates over time. But I've been wrong on that for some time, I may be wrong for a long time in the future." Resolution (my reading): he states each macro call with error bars, in writing, and sizes it so it cannot hurt the fortress; the discipline is not to avoid holding any macro view but never to bet the company on one. Elections: "I can't think of when I've really done much about purchases or sales in connection with any election" (CNBC May 2017; the GDP-print line is under Macro).
quotes: I don't think they can coexist with really low inflation rates over time. But I've been wrong on that for some time, I may be wrong for a long time in the future.

title: Dated exceptions to the no-forecast rule (2002 to 2006, 2019)

text: [Process, people and communication] **Concentrate when conviction is real; act as if you have 20 punches.** "I could improve your ultimate financial welfare by giving you a ticket with only 20 slots in it… and once you'd punched through the card, you couldn't make any more investments at all" (Munger recounting Buffett, USC 1994). "if you… find five to ten sensibly-priced companies that possess important long-term competitive advantages, conventional diversification makes no sense for you" (1993). He put about 40% of the Partnership into American Express after the 1963 salad-oil scandal (1994). In 1998: "If you really know businesses, you probably shouldn't own more than six of them… Very few people have gotten rich on their seventh best idea. But a lot of people have gotten rich with their best idea."

title: Concentrate when conviction is real; act as if you have 20 punches

text: [Process, people and communication] **Bet on the jockey; align the incentives; eat your own cooking.** "I never look at where a candidate has gone to school. Never!" (2024). "We do not use options or other one-sided forms of compensation; if you lose money, so do we" (2024); "alignment means being a partner in both directions, not just on the upside. Many 'alignment' plans flunk this basic test, being artful forms of 'heads I win, tails you lose'" (1994). He adds a caution on reading people: "People are not that easy to read. Sincerity and empathy can easily be faked" (2023), and an 1863 line from Hugh McCulloch: "Never deal with a rascal under the expectation that you can prevent him from cheating you."

text: [Process, people and communication] **Delegate by handing over the baton.** On Lou Simpson (GEICO equities, 20.3% a year from 1980 to 2004 against 13.5% for the S&P): "When Charlie and I assign responsibility, we truly hand over the baton." "I typically learn of Lou's transactions about ten days after the end of each month. Sometimes, it should be added, I silently disagree with his decisions. But he's usually right" (2004). The 2001 admission: "I manage most of Berkshire's equity portfolio, and my results were poor, just as they have been for several years," while "Lou's performance has been far better than mine."
quotes: When Charlie and I assign responsibility, we truly hand over the baton.

title: Delegate by handing over the baton

text: [Process, people and communication] **Manager span of control and "merit badges."** "If I have one person reporting to me and he is a lemon, that's one too many, and if I have managers like those we now have, the number can be almost unlimited" (1995). "We distribute merit badges, not lottery tickets: In none of Berkshire's subsidiaries do we relate compensation to our stock price" (1997). Eddie Bennett, the batboy who joined winning teams, is the model: "to be a winner, work with winners" and "My job is to stay out of their way and allocate whatever excess capital their businesses generate. It's easy work" (2002). Managers are asked to run their companies "as if these are the sole asset of their families and will remain so for the next century" (1999); no show-and-tell presentations, no budgets to be approved by headquarters (1999).

My job is to stay out of their way and allocate whatever excess capital their businesses generate. It's easy work
as if these are the sole asset of their families and will remain so for the next century
title: Manager span of control and "merit badges."

text: [Process, people and communication] **Reputation is the bright line / the front-page test.** Taking over scandal-hit Salomon in 1991: "Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding; lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless." The operational test: before any act, ask whether you would be willing to see it appear "on the front page of [your] local paper" read by "spouses, children, and friends, with the reporting done by an informed and critical reporter" (1991 testimony). He asked "every Salomon employee to be his or her own compliance officer."
quotes: Lose money for the firm, and I will be understanding; lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless.
on the front page of [your] local paper
spouses, children, and friends, with the reporting done by an informed and critical reporter
every Salomon employee to be his or her own compliance officer.
title: Reputation is the bright line / the front-page test

text: [Process, people and communication] **Equal-information rule and Friday-night disclosure.** No earnings guidance and no one-on-one calls with large holders; "Our goal is to have all of our owners updated at the same time" (Owner's Manual). Financial data goes out late Friday or early Saturday: "There is no one more important to us than the shareholder of limited means who trusts us with a substantial portion of his savings" (2015).
quotes: Our goal is to have all of our owners updated at the same time
There is no one more important to us than the shareholder of limited means who trusts us with a substantial portion of his savings
title: Equal-information rule and Friday-night disclosure

text: [Process, people and communication] **Do not let a headline stand for the whole letter.** On the 2009 letter's one-line sentence that got half-quoted ("We are certain, for example, that the economy will be in shambles throughout 2009 – and probably well beyond – but that conclusion does not tell us whether the market will rise or fall"), the media quoted only the first half; the Dow closed the day of the letter at 7,063 and finished the year at 10,428: "I regard this as terrible journalism." The lesson for him: "Those who invest only when commentators are upbeat end up paying a heavy price for meaningless reassurance" (2009).
quotes: We are certain, for example, that the economy will be in shambles throughout 2009 – and probably well beyond – but that conclusion does not tell us whether the market will rise or fall
I regard this as terrible journalism.

title: Do not let a headline stand for the whole letter

text: [Process, people and communication] **Bad-news culture.** "Just tell me the bad news; the good news will take care of itself" (Munger's dictum, quoted 1995). (His 2004 whistleblower-line admission is under Governance.) In 2017, Berkshire's hotline received "about 4,000 complaints of one sort or another," routed to the head of internal audit, anonymous with "no retribution": "a pretty good percentage of the time it lead to something pretty big."
quotes: Just tell me the bad news; the good news will take care of itself
about 4,000 complaints of one sort or another,
a pretty good percentage of the time it lead to something pretty big.
title: Bad-news culture

text: [Process, people and communication] **Know when to shut down vs. subsidize a weak business.** "I won't close down businesses of sub-normal profitability merely to add a fraction of a point to our corporate rate of return. However, I also feel it inappropriate for even an exceptionally profitable company to fund an operation once it appears to have unending losses in prospect. Adam Smith would disagree with my first proposition, and Karl Marx would disagree with my second; the middle ground is the only position that leaves me comfortable" (1985, closing the textile mill). (The 1969 Partnership refusal to liquidate is under Pivot vs. persevere.) The Owner's Manual's statement of the exception: closed in the mid-1980s "after 20 years of struggling" only because it was "doomed to run never-ending operating losses."

title: Know when to shut down vs. subsidize a weak business

text: [Process, people and communication] **Know when to stop playing a game you no longer understand.** The 1969 Partnership wind-down: "I am not attuned to this market environment and I don't want to spoil a decent record by trying to play a game I don't understand just so I can go out a hero." The same discipline drives his 2023 crypto abstention. The 2023 letter applies the same honesty to scale: "Outside the U.S., there are essentially no candidates."
quotes: I am not attuned to this market environment and I don't want to spoil a decent record by trying to play a game I don't understand just so I can go out a hero.
Outside the U.S., there are essentially no candidates.
title: Know when to stop playing a game you no longer understand

text: [Pivot vs. persevere (when to kill a business)] Distinguish a temporary rough patch from a structurally doomed one; subsidize neither indefinitely.

[Pivot vs. persevere (when to kill a business)] **Berkshire textiles (1965 to 1985).** He funded it long past sense: "I wanted the business to succeed and wished my way into a series of bad decisions… wishing makes dreams come true only in Disney movies; it's poison in business" (2012). He shut it in 1985 admitting he "should be faulted for not quitting sooner." In December 1969 he had explicitly refused to liquidate: "I have no desire to trade severe human dislocations for a few percentage points additional return per annum" (about 1,100 employees), though compulsory additional investment or sustained operating losses "might have to be" a different decision (BPL Dec 1969). In 2017 he still counted the human cost: "it wasn't any fun eventually getting rid of 2,000 people working at Berkshire Textile Mills" (CNBC May 2017), and asked about his worst trade he answered "Yeah, but I have plenty of other competitors" (meaning Berkshire itself). The exchange on textiles: "What kind of an idiot would go into textiles in New England?" (Munger) and "The guy on your right" (Buffett).

text: [Pivot vs. persevere (when to kill a business)] **Waumbec Mills (1979).** He expanded the textile commitment by buying Waumbec (Manchester, NH) below working capital and "got very substantial amounts of machinery and real estate for less than nothing." "But the purchase was a mistake. While we labored mightily, new problems arose as fast as old problems were tamed." Lesson: "Both our operating and investment experience cause us to conclude that 'turnarounds' seldom turn" (see Mental models for the full quote and the dated tension with 1989 and 2023).

title: Waumbec Mills (1979)

text: [Pivot vs. persevere (when to kill a business)] **Dexter Shoe (1993, 1999, 2001, 2014, 2015).** He called shoes "a cyclical problem, not a secular one" in 1995 and was wrong; the 2001 letter lists the three decisions that hurt: "(1) buying it in the first place; (2) paying for it with stock and (3) procrastinating when the need for changes in its operations was obvious. I would like to lay these mistakes on Charlie (or anyone else, for that matter) but they were mine." In 2000 he charged off all the remaining Dexter accounting goodwill ("We may regain some economic goodwill at Dexter in the future, but we clearly have none at present"). The 2014 verdict is the dollar figure (of the stock used to pay for it: "shares I used for the purchase are now worth about $5.7 billion. As a financial disaster, this one deserves a spot in the Guinness Book of World Records") and the 2015 letter adds the human cost: "When low-cost competition drove shoe production to Asia, our once-prosperous Dexter operation folded, putting 1,600 employees in a small Maine town out of work."

text: [How to price (your own product, underwriting, a retail margin)] Price to exposure, never to volume or recent experience.

[How to price (your own product, underwriting, a retail margin)] **Insurance.** Price to exposure, not recent experience: the 9/11 admission and the three underwriting rules are under Insurance, float and underwriting (2001). GEICO prices to pass savings through rather than to maximize margin: in 1997 its underwriting margin was 8.1% against a deliberate 4% target, so rates were cut; in 1998 the margin was 6.7%, "better than we had anticipated" (and better than he wished, my paraphrase), so rates fell 3.3% with more cuts planned (1997, 1998).
quotes: better than we had anticipated
title: Insurance

text: [How to price (your own product, underwriting, a retail margin)] **Retail.** Mrs. Blumkin's rule: "If you have the lowest price, customers will find you at the bottom of a river" (2003). Borsheim's gross margin was "fully twenty percentage points below that of its major rivals" (2004). See's raises prices without losing the franchise, but he worries about volume: in 1983 same-store pounds were down 0.8% and about 8% cumulatively since 1979, and he refuses to cut quality: "We regard product quality as sacred" (1983).
quotes: If you have the lowest price, customers will find you at the bottom of a river
fully twenty percentage points below that of its major rivals
We regard product quality as sacred
title: Retail

text: [How to price (your own product, underwriting, a retail margin)] **A newspaper's news hole.** He refuses to cut the Buffalo News's 50% news hole for margin (page for page it gave readers over 25% more news than the typical paper), and treats a newspaper's penetration ratio as the best measure of its franchise strength; the News ranked number one in weekday penetration among the 100 largest U.S. papers and its Sunday circulation went from 270,000 (1976) to 376,000 (1984) (1983, paraphrase).
title: A newspaper's news hole

text: [When to sell a winner] Almost never. "If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes" (1996). Selling to lock gains forfeits the tax-deferred compounding engine; "one wonderful business can offset the many mediocre decisions that are inevitable" (2023). A senior security that matures is not "sold" (1995). He names his own reverse mistakes with the price tag attached:
quotes: If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes

text: [When to sell a winner] **GEICO, 1951 to 1952.** At 20 he took the train to Washington on a Saturday in January 1951, pounded on a closed door until a custodian appeared, and spent "four hours or so" with Lorimer Davidson learning why direct marketing gave GEICO a cost advantage agents could not copy: "After my session with Davy, I was more excited about GEICO than I have ever been about a stock." He bought 350 shares for $10,282 (by year end worth $13,125, more than 65% of his net worth; he already had more than 50% in it), then sold all in 1952 for $15,259 to switch into Western Insurance Securities at "slightly more than one times its current earnings." "But in the next 20 years, the GEICO stock I sold grew in value to about $1.3 million, which taught me a lesson about the inadvisability of selling a stake in an identifiably-wonderful company" (1995).

text: [When to sell a winner] **Disney, 1966 to 1967.** In 1966 Disney's market value was under $90M, pre-tax earnings about $21M, more cash than debt, with the $17M Pirates of the Caribbean ride about to open: "a company selling at only five times rides!" The Partnership bought a significant amount at a split-adjusted $31. "In 1967 I sold out at 48 per share." And: "That decision may appear brilliant, given that the stock now sells for $66. But your Chairman was up to the task of nullifying it" (1995).

text: [Focus vs. diversify (advice to others and to himself)] **Ground Rule 7 as an expected-value calculation (BPL Nov 1965 and Jan 1966).** "We diversify substantially less than most investment operations. We might invest up to 40% of our net worth in a single security under conditions coupling an extremely high probability that our facts and reasoning are correct with a very low probability that anything could drastically change the underlying value of the investment." The reasoning: with 50 uncorrelated ideas each worth 15 points over the Dow he would put 2% in each, but "We have to work extremely hard to find just a very few attractive investment situations." Position sizing is set so any single position (or correlated group) has only a "tiny" probability of making the whole portfolio more than ten points worse than the Dow. "any portfolio encompassing one hundred stocks (whether the manager is handling one thousand dollars or one billion dollars) is not being operated logically." "Noah School of Investing - two of everything. Such investors should be piloting arks." And Billy Rose's line: "You've got a harem of seventy girls; you don't get to know any of them very well."

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] Prefer friendly cash purchases of whole businesses run by managers who want to keep running them, evaluated "on an all-equity basis… We also never factor in, nor do we often find, synergies" (2017). The method is passive and referral-driven: "Our acquisition technique at Berkshire is simplicity itself: We answer the phone" (2000); "At Berkshire, our carefully-crafted acquisition strategy is simply to wait for the phone to ring" (1999); "We buy to keep" and have no "exit" strategy (2002). On hostile deals, even justified ones: "We, though, will leave these 'opportunities' for others. At Berkshire, we go only where we are welcome" (2015). Because Berkshire analyzes all purchases on an all-equity basis, when LBO financing collapsed in 2000 "our evaluations did not change, which means we became considerably more competitive" (2000).

Such a policy might seem axiomatic. Why, you might ask, would anyone issue dollar bills in exchange for fifty-cent pieces?" (1982). Reviewed action in 1997: every Berkshire stock-only merger (excluding Diversified Retailing and Blue Chip Stamps) left owners "slightly worse off" than no deal, while the cash deals (National Indemnity 1967, See's, Buffalo News, Scott Fetzer, GEICO) did "incredibly well." Reason: Berkshire's roster is full of ".380 hitters," so a deal adding a ".350 hitter" requires trading one. "Though it hurts me to say it, when I've issued stock, I've cost you money." A premium makes sense only if "a) its stock is overvalued relative to the acquiree's or b) the two enterprises will earn more combined than they would separately."

The target, a smaller similar bank, wanted nearly three times book in stock while the acquirer traded near book: "the owner of the small bank became richer, we became poorer." Munger's line: "Are we supposed to applaud because the dog that fouls our lawn is a Chihuahua rather than a Saint Bernard?" Management's rationalization: "We need to show that we are in the hunt. Besides, it's only a small deal." His fix: "Directors should hire a second advisor to make the case against the proposed acquisition, with its fee contingent on the deal not going through" and, failing that, "Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut" (2009).

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Illinois National Bank (1969) and the forced sale (1979).** Bought in 1969 for the Rockford bank; the Bank Holding Company Act required divestiture by Dec 31, 1980. In 1969 Boston's First National answered his $10M request at once ("they would supply the money for our purchase and that we would work out the details later") while a New York bank never responded; in 2001 FleetBoston did the same for Berkadia: "you've got the money and we'll work out the details later" (2001). The bank "earned approximately 2.3% on average assets last year, a level again over three times that achieved by the average major bank." Gene Abegg, then 82, ran it. The Fed held that in a spin-off no Berkshire officer or director could serve at the bank.
quotes: they would supply the money for our purchase and that we would work out the details later
you've got the money and we'll work out the details later
earned approximately 2.3% on average assets last year, a level again over three times that achieved by the average major bank.
title: Illinois National Bank (1969) and the forced sale (1979)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Selling Illinois National: choose the buyer, accept the cost (1979).** Forced by the Bank Holding Company Act, his decision rule for the sale: "We will be most choosy about any purchaser, and our selection will not be based solely on price. The bank and its management have treated us exceptionally well and, if we have to sell, we want to be sure that they are treated equally as well." And the cost: "we do not expect to be able to fully, or even in very large part, replace the earning power represented by the bank from the proceeds of the sale of the bank. You simply can't buy high quality businesses at the sort of price/earnings multiple likely to prevail on our bank sale" (1979).
quotes: We will be most choosy about any purchaser, and our selection will not be based solely on price. The bank and its management have treated us exceptionally well and, if we have to sell, we want to be sure that they are treated equally as well.

we do not expect to be able to fully, or even in very large part, replace the earning power represented by the bank from the proceeds of the sale of the bank. You simply can't buy high quality businesses at the sort of price/earnings multiple likely to prevail on our bank sale
title: Selling Illinois National: choose the buyer, accept the cost (1979)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Blue Chip Stamps (1970), the control purchase that went to zero.** Sales $126M, about 60 billion stamps licked, a 116-page rewards catalog: "When I was told that even certain brothels and mortuaries gave stamps to their patrons, I felt I had finally found a sure thing." Sales fell to $19.4M (1980), $1.5M (1990), then "fell another 98%"; in 2006 "all of $25,920 (no zeros omitted) came from Blue Chip." "No quitter, I redoubled my managerial efforts" (2006). (Blue Chip's float funded See's, Wesco and the Buffalo News; the 1983 appendix prices the See's piece.)
quotes: When I was told that even certain brothels and mortuaries gave stamps to their patrons, I felt I had finally found a sure thing.
fell another 98%
all of $25,920 (no zeros omitted) came from Blue Chip.
No quitter, I redoubled my managerial efforts
title: Blue Chip Stamps (1970), the control purchase that went to zero

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Nebraska Furniture Mart (1983).** Bought 90% from Rose Blumkin ("Mrs. B"), then 90, who had arrived from Russia, had no formal education and no English, and started in 1937 with $500 saved from selling used clothing; sales "over $100 million" from one 200,000 square foot store, more than all Omaha competitors combined. He left 10% with the family in management and optioned 10% to key young family managers; Mrs. B stayed chairman and kept selling carpet seven days a week. The deal was "quickly made" because he had "admired both the family and the business for decades." Why the model works: "built upon exceptional value to the customer that in turn translates into exceptional economics for its owners." Character evidence: when early resources ran out she sold furniture from her home "to pay creditors precisely as promised," and after proving she could profitably sell carpet at a huge discount she "sold the judge $1400 worth of carpet." He quotes Pascal on being unable to stay quietly in one room and adds "Even Pascal would have left the room for Mrs. Blumkin" (1983). The 'Berkshire Weekend' sales at NFM went from $5.3M (1997) to $25.1M (2004) and $30M (2006).
quotes: over $100 million
admired both the family and the business for decades.
built upon exceptional value to the customer that in turn translates into exceptional economics for its owners.
to pay creditors precisely as promised,
sold the judge $1400 worth of carpet.
Even Pascal would have left the room for Mrs. Blumkin
title: Nebraska Furniture Mart (1983)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Scott Fetzer (1985): the anti-auction.** A major banker had failed to sell it; after Buffett wrote to CEO Ralph Schey, "I had never met Ralph, but within a week we had a deal." The engagement letter still owed the bank $2.5 million and the banker offered the sales "book"; Munger answered "I'll pay $2.5 million not to read it" (1999). Net price $230 million; Schey (hired at 61) ran it 15 years and "the company distributed $1.03 billion to Berkshire" (2000).
quotes: I had never met Ralph, but within a week we had a deal.
I'll pay $2.5 million not to read it
the company distributed $1.03 billion to Berkshire
title: Scott Fetzer (1985): the anti-auction

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **GEICO (1976 to 1996).** In the early 1970s management "made some serious errors in estimating their claims costs," which "almost caused it to go bankrupt"; Jack Byrne became CEO in 1976 (1995). "Because I believed both in Jack and in GEICO's fundamental competitive strength, Berkshire purchased a large interest": $45.7M for 33.3% by year end 1980, no purchases for 15 years, and a stake that grew to about 50% through GEICO's own buybacks. In 1995 Berkshire agreed to pay $2.3B for the other half. "That is a steep price," justified by the same moat, Tony Nicely (insurance) and Lou Simpson (investments, 22.8% a year from 1980 to 1995 against 15.7% for the S&P); expense ratio 23.6% of premiums (1995).
quotes: made some serious errors in estimating their claims costs,
almost caused it to go bankrupt
Because I believed both in Jack and in GEICO's fundamental competitive strength, Berkshire purchased a large interest
That is a steep price,
title: GEICO (1976 to 1996)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **GEICO's customer-acquisition economics (1999).** Marketing spend rose from $33M and 652 phone counselors (1995) to $143M and 2,162 counselors (1998) and $242M and 2,631 counselors (1999); "we would happily commit $1 billion annually to marketing if we knew we could handle the business smoothly and if we expected the last dollar spent to produce new business at an attractive cost." Advertising buys "a direct relationship with a huge number of households that, on average, will send us $1,100 year after year"; in 1999 customers added 766,256 and GEICO "gained $590 million of cash from operating earnings and the increase in float."
quotes: we would happily commit $1 billion annually to marketing if we knew we could handle the business smoothly and if we expected the last dollar spent to produce new business at an attractive cost.
a direct relationship with a huge number of households that, on average, will send us $1,100 year after year
gained $590 million of cash from operating earnings and the increase in float.
title: GEICO's customer-acquisition economics (1999)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **GEICO's two-variable incentive plan and the advertising ceiling (1999, 2004, 2015).** Compensation is on two variables only: policyholder growth and profit on seasoned (more than one year old) business, so, as he told associates, "we will foot the bill for new business"; profit sharing was 28.4% of salary ($113.3M) in 1999 and 24.3% ($191M) in 2004. The 1999 limit he named: "inquiries per ad fall for all of us" as advertising rises, and about 40% of people checking rates find they can save; the referral floor, "we probably could maintain our policy count by spending as little as $50 million annually." Also an insurance-industry history lesson (2004, 2015): "Though the early bird gets the worm, the second mouse gets the cheese," and "It was clear to me that GEICO would succeed because it deserved to succeed."
quotes: we will foot the bill for new business
inquiries per ad fall for all of us
we probably could maintain our policy count by spending as little as $50 million annually.
Though the early bird gets the worm, the second mouse gets the cheese,
It was clear to me that GEICO would succeed because it deserved to succeed.
title: GEICO's two-variable incentive plan and the advertising ceiling (1999, 2004, 2015)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Gillette preferred (1989) and the Salomon and USAir convertibles (1987 to 1989).** See the Named mistakes ledger.
title: Gillette preferred (1989) and the Salomon and USAir convertibles (1987 to 1989)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Helzberg's Diamond Shops (1995): acquisitions by walking around.** A week after the 1994 meeting, Buffett crossed 58th and Fifth in New York when Barnett Helzberg Jr., who owned four Berkshire shares, stopped him; Helzberg's had 134 stores in 23 states, founded in 1915, with sales of $10M (1974), $53M (1984) and $282M (1994). Barnett, 60, wanted diversification. Berkshire bought it in 1995 in a tax-free stock exchange, the only structure Barnett wanted, and "we would not have bought the business if Jeff [Comment] had not been there to run it." "Buying a retailer without good management is like buying the Eiffel Tower without an elevator." Screening rule: when people say they have a business, "it usually turns out they have a lemonade stand," so he only asked for particulars (1995). Ben Bridge Jeweler followed in 2000, agreed "by phone, prior to any face-to-face meeting" on referral from Barnett Helzberg, with same-store sales +9%, +11%, +13%, +10%, +12%, +21% and +7% over seven years (2000).
quotes: we would not have bought the business if Jeff [Comment] had not been there to run it.
Buying a retailer without good management is like buying the Eiffel Tower without an elevator.
it usually turns out they have a lemonade stand,
by phone, prior to any face-to-face meeting
title: Helzberg's Diamond Shops (1995): acquisitions by walking around

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **R.C. Willey (1995, 1999, 2001, 2004, 2005).** Irv Blumkin told Bill Child of the Blumkin family's good Berkshire experience; in early 1995 Child mentioned estate-tax and diversification reasons to sell. Child took over from his father-in-law in 1954 at sales of about $250,000; 1995 sales were $257M, over 50% of Utah furniture. Process: "Bill sent me some figures, and I wrote him a letter indicating my idea of value. We quickly agreed on a number, and found our personal chemistry to be perfect" (1995).
quotes: Bill sent me some figures, and I wrote him a letter indicating my idea of value. We quickly agreed on a number, and found our personal chemistry to be perfect
title: R.C. Willey (1995, 1999, 2001, 2004, 2005)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **R.C. Willey's Boise and Las Vegas stores: the founder's capital at risk (1999 to 2004).** In 1997 Child wanted a Boise store and offered to build it at his own risk ($9M in the 1999 letter, $11M in the 2001 letter; the discrepancy is in the sources) and sell it at cost; Buffett offered to take the downside and "Bill said nothing doing." Opened August 1999, "immediately became a huge success"; Child transferred it at cost and "refused to take a dime of interest on the capital he had tied up over the two years." Las Vegas then "outsells all others in the R.C. Willey chain" at "twice what I had anticipated" (2001); a second store 20 minutes away that Buffett predicted would cannibalize ("In truth, I thought they were mistakes") does 26% more volume than any other store in the chain (2004). "Today, when I pontificate about retailing, Berkshire people just say, 'What does Bill think?'" (2001). NFM's new Kansas City store "will keep this store open on Sundays" (2001).

immediately became a huge success
refused to take a dime of interest on the capital he had tied up over the two years.
outsells all others in the R.C. Willey chain
twice what I had anticipated

title: R.C. Willey's Boise and Las Vegas stores: the founder's capital at risk (1999 to 2004)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Star Furniture (1997) and Jordan's (1999).** Star (Houston, Melvyn Wolff and Shirley Toomin, 12 stores, family since 1924) was done "in a single, two-hour session" in New York: "I had no need to check leases, work out employment contracts, etc. I knew I was dealing with a man of integrity and that's what counted" (closed July 1, 1997). Jordan's (Tatelman brothers, family business since 1927, "shoppertainment," the highest sales per square foot of any major U.S. furniture operation) was found by the "any more at home like you?" chain. Berkshire bought assets for cash so goodwill amortizes over 15 years for tax, "a procedure that will maximize the cash produced for our shareholders but minimize the earnings we report to you" (1999).
quotes: in a single, two-hour session
I had no need to check leases, work out employment contracts, etc. I knew I was dealing with a man of integrity and that's what counted
any more at home like you?
a procedure that will maximize the cash produced for our shareholders but minimize the earnings we report to you
title: Star Furniture (1997) and Jordan's (1999)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **International Dairy Queen (1998).** 5,792 stores in 23 countries; trigger: an owner (Luther) had died and his estate needed to sell; a cash-or-Berkshire-stock choice patterned on the FlightSafety deal and tilted toward cash (only 45% chose cash). "We have put our money where our mouth is": Buffett was a regular at the Omaha DQ (1997). Decision pattern: he buys what he uses.
quotes: We have put our money where our mouth is
title: International Dairy Queen (1998)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **NetJets (1998, $725M).** Buffett was a customer first: Frank Rooney recommended it; "It took Rich about 15 minutes to sell me a quarter (200 hours annually) of a Hawker 1000"; his family flew 900 hours on 300 trips; he made a testimonial ad "long before I knew there was any possibility of our purchasing the business" and asked Rich Santulli to call if he ever wanted to sell. Santulli phoned in May 1998. Moat logic: the largest operator (1,000 customers, 163 aircraft, 31% of corporate jet orders in 1997) sells multiple manufacturers' planes while two rivals "prescribe" their own house brand; FlightSafety supplies pilot training. He sold the Berkshire plane. "Alice, you aren't buying it; your heirs are" (the Aunt Alice and fur coat joke) (1998). On selection: "I viewed the selection of a flight provider as akin to picking a brain surgeon: you simply want the best" (2004); "Once a customer has tried us, going back to commercial aviation is like going back to holding hands" (2003). The later losses are in the ledger.
quotes: It took Rich about 15 minutes to sell me a quarter (200 hours annually) of a Hawker 1000
long before I knew there was any possibility of our purchasing the business
Alice, you aren't buying it; your heirs are
I viewed the selection of a flight provider as akin to picking a brain surgeon: you simply want the best
Once a customer has tried us, going back to commercial aviation is like going back to holding hands
title: NetJets (1998, $725M)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **General Re (1998, $22B).** The largest U.S. property-casualty reinsurer (plus 82% of Cologne Re). Berkshire took over the investment portfolio but not underwriting; asked Gen Re to retain more of its business: "Berkshire, in contrast, happily accepts volatility, just as long as it carries with it the expectation of increased profits over time," and "we are a Fort Knox of capital, and that means volatile earnings can't impair our premier credit ratings." After closing, Gen Re dumped about 250 stock positions, incurring $935 million of taxes, because "We don't back into decisions" (1998). He bought it with minimal due diligence (the "home office" line under Decision heuristics, U. Florida talk, Oct 1998; the letter gives $22 billion at closing). **[CHECK, dated]** The 1998 optimism ("Berkshire can add absolutely nothing to the skills of General Re's and Cologne Re's managers") became, in 2001 to 2003, the admission that Gen Re was "grossly mispricing" and underreserved; see Named mistakes.
quotes: Berkshire, in contrast, happily accepts volatility, just as long as it carries with it the expectation of increased profits over time,
we are a Fort Knox of capital, and that means volatile earnings can't impair our premier credit ratings.
We don't back into decisions
Berkshire can add absolutely nothing to the skills of General Re's and Cologne Re's managers
title: General Re (1998, $22B)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **MidAmerican Energy (1999 to 2005).** Walter Scott Jr. introduced it at a California conference in September 1999; Buffett read public reports and "had two short meetings with Walter and David Sokol," then said he would deal "at an appropriate price." The structure was forced by the 1935 holding-company act: an 11% fixed-income security, common stock and exchangeable preferred that gave Berkshire "just under 10% of the voting power of MidAmerican but about 76% of the equity interest," about $2B in all, with Walter and family buying about $280M of stock for cash (1999). In 2003 Berkshire owned 80.5% (fully diluted), voting limited to 9.9% under PUHCA, with $1.578B of junior debt owed to Berkshire at 11%; the U.K. unit went from 6,800 employees at denationalization (March 31, 1990) to 2,539 serving the same customers (2003).
quotes: had two short meetings with Walter and David Sokol,
at an appropriate price.
just under 10% of the voting power of MidAmerican but about 76% of the equity interest,
title: MidAmerican Energy (1999 to 2005)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Northern Natural Gas (2002): the Enron pipeline bought in three days.** An Enron history (1985 InterNorth merged with Houston Natural Gas on a promise to stay in Omaha; Ken Lay renamed it Enron and moved it to Houston within a year); Enron put it up as collateral for a Dynegy loan; Dynegy wanted "a quick and certain cash sale"; call Friday July 26, contract July 29, "Dynegy phoned the right party" (2002).
quotes: a quick and certain cash sale
Dynegy phoned the right party
title: Northern Natural Gas (2002): the Enron pipeline bought in three days

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Kern River, PacifiCorp and the turn to capital-intensive utilities (2002 to 2009).** Kern River ($1.2B expansion) and PacifiCorp (2005, $3.4B of MidAmerican stock plus $1.7B of borrowing): "You can't expect to earn outsized profits in regulated utilities, but the industry offers owners the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns" (2005). The 2009 shift: "In earlier days, Charlie and I shunned capital-intensive businesses such as public utilities," now accepted for the expectation of "ever-increasing amounts of cash" and "reasonable expectations of earning decent returns on the incremental sums they invest" (2009).
quotes: You can't expect to earn outsized profits in regulated utilities, but the industry offers owners the opportunity to deploy large sums at fair returns
In earlier days, Charlie and I shunned capital-intensive businesses such as public utilities,
ever-increasing amounts of cash
reasonable expectations of earning decent returns on the incremental sums they invest
title: Kern River, PacifiCorp and the turn to capital-intensive utilities (2002 to 2009)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **The 2000 wave: eight businesses, $8 billion, 97% cash.** CORT Business Services: a one-page fax on Nov 23, 1999 from airplane broker Bruce Cort with a Washington Post article on a failed buyout; Buffett "printed out its SEC filings" that day, met CEO Paul Arnold Nov 29, and bought through Wesco for about $386M cash: "a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price (going by that on the failed deal) that made sense." U.S. Liability (introduced by Ron Ferguson of General Re, half stock half cash by phone).
quotes: printed out its SEC filings
a fine though unglamorous business, an outstanding manager, and a price (going by that on the failed deal) that made sense.
title: The 2000 wave: eight businesses, $8 billion, 97% cash

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Justin, Shaw, Benjamin Moore and Johns Manville (2000).** Justin Industries (boots and Acme brick): a stranger's May 4 fax from Mark Jones; bought for $570M cash; Acme makes over a billion bricks a year in 22 plants, about 11.7% of national output; 75% of Texans name Acme. Shaw Industries: after Buffett refused an uncapped asbestos policy for a prospective merger partner ("we would never issue a policy that lacked a cap"), the carpet maker's owners kept at least 5% and Berkshire owns 87.3%. Benjamin Moore: call from a director he knew from Salomon; "we made a $1 billion cash offer on the spot." Johns Manville: LBO financing collapsed Friday Dec 8; "The following Monday" Buffett and Munger made an all-cash offer with no financing contingencies; trustees voted the next day; about $1.8B.
quotes: we would never issue a policy that lacked a cap
we made a $1 billion cash offer on the spot.
The following Monday
title: Justin, Shaw, Benjamin Moore and Johns Manville (2000)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Why sellers pick Berkshire, and the anti-synergy promise (2000).** "We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him"; a Rembrandt owner prefers choosing the permanent home to having "a trust officer or uninterested heirs auction it off" (2000). The anti-synergy promise to Ben Bridge's family: "No one wanted another jewelry chain to come in and decimate the organization with ideas about synergy and cost saving (which, though they would never work, were certain to be tried)."
quotes: We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him
a trust officer or uninterested heirs auction it off
No one wanted another jewelry chain to come in and decimate the organization with ideas about synergy and cost saving (which, though they would never work, were certain to be tried).
title: Why sellers pick Berkshire, and the anti-synergy promise (2000)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Fruit of the Loom (2001), from Graham-Newman in 1955.** Backstory: Buffett was one of five employees of Graham-Newman when Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron (P&R) bought Union Underwear (licensee of the Fruit of the Loom name) for $15M, with "Fully $9 million of the remaining $12.5 million due" satisfied by non-interest-bearing notes payable from 50% of any earnings above $1 million: "(Those were the days; I get goosebumps just thinking about such deals.)" Fruit later earned over $200M pre-tax. Why it failed: John Holland ran it in its best years; after he retired in 1996 "management loaded the company with debt, in part to make a series of acquisitions that proved disappointing. Bankruptcy followed."
quotes: Fully $9 million of the remaining $12.5 million due
(Those were the days; I get goosebumps just thinking about such deals.)
management loaded the company with debt, in part to make a series of acquisitions that proved disappointing. Bankruptcy followed.
title: Fruit of the Loom (2001), from Graham-Newman in 1955

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Fruit of the Loom: buying the debt, then the company (2001).** Berkshire bought public and bank debt at about 50% of face early in the bankruptcy (about a 15% current return, reaching 10% of the senior debt, "probably end up returning us about 70% of face value"), then made a whole-company bid "to which we attached no financing conditions, even though our offer had to remain outstanding for many months," with the proviso that "John had to be available to continue serving as CEO after we took over. To us, John and the brand are Fruit's key assets." "What goes around truly does come around" (2001).
quotes: probably end up returning us about 70% of face value
to which we attached no financing conditions, even though our offer had to remain outstanding for many months,
John had to be available to continue serving as CEO after we took over. To us, John and the brand are Fruit's key assets.
What goes around truly does come around
title: Fruit of the Loom: buying the debt, then the company (2001)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Acme Boot, P&R's second Graham-Newman-era deal (told in 2001).** Acme Boot, P&R's second deal (price $3.2M, sales $7M, also part paid in non-interest notes), became "the world's largest bootmaker," then "eventually hit the skids and never recovered"; H.H. Brown bought its inventory and trademarks for $700,000 in December 2001. Graham and Dodd quote Horace: "Many shall be restored that now are fallen and many shall fall that are now in honor."
quotes: the world's largest bootmaker,
eventually hit the skids and never recovered
Many shall be restored that now are fallen and many shall fall that are now in honor.
title: Acme Boot, P&R's second Graham-Newman-era deal (told in 2001)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **FINOVA and Berkadia (2001).** Late 2000 Berkshire began buying FINOVA's obligations ($11B outstanding), 13% "at about two-thirds of face value": "We expected the company to go into bankruptcy, but believed that liquidation of its assets would produce a payoff for creditors that would be well above our cost." With Leucadia, a prepackaged plan paid creditors 70% of face plus full interest and a 7.5% note for the remaining 30%; the vehicle Berkadia borrowed $5.6B from FleetBoston and relent to FINOVA with a priority claim at a spread of about two points (90% Berkshire, 10% Leucadia); Berkshire guaranteed 90% of Berkadia's borrowing; an offer for up to $500M of new bonds was withdrawn when the NYSE closed the week of 9/11. The resulting $6B loan was oversubscribed by 17 banks: "if you ever need $6 billion, just give Chad a call - assuming, that is, your credit is AAA."
quotes: at about two-thirds of face value
We expected the company to go into bankruptcy, but believed that liquidation of its assets would produce a payoff for creditors that would be well above our cost.
if you ever need $6 billion, just give Chad a call - assuming, that is, your credit is AAA.
title: FINOVA and Berkadia (2001)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **XTRA and Larson-Juhl (2001).** XTRA was bought by tender offer expiring September 11, 2001, with an "out" if markets closed; its CEO Lew Rubin knew Berkshire could back away while his son-in-law in the World Trade Center was unaccounted for; Berkshire completed the deal. Larson-Juhl: a December 3 call from Craig Ponzio (sales from $3M to $300M since 1981), "in ninety minutes we reached an agreement. In ten days we had signed a contract."
quotes: in ninety minutes we reached an agreement. In ten days we had signed a contract.
title: XTRA and Larson-Juhl (2001)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **The Pampered Chef (2002).** Doris Christopher founded it in 1980, borrowing $3,000 against her life insurance policy ("all the money ever injected into the company"); the first party had $175 of sales, first-year sales $50,000, and 22 years later more than $700M and 67,000 consultants. Sheila O'Connell Cooper was CEO for two years. "It took me about ten seconds to decide that these were two managers with whom I wished to partner" (2002); Buffett attended a party himself. Entry criteria: "economic characteristics ranging from good to great, run by managers ranging from great to great," plus "a sensible purchase price."
quotes: all the money ever injected into the company
It took me about ten seconds to decide that these were two managers with whom I wished to partner
economic characteristics ranging from good to great, run by managers ranging from great to great,
a sensible purchase price.
title: The Pampered Chef (2002)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Clayton Homes (2003), found through a student gift.** Prof. Al Auxier brings about 40 University of Tennessee finance students to Omaha each year; in February 2003 their thank-you gift was Jim Clayton's autobiography. He already knew Clayton was "the class act of the manufactured housing industry" from knowledge acquired "after earlier making the mistake of buying some distressed junk debt of Oakwood Homes": "At the time of that purchase, I did not understand how atrocious consumer-financing practices had become throughout most of the manufactured housing industry. But I learned: Oakwood rather promptly went bankrupt."
quotes: the class act of the manufactured housing industry
after earlier making the mistake of buying some distressed junk debt of Oakwood Homes

At the time of that purchase, I did not understand how atrocious consumer-financing practices had become throughout most of the manufactured housing industry. But I learned: Oakwood rather promptly went bankrupt.
title: Clayton Homes (2003), found through a student gift

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Clayton Homes: the offer made from a book (2003).** He phoned CEO Kevin Clayton, judged him "both able and a straight-shooter," and "I made an offer for the business based solely on Jim's book, my evaluation of Kevin, the public financials of Clayton and what I had learned from the Oakwood experience." The board was receptive because lenders had fled. The diagnosis: "Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn't have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent." Full circle: Clayton agreed to buy Oakwood's assets, so Berkshire's discounted Oakwood debt likely returned a small profit. Each of the 40 students got a "PhD (for phenomenal, hard-working dealmaker)" and a B share; Auxier got an A share.
quotes: both able and a straight-shooter,
I made an offer for the business based solely on Jim's book, my evaluation of Kevin, the public financials of Clayton and what I had learned from the Oakwood experience.
Much of its volume a few years back came from buyers who shouldn't have bought, financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent.
PhD (for phenomenal, hard-working dealmaker)

text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Clayton Homes after the purchase: financing and lending discipline (2003, 2004, 2015).** The $1.7B acquisition; Berkshire then borrowed $2B and re-lent it to Clayton at a markup (see Raise vs. bootstrap / leverage; 2003, 2004). text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **McLane (2003): $23 billion of sales at about a 1% pre-tax margin.** Banker Byron Trott told him in early spring that Wal-Mart wished to sell. text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Forest River (2005) and Business Wire (2005).** Forest River (RV maker, $1.6B sales, Pete Liegl): a two-page fax on June 21, figures the next morning, an offer that afternoon, a handshake on June 28; Liegl's earlier LBO sale had sunk the business into bankruptcy until he repurchased it. text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Kraft Heinz (2013 to 2019).** Berkshire owned about 53% of Heinz at a cost of $4.25B; after the Kraft merger it owned 325.4M shares (about 27%) costing $9.8B, and GAAP forced a $6.8B write-up though "we sold no Kraft Heinz shares," "an outcome only an accountant could love." The preferred ($720M a year, carried at $7.7B) was redeemed at $8.32B: "good news for Kraft Heinz and bad news for Berkshire." Philosophy contrast with 3G (Lemann, Behring, Hees): they buy bloated companies and cut fast; Berkshire buys businesses "long been run by cost-conscious and efficient managers." Munger's line used to justify non-interference: "If you want to guarantee yourself a lifetime of misery, be sure to marry someone with the intent of changing their behavior" (2015). The 2019 reckoning is in the ledger.
