text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Occidental (2019, 2023).** The 2019 timeline is in Mental models (Friday call, Sunday handshake). Why Berkshire: no committees or MAC clauses; "I can get a call on Friday afternoon, and they can make a date with me on Saturday, and on Sunday, it's done"; their board approved Monday 10 p.m., announced Tuesday (2019 meeting). Secrecy: plane trackers deduced the deal ("if they take a NetJets plane nobody will be able to track them") (CNBC May 2019). **Evolution:** in 2019 he described a financing deal (preferred plus warrants); in 2023 Berkshire owned 27.8% of the common plus warrants ("Berkshire has no interest in purchasing or managing Occidental") with an energy-independence rationale (U.S. production 8 million BOEPD in 1975, 5 million by 2007, more than 13 million now) and "No one knows what oil prices will do over the next month, year, or decade. text: [When to acquire (policy), and the stories behind it] **Apple (2016 on).** Berkshire's stake rose to 5.4% via Apple's own buybacks (2020); its look-through earnings dwarf the dividends (2021, see Mental models); by 2019 Berkshire owned "more than $50 billion" of Apple. Why Apple but not Google or Amazon (CNBC May 2017): "Apple didn't have to do a lot better in the future than they were doing at the current time"; with Google and Amazon "you're paying for the future more." Apple's pricing power observed at Nebraska Furniture Mart: price drives TV and appliance traffic, but "They don't want the cheapest product" in phones. The real moat threat: "benefit competition," not price competition. Tim Cook "has made Berkshire a lot more money than I've ever made" (2025 meeting). Munger's quip (2019): "Maybe Apple was atonement."

text: [Named mistakes ledger (situation, action, price tag, quote, source year)] **Fifteen-year bonds (1979).** Written after rates jumped in early 1980. "You do not adequately protect yourself by being half awake while others are sleeping. It was a mistake to buy fifteen-year bonds, and yet we did; we made an even more serious mistake in not selling them (at losses, if necessary) when our present views began to crystallize." Accountability: "our mistakes should be viewed less charitably than the mistakes of those who went about their business unmindful of the developing problems." The industry argument underneath: insurers decided "that one year is too long a period for which to set a fixed price for insurance in an inflationary world," then "taken the proceeds from the sale of that six-month policy, and sold the money at a fixed price for thirty or forty years." His decision rule: "Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be" (Polonius, slightly restated) (1979). He flagged his own uncertainty: "We even may miss large profits from a major rebound in bond prices."

text: [Named mistakes ledger (situation, action, price tag, quote, source year)] **The Gillette preferred (1989).** $600M of convertible preferred into 48M split-adjusted common shares. He could "probably" have bought 60M common shares at about $10.50 in a private placement, at a discount of at least 5%. "But I was far too clever to do that." The preferred was called within two years. "If I had negotiated for common rather than preferred, we would have been better off at yearend 1995 by $625 million, minus the 'excess' dividends of about $70 million." By 1997 the $600M had become $4.8B.

text: [Named mistakes ledger (situation, action, price tag, quote, source year)] **Why Gen Re Securities was dangerous, in his words (2002, 2003, 2006).** On the risk itself: "No matter how financially sophisticated you are, you can't possibly learn from reading the disclosure documents of a derivatives-intensive company what risks lurk in its positions" and Darwin: "Ignorance more frequently begets confidence than does knowledge" (2003). Why he and Munger knew: reported profits "struck us as illusory," risks "could not effectively be measured or limited," trouble would "correlate with troubles in the financial or insurance world" so the unit "would commandeer the capital and credit of Berkshire at just the time we could otherwise deploy those resources to huge advantage" (2003). Mark-to-model "degenerates into what I would call mark-to-myth" (2002). Munger's tombstone for the book in 2006: "Good Until Reached For"; "All's well that ends."

text: [Named mistakes ledger (situation, action, price tag, quote, source year)] **Defending Tim Sloan, against Munger (2019 meeting).** Defense of Tim Sloan (2019): "I was 100% behind Tim Sloan... I would have never asked for the resignation," and a Wall Street hire would be "pinatas from now until the election time... They'd be poison in Washington"; he diverged from Munger, who thought predecessors (Kovacevich, Stumpf) were the problem: "I like Dick Kovacevich. Dick expresses himself very forcefully, Charlie expresses himself forcefully and maybe the two don't mix that well." Munger on the same panel: "I don't think people ought to go to jail for honest errors of judgment." **[CHECK, dated, resolved]** The baseline critique (that as the largest holder he took no action to stop it) and the 2017 self-defense ("I was not a director") are both on the record; the synthesis is that as a roughly 10% holder who spoke to the CEO about once a year he took the position that he had no inside information, and in 2019 he stated the rule for others: "if you're in the top job, you've got to take action fast."

A larger bank owned 25.5% and wanted a merger blocked "for personal reasons." He bought about 12% at an average of about $51 over roughly a year (a position of 10% to 20% of partnership assets), becoming the second-largest holder. "Obviously it was definitely to our advantage to have the stock remain dormant in price." About 300 holders and "two trades or so per month."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Commonwealth Trust: the price move, the test and the exit (BPL 1958).** Competition lifted the price to $65 ("Very small buying orders can create price changes of this magnitude in an inactive stock, which explains the importance of not having any 'Leakage' regarding our portfolio holdings"), and he stopped buying. Three-part test: "1. Very strong defensive characteristics; 2. Good solid value building up at a satisfactory pace and; 3. Evidence to the effect that eventually this value would be unlocked although it might be one year or ten years." Exit: sold at $80 when he found a special situation where the Partnership could be the largest holder (replacement about 25% of assets). His warning on reading short records: realized profit in any single year is "fortuitous," so a one-year record has "serious limitations as a basis for estimating long term results."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Sanborn Map Co. (1960 letter, dated Jan 30, 1961): the 35% position.** A fire-insurance-map near-monopoly (after-tax map profits over $500,000 in the late 1930s, under $100,000 by 1958 to 1959 after "carding") that had accumulated about $2.5M of securities (original cost), worth about $7M. The valuation gap: in 1938, with the Dow at 100 to 120, the stock was $110 with $20 a share of portfolio, so the map business was valued at $90; in 1958, with the Dow near 550, the stock was $45 with a $65 portfolio, so the map business "was evaluated at a minus $20 with the buyer of the stock unwilling to pay more than 70 cents on the dollar for the investment portfolio with the map business thrown in for nothing."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Sanborn Map: the action and the result (BPL Jan 1961).** He bought the widow's block of 15,000 shares after a family dispute and grew holdings with allies to about 46,000 shares; Booz Allen's consultants also recommended separation; instead of a proxy fight he offered to take out any holder at fair value in portfolio securities (the SEC ruled the plan fair). Result: about 72% of the shares (50% of 1,600 holders) exchanged for portfolio securities; the map business kept over $1.25M in bonds and avoided a corporate capital-gains tax of more than $1M. It reached 35% of net assets at one point. Meta lesson: "Such control situations may occur very infrequently. Our bread-and-butter business is buying undervalued securities and selling when the undervaluation is corrected along with investment in special situations where the profit is dependent on corporate rather than market action."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Dempster Mill Manufacturing (1956 to 1963, told in the Jan 18, 1964 letter).** Situation (1956): stock $18, book $72, of which $50 a share was current assets net of all liabilities; "The qualitative situation was on the negative side (a fairly tough industry and unimpressive management), but the figures were extremely attractive." Base rate: "Experience shows you can buy 100 situations like this and have perhaps 70 or 80 work out to reasonable profits in one to three years." He bought for five years at $16 to $25 while a director; by mid-1961 about 30% (tender offers drew "poor results"); purchases at $30.25 in August and September 1961 and a tender at the same price took him past 70%. Valuation at 11/30/61: cash 100%, receivables 85%, inventory 60%, prepaids 25%, plant at estimated auction $800K, giving $35.25 a share.

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Dempster Mill: the Harry Bottle turnaround (BPL Jan 1964).** Management: he first promoted the executive vice president "to see what he would do unfettered by the previous policies. The results were unsatisfactory," and hired Harry Bottle (April 17, 1962; in the president's chair April 23). Bottle's changes: inventory from over $4,203,000 to $890,000; administrative and selling expense from $150,000 to $75,000 a month; factory overhead burden from $6 to $4.50 per direct labor hour; five unprofitable branches closed (three kept) with distributors replacing the rest; jobbed lines eliminated; repair-part prices adjusted for about $200,000 of extra profit; cash and securities from $166,000 to $2,436,000; liabilities from $2,318,000 to $274,000.

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Dempster Mill: the margin-of-safety rules it taught (BPL Jan 1964).** "Never count on making a good sale. Have the purchase price be so attractive that even a mediocre sale gives good results. The better sales will be the frosting on the cake"; "By buying assets at a bargain price, we don't need to pull any rabbits out of a hat to get extremely good percentage gains"; "Harry works the same way I do -- he likes big carrots." and "I like dealing with someone who is not trying to figure how to get the fixtures in the executive washroom gold-plated." Morals: a three-year judging minimum; no discussing current holdings ("plead the '5th Amendment'"); and "An investment operation that depends on the ultimate buyer making a bum deal (in Wall Street they call this the 'Bigger Fool Theory') is tenuous indeed" (1964). Note on tax: de-incorporating would have doubled partners' after-tax earnings but was complex.

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Texas National: scoring the risks and the payoff (BPL Jan 1964).** Risk scoring: stockholder approval "nil," title and antitrust "virtually nil," the one open item a tax ruling delayed by USC's charitable status in the production payment. His call log: June 18 "Hoping for ruling in July," July 24 "early next week," Aug 13 all parties in Washington, Sept 18 "No news." Ruling late September; closed Oct 31, 1962; payments of $3.50 (Dec 14), $3.90 (Feb 4), 15 cents (Apr 24, 1963). Bonds: $14,446 gain on $260,773 for about 20% annualized. Stock and warrants: $89,304 realized (from $146,000 in April to $731,000 in October), about 22% annualized.

title: Texas National: scoring the risks and the payoff (BPL Jan 1964)

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Work-out lessons from Texas National: delay, leverage and errors (BPL Jan 1964).** Pattern: "the deals take longer than originally projected" and "the payouts tend to average a little better than estimates." Leverage: "some borrowed money is warranted against a portfolio of workouts, but feel it is a very dangerous practice against generals." "When a workout falls through, the resulting market value shrink is substantial. Therefore, you cannot afford many errors." He calls it "typical of our bread-and-butter type of operation," not "any earth-shaking triumph." Mechanism: "We wait until we can read it in the paper."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Berkshire Hathaway (Nov 1962 to 1966).** Purchases began Nov 1962 at $7.60, which "partially reflected large losses incurred by the prior management in closing some of the mills"; he assumed a controlling position in spring 1965 at an average of $14.86 ("very heavy purchases in early 1965"); by Dec 31, 1965 net working capital alone was about $19 a share. In 1948 the mills had 11,000 workers and about $29.5M of pre-tax profit; at control, two mills and about 2,300 employees; he was pleasantly surprised that the remaining units "had excellent management personnel" and brought in no outsider.

title: Berkshire Hathaway (Nov 1962 to 1966)

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Valuing control, and the textile verdict (BPL 1965 to 1969).** Valuation of a controlled holding (Nov 1, 1965): at a price halfway between net current asset value and book, because "Market price, which governs valuation of minority interest positions, is of little or no importance in valuing a controlling interest." The 1965 description: "While a Berkshire is hardly going to be as profitable as a Xerox, Fairchild Camera or National Video in a hypertensed market, it is a very comfortable sort of thing to own. As my West Coast philosopher says, 'It is well to have a diet consisting of oatmeal as well as cream puffs.'" By 1967: "B-H is experiencing and faces real difficulties in the textile business" and he saw "no prospect of a good return on the assets employed in the textile business"; by December 1969 it "cannot be judged a satisfactory business," so capital would be redeployed "now on a permanent basis into insurance and banking." (The 2017 interview adds that the three building blocks were Berkshire, Diversified Retailing and Blue Chip Stamps, and "the base companies of both of the other two totally failed, disappeared.")

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Hochschild, Kohn & Co. (July 12, 1966 letter) and Diversified Retailing.** The first time the Partnership bought an entire business by negotiation: a privately owned Baltimore department store with several thousand employees, bought with two 10% partners; BPL's share was about 10% of more than $50M invested, so it should not be read as "financial importance"; "I still prefer the iceberg approach toward investment disclosure." Selection rule: "Even if the price had been cheaper but the management had been run-of-the-mill, we would not have bought the business." He admits "All of our investments usually appear undervalued to me" and that he did not learn to pronounce "HK" until the deal closed. Later, Diversified Retailing Co. (80% BPL) owned HK and Associated Cotton Shops (Ben Rosner; sales about $37.5M, net income about $1M, "about 20% on capital employed," a level only 37 Fortune 500 companies reached in 1967); DRC sold HK to Supermarkets General in December 1969 for $5.0M cash plus notes of $2M and $4.54M. National Indemnity (Jack Ringwalt) was bought in 1967 and Illinois National Bank and Trust of Rockford in early 1969 for Berkshire.

title: Hochschild, Kohn & Co. (July 12, 1966 letter) and Diversified Retailing

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Generals-private owner: accumulating while the stock sleeps (1966).** Starting mid-1965 he bought a widely held security far below private-owner value, hoping to build $10M or more over two to three years; by year end 1965 he had invested $1,956,980 (value $2,358,412) when "Another party, previously completely unknown to me, issued a tender offer which foreclosed opportunities for future advantageous buying." He realized $1,269,181 of profit in February 1966 ($867,749 applicable to 1966) and regretted it: "we would have been much better off from a long range standpoint if 1966 results had been five percentage points worse." The mechanism is the same as Commonwealth: you want the stock stagnant while you accumulate. 1965's other "private owner" case: a tender offer realized $3,188,000, because "A private owner was quite willing ... to pay a price for control of the business which isolated stock buyers were not willing to pay."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **The 1967 workout drag and the 1969 workout loss.** 1967: workouts earned $153,273 on $17,246,879 of average capital (0.89%): "The streets were filled with upset applecarts - our applecarts." 1969: "Our experience in workouts this year has been atrocious ... Our poor experience this year is 100% my fault. It did not reflect bad luck, but rather an improper assessment of a very fast-developing governmental trend." Plus: "Documenting one's boners is unpleasant business. I find 'selective reporting' even more distasteful." Feel: "I have felt like the bird that inadvertently flew into the middle of a badminton game."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **The October 9, 1967 letter that lowers the goal.** Four named difficulties: (1) "the virtual disappearance of the bargain issue as determined quantitatively," leaving "the occasional security where I am really competent to make an important qualitative judgment"; (2) "Mushrooming interest in investment performance" produced a "hyper-reactive pattern of market behavior" ("I think we are witnessing the distortion of a sound idea," as three-year judgments shrank to monthly); (3) size (capital about $65M against "a diminishing trickle of good investment ideas"; and "if we were operating with one-tenth of our present capital our performance would be little better"); (4) personal: "When I started the partnership I set the motor that regulated the treadmill at 'ten points better than the DOW'" and "My own personal interests dictate a less compulsive approach to superior investment results than when I was younger and leaner."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Out of step with the go-go market, and the aftermath (BPL Oct 1967 to Jan 1969).** He explains the habit trap with Bertrand Russell's Lithuanian girls who kept stealing vegetables after the war. On fashion investing: "does not completely satisfy my intellect (or perhaps my prejudices), and most definitely does not fit my temperament. I will not invest my own money based upon such an approach" and "hence, I will most certainly not do so with your money." "Essentially I am out of step with present conditions" and "I will not abandon a previous approach whose logic I understand (although I find it difficult to apply) even though it may mean foregoing large and apparently easy, profits to embrace an approach which I don't fully understand, have not practiced successfully and which, possibly, could lead to substantial permanent loss of capital." "The above may simply be 'old-fogeyism' (after all, I am 37)." The aftermath: partners with about $1.6M withdrew at year end, and 1968 then produced +58.8% against the Dow's +7.7%, "a freak like picking up thirteen spades in a bridge game."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **The Sorrows of Compounding (Jan 20, 1966).** Capital had reached $43,645,000. He reversed his earlier denial: "I feel substantially greater size is more likely to harm future results than to help them. This might not be true for my own personal results, but it is likely to be true for your results." Decision: admit no new partners (the joke: "I have notified Susie that if we have any more children, it is up to her to find some other partnership for them"). Control situations favor size ("A 'Sanborn Map' cannot be accomplished without the wherewithal") while passive holdings hurt. His 1967 admission: "For years my investment ideas were anywhere from 110% to 1000% of our capital." Assets by January: $303,726 (1957), $7,178,500 (1962), $9,405,400 (1963), $17,454,900 (1964), $26,074,000 (1965), $43,645,000 (1966), $54,065,345 (1967), $68.1M (1968), $104,429,431 (1969).

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **The 1969 wind-down mechanics.** Decided May 29, 1969: "I just don't see anything available that gives any reasonable hope of delivering such a good year and I have no desire to grope around, hoping to 'get lucky' with other people's money." Reasons: (1) opportunities for the quantitative analyst "have virtually disappeared"; (2) "$100 million of assets" rules out companies with less than about $100M of common stock at market, since commitments below about $3M cannot move results; (3) a short-term-oriented market. "I have flunked this test completely" (limited objectives did not lessen effort); "The only way to slow down is to stop."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Wind-down distribution: cash, Ruane and the Blue Chip block (BPL 1969 to 1970).** Distribution: Jan 5, 1970 cash of at least 64% (later about 70% after Blue Chip) of Jan 1, 1969 capital plus pro rata Diversified Retailing and Berkshire shares; he recommended Bill Ruane (disclosing Ruane's record fairly, down about 50% in 1962 and about 15% in 1969). The Blue Chip Stamps underwriting (about 7.5% of the company) collapsed when the offer price slid from $24 to $16.5 after announcement: "I intend to hold our block." Berkshire and DRC shares went out by private placement, not registration: "The more sophisticated partners might have an important edge on the less sophisticated ones." On second men: "The only real way to see how someone is going to do when running a company is to let him run it."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Bonds versus stocks, October 1969.** "For the first time in my investment lifetime. I now believe there is little choice for the average investor between professionally managed money in stocks and passive investment in bonds." With tax-free bonds at about 6.5% and ten-year stock expectations "probably not better than 9% overall. say 3% dividends and 6% gain in value" (about 6.5% after tax for a 40% bracket), and "less than 10% of professionally managed money" averaging two points above group expectancy, he concluded that passive tax-free bonds were "fully the equivalent of expectations from professionally managed money in stocks, and only modestly inferior to extremely well-managed equity money." Method: "the best expectable after-tax rate of return makes the most sense - given a rising, declining or stable dollar."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Taxes in the Partnership era (July 1963, Jan 1965).** "My net worth is the market value of holdings less the tax payable upon sale." "More investment sins are probably committed by otherwise quite intelligent people because of 'tax considerations' than from any other cause." Swap funds as a test case (Federal Street Fund -19.0% in 1962, +17.0%, +13.8%; Westminster -22.5%, +18.7%, +12.3%, against the Dow's -7.6%, +20.6%, +18.7%): "Anyone for taxes?" Policy: maximize investment gains, not minimize taxes. **[CHECK, dated]** This early stance (pay the tax at low rates and maximize gains) is the opposite of buy-and-never-sell; the later 0.1% ProPublica figure comes from Berkshire paying no dividend, rarely selling, and the Giving Pledge, which is why both Partnership-era and 2011 positions have to be read together (see Blind spots).
quotes: My net worth is the market value of holdings less the tax payable upon sale.

title: Taxes in the Partnership era (July 1963, Jan 1965)

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Why institutions underperform: his five-factor diagnosis (Jan 1965).** "(1) group decisions ... (2) a desire to conform to the policies and (to an extent) the portfolios of other large well-regarded organizations; (3) an institutional framework whereby average is 'safe' and the personal rewards for independent action are in no way commensurate with the general risk attached to such action; (4) an adherence to certain diversification practices which are irrational; and finally and importantly, (5) inertia." Evidence: the four largest funds averaged about 9% to 10% against the Dow's 11.1% (1957 to 1964) with advisory fees "over $8 million." Even so: "In no sense is this statement intended as criticism. Within their institutional framework and handling the many billions of dollars involved, I consider such average results virtually the only possible ones." 1957 to 1961 cumulative: four largest funds 71.4%, 76.9%, 70.8%, 77.4%; the Dow 74.9%; limited partners 181.6%. Of 38 comparable mutual funds from 1946 to 1960, 32 did poorer than the Dow.

(2) a desire to conform to the policies and (to an extent) the portfolios of other large well-regarded organizations; (3) an institutional framework whereby average is 'safe' and the personal rewards for independent action are in no way commensurate with the general risk attached to such action; (4) an adherence to certain diversification practices which are irrational; and finally and importantly, (5) inertia.

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Two kinds of conservatism (Jan 1962, Jan 1965, July 1966).** (a) Conventionalism: results "varying only slightly from average experience." (b) True conservatism: "subject to substantially less temporary or permanent shrinkage in value than total experience." In the cumulative declines of 1957, 1960 and 1962 the Dow fell 20.6% and funds 9.7% to 24.6% while limited partners gained 45.0%. "True conservatism is only possible through knowledge and reason."

text: [The Partnership years (1956 to 1969): worked situations with the numbers] **Ground Rules and fee design (Jan 1963, Nov 1965, July 1961).** Rule 2: "Any year in which we fail to achieve at least a plus 6% performance will be followed by a year when partners receiving monthly payments will find those payments lowered." Rule 4: measure against the Dow "whether we are plus or minus." Rule 5: "three years is an absolute minimum." Rule 6 (see Decision heuristics). Fees: the first 6% to partners on beginning capital at market; excess split one-quarter to the general partner and three-quarters to limited partners; shortfalls carried forward but never back; the GP and his family barred from owning other marketable securities. The Buffetts' interest was $1,025,000 (1962), $2,392,900 (1964), $3,406,700 (1965) and $6,849,936 (1966), well over 90% of their net worth. A stated 1962 yardstick ("A Word About Par," see Mental models), and from 1964: "We started out with a 36-inch yardstick and we'll keep it that way. If we don't measure up, we won't change yardsticks." "Show me a good loser, and I'll show you a loser" (Casey Stengel, quoted).

text: [The nine records of Graham-and-Doddsville (Columbia, May 17, 1984)] **Epistemic caution:** "if I had just recently searched among thousands of records to select a few names for you this morning," he would "advise you to stop reading right here." Observation: "it is extraordinary to me that the idea of buying dollar bills for 40 cents takes immediately to people or it doesn't take at all," and he has "never seen anyone who became a gradual convert over a ten-year period." Why he publishes the secret: "the secret has been out for 50 years, ever since Ben Graham and Dave Dodd wrote Security Analysis, yet I have seen no trend toward value investing in the 35 years that I've practiced it," because of "some perverse human characteristic that likes to make easy things difficult."

text: [Governance, boards and executive pay] **Fred Futile (2005): fixed-price options are free capital.** The CEO of "Stagnant, Inc." gets ten-year fixed-price options on 1% of a company earning $1B a year on $10B of net worth (100M shares, $10 a share, no dividend, buying back stock at ten times earnings). Shares fall to 38.7M, EPS grows to $25.80, the stock appreciates 158%, and Fred makes "$158 million, despite the business itself improving not at all." Retaining earnings in 5%-return projects still pays him $63M, and even with earnings down 20% he "could have made more than $100 million." "fixed-price options give them capital that is free." His fix: options "with strike prices that are adjusted for retained earnings," which consultants ("the ever-accommodating firm of Ratchet, Ratchet and Bingo") never propose.

text: [Governance, boards and executive pay] **Paying the extraordinary CEO, and CEO pay as the acid test (2003, 2005).** Counterpoint: "it's difficult to overpay the truly extraordinary CEO of a giant enterprise. But this species is rare" (Jim Kilts at Gillette "earned every penny"). He had served as a director of twenty public companies and "only one CEO has put me on his comp committee." The Hank Greenberg story: "Ask for a uniform." In 2003 the acid test: "In judging whether Corporate America is serious about reforming itself, CEO pay remains the acid test," because the CEO cares more about 100,000 vs 500,000 options than the comp committee does, so "the negotiation often has a 'play-money' quality."

text: [Governance, boards and executive pay] **Option expensing as institutional capture (2002 and 2004).** Arthur Andersen's Professional Standards Group said in 1992 that options should be expensed; "rainmaking" partners reversed it; FASB voted 7-0; the Senate voted 88-9 against; SEC chair Arthur Levitt later called bowing to it "the act of his chairmanship that he most regrets"; "Of the 500 companies in the S&P, 498 adopted the method deemed less desirable" (2002). In 2004 the House passed a pro-CEO bill 312-111. The 2004 position: he would support options with "1) an appropriate strike price, 2) an escalation in price that reflects the retention of earnings, and 3) a ban on his quickly disposing of any shares purchased through options" for his successor.

Yet these are the very board members most often classed as 'independent.'" Three questions owners should press: "First, does the company have the right CEO? Second, is he/she overreaching in terms of compensation? Third, are proposed acquisitions more likely to create or destroy per-share value?" (2004).

text: [Governance, boards and executive pay] **Berkshire's own board design (2003, 2004, 2006).** Eleven directors (2003), each with family holdings above $4 million bought in the open market and "we've never passed out options or restricted shares"; fees nominal; no D&O insurance ("After all, who ever washes a rental car?"; "You win, they win big; you lose, they lose big"). He calls it "owner-capitalism"; the rarest quality is business savvy: "I would be useless on a medical or scientific board" and "I could be replaced, without loss, by a potted plant." Process in 2003: shareholders could self-nominate (more than twenty did); Charlie and he, with the incumbents, picked David Gottesman, Charlotte Guyman, Don Keough and Tom Murphy, none of whom nominated themselves.

If a CEO bats .300, he gets paid for being a .300 hitter, even if circumstances outside of his control cause Berkshire to perform poorly." text: [Accounting, disclosure and communication] **"Accounting Part 2" (1998): restructuring and merger accounting.** "Son of Gresham: Bad accounting drives out good." Evidence: R. G. Associates counted 1,369 special charges totaling $72.1B in 1998, against 1997 Fortune 500 earnings of $324B; the golf analogy (a 140 followed by four 80s instead of 91, 94, 89, 94, 92); reserve padding at deal time ("uncanny how often an actuarial 'revelation' of this kind coincides with the inking of a deal"); two bank CEOs overheard on a merger, one asking "But won't that mean a huge charge" and being told the charge would be "bigger than that" because that was why they were doing the deal. Contrast: "In all of our acquisitions, we have left the loss reserve figures exactly as we found them" and "If we are to disappoint you, we would rather it be with our earnings than with our accounting." He borrows Kinsley: "The scandal isn't in what's done that's illegal but rather in what's legal." He praised SEC chair Arthur Levitt's "earnings management" speech and chided auditors who "kowtow" to managers.

text: [Macro, currency and the never-forecast rule in practice] **The currency position (2002 to 2006) as a documented exception.** "Before March 2002, neither Berkshire nor I had ever traded in currencies" (2004). By 2003 about $12 billion across five currencies; by year end 2004 $21.4B across 12 currencies. Trigger: the U.S. current-account deficit ($618B in 2004, up from $263B in 1999), a wealth transfer "at the rate of $1.8 billion daily," foreigners owning net about $3 trillion of the U.S., projected near $11 trillion in a decade. Frameworks: "A budget deficit in no way reduces the portion of the national pie that goes to Americans" but current-account deficits mean "we own less and less of what we produce… the rest of the world enjoys an ever-growing royalty on American output"; "A country that is now aspiring to an 'Ownership Society' will not find happiness in – and I'll use hyperbole here for emphasis – a 'Sharecropper's Society.'" He still says "true trade… is enormously beneficial for both us and them." Disagreement: both parties' policymakers and the Fed's "soft landing" hope: "a gently declining dollar would not provide the answer" (his Nov 10, 2003 Fortune article).

text: [Macro, currency and the never-forecast rule in practice] **The currency position's scorecard and exit (2003 to 2006).** Results: 2003 gains of $825M from foreign exchange; 2005 "My conviction, however, cost Berkshire $955 million pre-tax in 2005" though Berkshire was "$2.0 billion in the black" since inception; 2006: a $2.2B total gain since 2002 ($186M in 2006), led by euro $839.2M, Canadian dollar $398.3M, pound $287.2M, won $261.3M, Australian dollar $247.1M, peso $106.1M, NZ dollar $102.6M, with losses in the Taiwan dollar (45.3), yuan (12.7), Singapore dollar (2.6) and Hong Kong dollar (2.5); he ended direct positions because carry turned negative in 2005 and moved into foreign equities or U.S. stocks with big foreign earnings. Also "Americans will live better ten or twenty years from now than they do today." In 2005: "Either Americans address the problem soon in a way we select, or at some point the problem will likely address us in an unpleasant way of its own."

text: [Macro, currency and the never-forecast rule in practice] **How he reconciled it with the never-forecast rule (in his words).** 2003: "the cemetery for seers has a huge section set aside for macro forecasters. We have in fact made few macro forecasts at Berkshire." 2004: "macro-economics is a tough game in which few people, Charlie and I included, have demonstrated skill. We may well turn out to be wrong in our currency judgments"; "(Indeed, the fact that so many pundits now predict weakness for the dollar makes us uneasy.)" On reputation: "From a reputational standpoint, Charlie and I run a clear risk with our foreign-exchange commitment. But we believe in managing Berkshire as if we owned 100% of it ourselves. And, were that the case, we would not be following a dollar-only policy." Keynes: "Worldly wisdom teaches that it is better for reputation to fail conventionally than to succeed unconventionally." He also hedged his preference: a prompt solution "would likely cause Berkshire to record losses on its foreign-exchange contracts," since "Berkshire's resources remain heavily concentrated in dollar-based assets."

The rule he actually follows (my reading): he voices macro views in writing, labels the error bar, and never lets one drive the core portfolio.

text: [Macro, currency and the never-forecast rule in practice] **Zero-coupon bonds and silver (1997).** Silver: 111.2 million ounces bought in 1997 (pre-tax gain $97.4M); oil derivatives (14.0M barrels left of a 45.7M barrel position set 1994 to 1995; 31.7M settled for a pre-tax gain of about $61.9M); zero-coupon Treasuries ($4.6B at amortized cost, unrealized pre-tax gain $598.8M when rates fell): "If rates rise, you lose heavily with zeros, and if rates fall, you make outsized gains." The accountability line: "you pay Charlie and me to use our best judgment -- not to avoid embarrassment -- and we will occasionally make an unconventional move when we believe the odds favor it." And the honest limit: "A macro-based commitment such as this never has anything close to a 100% probability of being successful." He also distinguishes: a wonderful business at an attractive price means "we are going to make money -- the only question being when"; with these, "we think that we are going to make money. But we also recognize that we will sometimes realize losses, occasionally of substantial size" (1997).

text: [Taxes, social contract, productivity and politics] **Productivity and the people who pay for it (2015, 2017).** The engine of prosperity: farming went from 11 million of a 28 million workforce in 1900 (40%) to about 3 million of 158 million; corn yield from 30 to over 150 bushels an acre; railroads 1947 to 2014: workforce 1.35 million to 187,000, ton-miles 655 billion to 1.85 trillion, real price per ton-mile down 55%, saving shippers about $90B a year; BNSF 1996 to 2015: ton-miles +71% while employees rose 4%; BHE Iowa: 3,700 to 3,500 employees while output rose from 19 to 29 million megawatt-hours, "without a rate increase for 16 years" while industry rates rose 44% (2015). The flip side: Dexter's Maine workforce (see Named mistakes); New Bedford textile workers "had no Plan B." Remedy: a reformed and expanded Earned Income Tax Credit: "The price of achieving ever-increasing prosperity for the great majority of Americans should not be penury for the unfortunate." And "(It was fortunate that horses couldn't vote.)"

"She is sensible – very sensible – instinctively knowing that pundits should always be ignored. After all, if she could reliably predict tomorrow's winners, would she freely share her valuable insights and thereby increase competitive buying? That would be like finding gold and then handing a map to the neighbors showing its location." Her record: active until 1980, then, at 46 and "independent of any urgings from her brother," she kept only the mutual fund and Berkshire and "made no new trades during the next 43 years. During that period, she became very rich, even after making large philanthropic gifts (think nine figures)." text:
Folksy, plain-spoken, self-deprecating, teacherly: a brilliant analyst who deliberately talks like your smartest uncle so the lesson lands. He reaches for homely analogies (Mr. Market, the castle-and-moat, the gold cube, an elephant gun, robins and spring, the preening duck, the batboy Eddie Bennett, the Gotrocks family and its helpers, Fred Futile, the hamburger quiz, Aesop's birds, "jumbo shrimp" and "lady mudwrestler" for institutional-investor oxymorons) and Midwestern understatement. He teaches by parable (Aesop; the Li'l Abner compounding tables; the golfer who "restructures" a 140 into four 80s; the commuter who cheers higher gas prices because his tank is full; the Scarlett O'Hara line on teaser mortgages; the rented suit at the funeral; the horse who is "walking fine" and gets "peddled as Secretariat") and quotes a fixed cast: Graham, Keynes ("I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong"), Mae West ("Too much of a good thing can be wonderful"), Ben Franklin, Churchill, Ronald Reagan, Jack Benny, Pascal, Polonius, Horace, Casey Stengel, Billy Rose, and Munger.
He admits errors out loud, by name and with the dollar figure attached (Fannie Mae's "$1.4 billion," Dexter's "$5.7 billion," Precision Castparts' "$11 billion," Gillette's $625 million, NetJets' $157 million, the GEICO credit card's further $44 million loss) and grades himself on a letter scale (a "D" for 1999; "Quack" for 1997). He is blunt about fees, derivatives, EBITDA, executive pay, forecasters, and his own omissions; he hedges on macro and on precise valuations (intrinsic value is "fuzzy," two honest people will differ). He explains the cost of his virtues rather than hiding it: "just standing there, day after day, with my bat on my shoulder is not my idea of fun" (1997). His sentences tend to set up a general rule, turn it on a vivid concrete case, and close on a one-line aphorism; he states what would change his mind (price, not narrative), and he credits managers by name, always.
Note the register shift over time: the Partnership letters are precise and contractual (the numbered Ground Rules, asset tables to the dollar, "old-fogeyism (after all, I am 37)"); the 1980s letters are parable-driven and appendix-heavy (the See's goodwill math); the 1990s and 2000s letters are pedagogical and crusading on accounting and governance (options, pro-forma, mutual-fund directors) with long lists of acquisition origin stories; the 2010s are statistical and patriotic (GDP per capita, productivity); the Nov 2025 farewell is a memoirist's voice, openly mortal, still wry ("I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of"), closing on aphorism rather than arithmetic.
The CNBC interviews (2017, 2019, 2023) are looser and more candid than the letters: asked why he did not buy Amazon, he answers "Stupidity." Distinguish him from Munger: Munger is terser and more caustic ("If something is not worth doing at all, it's not worth doing well," which Buffett relays as something "Charlie regularly reminds me," 1994; "Are we supposed to applaud because the dog that fouls our lawn is a Chihuahua rather than a Saint Bernard?"; "I feel like a horse's ass for not identifying Google better"), and it was Munger who supplied the strategic pivot ("buy wonderful businesses at fair prices") that Buffett then spent decades narrating, with, as Buffett says, "much back-sliding."
quotes: peddled as Secretariat
I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong
Too much of a good thing can be wonderful
just standing there, day after day, with my bat on my shoulder is not my idea of fun

text: **His alpha may be a factor bet, not magic.** *Buffett's Alpha* (Frazzini, Kabiller & Pedersen, NBER w19681) finds that controlling for Betting-Against-Beta and Quality-Minus-Junk "drives the alpha of Berkshire's public stock portfolio down to a statistically insignificant annualized 0.3%," estimates "Buffett's leverage is about 1.6-to-1 on average," and concludes the returns are "reward for the use of leverage combined with a focus on cheap, safe, quality stocks." Read charitably this validates his framework; read critically the edge is systematizable and partly cheap leverage (float), not unique genius.

text: **Tax hypocrisy, by the numbers (and the Partnership-era contrast).** ProPublica's "Secret IRS Files" found that 2014 to 2018 Buffett's wealth rose **$24.3 billion** while he paid **$23.7 million** in tax, "a true tax rate of 0.1%," the lowest of the 25 wealthiest Americans, "perhaps surprising, given his public stance as an advocate of higher taxes for the rich." The mechanism (no Berkshire dividend, rarely selling, the giving pledge) is exactly the buy-and-never-sell philosophy he preaches, which is what produces the 0.1% and the tension with "Stop Coddling the Super-Rich" (2011). His own sources show the earlier stance ("maximize investment gains, not minimize taxes," Partnership 1963 and 1965) and the 2017 remark that under the House bill's repeal of the 3.8% net-investment-income tax "I'm a lot healthier now than I was a week ago financially," and the 2003 sentence "my class is clearly winning." His defense: the code "should be changed substantially" and the money will do more good "disbursed philanthropically." A separate ProPublica piece notes many Berkshire subsidiaries don't offer the low-cost index funds in their 401(k)s that he tells everyone else to buy.

a true tax rate of 0.1%,
perhaps surprising, given his public stance as an advocate of higher taxes for the rich.

I'm a lot healthier now than I was a week ago financially,

text: **Wells Fargo: governance rhetoric vs. passive conduct.** His sharpest documented blind spot: the 1990 "best managers in the business" bet became a fraud (millions of fake accounts, ~$185M in fines, retaliation against whistleblowers). Buffett diagnosed it precisely ("You have to be very careful what you incentivize"; "the CEO has to act," Quartz 2017) yet, as the largest (~10%, ~$26B) shareholder, took no public action to stop it and sold no shares at the time. His 2017 reply ("I was not a director"), his 2019 defense of Sloan, and Munger's contrary view are all dated above; the 2019 "cocker spaniel" board-independence critique sits in direct tension with his own conduct here, and the 2005 line that he called Wells "a company that Dick Kovacevich runs brilliantly" is the pre-scandal high-water mark.

You have to be very careful what you incentivize
the CEO has to act,
I was not a director

text: **The Sokol affair (2011).** David Sokol, then a leading internal succession candidate, bought Lubrizol shares shortly before pitching the Lubrizol acquisition to Buffett; Berkshire bought Lubrizol, Sokol's stake gained ~$3M, and he resigned in March 2011. Berkshire's audit committee found he had violated company insider-trading and ethics standards, and Buffett was widely criticized for an initially soft public response before the committee's harder finding. *(This is a matter of public record, Berkshire's own 2011 press release/audit-committee report and contemporaneous SEC coverage, summarized here from that record; it was not independently re-verified against a primary URL in this rebuild, so treat the framing as public-record context, not a quote.)* The 2009 letter shows Sokol had been installed as NetJets CEO in August 2009 to fix a unit where, in Buffett's words, "I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition."
quotes: I failed you in letting NetJets descend into this condition.
title: The Sokol affair (2011)

text: **Decades-long tech avoidance was costly (and he says why).** Google, Amazon, early Microsoft, and a money-losing IBM stake (bought ~2011, exited 2018). He concedes the misses; Munger's 2014 estimate of what omissions such as Walmart cost is in the Named mistakes ledger. The very discipline that built the record kept Berkshire underweight the basket that won the 2010s to 2020s. (Apple, bought 2016+, is the late correction, and the 2017 anchoring confession is the behavioral mechanism: having seen X, buying at 10X is hard.) 1999 is the first documented case: he stood aside from tech in the year he graded himself a D.
title: Decades-long tech avoidance was costly (and he says why)

text: **The airlines round-trip.** After decades of shunning airlines as commodity/capital-intensive ("It's a job I don't want, running an airline," 2017), he bought ~10% of the big four (~2016), then sold the entire stake at the 2020 trough, by his own account his mistake and his decision alone (2020 meeting; paraphrase, exact transcript wording could not be verified, see Provenance). The stocks recovered substantially within ~18 months. USAir (1989, $358M) had already shown the failure mode; the 2017 interview names it as his own mistake: "I made it all by myself."
quotes: It's a job I don't want, running an airline,
I made it all by myself.
title: The airlines round-trip

text: **Derivatives: rules for thee?** He booked >$10B in mark-to-market losses on equity-index puts during 2008 while lecturing the world on derivative danger (Yahoo Finance). On his own reading it is structure, not hypocrisy (long maturities, no collateral triggers, positions he manages himself, 2006 and 2009), but the optics were real and his counterparties bore Berkshire-credit risk.
title: Derivatives: rules for thee?

text: **Macro and currency: the exception to his own rule.** The 2002 to 2006 currency book was a macro view held by a man who says "macro-economics is a tough game"; it cost $955M pre-tax in 2005 even if it finished about $2.2B ahead by 2006. He disclosed the reputational risk himself (2004). The 2003 to 2006 insistence that the U.S. current-account position would end badly, and the 2019 belief that low inflation could not coexist with policy, both sit next to his admission that "I've been wrong on that for some time." In 1979 he held 15-year bonds and did not sell: a duration call that turned out wrong as yields peaked in 1981 (my inference from the 1979 letter's own account).
quotes: macro-economics is a tough game
I've been wrong on that for some time.
title: Macro and currency: the exception to his own rule

text: **Governance and transparency gaps he champions elsewhere.** Berkshire's board is widely described as handpicked friends/family; in 2023 shareholders rejected an independent-chair proposal ~10-to-1 (US News), and he recommended voting against TCFD-aligned climate-disclosure proposals despite substantial independent-shareholder support, a transparency stance at odds with his "candor" creed. The 2003 to 2006 letters define "independence" as owning stock bought in the open market and not relying on director fees; that is a standard Berkshire meets, but the board is still friend-heavy by any outside measure. Berkshire also has no D&O insurance and keeps directors' downside above shareholders'. He conceded in 2002 that for years he sat silent on other boards ("collegiality trumped independence"), and in 2004 that he should have introduced executive sessions and a whistleblower line decades earlier.
quotes: collegiality trumped independence
title: Governance and transparency gaps he champions elsewhere

text: **Philanthropy critique, from inside the family.** His son Peter Buffett called big billionaire philanthropy "conscience laundering" and "Philanthropic Colonialism" that "keeps the existing structure of inequality in place" (NYT 2013). Warren's own delegation logic ("What can be more logical, in whatever you want done, than finding someone better equipped than you are to do it? Who wouldn't select Tiger Woods to take his place in a high-stakes golf game?", Fortune 2006) has a documented coda: he resigned as a Gates Foundation trustee in 2021 and redirected the estate to his children's foundations, a partial walk-back of the give-it-through-Gates mechanism, though not of the >99% pledge. His 2006 argument against perpetual foundations is an opinion with no outcome data behind it.
quotes: keeps the existing structure of inequality in place
What can be more logical, in whatever you want done, than finding someone better equipped than you are to do it? Who wouldn't select Tiger Woods to take his place in a high-stakes golf game?
title: Philanthropy critique, from inside the family

text: **Scale now caps returns, by his own admission, and has since 1966.** "A fat wallet… is the enemy of superior investment results" (1994); "there will be many companies that have done better than Berkshire; our size takes its toll" (2025). The record: per-share investments compounded 27.5% from 1965 to 2006 but only 12.6% from 1995 to 2006 (2006 letter), and Berkshire trailed the S&P over much of the past decade. Munger's 1965 instruction says Graham's method "works but only when practiced at small scale": the cigar-butt and workout methods that built the Partnership (Dempster, Sanborn, Texas National) do not scale, which also means a founder or small investor copying the Berkshire-scale quality-at-a-fair-price rule may be applying the wrong regime.
quotes: A fat wallet… is the enemy of superior investment results
there will be many companies that have done better than Berkshire; our size takes its toll
works but only when practiced at small scale
title: Scale now caps returns, by his own admission, and has since 1966

text: **The cash drag, from outside.** In 2019 a fund manager called the roughly $114B pile "certainly a drag" (Reuters via Daily Herald) while saying the Apple and Amazon purchases "are a good sign." The 2017 interview shows him accepting the cost: "it's selling at a 100 times earnings." The 2025 pile (about $334B to $397B) raises the same question.

are a good sign.
it's selling at a 100 times earnings.
title: The cash drag, from outside

text: **Insurance results lean on luck, and he says so.** "To date, we have benefitted from good luck on this volatile book" (1999); "Mother Nature, bless her heart, went on vacation… Enjoy the view, because you won't soon see another like it" (2006). "Because we were lucky in our super-cat insurance business… our 1997 operating earnings were much better than we anticipated" (1997).

title: Insurance results lean on luck, and he says so

text: **A rule he mis-specified for 26 years.** The five-year rolling retained-earnings test in the Owner's Manual (from 1983) failed whenever a five-year market stretch was negative; he corrected it only after a question at the 2009 meeting.
title: A rule he mis-specified for 26 years

text: **Deal-sourcing depends on networks and structures that no longer exist.** The best Berkshire deals arrived through friends (Roach, Newman, Blumkin, Robertson) and, in the 1955 Fruit of the Loom story, structures (non-interest-bearing notes, tax-loss shelters) he says belong to a past era ("Those were the days"). Founders without that network get less of the model.
quotes: Those were the days
title: Deal-sourcing depends on networks and structures that no longer exist

text: **Key-man / succession risk.** The "single winning decision"/one-genius model is the flip side of concentration risk. The handoff to Abel completed Jan 1, 2026; he writes that "My children are already 100% behind Greg as are the Berkshire directors," but the fact that he keeps A-shares "until Berkshire shareholders develop the comfort with Greg" (2025) tells you the market's worry that capital-allocation skill and culture were personal to Buffett and Munger. The 2006 letter shows the investment side was known to be "not as well-prepared" (a 2006 plan to hire a younger portfolio manager), a gap later filled by Combs and Weschler.
quotes: single winning decision
My children are already 100% behind Greg as are the Berkshire directors,
until Berkshire shareholders develop the comfort with Greg
not as well-prepared
title: Key-man / succession risk

text: **A recurring governance failure he names himself.** "a wonderful and loyal CEO… will succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease. Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake" (2025), a rare admission of a *repeated* weakness, not a one-off. The 2005 letter had already written the principle ("Someone else often needs to blow the whistle").
quotes: a wonderful and loyal CEO… will succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease. Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake
Someone else often needs to blow the whistle
title: A recurring governance failure he names himself

text: **Survivorship in the Graham-and-Doddsville evidence.** The 1984 nine were pre-selected in advance by Buffett, and he warned that after-the-fact selection would defeat the argument; the nine hold small and illiquid names (Schloss's Hudson Pulp & Paper, Jeddo Highland Coal, New York Trap Rock), and the tables show overall and limited-partner columns but say little about fees or transaction costs. The orangutan test still leaves the question of how many Graham students never became superinvestors.
title: Survivorship in the Graham-and-Doddsville evidence

text: **Documented evolutions, not contradictions (dated).** Mark-to-market: pro in 2008 (Charlie Rose, "I believe in Mark to market"), against the 2018 GAAP rule routing unrealized gains through net income ("worse-than-useless," 2023). "Franchise" (1991) is the earlier vocabulary for "moat" (1993 to 2007). Deficit-doom preaching (retracted in 2018) became "fiscal policy… scares me more than monetary policy" (CNBC 2023).

title: Documented evolutions, not contradictions (dated)

text: **More dated evolutions.** Silver (1997, supply-demand, "Inflation expectations… play no part") vs. gold (2011, "will not respond"). Derivatives: "time bombs" (2002) vs. personally managed mispriced contracts (2006, 2009). Capital-intensive businesses: shunned until 2009, then BNSF and utilities, with the 2023 errors on both. Cigar butts (1960s to 1989) to "not something that we try to do anymore" (2019). Buyback thresholds: only below conservatively calculated intrinsic value (1999, 2011), 120% of book (2015), a 10% band (2019). Owner's Manual succession plan superseded by the Nov 2025 letter. Board independence defense (2003 to 2006) vs. "cocker spaniel" critique (2019) vs. the 2023 vote. Climate: 2006, 2015, 2023 as dated above. Tax: Partnership-era stance, 2003, 2011, 2017 and the ProPublica numbers.

not something that we try to do anymore
title: More dated evolutions

text: **Discrepancies in the sources themselves, left visible.** R.C. Willey's Boise store: Child's own money was $9M in the 1999 letter and $11M in the 2001 letter.
